Queer without fear. Interdependent and here. Divergent and proud. Living out loud. Plucky pluralism, for human organisms. Becoming and belonging, with ribald songing. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so. The street has a name, and it is not ours. Danny the Street is a character in DC Comics’ Doom Patrol, created in 1990 by Grant Morrison and Richard Case: a living street who turns up wherever somebody needs shelter and rearranges what is on them to suit whoever has arrived. Rooms that refuse to match, a field for anybody who would rather not be on a street at all, a shopfront with the keys in the door — that is all Danny’s, and we would like it on the record. Where Danny came from, and what they have been since → WHERE IS EVERYTHING? THE MAP → The whole street as a model in white card on a cutting mat, from the treeline at one end to the last streetlight at the other, with every room behind a room standing where it stands. Pick anything up to go there. The foot of every page has a Where am I? that opens it at the page you are on.
The rooms

THE PEBBLE BOARD → Community show-and-tell under glass on the pavement. Songs, art, jokes, recipes and things worth keeping, brought by our people for each other. A new edition goes up when there is a new gathering; the old ones stay in the rack underneath. THE BRASS TACKS BOARD → News, notices, events and celebrations, posted by our moderators with their names on them, and kept until they are taken down. Anybody can read it, and it has a feed of its own. NOW PLAYING → A poster column beside the board, with one bill pasted round it: every room on the street with something in it to press and play, in the campgrounds and down the road too, and what each one puts on first. THROUGH THE GATE: THE GARDEN → Midday, and one bed for every site we publish — what grows on each of them, whose hands are in it, and a spider that will answer questions about the lot. Everything out there links off this street. WHERE THE BUILDINGS STOP: THE LOTS THROUGH THE FENCE Open ground at the far end of the street, side by side and each next door to the next, with a gate into each. The Run →A dog park in a dog’s colours, with every dog from the shelter out for a run. The Truck Stop →Truckin’ Food Court: five trucks round a porch, each doing one thing several ways, and nothing with a price on it. The Green →A wood, a pond and an accessible boardwalk round it, just after the rain. The Pile →A junk playground, and everything on it is whatever you say it is. THE CAMPGROUNDS → Past the treeline, where the street runs out. Pitches in a field, for the ones who would rather not live on a street at all. THE OUTSKIRTS → Past the last streetlight, where the kerb gives up. The mystical, the eldritch and the after-dark keep premises out there — including a drive-in screen standing in black water, where it is always Halloween. DOWN: ARLESGLAD CAVERNS ↓ By lift, or by the stair beside it. Under the street there is a cavern lit only by its handrail, for everything that needs things to stay the same.
WHAT THIS STREET IS FOR

Every other site we run is careful on purpose — careful palettes, careful sourcing, careful attribution, careful hedging. Those sites are load-bearing and they stay. This one is the other half of the same lung. It has no single design system, deliberately. The street is the system; the rooms refuse to share one. And it has edges — the garden through the gate in the wall, where the sites we publish grow, and one at each end of the road: the campgrounds past the treeline, for anybody who would rather not be on a street at all, and The Outskirts past the last streetlight the other way, where the after-dark keeps premises. At the far end, where the buildings stop, there is open ground: lots side by side behind a fence, the Run, the Truck Stop, the Green and the Pile. And under all of it, by lift or stair, Arlesglad Caverns, for everything that needs things to stay the same. Two things stay careful even here: attribution, because that is a licence and not a house style, and contrast, because clashing is not the same as illegible. Everything else went out the window. See the liner notes.

The Map
The whole street as a model in white card, standing on a cutting mat, and never finished.
mm-how-h
How to read it

The street runs down the middle of the board from the treeline end at the top to the far end at the bottom, with the shopfronts standing on both sides of it in the order they stand on the front page. A small building behind a big one is a room behind a room. Past the treeline, off the top of the board, is the campground’s field with its pitches; past the last streetlight, off the bottom, is the road out of town with its turnings. The lift beside the stoop goes down to the caverns under the street, which are the smaller board at the foot of the model, one plate for every level. Everything standing on the mat is a link: pick one up and it takes you there. Follow Where am I? at the foot of any page on the street and the model opens at that page, with a flag on it saying you came from there.
mm-why-h
Why nothing on it is painted

Every room on this street is its own world, with its own light, its own colours and its own typefaces, and no two of them alike. A model that tried to paint them all would be telling you they belonged to one set. So the whole thing is one white card under one lamp, the only colour on the table is the mat and the pins, and every room is left to be itself when you get there. Nothing on it was placed by hand, either. The shopfronts come off the front page in the order they stand, the pitches off the campground’s own board and the turnings off the road’s own signs, and the gate to the garden stands halfway down however long the street happens to be. A room cannot open on this street without going up on the model, because the build refuses until it has.

Danny the Street

Doom Patrol · DC Comics · 1990 · not ours This site is a street with rooms on it that agree about nothing, and that was never our idea. It is Danny's. Danny the Street is a character in DC Comics’ Doom Patrol: a living street who turns up wherever somebody needs shelter, rearranges what is on them to suit whoever has arrived, and talks by changing the words written on their own surfaces. We borrowed the architecture and put a marquee across the top of the front page saying so. This page is where the name came from, what Danny has been since, and which parts are ours to take.
What Danny is

A living, sentient piece of urban geography, who can place themselves into any city’s layout without disturbing it — the buildings and the roads simply make room. Danny does it mostly at night, when nobody is looking, which means you can turn a corner on the way to work and find that you are walking down somebody. What is on Danny is a joke with an argument inside it. The shopfronts are relentlessly masculine — a gun shop, an army and navy store, a hardware shop — and every one of them is hung with frills, lace, flowers and fairy lights. The street is in drag. That is the whole character in one image, and it is why a site about being unassimilable is laid out as a row of shops that do not match. Danny has no voice and no face, so Danny speaks by rearrangement. Words appear in shop windows. A sentence turns up typed on a typewriter that happens to be there. Letters form out of the vapour coming off a manhole, or out of a scatter of broken glass. The English is thick with Polari, the slang carried through fairgrounds, the merchant navy, the theatre and gay Britain when being understood by the wrong person was dangerous — a way of speaking designed to be read only by people who could read it. This is the part we stole most directly. On this street the page is the speech: there is no house style sitting above the rooms telling you what the site is, only the surfaces, each one saying a different thing in a different hand.
Where Danny came from

Danny first appeared in Doom Patrol (volume 2) #35, cover-dated August 1990, written by Grant Morrison and drawn by Richard Case. Morrison had taken the title over with #19 in 1989 and turned a superhero book about damaged people into a book about people the world has no slot for — which is the only kind of superhero book that was ever going to produce a street. The name is a pun. Danny is named after Danny La Rue, the drag performer, whose stage surname is French for the street. Morrison has said as much in interviews since, and the joke tells you what the character is for: a female impersonator who is also a literal thoroughfare, so that the place and the person are the same thing and neither can be separated out for tidying. The story Danny arrives in is a story about normalcy as the enemy. Danny and the people living there are hunted by Darren Jones and the Men from N.O.W.H.E.R.E., whose project is a world that behaves like a 1950s situation comedy. The Doom Patrol turn up to defend the street; what actually finishes Jones is the street’s own cabaret. A Disabled people’s organisation could not invent a better origin story if it tried: the antagonist is enforced ordinariness, and the defence is a floor show. Flex Mentallo, who debuts in the same issue, is sheltered on Danny through the breakdown that follows his first failure. That is the other half of the character. Danny is not a base of operations. Danny is housing.
What Danny has been since

Danny is destroyed and reassembled more often than most characters get published, and every form keeps the same job. 1990 Danny the Street. Doom Patrol (vol. 2) #35, by Morrison and Case. Later in that run Danny the World. Danny leaves this universe for an alternate Earth and becomes a whole one, pledged to shelter the people who need it across dimensions. Morrison’s last issue ends with a member of the team being brought home to live on Danny. Volume 5 Danny the Brick. Danny is levelled in Doom Patrol (vol. 5) #7. Crazy Jane gets out carrying one brick out of one of Danny’s buildings, with Danny’s sentience still in it, and carries Danny around in a pocket. 2012 Danny the Street again, briefly. Reintroduced in Teen Titans (vol. 4) #3, January 2012, in DC’s New 52 continuity, and later suggested to have survived as Danny the Alley. 2016 on Brick, World, Dannyland, Ambulance. In Gerard Way’s Doom Patrol for DC’s Young Animal imprint, Danny goes from the brick back to a world, becomes an amusement park called Dannyland, manifests the comic-book character Casey Brinke into reality, and turns up as Danny the Ambulance. A street, a world, a brick, an alley, a funfair and an ambulance. The thing that stays constant is not the shape; it is that whatever Danny is this month has a door in it.
Danny on television

Danny appears in the first three seasons of Doom Patrol (2019–2023), made for DC Universe and then HBO Max, as a fugitive from the Bureau of Normalcy — the show’s version of the Men from N.O.W.H.E.R.E., with the name saying the quiet part out loud. The episode is “Danny Patrol”, season 1, episode 8, first shown on 5 April 2019, written by Tom Farrell and directed by Dermott Downs. This Danny is explicitly genderqueer and uses they/them pronouns, and the people who live on them are the Dannyzens — among them Maura Lee Karupt, a drag queen and a former Bureau agent who left the agency for the street it was hunting. Later seasons break Danny down to a brick and then rebuild them as an ambulance, which is the comics doing what the comics do. There is one more screen version, and it is the odd one out: an episode of Teen Titans Go! called “Stickiest Situation”, in which Danny can talk out loud and move parts of themselves like limbs. It is the only Danny with a voice.
He, they, and which Danny is which

The comics write Danny as he, and describe the character in the vocabulary that was available in 1990 — a word for cross-dressing that has since aged into an insult in most of the mouths that use it. The television version is genderqueer and uses they/them. Both of those are facts about other people’s work and we are not here to adjudicate them. Asked in 2020 why Danny had landed so hard with viewers, Morrison put it this way: “Back in the day when he was created in the late 1980s, we didn’t have terms like ‘genderqueer’ or ‘non-binary,’ they just didn’t exist.” Grant Morrison, interviewed by Kimberly Ricci, Uproxx, 11 August 2020 The Danny in our marquee uses they/them. That is a decision about this site rather than a correction of anybody’s canon: the street we borrowed is the one that shelters people whose category does not exist yet, and on a site run by and for neurodivergent and Disabled people, defaulting to they is what we would do for a person whose pronouns we had not been told. Danny has been a street, a world, a brick and an ambulance; they is the pronoun that survives all six.
What we took, and what we did not

We took the architecture. No single design system, on purpose: the rooms here share a base of ground rules and then refuse to look like each other, because the street rearranges itself for whoever walks down it. We took the rooms behind rooms, the field past the treeline for people who would rather not live on a street at all, and the empty shopfront with the keys in the door. We took the idea that a surface can be a way of speaking. We did not take Danny. Danny the Street belongs to DC Comics, and nothing of theirs is on this page: no panels, no artwork, no dialogue. Every drawing here is ours and every one of them is a drawing of a road, which is a thing nobody owns. The one quotation above is an interview, quoted short and credited in full. What this page is, is a namesake credit — the same habit the liner notes keep for every song, typeface and borrowed phrase on the site, applied to the borrowed thing that is holding the whole building up. And we did not take the vocabulary. 1990 was doing its best with the words it had. We have better ones and no excuse.

ROOM RULE

The vibe, not the lyrics — the same rule as the dancefloor next door. We name the artist, link the song, and let them keep their own words. Chappell Roan is not affiliated with Stimpunks and does not endorse us; this is a room named after somebody whose work we like, which is homage and not licence. Nothing here is hosted by us and nothing here is ours.
WHY A CHAPEL

Because the two things in the title are usually kept apart. Pleasure gets treated as the frivolous one and inclusion as the serious one, and Disabled people are handed the serious one and told the other is a reward for good behaviour. This room puts them in the same building on purpose: unabashed pleasure is not the opposite of righteous inclusion, it is what inclusion is for. A movement that can only ask for access and never for joy has agreed to a smaller life than it is owed. The chapel is the joke and the argument at once. Camp has always understood that the sacred and the sequinned are the same gesture done at different volumes, and a Disabled people’s organisation building a rhinestone Vatican off its own dancefloor is us saying which volume we prefer. Club Chronic

Punk music · punk community · a vivifying overlap Freaks to the front. Bring your stims and glims. Bring your pain and suffering. Bring the agony and the ecstasy of existence. Bring your authentic self or selves. Shed your masks or wear them boldly.
The scene is the thing, not the sound

Punk documentaries are all secretly the same documentary, and it is not about music. Community comes together to build inclusive spaces. Community rebounds after losing spaces. Community fights off skinheads with bats and pipes to keep spaces safe. Community learns how to DIY together. Thirty years of the East Bay, and the thing everybody in it keeps saying is that they came looking for somewhere to be, and when there was nowhere they built one on Gilman Street and ran it themselves. That is the whole method and it is why a disability organisation has a punk club in it. A scene that has to build its own door ends up thinking very clearly about who the door is for. The social model of disability says the same thing in duller words: the barrier is not in you, it is in the stairs, and the stairs were built by somebody who could have built a ramp. Punk worked that out on the ground, about venues, decades before most of us met the theory. Our own essay on this is where the playlist got its name. Lorne, in This Is What Trans Punk Looks Like, puts it better than any of our paragraphs: “To be a queer person is inherently a very punk thing. I think to be a punk person is also inherently a queer thing. There’s a lot of really vivifying overlap there between those two things for me.” Vivifying overlap is the phrase this room is built on. It is the same shape as neuroqueer: not two identities that happen to be in the same person, but each one making the other more itself. And it is not a fable. The Linda Lindas were eleven and thirteen in a public library when they played Racist, Sexist Boy, and the reason that song exists is that a boy said a thing to Mila and, in her words, “we were really angry, and we decided to write a song about it.” Their tagline is we rebuild what you destroy. Punk’s inclusiveness was never automatic and never finished — it has been fought for from the inside, repeatedly, by the people the scene kept leaving out. That is the part worth inheriting.
The door policy

You are not admitted on condition that you turn out to be fine. Nobody checks first. The weird thing about you is not something this room agrees to overlook — it is roughly what the room is for. Nothing plays until you press play. Same rule as every other room here. No request reaches YouTube or Spotify before you press something, and every record in the rack says how long it runs before you do. Nothing in here strobes, at any setting. A punk club has exactly one obvious ambient effect and it can cause seizures, so this room has none at all. The dial still works everywhere else; there is simply nothing in here for it to turn up. A room whose whole argument is come in as you are cannot have a light in it that puts somebody on the floor. A loud room is itself an access barrier, and we would rather say it than have it discovered. For a lot of us the gig described upstairs is unsurvivable — volume, crowds, no exit, no quiet room, no seat. A scene that lets anybody in and then builds the only entrance out of volume has not finished the job. That is why this club is a page: you can turn it off, leave it mid-song, and nobody notices. Not inspiration. Nobody here is anybody’s evidence that attitude conquers all.

THE LAST LINE OF THE COURSE

— Rainbow Shiner, written by Laura Harris, Betsy Wright and Mary Timony, performed by Ex Hex on It’s Real, 22 March 2019. Buy it from the band. Words this sheet borrowed, each one a door into the glossary: autigender · neuroqueer · bricolage · minority stress · neuronormativity · chosen family · queer The same impulse that tells an Autistic kid to put their hands down tells a trans kid their gender is a phase. Both are orders to perform a self that is not yours. Both name the performance normal and the person underneath disordered. Two rainbows. Two coming-out stories. Two sets of people deciding what we are allowed to be. Gender-diverse people are far more likely to be Autistic, and Autistic people are far more likely to be gender-diverse. We are not a coincidence the literature keeps stumbling over. We are a population the pathology paradigm was never built to hold. The hand stilled and the gender denied come from one root.
SEVEN LESSONS, SEVEN LINES

One idea per line is the course’s own device, not ours. The hand stilled and the gender denied were trained in the same room. Gender is not a binary or even a line. It is a copia, an identity you assemble. Two stigmas compound: more stressful situations, fewer resources to meet them. Neuroqueering queers neuronormativity and heteronormativity in the same move. Chosen family is not a consolation prize. It is how we cope and survive. Queer is a horizon of possibility, not a class of pathologies. Bathroom bills hurt Disabled, neurodivergent and trans people in one stroke. Distilled by Stimpunks from our own course. Monotropism

5 passages, written for this room and read by Ryan Boren. the glossary entry. 5 of 5 recorded. What monotropism is Monotropism is a theory of Autistic attention, made by Autistic people — Dinah Murray, Wenn Lawson and Mike Lesser. The short version: attention is a resource, and some of us spend it deeply on a few things rather than thinly across many. That is the whole claim. Most of what gets said about us follows from it. The A side: what the instrument reports This is the A side. What follows is not our description. It is the one the clinic writes down. Restricted interests. Preoccupation. Poor attention switching. Rigidity. Resistance to transition. Failure to respond to name. Every one of those is a real observation. Every one is also a measurement, reported as though it were a property of the person rather than a property of the instrument. The B side: the same wall This is the B side. Same person, same afternoon, different instrument. Attention pulled hard toward a few things, with not much left over for the rest. Interruption is expensive, because leaving a tunnel costs more than staying in one. The name went unanswered because it arrived from outside the tunnel — not because it did not matter. Nothing in that list is a deficit. It is a description of where the attention went. Both are measurements Leave it open and you get both patterns at once, which is the honest picture. The two readings describe the same behaviour. They are not equally true. One of them knows it is a measurement. The other reports itself as the whole truth. A love language Listening to the monotropic people in your life infodump about their SpIns is a love language.

Developmental Pace

5 passages, cut from our own glossary entry and to be read by Helen Edgar. the glossary entry. 0 of 5 recorded. What developmental pace is Developmental pace is the rate at which a person arrives — at a skill, a concept, a capacity — and it varies enormously between people, and within one person across different domains. Not recorded yet. The words are here; the voice is not. This slot stays visibly empty rather than quietly closed up. The A side: what the ruler reports Pace is ordinary variation. School treats it as a fixed background condition: children are grouped by birth date, taught the same content at the same time, and marked on the distance between where they are and where the timetable says they should be. That distance gets recorded against the child. So a single label — ahead, behind, at grade level — is a summary of a shape it cannot represent. It averages the peaks and the troughs into one number and then treats that number as the child. Not recorded yet. The words are here; the voice is not. This slot stays visibly empty rather than quietly closed up. The B side: not one number Developmental pace is not a single dial set slow or fast for a whole person. It is uneven by domain — which is what a spiky profile describes. A pace is not a property a child was issued at birth and can be measured against. It emerges from a person meeting an environment — which means the environment is half of it, and the half we can actually change. Not recorded yet. The words are here; the voice is not. This slot stays visibly empty rather than quietly closed up. Both are measurements “Behind” is information about the ruler, not about the learner. Not recorded yet. The words are here; the voice is not. This slot stays visibly empty rather than quietly closed up. What it is not An argument against age-graded expectations sits one careless line away from reading as an argument for lower ones. It is not that. Not recorded yet. The words are here; the voice is not. This slot stays visibly empty rather than quietly closed up.
WHY THIS IS NOT A METAPHOR

Quantum queering is not one field borrowing a little glamour from another. Barad makes the strong version of the claim: the queerness is not ours, projected onto matter. It is matter’s own. If queerness is in the nature of spacetimemattering, then it is not a deviation from the natural order — it is the natural order, and “acts against nature” becomes an incoherent charge. Barad also names the reaction: panicked attempts to contain, tame, or normalize what will not stay contained. We know that reflex. It is the same one that built the behaviorist clinic and the compliance classroom, one scale down.

The Polaroid Wall

The wall in Enid’s Room is grey rectangles. They are placeholders for photographs of our community, and they stay grey until somebody sends one — because the one thing a wall like this cannot be filled with is stock photography of strangers pretending to be us.
WHAT WE ARE ASKING FOR

A photo of you, or of you and your people. Not a good photo. Not a flattering one. The one where nobody made you smile. There is no standard to meet. Blurry is fine, badly lit is fine, half a face is fine, a photo of your hands or your dog or the ceiling you were looking at is fine. This is a wall in a room named after a character who does not match the house.
What we promise

What we promise about the photographs, and what makes each promise true The promise What makes it true rather than nice It comes down when you say so One message. No reason required, no conversation, no asking whether you are sure. This is why your photo is excluded from the site’s Creative Commons licence: CC BY-SA cannot be revoked, so a photo published under it could not be taken back even after you withdrew. Yours carries no onward licence at all. Nobody else gets to reuse it The rest of this site invites reuse. Your photograph does not. It stays yours and the photographer’s, used here with permission and nowhere else. You write the caption and the alt text Both. You know what is in the picture and what you want said about it. We will not describe you in our words, and we will not publish a photo with no description at all — a picture nobody can hear is not on a Disabled people’s site by accident, it is there by neglect. Your name is however you write it Full name, first name, handle, or nothing at all. Anonymous is a real option and does not make the photo worth less. The location data is removed Photos carry hidden metadata — where you were, when, on what device. We strip it before publishing, and our own tool refuses to publish a file that still has it. Sending us a photo should not tell the internet where you live. Everything else this site keeps about anybody, including the people who only visit, is on the privacy page.
What we need with the photo

Four things, and the tool that builds the wall will not publish a photo missing any of them: A description of what is in the picture, for anybody who cannot see it. A sentence is plenty. A caption, if you want one — the handwriting under the photo. This can be a joke. Who is in it, named the way you want to be named, or marked anonymous. Who took it, if that is somebody else, and their permission too. A photographer owns their photograph; being in a picture is not the same as owning it.
Photographs of young people

We publish photographs of young people who are doing the work and who have said yes themselves. A lot of Stimpunks volunteers and self-advocates are teenagers, and a rule that kept them off our pages would take the credit for their own activities away from them and hand it to the adults standing next to them. Nothing about us without us has no lower age bound. Two things do not move. The young person gives the consent, not a parent on their behalf. A parent can be part of the conversation and often is, but an adult’s yes is not a substitute for theirs — and the worry that first put a rule here, that somebody else makes a permanent public decision for you, is answered by asking the person themselves rather than by keeping them off the wall. And withdrawal works for them exactly as it does for everybody else, for as long as they want it: say so once, and the photograph is deleted rather than hidden. That is what the photographs carrying no onward licence is for. Where somebody is too young to give that consent themselves, we do not publish the photograph, and a parent cannot give it for them.
What we are not going to do

Ask for a better photo. Crop you. Filter you. Put your photo in a fundraising appeal, a grant application, or an advertisement. Use it to represent Disability in the abstract to somebody who needs a stock image. Keep a copy after you have asked us to stop.

THE SOUND BOARD

Nine keys, three by three where there is room for it and one column on a phone. The first six make one noise each, for as long as you keep pressing them. The last three have moods, and each one shows the mood it is about to play. The last three keys are not a feelings chart. Nobody here is being asked to identify an emotion, match it to a face, or perform one, and there are no faces anywhere on this board. What changes between the moods is the shape of a noise — a hum that lifts, a hum that sags, a hum with a buzz in it. A sad noise is a perfectly good thing to want. You can leave a key on angry and go and do something else. Nothing is counted and nothing is kept. Press one key ninety times or press all nine once; the board has no memory, no total and nothing to finish. At MAX GLITTER every key throws something different across itself. At Gentle it throws nothing and says exactly the same words.

THE ARCADE

A grape carpet, a marquee, and cabinets standing on it playing to nobody. Walk up to one. Every machine in here is a room of its own behind the glass — they share a body and a carpet, the way cabinets in an arcade do, and nothing else.
The cabinets

QUILL DRIFT Loose quills drift across a dark field. Steer Esmx the Porkypine and they join the mane on contact — the only verb this one has, because a porcupine cannot throw a quill. PLAY → OTTERLY ADORBS An otter, a kelp bay, and twirls, somersaults, dives and fish at feeding time. Floating on your back fills nothing up, which is the point of it. PLAY → PENGUIN PEBBLING A shore, some pebbles, and neighbours with nests. Carry something over and give it to somebody. Nothing is counted and nothing is owed back. PLAY →
WHAT EVERY MACHINE IN HERE WILL NOT DO

None of them will time you. No clock, no lives, no score, no streak, no best-ever, and nothing you can fail. None of them will chase you. There is nothing in any of these games trying to beat you, take anything back, or arrive while you are not looking. None of them will make a noise. Not one, ever, at any setting. An arcade that is silent by choice seemed better than one that is silent until it isn’t. None of them will remember you. The cabinets store nothing and send nothing, and closing the tab is the whole of quitting. Nothing moves until you press start. Each screen is dark when you walk up to it, which is the same consent the jukebox two doors down runs on. Each cabinet also has refusals of its own, written on its own page, because they come out of what that particular game is about.
THE DIAL AND THE SPEED KNOBS

These do different jobs. The dial governs the room — the glow behind the cabinets, the marquee bulbs. Each cabinet has its own speed knob, and the player holds that. The dial picks the knob’s starting position — Slow if you arrived on Gentle — and then stops having an opinion. All three speeds are here at every dial setting. A Gentle that quietly handed you a different game would be the “lite version” mistake with a joystick on it. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. WHAT QUILL DRIFT WILL NOT DO

It will not let you throw anything. Porcupines cannot shoot their quills — they cannot throw them, fire them or launch them; a quill comes away in whatever touched it. A spiky mascot invites exactly the opposite reading, so this game has no such verb in it. Contact is the only mechanic. It will not chase you. There is nothing else on that field. Nothing arrives to take a quill back, and there is no way to lose one. It will not time you. No clock, no lives, no score, no streak, no best-ever. The count is a count of what you have, and it only goes up. It will not make a noise. Not one, ever, at any setting. An arcade that was silent by choice seemed better than an arcade that was silent until it wasn’t. It will not remember you. The game stores nothing and sends nothing, and closing the tab is the whole of quitting.
WHO ESMX IS, AND WHY THERE IS A GAME AT ALL

Esmx the Porkypine — part pig, part porcupine, with a bit of goblin in there — is the Stimpunks Foundation’s community mascot. We commissioned them; the artist is Kaya Oldaker, and her name goes on the drawing wherever it appears, because attribution here is a licence and a courtesy rather than a question of who holds the rights. Esmx’s pronouns are they/them, and the name comes from Esmeralda Weatherwax and the Witches of Discworld. The x is deliberate. Esmx’s mane evokes the spiky profile, and the spikes are a mix of the autism spectrum’s colours and the LGBT+ flag’s, because there is heavy overlap between the two. Kaya’s notes say the spikes trail off and separate, as if they are made of energy, and that they can trail off and create patterns. A game about loose quills drifting across a dark field is that sentence with a d-pad attached. An arcade in particular, because Kaya says so: Esmx resembles a Sonic character or a Pokémon on purpose, due to their popularity within the Autistic community. This room is not a costume we put on the mascot. It is where the mascot already came from.
WHY THIS IS A NEW DRAWING

Esmx is ours to reproduce — we hold the rights and Kaya’s originals are a download away. The Esmx on that screen is built from scratch in this room’s line anyway, the way the Quillery’s eight were, and not because anybody needed permission. A pasted PNG would have been the only thing in this arcade that came from somewhere else, in a room whose whole argument is that it shares nothing with the rooms next door. And a variant is the thing the licence goes out of its way to ask for: feel free to customise! Make variants of Esmx to represent your community. Taking our own invitation seemed like the least we could do with it. The marks we kept are the ones that make Esmx Esmx: the snout, the earring in one ear, the chunk out of the other, and a mane that comes apart at the tips. The original, every official variant, the blank template and the download are on Esmx’s own page. If you share any of them, include alt text — Kaya asked, and honouring a licence is the easy half of honouring a maker. “Esmx” by Kaya Oldaker is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0; this variant likewise. That credit line is the one on Esmx’s own page and it stays on ours — owning a commission is not a reason to stop saying whose hand drew it. The quill facts behind the house rules are in the Quillery, which sources them. Full credits are in the liner notes.
THE DIAL AND THE SPEED KNOBS

These do different jobs. The dial governs the room — the glow behind the cabinets, the marquee bulbs. Each cabinet has its own speed knob, and the player holds that. The dial picks the knob’s starting position — Slow if you arrived on Gentle — and then stops having an opinion. All three speeds are here at every dial setting. A Gentle that quietly handed you a different game would be the “lite version” mistake with a joystick on it. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so — and nothing in this room makes a sound at all.

WHAT OTTERLY ADORBS WILL NOT DO

Floating will not fill anything up. No meter, no stamina, no bonus afterwards. The zine this is built on refuses rest so you can produce in as many words — the otter is not recharging in order to forage better tomorrow — so wiring a reward to rest would have put a sentence on this page that another of our pages spends a spread refusing. It will not rank the otters. The other three keep their own rhythms and none of them is the good one. Under pressure a real population does not converge on one best way to be an otter; it fans out into specialists, each better at its own thing (Tinker, Bentall & Estes, 2008). A leaderboard is the one thing this cabinet is built to refuse. It will not tell you how many blows a clam should take. Two observers on the California coast in 1964 watched otters take between 6 and 88 to open a mussel, averaging 35.5 (Hall & Schaller). Those are the numbers this uses. There is no correct number; there is your number. It will not make you carry a stone. Some otters never use one — they are on prey a stone would not help with, and the ones who do use a stone keep their teeth (Law et al., 2024). Both routes are here and neither is scored. It will not time you or make a noise, and it will not remember you. Feeding time arrives and leaves on its own; nothing is lost by ignoring all of it.
WHY OTTERS

Every Saturday the Stimpunks Solidarity Session leaves an otter cam running while the conversation drifts in and out — cameras on or off, some speaking, some in text, some just there. Nobody has to watch it. That is the part that makes it work. Helen Edgar wrote down what the cam was doing for her in Stimpunks Solidarity and Otters (Autistic Realms, 2026): somewhere to put her attention on a day when listening and speaking were both off the table, and a way to exist in parallel with people she wanted to be near. Then she noticed the resemblance — the otters float, juggle a stone, somersault off alone, drift back for a minute of shared play, and peel away again. Parallel play, and a cave and a watering hole in one animal. Helen’s reading is hers and is credited to her, not folded into our “we”. The findings behind the mechanics are in The Stone You Keep (Star Stuff No. 58), which sources every one of them. One thing that zine corrects and this cabinet follows: the widely repeated lifelong favourite rock, kept for years in a pouch under the arm, traces to popular retellings rather than to the primary literature. What the primary supports is a stone kept and reused across successive food items within a bout of feeding, and that is all this does.

WHAT JUST HAPPENED

Everything the screen does is also said in the strip under it. This list is not a total — it keeps the last few things and forgets the rest, which is the only honest way to log a practice that is explicitly not about volume.
WHAT PENGUIN PEBBLING WILL NOT DO

It will not count what you gave. No tally, no total, no streak, nothing at the end. The locution is not about volume, and a number beside it would quietly make it about volume. It will not require a pebble back. The neighbours bring you things on their own clock whether or not you have ever given them anything. That is the difference between pebbling and trading, and it is built as a timer rather than as a reward on purpose. There is no wrong thing to give anybody. Every pebble is taken and every one gets something different said back. There is no matching puzzle underneath this — giving is how you find out who somebody is, not a lock to pick. A pebble you keep is not a failure. You can carry one the whole time, or put it back down. Nothing notices. Nobody steals anything. Real Adélie and gentoo penguins nick stones off each other constantly, which is funny and true and belongs in a different game. This one is about the locution.
WHERE THIS COMES FROM, AND WHAT IT IS NOT

Penguin pebbling is one of the Five Neurodivergent Love Locutions, coined by Amythest Schaber (Neurowonderful) and documented by Stimpunks in 2022. The line most people meet it through is @brainsandspoons’: “I thought about you today. I remembered this thing about you. Here’s something I want to share with you specifically.” Helen Edgar wrote it up at Autistic Realms in 2023: a pebble, a twig, a flower, a photograph from a walk — not spending money. There is a glossary entry too. There is already a Penguin Pebbling game, and this cabinet is not it. Penguin Pebbling is a thirty-card game by Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms) and Ryan Boren (Stimpunks), 2026, built around all five locutions. Go and play that one; it is the better thing and it is a real deck you can print. This cabinet takes nothing from it — no cards, no prompts, no artwork, no five-locution structure — and the reason is a licence rather than modesty: the deck is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and this site is CC BY-SA 4.0. An adaptation would carry the non-commercial clause onto a page that cannot hold it, and relicensing is not ours alone to do. So this is built on the locution, which belongs to the community. And one honest thing about the penguins. Adélie and gentoo penguins really do build nests out of stones and carry them about, and they really do steal them from each other. The tidy romance — one penguin choosing the perfect pebble and presenting it to its beloved — is the popular retelling rather than the finding. The locution is named after the image and is not weakened by that. A metaphor does not have to be a finding. It is said here rather than quietly traded on.

The Latibulum
A burrow of belonging for burnouts. Every other door on this street opens onto a room. This one opens onto a hole in the ground, and going down into it is the point.
The word

Latibulum is Latin. Lewis and Short give it as “a hiding-place, lurking-hole, covert, den, of animals” — a badger’s sett, a fox’s earth, somewhere a creature goes when it has had enough of being findable. Then they give a second sense, the figurative one, and quote Cicero calling a place the latibulum et perfugium doloris mei: the hiding-place and refuge of his grief. So the word already does both jobs. It is where an animal goes to be unavailable, and it is where a person goes when something has knocked them flat. We did not have to stretch it. Ryan met the word at Walkabout Saga; the dictionary entry is Lewis and Short’s, on Perseus. In our own vocabulary this is a cave — the quiet end of a Cavendish Space, where the work is being unreachable for a while. Not a break room with a twenty-minute limit on it. Burnout does not run on a twenty-minute limit either.

Tai chi and qigong, taught entirely from a chair — Repulse Monkey, Parting the Horse's Mane, Cloud Arms, three repetitions of everything so that all the exercises become familiar. Everything in it is seated, and not as a modification: as the design. Nothing in it requires standing and nothing in it requires moving at all. Annette, of Itstimefitness. Nothing of it is hosted here; pressing is what sends the request.
Things to do with a bodymind

We are not minds riding around in bodies. We are bodyminds — nervous systems woven through with cognition, feeling and flesh — and a bodymind in a burrow has needs that deserve to be met. This shelf is lifted straight off our own Bodymind Break, which is where it belongs and where there is more of it. stretchReach for something. It does not have to be far, and it does not have to be up. flapHands talk. Stimming is regulation, not a symptom to be quiet about. fidgetSomething in your hands, turning. A ring, a zip, a corner of a blanket. meditateOr sit there badly. Nobody in this burrow is checking your posture. stim danceChair, floor, one hand, nothing. See Happy Flappy. body scanStart at the feet and work up. What it is, and how. eatThe unglamorous one. Something warm, something cold, something beige. drinkWater counts. So does the third tea you forgot about. peeGo now. It is on the list because it is always the thing being postponed. Nothing on that shelf is a button. No ticks, no streak, no progress bar, nothing that notices which ones you did. A shelf that kept score would have turned a bodymind break into a small unpaid job, which is the thing the break is a break from. In practical terms, supporting nervous system regulation means tending to and responding to the body’s needs first and foremost. This means prioritising physiological needs. Things like taking rest breaks, keeping warm, cooling down, regularly hydrating, moving when the body feels it needs to, and going to the toilet as soon as you need to. — Embodied Education: Creating Safe Space for Learning, Facilitating and Sharing, quoted on our own Bodymind Break.
What the burrow is

Nothing plays until you press play. Both of the things down here that can make a noise are silent, and have been since the page loaded. Until you press one, this page has asked YouTube for nothing on your behalf — no iframe, no cookie, no request — and both of them tell you how long they run before you decide. Nothing is counted. No visits, no minutes, no streak, no shelf of things you got through. A burrow that tallied your rest would be a burrow that had opinions about how much of it you were entitled to. Nothing is behind the dial. This room is quiet at every setting because it was built quiet, not because Gentle took anything off it. Turn it all the way up to MAX GLITTER and exactly one thing happens: the lamp breathes, slowly, and nothing else in here so much as leans. You can leave without telling anybody. There is nothing to sign, nothing to join, and nothing that notices you came. The street is still up there whenever you want it, and it will be just as loud as you left it. It is a hole in the ground and it is allowed to be. Hiding is not a failure state. It is what the word has meant since before anybody thought to be ashamed of it.
Who made the noise in here

“Ocean Waves” is by Adriel Jeremiah Wool, a Stimpunk, and it is his — used here with his permission and hosted by him, not by us. The seated tai chi class is Annette’s, of Itstimefitness; we found it for our own Campfire Learn Together on somatic practice and bodily survival knowledge. Neither of them is affiliated with this street beyond being on it. The shelf is our own Bodymind Break, and the quotation on it belongs to the page it is quoted from. Everything is collected in the liner notes. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so — and down here, MAX GLITTER is one lamp breathing.

The Jungle Room

Drop in. Space out. Belong here. A room with the cameras on and nobody presenting. Every screen in here is somebody else’s camera pointed at somewhere real, and every one of them is off until you open it.
Why a room is just a lot of screens

Every weekday our Watering Hole Hangs puts a nature cam up in the background and leaves it there. No slides, no presenter, no outcomes — people turn up, do their own thing near each other, and let the otters carry the social weight. That is body doubling, and it is one of the most underrated things neurodivergent people do for one another. A watering hole is the third of our three gathering modes: not the cave you go into alone, not the campfire gathered around a story, but the in-between place where community actually forms because nobody scheduled it to. Co-regulation happens there, quietly, and a bodymind settles in the presence of other bodyminds even at this distance. The cam is doing some of that work too. Something about water, movement, and animals going about their quiet lives — it earns its place in the background. This room is the cams, and only the cams. The groups below, their order, and the order inside each of them are lifted from that events page exactly as they stand there — it is a list somebody keeps, not one for this street to re-sort. The train cams on it are not here: a cab view down a Norwegian line is a fine thing to hang about in and it is not a watering hole. Everything else is. The galleries are built from data/jungle.json by tools/make-jungle.py.

What the room is

Nothing plays until you press play. Every screen above is a button. Until you press one, this page has asked YouTube for nothing on your behalf — no iframe, no cookie, no request, no pixel. Press one and exactly one becomes a video; the rest stay buttons. Nothing here says how long it runs, because none of it ends. Every other press-to-play control on this street carries a runtime, and that is the promise that lets you decide before you press. A live camera has no runtime to carry. Putting the length of whichever stream happens to be up today on the page would be a number that is wrong tomorrow, so the label says the true thing instead: it runs until you close it. The picture is whatever is happening there right now. Which is sometimes darkness, sometimes rain, sometimes an empty waterhole, and sometimes a cam between streams showing you the last one. None of that is a fault. A camera pointed at somewhere real is a camera that is often pointed at nothing, and sitting with nothing happening is most of what this room is for. Nothing is hosted here. Not one frame. The Den

He did not go to the studio. The studio came into the den. Green shag on the floor. Carved wood, fake fur, a waterfall of cut fieldstone on the north wall, and a jade lamp on either side of it. In 1976 somebody rolled recording equipment into this room, and the last two Elvis Presley albums came out of it.
The room, and then the records

Graceland has a den that Elvis Presley filled with Polynesian furniture after Blue Hawaii — carved wood, fur over the seats, plants, coloured glass, and an indoor waterfall of cut field stone on the north wall. People have been rude about it for fifty years. It is one of the great rooms. And then in 1976 it was turned into a recording studio, and the bulk of his final two albums were made in it: From Elvis Presley Boulevard, Memphis, Tennessee, out that May, and Moody Blue, out in July 1977. Felton Jarvis produced. The band was the touring band — James Burton, Ron Tutt, Jerry Scheff, Glen D. Hardin, John Wilkinson, Charlie Hodge, David Briggs — with J.D. Sumner & The Stamps, Kathy Westmoreland and Myrna Smith singing. They played it live in a room with the furniture still in it. That is the whole reason this is a room and not a link. A shag carpet is a joke; a discography made on top of one is a listening bench. House rules, in here

Nothing plays until you press play. Every one of those is a button, not a video. Until you press one this page has asked YouTube for nothing on your behalf — no iframe, no cookie, no request. Press one and exactly one becomes a song. Every button says how long it runs. Which is the rule the room you came through cannot follow, because a live camera never ends. These are songs with a length, so withholding it would be keeping back the one fact that lets you decide. The two generators enforce opposite checks and are making the same promise. The vibe, not the lyrics. Same rule as the dancefloor and the chapel. We name the artist, we link the song, and we let them keep their own words. And we name the people who wrote them, because Elvis Presley wrote none of these and a room that credited only the voice would be doing the exact thing this site keeps attribution for. Nothing is hosted here. Not one second of audio. Every button is a facade that points at Presley’s own official channels — the estate’s art-track channel and his VEVO — and the recordings stay where their owners put them. This room is not the room upstairs. Both are called the Jungle Room and both are green, and that is where it stops. Up there the green is the darkness and the light falls from above; down here the room is brown, the carpet is the brightest thing in it, and the list is set dark on the green. Same colour, opposite job.

The Raven

Eighteen stanzas, six lines each, and a bird that only knows the one word. Poe published it in January 1845 and it has been out of copyright for longer than most countries have had copyright. All twenty-six of Gustave Doré’s engravings are here, standing at the lines they illustrate, and so are three leaves of an 1865 printing. Set the whole thing in whichever voice you want: the picker holds every typeface on this street, which is the one place here where borrowing all of them is the joke rather than the failure.
The Raven, Philadelphia: Tyndale, Mitchell & Co., 1865

With illustrations engraved on wood by Scattergood. Scanned by Lehigh University and published by the Internet Archive under the Public Domain Mark 1.0 — an explicit statement that it may be reproduced, which is why these leaves are here rather than only linked to. The front cover Four stanzas, as they were set in 1865 A wood engraving, and the stanzas under it The whole book at the Internet Archive → There is also a facsimile of the poem in Poe’s own hand, six leaves of it, at the Library of Congress — and it is a link rather than a copy. That facsimile was printed in 1949 for an exhibition at Yale and carries “reproduction prohibited without permission” along the foot of its own first leaf. The poem is Poe’s and free; that printing of it is somebody else’s object. The difference between it and the 1865 book above is one line of metadata, and it is the whole difference between showing you something and pointing at it. Read it in Edgar Allan Poe · first published January 1845 · engravings by Gustave Doré, 1884 Doré’s edition printed the poem straight through and the plates after it, each captioned with the lines it illustrates. Here every plate sits at the lines its own caption quotes, which is our decision about reading rather than a reproduction of that book’s layout. The captions are his edition’s, word for word — which is how you can see that its text is not quite the one set below it. Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and weary, Over many a quaint and curious volume of forgotten lore— While I nodded, nearly napping, suddenly there came a tapping, As of some one gently rapping, rapping at my chamber door. “’Tis some visiter,” I muttered, “tapping at my chamber door— Only this and nothing more.” “Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and weary, / Over many a quaint and curious volume of forgotten lore.” Ah, distinctly I remember it was in the bleak December, And each separate dying ember wrought its ghost upon the floor. Eagerly I wished the morrow;—vainly I had sought to borrow From my books surcease of sorrow—sorrow for the lost Lenore— For the rare and radiant maiden whom the angels name Lenore— Nameless here for evermore. “Ah, distinctly I remember it was in the bleak December, / And each separate dying ember wrought its ghost upon the floor.” “Eagerly I wished the morrow;—vainly I had sought to borrow / From my books surcease of sorrow.” “Sorrow for the lost Lenore.” “For the rare and radiant maiden whom the angels name Lenore— / Nameless here for evermore.” And the silken sad uncertain rustling of each purple curtain Thrilled me—filled me with fantastic terrors never felt before; So that now, to still the beating of my heart, I stood repeating “’Tis some visiter entreating entrance at my chamber door— Some late visiter entreating entrance at my chamber door; This it is and nothing more.” “’T is some visiter entreating entrance at my chamber door— / Some late visiter entreating entrance at my chamber door.” Presently my soul grew stronger; hesitating then no longer, “Sir,” said I, “or Madam, truly your forgiveness I implore; But the fact is I was napping, and so gently you came rapping, And so faintly you came tapping, tapping at my chamber door, That I scarce was sure I heard you”—here I opened wide the door— Darkness there and nothing more. “Here I opened wide the door;— / Darkness there, and nothing more.” Deep into that darkness peering, long I stood there wondering, fearing, Doubting, dreaming dreams no mortals ever dared to dream before; But the silence was unbroken, and the stillness gave no token, And the only word there spoken was the whispered word, “Lenore?” This I whispered, and an echo murmured back the word, “Lenore!”— Merely this and nothing more. “Doubting, dreaming dreams no mortal ever dared to dream before.” Back into the chamber turning, all my soul within me burning, Soon again I heard a tapping something louder than before. “Surely,” said I, “surely that is something at my window lattice; Let me see, then, what thereat is and this mystery explore— Let my heart be still a moment and this mystery explore;— ’Tis the wind and nothing more.” “‘Surely,’ said I, ‘surely that is something at my window lattice; / Let me see, then, what thereat is.’” Open here I flung the shutter, when, with many a flirt and flutter, In there stepped a stately Raven of the saintly days of yore. Not the least obeisance made he; not a minute stopped or stayed he, But, with mien of lord or lady, perched above my chamber door— Perched upon a bust of Pallas just above my chamber door— Perched, and sat, and nothing more. “Open here I flung the shutter.” “A stately Raven of the saintly days of yore. / Not the least obeisance made he.” “Perched upon a bust of Pallas just above my chamber door— / Perched, and sat, and nothing more.” Then the ebony bird beguiling my sad fancy into smiling, By the grave and stern decorum of the countenance it wore, “Though thy crest be shorn and shaven, thou,” I said, “art sure no craven, Ghastly grim and ancient Raven wandering from the Nightly shore— Tell me what thy lordly name is on the Night’s Plutonian shore!” Quoth the Raven, “Nevermore.” “Wandering from the Nightly shore.” Much I marvelled this ungainly fowl to hear discourse so plainly, Though its answer little meaning—little relevancy bore; For we cannot help agreeing that no living human being Ever yet was blessed with seeing bird above his chamber door— Bird or beast upon the sculptured bust above his chamber door, With such name as “Nevermore.” But the Raven, sitting lonely on that placid bust, spoke only That one word, as if its soul in that one word he did outpour Nothing farther then he uttered; not a feather then he fluttered— Till I scarcely more than muttered: “Other friends have flown before— On the morrow _he_ will leave me, as my Hopes have flown before.” Then the bird said “Nevermore.” “Till I scarcely more than muttered, ‘Other friends have flown before— / On the morrow he will leave me.’” Startled at the stillness broken by reply so aptly spoken, “Doubtless,” said I, “what it utters is its only stock and store, Caught from some unhappy master whom unmerciful Disaster Followed fast and followed faster till his songs one burden bore— Till the dirges of his Hope that melancholy burden bore Of ‘Never—nevermore.’” But the Raven still beguiling all my sad soul into smiling, Straight I wheeled a cushioned seat in front of bird and bust and door; Then, upon the velvet sinking, I betook myself to linking Fancy unto fancy, thinking what this ominous bird of yore— What this grim, ungainly, ghastly, gaunt, and ominous bird of yore Meant in croaking “Nevermore.” “Then, upon the velvet sinking, I betook myself to linking / Fancy unto fancy.” This I sat engaged in guessing, but no syllable expressing To the fowl whose fiery eyes now burned into my bosom’s core; This and more I sat divining, with my head at ease reclining On the cushion’s velvet lining that the lamp-light gloated o’er, But whose velvet violet lining with the lamp-light gloating o’er _She_ shall press, ah, nevermore! “But whose velvet violet lining with the lamplight gloating o’er / She shall press, ah, nevermore!” Then, methought, the air grew denser, perfumed from an unseen censer Swung by Seraphim whose foot-falls tinkled on the tufted floor. “Wretch,” I cried, “thy God hath lent thee—by these angels he hath sent thee Respite—respite and nepenthe from thy memories of Lenore! Quaff, oh quaff this kind nepenthe and forget this lost Lenore!” Quoth the Raven, “Nevermore.” “‘Wretch,’ I cried, ‘thy God hath lent thee—by these angels he hath sent thee / Respite—respite and nepenthe from thy memories of Lenore!’” “Prophet!” said I, “thing of evil!—prophet still, if bird or devil!— Whether Tempter sent, or whether tempest tossed thee here ashore, Desolate, yet all undaunted, on this desert land enchanted— On this home by Horror haunted—tell me truly, I implore— Is there—_is_ there balm in Gilead?—tell me—tell me, I implore!” Quoth the Raven, “Nevermore.” “On this home by Horror haunted.” “Tell me truly, I implore— / Is there—is there balm in Gilead?—tell me—tell me, I implore!” “Prophet!” said I, “thing of evil!—prophet still, if bird or devil! By that Heaven that bends above us—by that God we both adore— Tell this soul with sorrow laden if, within the distant Aidenn, It shall clasp a sainted maiden whom the angels name Lenore— Clasp a rare and radiant maiden whom the angels name Lenore.” Quoth the Raven, “Nevermore.” “Tell this soul with sorrow laden if, within the distant Aidenn, / It shall clasp a sainted maiden whom the angels name Lenore.” “Be that our sign of parting, bird or fiend!” I shrieked, upstarting— “Get thee back into the tempest and the Night’s Plutonian shore! Leave no black plume as a token of that lie thy soul has spoken! Leave my loneliness unbroken!—quit the bust above my door! Take thy beak from out my heart, and take thy form from off my door!” Quoth the Raven, “Nevermore.” “‘Be that word our sign of parting, bird or fiend!’ I shrieked, upstarting.” “‘Get thee back into the tempest and the Night’s Plutonian shore!’” And the Raven, never flitting, still is sitting, still is sitting On the pallid bust of Pallas just above my chamber door; And his eyes have all the seeming of a demon’s that is dreaming And the lamp-light o’er him streaming throws his shadows on the floor; And my soul from out that shadow that lies floating on the floor Shall be lifted—nevermore! “And my soul from out that shadow that lies floating on the floor / Shall be lifted—nevermore!”

House rules

Nothing plays until you press play. The screen is a picture of a screen until you ask for a video. Tuning through the list with the set off sends nothing anywhere. Borrowing comes before buying. Every book here has a route that costs nothing, and it is the first link on the card. Nobody wrote these but the people who wrote them. Every cut on that screen names Jagger and Richards, because eight of them are covers and the performer’s name is the draw. The dark is not the mood, it is the lighting. Turn the dial down and the candles stop moving; the room stays exactly as dark, exactly as legible, and exactly as full.
Who made the noise in here

The novels belong to the people who wrote them and the notes on them are ours. “Paint It, Black” is Mick Jagger and Keith Richards’, 1966; the cello arrangement everything else is answering is Danny Elfman and Chris Bacon’s, for Netflix. Nothing musical is hosted here. The Raven is Poe’s and out of copyright; the manuscript facsimile stays at the Library of Congress. It is all collected in the liner notes. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so — and in here, MAX GLITTER is candles guttering and a sign on a bracket.

The Oracle Deck

Thirteen engravings, between 1514 and 1891, with a question on the back of each one. It asks. It does not answer. There are no reversals, no yes, no no, and nothing in here about what is going to happen to you — a deck on a Disabled people’s site that told somebody how their life was going to go would be doing the exact thing the rest of these pages exist to refuse. The build refuses a card that tries.
Cut the deck

One card, at random, from the thirteen below. Draw as many as you like; there is no spread, no position and no meaning attached to the order. If it hands you something that is not useful, that is allowed — put it back. The deck is face down. Nothing is shuffled until you ask for it.
The whole deck

Every card, face up, in the order they were cut — oldest plate first. Nothing on this page is behind the draw: a room that made somebody gamble to reach its contents would have put its contents behind chance, which is the “lite version” mistake holding a deck.
card-melencolia
The Melancholy

What have you been calling laziness? She is surrounded by every instrument she knows how to use and she is not using any of them. Five centuries before anybody wrote the word, this is a picture of a person who has run out. Albrecht Dürer (German, Nuremberg 1471–1528 Nuremberg), Melencolia I, 1514. Engraving. Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, 1943, 43.106.1. The Metropolitan Museum of Art · public domain.
card-moon-full
The Full Moon

What is lit whether or not you are ready to look at it? Mellan cut the whole face in a single spiralling line that starts at the nose and never lifts. It is the most technically insane thing in this deck and it is a picture of something everybody has already seen. Claude Mellan (French, Abbeville 1598–1688 Paris), Full Moon, 1635. Engraving; first state of two (BN). The Elisha Whittelsey Collection, The Elisha Whittelsey Fund, 1960, 60.634.36. The Metropolitan Museum of Art · public domain.
card-moon-waxing
The Waxing Moon

What is coming back that you had written off? Half of it is missing and half of it is arriving. Both of those are true of the same object on the same night. Claude Mellan (French, Abbeville 1598–1688 Paris), The Moon in its First Quarter, 1635. Engraving; first state of two (BN). The Elisha Whittelsey Collection, The Elisha Whittelsey Fund, 1960, 60.634.38. The Metropolitan Museum of Art · public domain.
card-moon-waning
The Waning Moon

What are you allowed to have less of? Waning is not failing. It is the same body doing the other half of the only thing it does. Claude Mellan (French, Abbeville 1598–1688 Paris), The Moon in its Final Quarter, 1635. Engraving; first state of two. The Elisha Whittelsey Collection, The Elisha Whittelsey Fund, 1960, 60.634.37. The Metropolitan Museum of Art · public domain.
card-carceri-title
The Threshold

What have you not opened yet? A title page is a door with writing on it. Piranesi's opens onto a set of prisons that do not exist, never connect to each other, and were etched by a man who described himself on it as an architect. Giovanni Battista Piranesi (Italian, Mogliano Veneto 1720–1778 Rome), Title Page, from "Carceri d'invenzione" (Imaginary Prisons), ca. 1749–50. Etching, engraving, sulphur tint or open bite; first state of nine (Robison). Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, 1937, 37.45.3(21). The Metropolitan Museum of Art · public domain.
card-carceri-round-tower
The Tower

Who told you the only way out was up? Every staircase in this picture leads somewhere, and no two of them agree about where. The architecture is not solvable and was never meant to be. Giovanni Battista Piranesi (Italian, Mogliano Veneto 1720–1778 Rome), The Round Tower, from "Carceri d'invenzione" (Imaginary Prisons), ca. 1749–50. Etching, engraving, sulphur tint or open bite, burnishing; first state of four (Robison). Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, 1937, 37.45.3(27). The Metropolitan Museum of Art · public domain.
card-carceri-pier-lamp
The Lamp

Who is keeping a light on for you? One lamp, in a building the size of a weather system, put there by somebody. It does not light the room. It was not going to. Giovanni Battista Piranesi (Italian, Mogliano Veneto 1720–1778 Rome), The Pier with a Lamp, from "Carceri d'invenzione" (Imaginary Prisons), ca. 1749–50. Etching, engraving, sulphur tint or open bite, burnishing; first state of seven (Robison). Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, 1937, 37.45.3(29). The Metropolitan Museum of Art · public domain.
card-meryon-vampire
The Watcher

What have you looked at so long that it has started looking back? Meryon called this one The Vampire. It has been up there since the restoration, resting its chin on its hands and watching the city get on with it, and it is the closest thing this library has to a colleague. Charles Meryon (French, 1821–1868), The Vampire, 1853. Etching in brown ink on green laid paper; fifth state of ten. H.O. Havemeyer Collection, Bequest of Mrs. H.O. Havemeyer, 1929, 29.107.108. The Metropolitan Museum of Art · public domain.
card-goya-sleep-of-reason
The Sleep

What did you decide while you were exhausted? The lettering on the desk says the sleep of reason produces monsters. The lynx is the detail nobody mentions: something in the picture is still awake. Goya (Francisco de Goya y Lucientes) (Spanish, Fuendetodos 1746–1828 Bordeaux), Plate 43 from "Los Caprichos": The sleep of reason produces monsters (El sueño de la razon produce monstruos), 1799. Etching, aquatint. Gift of M. Knoedler & Co., 1918, 18.64(43). The Metropolitan Museum of Art · public domain.
card-goya-bogey
The Bogey

Who taught you to be frightened of that? Goya's own note on this plate is contemptuous of the parent, not the ghost: a child taught to fear a thing that is not there grows into an adult who can be frightened by anybody holding a sheet. Goya (Francisco de Goya y Lucientes) (Spanish, Fuendetodos 1746–1828 Bordeaux), Plate 3 from "Los Caprichos": Here comes the bogey-man (Que viene el Coco), 1799. Etching, burnished aquatint. Gift of M. Knoedler & Co., 1918, 18.64(3). The Metropolitan Museum of Art · public domain.
card-redon-armor
The Armour

What are you still wearing indoors? It is drawn in charcoal, which means the armour is made of dust. Redon spent twenty years on what he called his blacks before he allowed himself any colour at all. Odilon Redon (French, Bordeaux 1840–1916 Paris), Armor, 1891. Charcoal and conté crayon. Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, 1948, 48.10.1. The Metropolitan Museum of Art · public domain.
card-redon-veil
The Veil

What are you not saying out loud yet? Something is there and it is not resolving. Redon's whole argument was that a picture is allowed to do that, and refused to explain any of them. Odilon Redon (French, Bordeaux 1840–1916 Paris), A Veil, a Printed Image, 1891. Lithograph. Rogers Fund, 1920, 20.30.1. The Metropolitan Museum of Art · public domain.
card-bresdin-samaritan
The Thicket

Who stopped for you? The parable is in there. So is everything else — Bresdin filled the whole plate with undergrowth until the act of kindness became something you have to look for, which is a fair description of how it usually works. Rodolphe Bresdin (French, Montrelais 1822–1885 Sèvres), The Good Samaritan, 1861. Lithograph; early impression of first state (Van Gelder). Rogers Fund and the Elisha Whittelsey Collection, The Elisha Whittelsey Fund, 1979, 1979.573. The Metropolitan Museum of Art · public domain.
Where the pictures came from

Every plate is a public domain work in the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Open Access collection, which releases images of public domain works under CC0. One collection rather than thirteen scrapbook sources, because that is what lets this page make a single rights statement somebody could actually check — and the build refuses a plate whose object page is anywhere else. CC0 asks for nothing; Dürer, Mellan, Piranesi, Meryon, Goya, Redon and Bresdin are named on every card anyway, which is this street’s habit and not their requirement. The card names, the questions and the notes are ours. It is all collected in the liner notes. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. There is no ambient layer in this room at any setting: thirteen rectangles on a plain ground do not need one, and a deck that moved while you were reading it would be a different and much worse object.

The Doomscroll

All the bad news · newest first · nothing since 1920 A feed of doom, ordered the way a feed is ordered: newest at the top, by the date each item was first published. It is also, as promised, a scroll. The joke is that this is exactly what the other kind of doomscrolling gives you — an endless column of the worst thing anybody could think of, arriving in reverse chronological order — except that all of this is four hundred years old, none of it is trying to sell you anything, and every single item is a person who sat down and made the dread into something with a shape. The date is when it went public, not when it was written, and for a third of this scroll the two are decades apart. Hopkins sat in a friend’s desk for twenty-nine years. Hardy’s sat in a drawer for thirty-one. Dickinson’s was not printed until four years after she died, retitled, tidied and a stanza short. A feed records when the news broke, so that is what this is ordered on, and each item says the other date where it is known. Every poem here is out of copyright everywhere — not just in the United States — which means every one of these writers has been dead more than seventy years. That rule cost this scroll its best opening item: T. S. Eliot’s The Hollow Men would have sat at the top, and it is public domain in America and will not be in much of Europe until the 2030s. A site that serves everybody cannot publish somebody’s whole poem on a technicality that only holds in one country. 1920 · first published in Poems (1920), edited by Siegfried Sassoon and Edith Sitwell
OFFICIAL LINE ON GLORY CONTRADICTED BY EVERYONE WHO WAS THERE

Filed from the front by a man who did not come home. Printed two years after he was killed, a week before the armistice. Dulce et Decorum est by Wilfred Owen, who died in 1918 — which is why the whole of it can be printed here
poem-dulce
Dulce et Decorum est

Wilfred Owen · 1920 Bent double, like old beggars under sacks, Knock-kneed, coughing like hags, we cursed through sludge, Till on the haunting flares we turned our backs And towards our distant rest began to trudge. Men marched asleep. Many had lost their boots But limped on, blood-shod. All went lame; all blind; Drunk with fatigue; deaf even to the hoots Of gas-shells dropping softly behind. Gas! GAS! Quick, boys!—An ecstasy of fumbling Fitting the clumsy helmets just in time, But someone still was yelling out and stumbling And flound'ring like a man in fire or lime.— Dim, through the misty panes and thick green light, As under a green sea, I saw him drowning. In all my dreams before my helpless sight He plunges at me, guttering, choking, drowning. If in some smothering dreams you too could pace Behind the wagon that we flung him in, And watch the white eyes writhing in his face, His hanging face, like a devil's sick of sin, If you could hear, at every jolt, the blood Come gargling from the froth-corrupted lungs, Bitter as the cud Of vile, incurable sores on innocent tongues,— My friend, you would not tell with such high zest To children ardent for some desperate glory, The old Lie: Dulce et decorum est Pro patria mori. First published in Poems (1920), edited by Siegfried Sassoon and Edith Sitwell. This text is from the first published edition, transcribed from Wikisource's scan-backed text — see it there. Wilfred Owen died in 1918, so the poem is out of copyright everywhere. 1920 · first published in The Dial, November 1920
CENTRE CONFIRMED NOT HOLDING; FALCON UNREACHABLE

Twenty centuries of stony sleep end early. Authorities decline to say what is on its way to Bethlehem. The Second Coming by W. B. Yeats, who died in 1939 — which is why the whole of it can be printed here
poem-second-coming
The Second Coming

W. B. Yeats · 1920 Turning and turning in the widening gyre The falcon cannot hear the falconer; Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold; Mere anarchy is loosed upon the world, The blood-dimmed tide is loosed, and everywhere The ceremony of innocence is drowned; The best lack all conviction, while the worst Are full of passionate intensity. Surely some revelation is at hand; Surely the Second Coming is at hand. The Second Coming! Hardly are those words out When a vast image out of Spiritus Mundi Troubles my sight: a waste of desert sand; A shape with lion body and the head of a man, A gaze blank and pitiless as the sun, Is moving its slow thighs, while all about it Wind shadows of the indignant desert birds. The darkness drops again but now I know That twenty centuries of stony sleep Were vexed to nightmare by a rocking cradle, And what rough beast, its hour come round at last, Slouches towards Bethlehem to be born? First published in The Dial, November 1920. This text is from Michael Robartes and the Dancer (Cuala Press), transcribed from Wikisource's scan-backed text — see it there. W. B. Yeats died in 1939, so the poem is out of copyright everywhere. 1918 · first published in Poems (1918), edited by Robert Bridges
MIND FOUND TO CONTAIN CLIFFS; NO RAILING FITTED

The most exact description of despair anybody has managed, sat in a friend's desk for twenty-nine years before it was printed. No worst, there is none by Gerard Manley Hopkins, who died in 1889 — which is why the whole of it can be printed here
poem-no-worst
No worst, there is none

Gerard Manley Hopkins · 1918 No worst, there is none. Pitched past pitch of grief, More pangs will, schooled at forepangs, wilder wring. Comforter, where, where is your comforting? Mary, mother of us, where is your relief? My cries heave, herds-long; huddle in a main, a chief Woe, world-sorrow; on an age-old anvil wince and sing— Then lull, then leave off. Fury had shrieked 'No ling- ering! Let me be fell: force I must be brief'. O the mind, mind has mountains; cliffs of fall Frightful, sheer, no-man-fathomed. Hold them cheap May who ne'er hung there. Nor does long our small Durance deal with that steep or deep. Here! creep, Wretch, under a comfort serves in a whirlwind: all Life death does end and each day dies with sleep. First published in Poems (1918), edited by Robert Bridges. This text is from Bridges' first edition, transcribed from Wikisource's scan-backed text — see it there. Gerard Manley Hopkins died in 1889, so the poem is out of copyright everywhere. 1898 · first published in Wessex Poems and Other Verses (1898)
SUN GOES WHITE OVER POND; NOTHING SALVAGEABLE

Dated 1867 under its own last line and left in a drawer for thirty-one years, which is its own kind of news. Neutral Tones by Thomas Hardy, who died in 1928 — which is why the whole of it can be printed here
poem-neutral-tones
Neutral Tones

Thomas Hardy · 1898 We stood by a pond that winter day, And the sun was white, as though chidden of God, And a few leaves lay on the starving sod, —They had fallen from an ash, and were gray. Your eyes on me were as eyes that rove Over tedious riddles solved years ago: And some words played between us to and fro— On which lost the more by our love. The smile on your mouth was the deadest thing Alive enough to have strength to die; And a grin of bitterness swept thereby Like an ominous bird a-wing. . . . Since then, keen lessons that love deceives, And wrings with wrong, have shaped to me Your face, and the God-curst sun, and a tree, And a pond edged with grayish leaves.
