Thomas Hardy died in 1928, so the poem is out of copyright everywhere. 1890 · first published in Poems (1890), edited by Mabel Loomis Todd and T. W. Higginson, printed there as “The Chariot”
LOCAL WOMAN ACCEPTS LIFT FROM STRANGER, ARRIVES CENTURIES LATE

Published four years after she died by editors who retitled it, tidied her punctuation and left a stanza out. This is their version; the missing stanza is the one with the gossamer gown. Because I could not stop for Death by Emily Dickinson, who died in 1886 — which is why the whole of it can be printed here
poem-stop-for-death
Because I could not stop for Death

Emily Dickinson · 1890 Because I could not stop for Death, He kindly stopped for me; The carriage held but just ourselves And Immortality. We slowly drove, he knew no haste, And I had put away My labor, and my leisure too, For his civility. We passed the school where children played, Their lessons scarcely done; We passed the fields of gazing grain, We passed the setting sun. We paused before a house that seemed A swelling of the ground; The roof was scarcely visible, The cornice but a mound. Since then 't is centuries; but each Feels shorter than the day I first surmised the horses' heads Were toward eternity. First published in Poems (1890), edited by Mabel Loomis Todd and T. W. Higginson, printed there as “The Chariot”. This text is from the 1890 first printing, transcribed from Wikisource's scan-backed text — see it there. Emily Dickinson died in 1886, so the poem is out of copyright everywhere. 1867 · first published in New Poems (1867)
TIDE OF FAITH REPORTED GOING OUT; NO REPLACEMENT SCHEDULED
Filed from a hotel window on the Kent coast. Begins calm and ends on a beach with armies on it. Dover Beach by Matthew Arnold, who died in 1888 — which is why the whole of it can be printed here
poem-dover-beach
Dover Beach

Matthew Arnold · 1867 The sea is calm to-night. The tide is full, the moon lies fair Upon the straits; on the French coast, the light Gleams and is gone; the cliffs of England stand, Glimmering and vast, out in the tranquil bay. Come to the window, sweet is the night-air! Only, from the long line of spray Where the sea meets the moon-blanched sand, Listen! you hear the grating roar Of pebbles which the waves draw back, and fling, At their return, up the high strand, Begin and cease, and then again begin, With tremulous cadence slow, and bring The eternal note of sadness in. Sophocles long ago Heard it on the Ægean, and it brought Into his mind the turbid ebb and flow Of human misery: we Find also in the sound a thought, Hearing it by this distant northern sea. The sea of faith Was once, too, at the full, and round earth's shore Lay like the folds of a bright girdle furled. But now I only hear Its melancholy, long, withdrawing roar, Retreating, to the breath Of the night-wind, down the vast edges drear And naked shingles of the world. Ah, love, let us be true To one another! for the world, which seems To lie before us like a land of dreams, So various, so beautiful, so new, Hath really neither joy, nor love, nor light, Nor certitude, nor peace, nor help for pain; And we are here as on a darkling plain Swept with confused alarms of struggle and flight, Where ignorant armies clash by night. WIND OUT OF A CLOUD BLAMED; WIDOWER STILL SLEEPING IN THE TOMB

Printed two days after the poet's own death, in the same paper that ran his obituary. No editor could have arranged that. Annabel Lee by Edgar Allan Poe, who died in 1849 — which is why the whole of it can be printed here
poem-annabel-lee
Annabel Lee

Edgar Allan Poe · 1849 It was many and many a year ago, In a kingdom by the sea, That a maiden there lived whom you may know By the name of Annabel Lee; And this maiden she lived with no other thought Than to love and be loved by me. I was a child and she was a child, In this kingdom by the sea: But we loved with a love that was more than love— I and my Annabel Lee; With a love that the winged seraphs of heaven Coveted her and me. And this was the reason that, long ago, In this kingdom by the sea, A wind blew out of a cloud, chilling My beautiful Annabel Lee; So that her highborn kinsman came And bore her away from me, To shut her up in a sepulchre In this kingdom by the sea. The angels, not half so happy in heaven, Went envying her and me— Yes!—that was the reason (as all men know, In this kingdom by the sea) That the wind came out of the cloud by night, Chilling and killing my Annabel Lee. But our love it was stronger by far than the love Of those who were older than we— Of many far wiser than we— And neither the angels in heaven above, Nor the demons down under the sea, Can ever dissever my soul from the soul Of the beautiful Annabel Lee: For the moon never beams, without bringing me dreams Of the beautiful Annabel Lee; And the stars never rise, but I feel the bright eyes Of the beautiful Annabel Lee; And so, all the night-tide, I lie down by the side Of my darling—my darling—my life and my bride, In the sepulchre there by the sea, In her tomb by the sounding sea. KING OF KINGS' WORKS REVIEWED; NOTHING BESIDE REMAINS
Filed to a weekly paper under a pen name. The pen name is forgotten and the pedestal is not. Ozymandias by Percy Bysshe Shelley, who died in 1822 — which is why the whole of it can be printed here
poem-ozymandias
Ozymandias

Percy Bysshe Shelley · 1818 I met a Traveller from an antique land, Who said, “Two vast and trunkless legs of stone Stand in the desart. Near them, on the sand, Half sunk, a shattered visage lies, whose frown, And wrinkled lip, and sneer of cold command, Tell that its sculptor well those passions read, Which yet survive, stamped on these lifeless things, The hand that mocked them, and the heart that fed: And on the pedestal these words appear: “My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings.” Look on my works ye Mighty, and despair! No thing beside remains. Round the decay Of that Colossal Wreck, boundless and bare, The lone and level sands stretch far away. First published in The Examiner, 11 January 1818, signed “Glirastes”. SUN EXTINGUISHED; SURVIVORS BURN THE FURNITURE, THEN EACH OTHER

Written in the year without a summer, when a volcano on the other side of the world took the weather away and nobody yet knew why. Darkness by George Gordon, Lord Byron, who died in 1824 — which is why the whole of it can be printed here
poem-darkness
Darkness

George Gordon, Lord Byron · 1816 I had a dream, which was not all a dream. The bright sun was extinguished, and the stars Did wander darkling in the eternal space, Rayless, and pathless, and the icy Earth Swung blind and blackening in the moonless air; Morn came and went—and came, and brought no day, And men forgot their passions in the dread Of this their desolation; and all hearts Were chilled into a selfish prayer for light: And they did live by watchfires—and the thrones, The palaces of crownéd kings—the huts, The habitations of all things which dwell, Were burnt for beacons; cities were consumed, And men were gathered round their blazing homes To look once more into each other's face; Happy were those who dwelt within the eye Of the volcanos, and their mountain-torch: A fearful hope was all the World contained; Forests were set on fire—but hour by hour They fell and faded—and the crackling trunks Extinguished with a crash—and all was black. The brows of men by the despairing light Wore an unearthly aspect, as by fits The flashes fell upon them; some lay down And hid their eyes and wept; and some did rest Their chins upon their clenchéd hands, and smiled; And others hurried to and fro, and fed Their funeral piles with fuel, and looked up With mad disquietude on the dull sky, The pall of a past World; and then again With curses cast them down upon the dust, And gnashed their teeth and howled: the wild birds shrieked, And, terrified, did flutter on the ground, And flap their useless wings; the wildest brutes Came tame and tremulous; and vipers crawled And twined themselves among the multitude, Hissing, but stingless—they were slain for food: And War, which for a moment was no more, Did glut himself again:—a meal was bought With blood, and each sate sullenly apart Gorging himself in gloom: no Love was left; All earth was but one thought—and that was Death, Immediate and inglorious; and the pang Of famine fed upon all entrails—men Died, and their bones were tombless as their flesh; The meagre by the meagre were devoured, Even dogs assailed their masters, all save one, And he was faithful to a corse, and kept The birds and beasts and famished men at bay, Till hunger clung them, or the dropping dead Lured their lank jaws; himself sought out no food, But with a piteous and perpetual moan, And a quick desolate cry, licking the hand Which answered not with a caress—he died. The crowd was famished by degrees; but two Of an enormous city did survive, And they were enemies: they met beside The dying embers of an altar-place Where had been heaped a mass of holy things For an unholy usage; they raked up, And shivering scraped with their cold skeleton hands The feeble ashes, and their feeble breath Blew for a little life, and made a flame Which was a mockery; then they lifted up Their eyes as it grew lighter, and beheld Each other's aspects—saw, and shrieked, and died— Even of their mutual hideousness they died, Unknowing who he was upon whose brow Famine had written Fiend. The World was void, The populous and the powerful was a lump, Seasonless, herbless, treeless, manless, lifeless— A lump of death—a chaos of hard clay. The rivers, lakes, and ocean all stood still, And nothing stirred within their silent depths; Ships sailorless lay rotting on the sea, And their masts fell down piecemeal: as they dropped They slept on the abyss without a surge— The waves were dead; the tides were in their grave, The Moon, their mistress, had expired before; The winds were withered in the stagnant air, And the clouds perished; Darkness had no need Of aid from them—She was the Universe. Chartered street, chartered river. The word turns up twice and means the opposite of free both times. London by William Blake, who died in 1827 — which is why the whole of it can be printed here

London

William Blake · 1794 I wander thro' each charter'd street, Near where the charter'd Thames does flow, And mark in every face I meet, Marks of weakness, marks of woe. In every cry of every Man, In every Infant’s cry of fear, In every voice, in every ban, The mind-forg'd manacles I hear. How the Chimney-sweeper’s cry Every black'ning Church appalls; And the hapless Soldier’s sigh Runs in blood down Palace walls. But most, thro' midnight streets I hear How the youthful Harlot’s curse Blasts the new born Infant’s tear, And blights with plagues the Marriage hearse. First published in Songs of Experience (1794). Printed two years after the poet died, which he would have enjoyed. Ends by telling death that death is the one who dies. Death be not proud by John Donne, who died in 1631 — which is why the whole of it can be printed here
poem-death-be-not-proud
Death be not proud

John Donne · 1633 Death be not proud, though some have callèd thee Mighty and dreadfull, for, thou art not so, For, those, whom thou think'st, thou dost overthrow, Die not, poore death, nor yet canst thou kill me. From rest and sleepe, which but thy pictures bee, Much pleasure, then from thee, much more must flow, And soonest our best men with thee doe goe, Rest of their bones, and soules deliverie. Thou art slave to Fate, Chance, kings, and desperate men, And dost with poyson, warre, and sicknesse dwell, And poppie, or charmes can make us sleepe as well, And better than thy stroake; why swell'st thou then; One short sleepe past, wee wake eternally, And death shall be no more, death, thou shalt die. The oldest thing on this scroll and the only one still in its own spelling — including the quarto's famous slip, “Bare rn'wd quiers”, which editors since have read as bare ruin'd choirs. Sonnet 73 by William Shakespeare, who died in 1616 — which is why the whole of it can be printed here
poem-sonnet-73
Sonnet 73

William Shakespeare · 1609 That time of yeeare thou maist in me behold, When yellow leaues, or none, or few doe hange Vpon those boughes which shake against the could, Bare rn'wd quiers, where late the sweet birds sang. In me thou seest the twi-light of such day, As after Sun-set fadeth in the West, Which by and by blacke night doth take away, Deaths second selfe that seals vp all in rest. In me thou seest the glowing of such fire, That on the ashes of his youth doth lye, As the death bed, whereon it must expire, Consum'd with that which it was nurrisht by. This thou perceu'st, which makes thy loue more strong, To loue that well, which thou must leaue ere long. First published in Shake-speares Sonnets (1609). That is the bottom of the scroll. Three hundred and eleven years of it, and thirteen items. Not one of them was a notification. Every text was transcribed from Wikisource and every item names the printing it came from, because these poems exist in several and they differ — which is why The Darkling Thrush is not on here at all. Wikisource’s page for it names no printing and says so itself, and a text nobody can trace is the one thing a scroll built out of dates cannot carry. The headlines and the lines under them are ours and are meant to be funny; the poems are not ours and are not. The Mopery is back up the stairs, and the street is past that. It is very loud out there. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. There is no ambient layer on this scroll at any setting. Paper does not move, and a feed that moved by itself is the thing this room is a joke about. Liner notes · Changelog · a Stimpunks Foundation street.

The Adventurer’s Guild

Job board Hints at every job No score kept Rooms: all of them Somebody has come onto this street and filed everything. Ruled boxes, square corners, a class in the margin, a stamp for a job that is done. It is the only tidy room here and it is tidy the way a form is tidy, which on a street whose whole architecture is that nothing matches is the strangest thing anybody could have built. Every job below sends you to a marker standing in one of the rooms — a small drawing of something lying about in there, drawn in that room’s own colours, because no two rooms on this street look alike and neither do their markers. Open the marker and it gives you a quest code. Bring the code back here. Hand in a quest code Spaces and capitals do not matter. If you followed a link from a marker the code is already in the box — press the button when you are ready, because pressing it is the only thing that makes a noise. Quest code Your browser is not letting this page store anything, so stamps will not survive you leaving. Everything still works; it just will not be here when you come back. Nothing about this is kept anywhere but your own browser in the first place.
House rules

Nothing here is scored. No total, no percentage, no streak, no rank you climb, and nothing that expires. The board stamps a job when you hand its code in and that is the entire bookkeeping. One job is a perfectly good number of jobs to do. The difficulty class is how far you walk. I is on the street, II is through a door off another room, III is off the street altogether — the field past the treeline at one end, the road past the last streetlight at the other, or the caverns underneath. It says nothing whatever about the person doing it, which is why it is measured in doors. Every job has hints, and some have a question. A question is answered by a sentence already published on the page you are standing on — that is the point of asking. The hints are at the job, the question’s own hints are at the marker, and every question has a “give me the answer” way out. Taking it is a real way through this and not a lesser one. The fanfare does what the dial says, and the words never change. At Gentle handing a code in says its piece and does nothing else. At Regular it chimes. At MAX GLITTER it chimes properly and throws sparks up the page. You get the same sentences at all three. Nothing in here flashes or strobes, at any setting. That is Club Chronic’s rule, and it holds everywhere on this street except in one room: the Rebellion Rave Room has a strobe, and it is off until you switch it on and say yes. The markers are not hidden. They are quiet, which is a different thing: every one is a full-size control in the tab order with a real name on it, and every one opens without JavaScript. A secret only a sighted mouse user can find is not a secret.

Swaying Sweetgrass There is a firefly low in the grass at pitch 02. That room points at a book it will not play for you, and it will want you to know why before it lets the firefly go. Takes three minutes, and some reading · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is not on the street. Go out past the treeline to the campgrounds first. Hint 2 It is pitch 02, the meadow with the path through it. Where exactly it is Low in the grass at the very bottom of the meadow, below the clearing. That room also carries a correction to our own glossary near the top rather than in a footnote: two of our entries attribute a phrase to Barry Lopez that he never wrote. When two of our own pages disagree, the one that checked wins. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
The fourth learning space

The Solarpunk Hermitage There is a sunflower head drying on a hook outside the hermitage at pitch 03. Three of the four primordial learning spaces are laid out inside that cabin. The fourth is not in there, and the room will tell you where it is. Takes three minutes, and some reading · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is not on the street. Go out past the treeline to the campgrounds first. Hint 2 It is pitch 03, the cabin on wheels with the panels on the roof. Where exactly it is At the very bottom of the page, below the last of the cabin. It is the only room on this street lit by morning. Every other world here is a dark ground with light applied to it; a cabin that runs on the sun and reads as midnight would be an argument against itself. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
Who lit the woodland tea room?

Brew and Stew There is a tea room in a cabin on the Campgrounds, at the edge of the trees, and there is no flame in it anywhere. Go and sit in it, and come back with what gives it its light. Takes three minutes, and a pot of tea if you want one · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is not on the street. Go out past the treeline to the campgrounds first. Hint 2 Pitch 04 on the board, the cabin with its window dark. Where exactly it is On the floor of the room, before the sign-off. Nobody lit it: the light grows in the cabin's own wood, a pale glow in the joints between the logs, in the moss and in the little mushrooms at the foot of the walls, and the stove is shut iron, giving the room its warmth and none of its light. Difficulty class Ion the street
The two habits that survived

The Liner Notes There is a colophon mark at the foot of the liner notes. This street dropped most of the care its sibling sites run on and kept exactly two things. Name the one that is not contrast. Takes two minutes, and some reading · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is one of the pages linked from the pavement at the foot of the street. Hint 2 Go to the very bottom of the credits. Where exactly it is At the very bottom of the page, below the last credit. Contrast survived for a reason that is not the obvious one. This is a Disabled people's organisation, and a glitter-maximalist site that excluded the people it is for would be a self-own of exactly the kind we exist to name. The fix was never to tone it down — it was the dial. Difficulty class Ion the street
What a spider's best answer is

The Garden Somebody has dropped a blank plant label on the path in the garden, which is through the gate in the wall between two of the shopfronts. Pick it up. While you are in there, settle what that room says the garden spider is for, because it is careful about it and the sentence is worth carrying back out with you. Takes two or three minutes, most of it one paragraph · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is not behind a shopfront. There is a gate in the wall between two of them, down past the noticeboard. Hint 2 Through the gate is the garden, where every bed is one of the other sites we publish. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the garden, on the path below the hedge and the dial. A glossary exists to give somebody a word for an experience that usually goes unnamed, and a tool that can route them from the experience to the word is doing that job one step earlier. What it must never do is stand in for the page at the other end, which is why that room says out loud that it can be wrong and links the ethics pages where we hold the line. Difficulty class Ion the street
Which printing it was

The Zibaldone There is a shopfront on the street with a commonplace book left open on the desk in it. A nib has been put down beside the book. Pick it up, and while you are there settle the question the whole room turns on: one of the quotations in that book had to be traced to a particular printing before it could go in, because the obvious guess was wrong. Takes two or three minutes, most of it one list · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is a shopfront on the street, with the only pale window in the row. Hint 2 The book is open on a desk, and the nib is down at the foot of the page. Where exactly it is Below the attribution slip, at the bottom of the room. Naming the printing is not pedantry, it is the difference between quoting somebody and quoting somebody's editor. A quotation that names only its title cannot be checked by anybody, which is how a misquotation travels for a century in perfectly good faith. Difficulty class Ion the street
The words are not in the hole

The Rabbit Hole There is a shaft at the end of the street with seven recordings hanging in it, all of them of one song or of the record that song came out of. Go down it and count the lyrics. Takes a couple of minutes, and longer if you press something · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is a storefront on the street, not behind another room. Hint 2 The marker is on the wall of the shaft like everything else in there — keep going down past the engravings, the presses and the trail. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the page, under the dial. A room can carry a recording without carrying the words to it, and the difference is a legal one rather than a matter of taste. It is also the one place on this street where a room deliberately does less than the page it was built from. Difficulty class Ion the street
What the server says instead of no

The Healing Checkpoint There is a save room on the street with a bed in it and no monsters. It is numbered after an HTTP status code, and that status code has a companion that turns a refusal into a time. Go and find out what the companion is called. Takes a couple of minutes, and as long as you like after that · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is a storefront on the street, not behind another room — although there is also a back stair up to it from this board. Hint 2 The room explains its own number in a section of its own. The answer is a header name, and it is printed in bold there. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the page, under the dial. A status code can be a kindness. 429 is the one thing a computer says that blames a rate rather than a person, and the header beside it turns a no into a when — which is most of what anybody at capacity is actually trying to say. Difficulty class Ion the street
The letter that is a hole

The Foundry There is a type foundry on the street. Its own nameplate is set in a face that is not drawn the way the others are, and the room explains what it is instead. Go and read the two paragraphs about it. Takes a few minutes, and a long time after that if you start pulling proofs · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 A shopfront on the street, between the save room and the empty one. Hint 2 The room has a short section about its own display face, under the bench and the proof. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the page, under the dial. A letterform can be shaped by what it is cut into rather than by what anybody wanted it to look like. The bridges across a stencil are not styling: they are the only thing holding the middle of the letter in. Difficulty class Ion the street
The joke in the street's own name

Danny the Street This street is named after somebody and the name is a pun in two languages. There is a page about it, reached from a line under the dial on the front page rather than through any door. Go and find out who the joke is about. Takes five minutes, or twenty if you read the whole history · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 Not behind a door. It is linked from the front page, in the paragraph under the loudness dial. Hint 2 The page has a section called Where Danny came from, and the answer is in the paragraph that begins with the word pun. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the page, under the dial. The street you are standing on is named after a drag performer by way of a French pun, which means the architecture of this site — rooms that refuse to match, and a street that rearranges itself for whoever turns up — was somebody else's idea first and is credited rather than quietly absorbed. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
The far end of the street

The Outskirts The street has two edges. Everybody finds the field past the treeline; far fewer walk the other way, out past the last streetlight, where the kerb gives up and becomes a verge. Go and read the road, and find out what is actually lighting it. Takes five minutes, and there is nothing to press · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is not on the street. Leave by the far end rather than the treeline end — the link is under the shopfronts, past the noticeboard and the gate. Hint 2 The answer is in the list at the top of the road, in the item about how far you can see. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the road, under the section about the unlit signs. The street has an edge at each end and they are not the same kind of edge — a field you walk into at one, a road you drive out of at the other — which is also why the guild's class III stopped saying past the treeline and started naming both. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
What the band did without

Black Leather Lagoon Down the first turning off The Outskirts there is a drive-in screen standing in black water, and an appreciation of the band it is named after. That appreciation makes a point of something the band deliberately did not have, for years, on purpose. Go and find out what. Takes ten minutes, or an hour if you start pressing the records · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is off the street — out past the last streetlight, then the first turning. Hint 2 The answer is in the appreciation at the top, in the short paragraph that is entirely about a thing that was missing. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the rack of records. A band can remove the part everybody treats as structural and keep going for thirty years, and the missing piece becomes the sound rather than a fault in it. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
The tree nobody will cut

Sithen Second turning off the road out of town there is a ring of earth standing in a field, and one kind of tree growing on it that people across a whole country decline to touch. A motorway was moved rather than fell one. Go and find out which tree. Takes ten minutes, and there is nothing to press out there · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is off the street — past the last streetlight, then the second turning. Hint 2 The answer is in the documented half of the page, the part about earthworks rather than the part about rules. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the section about why the door is not opened. There is a tree in Ireland that a motorway was routed around, and the paperwork for that accommodation was a shrug — which is worth holding next to what is usually asked of a Disabled person before anything gets moved. Difficulty class Ion the street
Counsel, not commandment

Covenstead There is a kitchen on this street with the good china out and not one cup matching the next. One of the things laid on that table is famous, and the word at the front of it is the whole reason it never hardened into a rule. Go and find out what that word means. Takes ten minutes, and the kettle is already on · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts — the one with the pale window. Hint 2 It is the second thing on the table, the one first recorded publicly in 1964. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the section about whose these all are. The best-known line of a living religious tradition is phrased as advice rather than as an order, and has stayed that way — which is a rarer thing than it sounds if you have spent much time being handed rules that were described to you as guidance. Difficulty class Ion the street
The desks are for sitting at

Dead Tired Society There is a room on this street with the big lights off and the door wedged ajar, where a society of the burnt out meets on the floor. Its standing orders have something to say about the desks. Go and find out who stands on them. Takes five minutes, lying down if you like · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts — the dark one with a sliver of light in its awning. Hint 2 The standing orders are near the top of the room, just under the drawing of the doorway. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the section about whose these are, where the door would swing. A room can make a point of what it will not ask you to do. That one will not ask anybody to stand up — for themselves, for the room, or on a desk — and passing, there, is a whole turn. Difficulty class Ion the street
Who ordered?

Laughingstock There is a comedy club on the street, down a ramp rather than a flight of stairs, where the only thing standing in the spotlight is what the comics said. One of them was at a restaurant when the server asked his friend what he would have. Go and find out what the friend said. Takes five minutes, or a full hour if you stay for a special · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts — the one with a neon sign in the window. Hint 2 Josh Blue’s lines are in the spotlight near the top of the room, under his name. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the dial, where a set list would be taped down. Talk to the comic, not to whoever came in with them — which is one of that club’s house rules, and a good one for anywhere with tables in it. Difficulty class Ion the street
Where the attention goes

The Lightbulb Picture House There is a picture house on the street where the house lights never go down, and one of the films on its rack draws autistic attention as something out in space. Go and find out what. Takes five minutes, or four more if you watch the film · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts — the one with a row of warm bulbs in its awning. Hint 2 It is on the first rack, between Screen One and Screen Two, and the film is the one about monotropism. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the picture house, under the dial, where somebody left them on a seat. Attention that goes deep takes time to come back from. That is monotropism, and it is why a relaxed screening lets you walk in late and leave early. Difficulty class Ion the street
Same again

Samefood Cafe There is a café on the street whose kitchen knows its regulars, and whose specials line says what today’s special is — for everybody who walks in. Go and read it. Takes as long as a cup of coffee, the same cup as last time · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts — the pale one whose awning is a tray of little wells. Hint 2 The specials line is right under the café’s name, above the drawing of the table. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the café, under the section about whose these are, where something slipped off a tray. A special does not have to be one dish for everybody. A café can default to the same thing every time and still make it a different thing for every guest, because it knows its regulars — and for a great many of us the same again is how eating becomes possible at all. Difficulty class Ion the street
The question nobody asks

The Collection Collection There is a dark gallery on the street full of other people’s collections, each under a lamp of its own, and its house rules say there is one question nobody in there will ever ask you about yours. Go and find out which. Takes as long as it takes to walk past a row of cabinets without counting them · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts — the dark one whose awning is a row of unlit bays. Hint 2 The house rules are further down the gallery, after the cabinets. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the gallery, under the section about whose these are, where a label has come loose. A collection does not have to be counted to count. The gallery shows what people keep, lit the way they choose, with no totals, no prices and no ranking — because a number beside somebody’s things turns something they love into an inventory. Difficulty class Ion the street
Say it plainly

Vital Plant Living There is a kitchen on the street whose name over the door is a translation, and the room says so near the top. Go and find out what the old name's first word comes from. Takes about as long as it takes to read a menu board · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the turmeric one whose awning is a row of pots. Hint 2 Near the top of the kitchen, under the lede, there is a panel about where its name comes from. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the kitchen, under the section about whose these are, where something fell off the shelf over the counter. A name can be a translation and say so. Borrowing a word from somebody's faith for a menu that does not keep it would be a claim about the food; saying what the word means in plain English, and crediting where it came from, is the honest version. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
What the rocks give back

Looming Rocks Amphitheatre Third turning off the road out of town there is an open-air stage with something enormous on either side of it, and a lighting rig that points the wrong way. The rocks glow after dark. Go and find out what is actually doing the glowing, and which half of that story the room admits it made up. Takes ten minutes to read, or nine hours if you press everything · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 Off the street — past the last streetlight, then the third turning. Hint 2 It is in the section about what the rocks are, in the paragraph that begins by saying which half is real. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the section about whose all this is. A real property of a living thing is doing the work that looks most like special effects — and the room is careful to say which half of its own story is invented, which is the same care the herbarium two areas over takes about naming a plant. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
Who holds the volume

Dance, Punks Fourth turning off the road out of town there is a crowd dancing on an old airstrip, and not one sound of it reaches the verge. Go and find out who decides how loud it is. Takes ten minutes, and nothing plays unless you put a headset on · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 Off the street — past the last streetlight, then the fourth turning. Hint 2 It is in the section about why the room is silent, near the top. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the part about whose all this is. A loud room is an access barrier, and one way round it is to give every person in the crowd their own volume — which is what the dial on every page here is for, too. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
What the clock is missing

The Small Hours Fifth turning off the road out of town there is a diner with every light on, at an hour when everything else is shut. Something is missing from the clock over its counter. Go and find out what, and why nobody in there minds. Takes ten minutes, and there is nothing to press · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 Off the street — past the last streetlight, then the fifth turning. Hint 2 It is in the heading of the first window you come to. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the part about whose all this is. Crip time bends the clock to meet the body rather than the body to meet the clock — and some of us are simply awake when the town is not. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
What a repeater does

The Repeater Sixth turning off the road out of town, a track goes up to a ridge with a mast on it and nothing lit but two red lamps. Go and find out what the thing on the ridge does with a signal it hears. Takes ten minutes, or as long as you like with the line open · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 Off the street — past the last streetlight, then the sixth turning, and up the track. Hint 2 It is in the second paragraph at the top of the room. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the part about whose all this is. Far off is not the same as cut off. Signal is a mode of connection in its own right, and no mode sits at the top. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
Not charity

Nothing For Sale Seventh turning off the road out of town there is a lay-by with a ring of cars in it, headlights on, and tables in the middle with everything on them free. Go and find out what the room says it is instead of. Takes ten minutes, and there is nothing to press · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 Off the street — past the last streetlight, then the seventh turning. Hint 2 It is the first heading in the room. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the part about whose all this is. Mutual aid goes sideways and charity comes down. Solidarity, not charity, and no proof of worthiness required. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
Under the street

Arlesglad Caverns The street has an edge at each end, and a third one that is not at either end: straight down, by the lift by the stoop or the stair beside it. Go down and read the caverns, and find out what is doing the lighting. Takes five minutes, and there is nothing to press · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is not on the street and not past either end of it. Look for the way down, under the shopfronts with the other things that are not doors. Hint 2 The answer is in the list called What is down here, in the item about light. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the caverns, under the section about where the name comes from. The street has three edges now and only two of them are at an end of it. The caverns are the one you reach by going down, which is also why the guild's class III names all three rather than growing a fourth class for the one that is underneath. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
The dark shop

Glow Go Gee Gaws Three floors down in the caverns there is a shop full of glow-in-the-dark toys, every one of them dark until you give it some light. Charge them, and find out which colour lasts longest. Takes five minutes, and a toy or two to hold up to the rail if you want · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is under the street. Take the lift down to the caverns and look for level B3. Hint 2 The answer is in the section called How long a glow lasts. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the shop, under the credit line. A glow-in-the-dark toy does not make light. It keeps some of the light you give it and hands it back, slowly, which is the only light on this street that runs down after you press. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
Where the knob stops

Rebellion Rave Room Out past the last streetlight, an old hangar by the airstrip has the only strobe on the street. Read the walls in the ante-chamber before you go in, and find out how far it goes. Takes five minutes, and nothing needs switching on · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is off The Outskirts, past the last streetlight. Look for turning 08. Hint 2 The answer is on the strobe and laser warning, in the ante-chamber. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the hangar, under Whose this all is. The one room on the street with a strobe in it relaxes a rule by holding the opt-in harder than anywhere else: off on every visit, two presses to start it, and Escape stops everything at once. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
What the machine takes

The Cooldown Room Beside the rave's ante-chamber there is a small soft room with a vending machine along one wall. Go and sit down in it for a minute, and find out what the machine takes. Takes a minute, and a couch · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is through the other door in the Rebellion Rave Room's ante-chamber, off The Outskirts. Hint 2 The answer is in the section called The machine. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under Whose this all is. A free vending machine does the one thing it was never built for. Taking from it puts nobody in anybody's debt. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
The cellar at the top of the lift

Big Steep Fermentables One floor down under the street there is a cellar with house styles of beer, wine and kombucha. Read how the pours are set out, and find out which one comes first. Takes five minutes, and there is nothing to press or to drink · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is under the street. Take the lift down to the caverns; this is the first level. Hint 2 The answer is in the introduction to Try our house styles. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the cellar, under the credit line. Every pour on this street says how strong it is before you take it, the same way every button says how long it runs before you press it. The number is what lets somebody decide. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
The farm under the street

Mycelium Munchies Two floors down in the caverns there is a mushroom farm with a restaurant at the end of it. Read why it is there, and find out what happens to the blocks the mushrooms grew on once they are finished. Takes five minutes, and there is nothing to press · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is under the street. Take the lift down to the caverns and look for level B2. Hint 2 The answer is in the section called Why a mushroom farm. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the credit line. A mushroom is the fruit and not the thing that grows. The part doing the work is the mycelium, the part nobody sees on a plate, which is a fair description of most of the work on this street. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
The bottom of the caverns

Stay Frosty Go all the way down: past every level of the caverns to the one at the bottom, where the temperature stops moving. Read the room's rules, and find out what the dial on the page does down there. Takes five minutes, and there is nothing to press · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is under the street. Take the lift by the stoop down to the caverns, and then go to the bottom of its panel. Hint 2 The answer is in the list called What never changes in here. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the credit line. The dial is the street's promise that loudness is yours to hold. In a room with nothing loud in it, the promise is kept by there being nothing to turn down, which is the one setting where Gentle, Regular and MAX look exactly the same. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
Behind the quiet room

Stay Breezy At the very bottom of the caverns there is a room where nothing moves, and a door at the back of it. Go through, and read the house rules of the room full of fans. Takes five minutes, and you can do it without switching a single fan on · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is under the street. Take the lift down to the caverns, go to the bottom, and look for the door at the back of the quiet room. Hint 2 The answer is in the house rules, in the one about the ceiling fans. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the credit line. The loudest room in the caverns and the quietest one share a wall, and both keep the same promise from opposite ends: nothing flashes, and nothing happens to you that you did not switch on. Difficulty class Ion the street
The door the radio waits outside

Community Center There is a radio on this street that follows you from room to room once you have switched it on. There is one door it will not go through. Find out which, and why. Takes about as long as it takes to read a noticeboard · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the powder-blue one with its blinds half down. Hint 2 Inside, under the front desk, there is a list of how the radio works. The last thing on it is a room. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the hall, under the section about whose this is, where something fell off the letterboard. A room's promise about itself holds even against the street's own furniture. The Healing Checkpoint says it writes nothing down about you, so the radio that remembers where you put it waits outside, rather than the room's promise being quietly narrowed to fit the radio. Difficulty class Ion the street
What the middle of the building is open to

Town Hall There is a town hall on the street, a round hall with rooms off it. Go in and find out what the top of its dome is open to. Takes about as long as it takes to look up · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street, in the row of shopfronts: the one with a round hole in its roof. Hint 2 Read the lede, and the section headed Why a hole in the roof. Where exactly it is The gavel is on the floor at the foot of the hall, before the sign-off. A private room and a public record are two different things, and a building can have a place for each: doors round the wall for what has to stay in the room, and the middle open to the sky. Difficulty class IIthrough a door
The seat nobody sits in

The Fishbowl Through a door off the Town Hall there is a fishbowl on a sunny sill. Go and find out what the circle in the middle always keeps. Takes about as long as it takes to feed a fish · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 Go into the Town Hall on the street, and through the Fishbowl's door. Hint 2 Read How a fishbowl goes. Where exactly it is The flake is on the sill at the foot of the room, before the sign-off. A conversation stays open when there is always room to come in. The fishbowl keeps one seat in the middle empty, and whoever takes it is joined by somebody else stepping back out. Difficulty class IIthrough a door
How the light gets in

Directors Through a door off the Town Hall there is a room for Stimpunks' directors, with no lamp in it. Go and find out what the light comes through. Takes about as long as it takes to read a name backwards · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 Go into the Town Hall on the street, and through the Directors' door. Hint 2 Read Why frosted glass. Where exactly it is The key is on the floor at the foot of the room, before the sign-off. A room can be private without being hidden. The door is not locked, the directors' names are on the wall, and the glass lets the light through while keeping the detail back. Difficulty class IIthrough a door
Whose lamp is biggest

Board Through a door off the Town Hall there is a room for Stimpunks' board, at one long table. Go and find out what every seat at it has in front of it. Takes about as long as it takes to count down a table · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 Go into the Town Hall on the street, and through the Board's door. Hint 2 Read Why a lamp at every seat. Where exactly it is The pencil is on the floor at the foot of the room, before the sign-off. A board is a table where every seat counts the same. Nobody's lamp is bigger, and there is no light over the head of the table. Difficulty class IIthrough a door
What lights the room that looks after the street

Moderators Through a door off the Town Hall there is a room for Stimpunks' moderators, above the street at night, with no lamp in it. Go and find out what it is lit by. Who made this noise

The trope is everybody’s and belongs to nobody; the rooms it points at are ours. This one sets Rye, a woodtype face for posted bills, and Public Sans, which was drawn for United States government forms — both under the SIL Open Font License, both credited with everything else in the liner notes. Nothing you do on this board leaves your own browser. The stamps have no account and no server behind them: they are a list of job names in your own local storage, and the button above throws them away. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so — and in here the dial decides how loudly a finished job is announced. It never changes what the board tells you.

The Feed

A board is set by somebody with a machine. It is a picture of the railway and it is not the railway. Stimpunks is not one site. There is the big one, and there are the small ones each built to take one kind of weight off it, and every one of them publishes an RSS feed nobody needs an account to read. This room is a hall of indicator boards, one wire per feed, showing what has most recently arrived on each; this street has two, its changelog and the Brass Tacks Board.
How this board is set, and what it will not do

It is a snapshot, and it is not pretending otherwise. None of these sites sends a browser the header that would let this page read its feed, so the page cannot fetch them — and the two ways round that are a proxy we do not run and a third-party reader we would be handing you to without asking. So a person runs a tool, the tool reads every feed, and the board is set. Every plate below carries the minute its own wire was read, and the hall carries the minute the whole board was set. Both of those numbers are generated from the same file the rows come out of, so neither can quietly go wrong while looking authoritative. A row is a name, a date and a destination. There are no summaries here, no excerpts and no first paragraphs. A departures board does not read you the contents of the train; it tells you where the train is going, and then you get on it. That is the metaphor and it is also the practical point — a room that pasted in everybody's opening lines would be republishing other people's writing onto one surface it does not own, which is the opposite of sending you to them. The tool that sets this board refuses a row carrying a summary field, because that edit is a friendly one and it will arrive: the rows look bare, somebody helpfully pastes the words back in, and the board has become a reader. Nothing here is ranked and no site's activity is added up. You will not find out from this room which of our sites has been getting on with it, because that is not a fact anybody here needs and a board that showed it would turn publishing into a race between our own people — most of whom are Disabled, several of whom are one person with a chronic illness, and all of whom publish at the speed their bodies allow. The running order is stimpunks.org's own, off the page where our sites are already collected by somebody deciding, and re-sorting it here by who was newest would be this room overruling a decision made somewhere else. Each wire names which feed it carries. Two of these sites publish more than one — a feed of the things themselves and a feed of the reasoning behind them — so “the latest from Star Stuff” is an ambiguous sentence, and a board that picked quietly between them would be answering a question you did not know it had been asked. Where there is a second feed, the plate says so and links it. And this street is on its own board. A room that listed every sibling and left itself off would be claiming to be the station rather than a platform in it, so stimpunks.world's changelog is read over the network like every other wire — which means this board can be out of date about this site too, and is.
Go and read them properly

Every wire above links its site and its feed. Put the feed in whatever reader you use and the arrivals come to you, on your own time, with no board in between and nothing here deciding what you see first. That is the better version of this room and we would rather you used it. stimpunks.org keeps a feeds page with the lot on it, including the socials, the repository commits and the bookmark archive, none of which is up here: a social post has no title, a commit is a different kind of thing from a published page, and a board that mixed all three would be a machine with three jobs.
Whose machine this is

The split-flap indicator board is Solari di Udine's machine — the flap boards that stood in railway stations and airports for decades, and the reason a certain clacking noise means something has changed to anybody over about thirty. This room is a picture of one drawn in CSS. It is not one of theirs, it is not affiliated with them, and it makes no noise at all. The sites on the board are Stimpunks Foundation's, several of them built with Helen Edgar of Autistic Realms, who is named here rather than folded into our “we”. Penguin Pebbling is hers and Ryan Boren's together. Every title on this board belongs to whoever wrote the page it points at, and this room holds none of their words — only their names, their dates and their doors. The credits are collected in the liner notes.
What moves in here

At Gentle the boards are simply already showing their words, which is what a board does for almost all of its life. At Regular each row settles once as the page arrives — one flap, downward, and then still. At MAX GLITTER they riffle on the way to settling, the way a real board runs through half the alphabet before it finds the letter it wants. Nothing in here flashes, strobes or pulses at any setting, and nothing makes a sound. The words on every row are identical at all three: the dial takes away the clatter, never the arrivals. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes or plays until you say so — and in here, MAX GLITTER is a board that riffles before it settles.

The Zibaldone

Somebody else already wrote it down. A commonplace book, left open on the desk. People copy lines into it — from poems, from books, from each other — and beside each one they write what it is for. Every line in here says where it came from and how we checked it, because a quotation nobody can trace is just a nice-sounding sentence with a famous name stuck on the end.
The word

Zibaldone is Italian, and it means roughly a heap of things — the name given to the miscellany notebooks Italians have kept since about the fourteenth century, of which Leopardi’s enormous one is the famous example. Merchants kept them. So did poets. They are unruled, unsorted and unfinished on purpose: recipes next to accounts next to a line of verse somebody liked. In English the same object is a commonplace book, which our own glossary has had an entry for since 2022. Montaigne kept one and more or less invented the essay out of it. Marcus Aurelius kept one and it turned into the Meditations. It is not a filing system. It is what you reach for when you cannot find your own words and somebody else’s will do. This room exists because somebody in our community asked for it: a quote bank, quotes for any state of mind. That is what this is. The desk and the rules are ours; the good lines are everybody’s.
What this book will and will not do

A bank of quotations is the most dangerous shape of page on this street, and not for any reason you would notice from the outside. So the rules are in the generator rather than in somebody’s good intentions, and they are written here so you can hold us to them. 30 words is the longest quotation this room will carry, and tools/make-zibaldone.py refuses a longer one rather than trusting anybody to remember. A bank of quotations is the shape of page that turns into republishing somebody’s book one reasonable-looking entry at a time. Where the line is not enough, the book is linked. No song lyrics. Music publishing enforces on quotation where prose publishing shrugs, the licensing is separate from the recording, and one line is a far larger fraction of a song than of a novel. Nothing musical is hosted anywhere on this street, and a quote bank is exactly where that promise would have been broken in the way that looked most harmless. The tool refuses a song; it is not left to care. Bring us the person talking about the song instead — that we can quote. Every line names its printing, not just its title. These texts differ between printings and a title is not a source. The Dickinson in this book is the proof: it is in the second series, not the first, and the only thing that found that out was going and looking. The Thoreau is the other proof — the version everybody quotes has somebody marching to a beat, and he wrote neither word. Every line says how it was checked, and when. The public domain ones were read out of the transcription named on the card. The contemporary ones were read off our own published pages. An unchecked quotation sitting among checked ones looking identical is the thing this room is built to prevent, so there is nowhere for one to hide. Nothing here is ranked, counted or voted on. No favourites, no most-copied, no top of the bank, no number on a card. A quote bank is the shape of thing that grows one, and this room will never grow a leaderboard — refusing one matters because a leaderboard would turn the one page meant to meet somebody where they are into a popularity contest between other people’s grief. There are no faces in this room. A quote bank for states of mind obviously wants a row of moods you pick from, and the obvious drawing for a mood is a face. A row of happy, sad and angry faces on a Disabled people’s site is the emotion flashcard that autistic people spend their childhoods being drilled with. So each card says what it is for in a sentence about a situation you might actually be in, and you read the ones that sound like your week. The quotations are set in type; only the margins are handwritten. The hand is for the keeper’s own asides. A passage set in a handwriting face is an access failure wearing atmosphere, so the tool refuses one.

The Rabbit Hole

You meant to look up one thing. Every other door on this street opens onto a room you can stand in. This one opens onto a shaft, and there is no floor at the bottom of it — just more page. The daylight you came in by is above and behind you, and there is less of it the further down you read. That is not a warning. That is the amenity.
Rabbit holing

Go down the rabbit hole (embrace serendipity). You have to embrace the accidental. — Ryan Holiday, The 5-Step Research Method I Used For Tim Ferriss, Robert Greene, and Tucker Max, quoted on our own entry
Rabbit holing

You didn’t mean to be here for three hours. You meant to look up one thing. Welcome to the rabbit hole. You’re among friends. Those two sentences are the opening of our own glossary entry, Rabbit Hole, and this whole room is built out of that page. Read it first if you would rather have the argument straight; everything down here is that argument with the lights turned off. The short version. For monotropic minds — and a great many Autistic and ADHD people are monotropic — the rabbit hole is not a detour. It is the destination. Monotropism describes attention that goes in depth rather than in breadth: everything gets pulled into one blazing interest tunnel, and off you go. The rabbit hole is what that tunnel looks like from the outside. From the inside it looks like flow. Which is why the research rabbit hole is its own genre, and a good one. One citation leads to another. One tab becomes seventeen. One question opens into a whole field you did not know existed. This is not a failure of discipline. It is how knowledge actually gets built — serendipitously, associatively, joyfully. And then you surface, blinking, and need to tell somebody — everybody — everything you found, which is the infodump: the rabbit hole speaking. Cal Newport’s name for the undistracted end of this is deep work, and we have no glossary page for it, so this sentence is where it gets credited and there is nothing of ours to link. Neurodivergent people were doing it a long time before it had a productivity branding deal. Rabbit holes are how some of us learn best. They are how some of us love best. Go deep.
Where the hole comes from

The metaphor is Lewis Carroll’s. Wikipedia’s article on the idiom puts it plainly: going down the rabbit hole means getting deep into something, or ending up somewhere strange — and it does not promise which. The image comes from Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland , 1865, where the whole adventure starts with somebody following a rabbit into a burrow without once considering how they were going to get out again. There is a name for the version of this that most of us do daily. Wikipedia calls it the wiki rabbit hole and defines it as a learning pathway — the route a reader travels by navigating from topic to topic, each one further from where they started than the last. Not a distraction with a cute name. A pathway, with a shape, that people deliberately go looking for. Our glossary entry illustrates that with Glenn Newcomer’s network diagram of a wiki rabbit hole, published on Wikimedia Commons under CC BY-SA 4.0. It is not copied in here, because the drawing beside the argument on that page is doing its job where it is, and this room would only be borrowing it. Go and look at it there.

What we are witnessing is the computational exploitation of a natural human desire: to look “behind the curtain,” to dig deeper into something that engages us. — Zeynep Tufekci, YouTube, the Great Radicalizer, The New York Times, 2018, quoted on our own entry
Be wary of the holes you rabbit

Our own entry says that line, and it is the reason this room is not simply an advertisement for going deep. There is a difference between a hole you dug and a hole that was dug for you. The appetite is the same appetite. What changes is who chose the next thing. A recommendation engine tuned to keep you in the tunnel is not serendipity, it is somebody’s revenue, and the tunnel it builds runs somewhere specific. Monotropic attention is not a vulnerability to be patched — but it is worth knowing that it is valuable to people who do not have your interests at heart. Which is what the rest of this street is for. Stimpunks rabbit holes are meant to take you behind the curtain of the edges inclusively and compassionately, and to hand you back out at the other end with somewhere of your own to go. There is a trail at the foot of this page and every step on it is a page a person wrote. This room has no recommendation engine, no autoplay, no next-up, and nothing that decides for you what comes after. Seven things are offered, all of them named, and nothing reaches YouTube until you press it.
Remember what the Dormouse said

Grace Slick wrote White Rabbit after a childhood of being read Carroll and an adulthood of playing one Miles Davis record until it came out again in something of her own. She has told that story herself, in the Wall Street Journal: she identified with Alice, she went from a planned and bland 1950s into a rock band without looking back, and she called it her own Alice moment, heading down the hole. It is the most famous piece of rabbit-holing in popular music and it is also a description of how a monotropic mind works on something. Anything I love I’m going to cram into my ears, nose and mouth until I use it up, she said, which is the infodump’s cousin. The words to it are not printed on this page, and that is deliberate. Our glossary entry has them; this street says in three places that nothing musical is hosted here, and a quote bank one door along refuses songs outright because song lyric reproduction is a minefield in the United States in a way prose is not. So you get the recordings, credited, and Slick’s own account of writing them, and the words stay where their publisher put them. The two section titles on this page that are her phrases are credited as hers, here. Feed your head

Three words of Grace Slick’s, used here as a heading the way our glossary entry uses them, and credited rather than borrowed quietly. The counterculture that produced that song also produced the personal computer, and the book that traces the second out of the first takes its title from the same place. John Markoff’s What the Dormouse Said is about people who learned how to learn on their own, and it makes the case that this turned out to be one of the most important things any of them ever did. Rebecca Wood’s Learning From Autistic Teachers puts the case for taking this seriously as pedagogy rather than treating it as a symptom: Note what those two say together. The first is about the person in the tunnel: a well-timed special interest is not indulgence, it is regulation, and it can head off a meltdown. The second is about everybody else: a hyperfixation that gets to be shared with somebody is a teaching relationship, and an extremely good one. Our white rabbit — also known as Space Bunny — stands for playfulness, curiosity, wonder, hope, and the possibility of expanding what anybody can learn. That is why there is a rabbit on this organisation’s pages at all. It is not a mascot for distraction. It is the thing you follow. So: feed your head. Follow the thing that is going somewhere in a hurry. Read one book cited in every book you read. Keep a commonplace book so you can find it again — there is a whole room of one on this street. And never once consider how in the world you are going to get out again.

hc-trope
What a healing checkpoint is

In a game it is the room with no monsters in it. A bonfire, an inn, a save point, a bed you can use as many times as you like: your health goes back to full, it costs nothing, and the game stops trying to kill you for as long as you stand there. TV Tropes calls it the Healing Checkpoint. The trope is everybody’s and belongs to nobody; the room is ours. A checkpoint in a game does three things, and this one does none of them. It restores you to full. This one restores nothing, because you are not a health bar. There is no meter in this room, nothing fills up, and nothing is better about you when you leave than when you came in. That is not the room falling short of the trope. It is the room declining a premise the trope smuggles in — that a person is a quantity that runs down and gets topped up. It saves your progress. This one saves nothing at all. No account, no cookie, no local storage, no record that you were ever here. The job board one floor down keeps a list of finished jobs in your own browser and says so; this room keeps nothing, and a checkpoint that remembered you would be keeping a record of how often you needed one. It sits before the hard part. There is no hard part. Nothing is waiting on the other side of this page, there is no next room you are being prepared for, and the way out goes back to the street you came in by. And here is the sentence the whole room is built to protect: rest is not for anything. Not so you can work better, not so you can come back stronger, not so you can be more use to anybody tomorrow. Star Stuff’s zine No. 58 spends a spread refusing exactly that framing, one of our games refuses it in its own code, and our Rest entry never once offers it. A room arguing that rest is owed cannot carry a single sentence saying what it is owed for, so the generator behind this page refuses that vocabulary outright rather than leaving it to anybody’s care.
Why the room is numbered 429

Because 429 Too Many Requests is the nicest thing a computer says to anybody. It was added to HTTP by Mark Nottingham and Roy Fielding in RFC 6585, in April 2012, and what it means is narrow and precise: the user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time. Not that the request was wrong. Not that the sender was wrong. Not that anything is broken. The rate is wrong, and a rate is a property of a situation rather than of a person. That is the difference between a 429 and a 400. A 400 says you made a mistake. A 403 says you are not allowed. A 500 says something inside has fallen over. A 429 says: this is more than can be done at this speed, and that is all it says. Which is a thing a great many Disabled people have spent a great deal of energy trying to explain about themselves to somebody holding a deadline. And the RFC gives the response a way to be kind. Alongside a 429 a server may send Retry-After — not a refusal, a time. Come back then. The door is not shut; the door is on a different clock. Which is crip time with a header name.
hc-slip
Retry-After

The one amenity in this room, and it is the same shape as the spoon drawer in the Playhouse: it hands out the sentences and not the thing itself. Five slips, borrowing the shape of a 429 so you do not have to compose one from scratch when composing anything is the problem. Open one, read it, take it or leave it. Nothing is sent anywhere. There is no form, no endpoint, no fetch and no storage in this room: opening a slip shows you some text, and the copy button — which only appears if you have JavaScript — puts that text on your own clipboard. Where it goes after that is entirely your business. The wording is a borrowing of HTTP’s shape and not a protocol; a real rate limiter is not allowed to send the last one. Retry-After: an hour the smallest one, and the one the RFC’s own example uses 429 Too Many Requests Retry-After: an hour Ask me again in an hour and I will have more of an answer. Retry-After: later today for the thing that is real but is not this minute 429 Too Many Requests Retry-After: later today Not now. Later today, if it keeps. Retry-After: tomorrow the most useful one, most days 429 Too Many Requests Retry-After: tomorrow Tomorrow. I am not ignoring you; I am at capacity. Retry-After: the weekend for the week that has already spent itself 429 Too Many Requests Retry-After: the weekend The weekend, or the next one. It will still be there. Retry-After: no date the honest one, and the one a real rate limiter is not allowed to send 429 Too Many Requests Retry-After: no date I do not know when. That is not a no forever, and it is not a yes with a date on it either.

The Foundry

Every typeface on this street, and the name of whoever drew it. This is a workshop rather than a shop. It is grey because iron is grey, it is lit through a dirty roof because that is how a workshop was lit before anybody could afford to light one properly, and there is nowhere in it to sit down. Every other room on this street uses a typeface. This is the room where the typefaces are the thing in the window. Put your own words on the bench, or take a passage out of The Playhouse, The Mopery or The Zibaldone, and set it in anything the street owns. Change the size, the leading, the tracking and the measure. Take a weight, a real italic, or the machine slant that is not one. Then pull a proof and print it, with the name of the person who drew the letters on the bottom of the page.
fo-bench-h
The bench

What to set Your own words Typing here moves the picker above to your own words. Nothing you type is stored, sent or remembered, and reloading the page empties it. The face Grouped the way each family’s own record groups it, not the way we would have. Choosing one is what downloads it: nothing here is fetched until you ask for it. Weight Every weight this street declares for this face. Several of these families are one file with a weight axis inside it, declared against two or three weights — the same bytes, genuinely different drawings — and this picker used to drop those, because it asked whether the bytes differed instead of whether the letters did. A weight that came out the same drawings as the regular would be a control that does nothing, so the offered weights are rendered and measured rather than assumed. Upright, italic or slanted An italic is not a leaning roman: it is a second alphabet, drawn separately, often with different letters in it altogether. Where this site holds no italic file the option says so and the machine slant is what is left — which is honest, and is what a phototypesetter did. Case Size 30px A foundry sold type by the size it was cast at. This one is pixels, and it is the only setting here that changes what you can read rather than how it looks. Leading 1.4 The strips of lead a compositor slid between the lines. Multiples of the size, so it stays right when you change it. Tracking 0em Space added to every letter at once. Metal type could only ever have more; this can have a little less. Measure 44ch How wide the column is, in characters. The oldest setting here and the one that does most of the work. Ink and paper Four pairs, and the measured contrast ratio of each one is printed on it. There is no colour picker in here: this is the one room on the street where somebody else chooses the colour of the text, which makes it the one room where an unreadable pair would be ours and theirs at once. Everything offered clears the bar for body text at any size. Printer’s black on proof paper 14.73:1 Vermilion on proof paper 7.77:1 Prussian blue on proof paper 9.86:1 Reversed out, bone on iron 10.65:1 Printing sends the proof and nothing else — not this bench, not the street, not the shelves below. It comes out black on white whatever is on the screen, because paper colour is a screen decision and a printer would spend your toner on it, and it carries a colophon saying what it is set in and who drew that.

Why this room is set in a stencil

Every other world on this street chose a display face for how it sounds. This one chose one for what it is. A stencil letter is a hole rather than a mark — a shape cut out of a sheet of metal so that it can be used again and again and come out the same every time — which is the whole idea of type, arriving about four hundred years early and in the wrong material. It is also what actually gets painted on a workshop’s crates and machinery, which is the other reason it is over the door. The bridges you can see holding the middle of an o in place are not a decorative flourish. Without them the counter — the enclosed space inside a letter — would fall out of the sheet, and there is no way round that in a stencil. Nobody drawing type in metal or on a screen has that problem, which is why nothing else here looks like this.
Why nothing here describes a typeface

There is no sentence beside any face saying what it looks like, what it is good for or what century it is pretending to be from, and that is a refusal rather than an omission. Writing a line of appreciation for every family on this street would mean inventing type history at scale, in the one format most likely to be believed — which is the same reason the herbarium two rooms over refuses to name a pressed plant to species. What this room can say truthfully is who drew it, what licence it travels under and which room here sets it, and all three are read off records rather than remembered. The specimen is the description.
An italic is not a slant

A real italic is a second alphabet. It was cut separately, it has different letters in it — look at a single-storey a, or at the way an f descends — and it was never made by leaning the roman over. A machine slant is exactly that leaning: the upright letters pushed sideways by a machine that has no idea what they are. Both are offered here and both are labelled, because the difference is the kind of thing this room exists to show you rather than to tell you. Where this site holds no italic file, the italic option says so and stops being offered. An italic control on a family with no italic is not an error anywhere: the browser answers by inventing one, nothing looks broken, and the room has quietly told you a lie about somebody’s typeface. And the slant is a font setting and never a transform — check-gentle.py reads rotation and skew out of the computed matrix and cannot be asked to take this room’s word for the difference between a tilted page and a slanted letter.
Every face here is self-hosted, and none of it is ours

Reading any page on this street makes no request to anybody’s font service. The files are in this repository, subsetted to Latin, and a face is downloaded only when something actually sets it — which in this room means when you pick it. Nobody who never opens the picker pays for a single one. None of these typefaces belongs to Stimpunks. Every one of them is somebody’s work, released under a licence that asks to be named, and the name beside each face here is verbatim from that family’s own record rather than typed from memory — including where the record credits a studio rather than a person, and including where it disagrees with the fuller credit in our liner notes. Most are under the SIL Open Font License; a few are under the Apache License 2.0, and the shelves below say which is which face by face, because “they are all OFL” is the sort of thing a site says once and stops checking.
Nothing here is counted

Not the faces, not the proofs pulled, not the sizes tried. This is the room on the street most likely to want to boast about how much type it holds, and a number in the window would be out of date the next time somebody adds a face and wrong in a way nobody would notice. There is also no favourite, no most popular and no ranking of one designer’s work against another’s.
