Covenstead

Merry meet, and merry part, and merry meet again A covenstead is where a coven meets. Not a temple and not an institution — somebody’s kitchen, in the afternoon, with one window open and the good china out. The group is the whole of the subject. Not one wise person at the front and not a congregation: a handful of people who do not entirely agree, meeting on purpose, to check their own thinking out loud in front of each other. Not one of the cups matches. That is not untidiness, it is the subject of the room sitting on the table.
Merry meet, and merry part, and merry meet again

Read the shape of that rather than the words. It is a greeting with the goodbye already built into it, and then a third clause that undoes the goodbye. The parting is agreed at the door, before anyone has arrived, so leaving is not a rupture and nobody has to negotiate it at the time or perform a reason. That is a better door policy than most groups manage, which is why it is the first thing on this page instead of the last. If you have ever left somewhere early and spent the entire walk home composing the apology, you already know exactly what it is worth. Here the going is assumed. So is the coming back, and the door is on the latch rather than locked.
What is on the table

Every tenet below says whose it is and when it turns up. The line at the foot of each one is ours, written for this room, and is not claimed to be part of anybody’s tradition — the same split the fairy fort up the road keeps, because a reader should not have to tell inherited from borrowed by tone alone. Where the tradition argues with itself, the room says so and does not settle it.
Merry meet, and merry part, and merry meet again

A greeting that contains its own goodbye, and then undoes it. A traditional Wiccan greeting and farewell, in common use. Read the shape of it rather than the words. The parting is built into the hello, so leaving is not a rupture and nobody has to negotiate it at the time. And the third clause settles what the parting meant: going is assumed, and so is coming back. That is a better door policy than most groups manage, and it is the reason this is the first thing on the table rather than the last. If you have ever left somewhere early and spent the walk home composing the apology, you already know what it is worth.
An it harm none, do what ye will

The Wiccan Rede, in its best-known couplet. First publicly recorded in a 1964 speech by Doreen Valiente; the wording varies between published versions. · 1964 The word rede is Middle English for counsel. It is advice, and it has stayed advice for sixty years rather than hardening into a code somebody can be thrown out for breaking. That is rarer than it sounds and it is most of why this room exists: a great many of us have been handed rules dressed as guidance, and the difference is whether anybody is standing over you to enforce it. Note also which way round it runs. The constraint comes first and the permission is enormous.
The Rule of Three

That what you send out returns to you three times over. Also called the Threefold Law or the Law of Return; a possible prototype appears in Gerald Gardner's 1949 novel High Magic's Aid. · 1949 at the earliest Contested, and the room is not going to settle it: It is not a universal article of faith. There are Wiccans who regard it as an over-elaboration on the Rede, and others who consider it a modern innovation built on Christian morality. It has also been compared to other ethics of reciprocity, including karma and the Golden Rule. We are not going to settle that from out here, and the reason for saying so plainly is that the flattened version is the one that travels. A tidy cosmic ledger where harm is repaid at a fixed exchange rate is a very easy thing for a website to assert in passing, for atmosphere, about somebody else's religion. What is on this table is the argument rather than the verdict.
First Sight
First Sight and Second Thoughts, that’s what a witch had to rely on: First Sight to see what’s really there, and Second Thoughts to watch the First Thoughts to check that they were thinking right.
Wintersmith, Terry Pratchett, 2006
First Sight

Seeing what is actually in front of you rather than what you expected to be there. Terry Pratchett’s, from the Discworld books. The sentence that names it is below. · 2006 It is harder than it sounds, because the expectation arrives first and feels exactly like observation. This street has been caught by that repeatedly and the catches are all in the changelog: a colour that was decided and never rendered, a channel name compared against nothing, a share card built from the wrong meta tag. In every one of them the page looked right to somebody who already knew what it was supposed to look like.
Second Thoughts
Second Thoughts to watch the First Thoughts to check that they were thinking right.
Wintersmith, Terry Pratchett, 2006
Second Thoughts

The thoughts that watch the first thoughts, to check that they were thinking right. Terry Pratchett’s, from the same sentence, and the half our sibling site built its method on. · 2006 Not doubt. Supervision. And this is the half you can build machinery for, which is the only reason this site has any: the contrast checkers, the class checker, the tools that refuse rather than guess. Star Stuff makes the point that matters most, and it is worth carrying here because it is about the limit of all that plumbing: only the second half can be automated. No checker will ever tell you that a beautiful pattern is doing your looking for you.
If I don't help them, who will?
You can’t not help people just because they’re stupid or forgetful or unpleasant. Everyone’s poor around here. If I don’t help them, who will?
A Hat Full of Sky, Terry Pratchett, 2004
If I don't help them, who will?
I store it in other people. It’s amazing what you can store in other people.
A Hat Full of Sky, Terry Pratchett, 2004
If I don't help them, who will?
A witch never expects payment and never asks for it and just hopes she never needs to.
A Hat Full of Sky, Terry Pratchett, 2004
If I don't help them, who will?
Even if it’s not your fault, it’s your responsibility. Witches deal with things.
A Hat Full of Sky, Terry Pratchett, 2004
If I don't help them, who will?

That the work goes to whoever needs it, including the people who will not thank you for it. The ethic of the Discworld witches, Terry Pratchett’s, collected and argued at length on our own philosophy page. This is the one that makes a coven different from a club. The witches of those books do the unglamorous half of care work, for people who are rude, forgetful or broke, and they keep a ledger that never quite balances on purpose. It is mutual aid with the accounting done out loud, and it is the reason a group that meets to check its own thinking is not merely a seminar.
Only the second half can be automated

That sentence is Star Stuff’s, and it is the most useful thing anybody we publish has said about how this site is built. Second Thoughts you can build machinery for. This street is largely made of that machinery: tools that measure contrast on the page as rendered rather than as written, a checker that refuses a class name two rooms have both claimed, generators that refuse to build rather than guess. Every one of them is a first thought being supervised. First Sight you cannot. No checker will ever tell you that a beautiful pattern is doing your looking for you, that an argument is wrong only in this context, or that a sentence which sounds like solidarity is quietly building a category of people. Those get caught by somebody willing to be disappointed by a finding they liked — and on this site they have been, repeatedly, and the catches are in the changelog rather than tidied away.
What is not in this room

No degrees and no initiation. Nobody is admitted, nobody is examined at the door, and there is no inner circle with the real version in it. A room you have to qualify for is the one thing this street will not build. Nothing is counted. Not visits, not how long you stayed, not how many of these you have read. A place people come back to cannot also be keeping a record of how often they needed to. Nobody is converted. This is a page about what a group of practices says, by people who are not members of them, and it is not an invitation to believe anything. The Wiccan material is somebody else’s religion and is treated as such. No spells, no rituals, no instructions. There is nothing here to perform. What is on the table are ideas about how to treat people and how to check your own thinking, which is the part that travels.
Whose these are

First Sight and Second Thoughts are Terry Pratchett’s, from the Discworld books, and so is the ethic of going to the people nobody else goes to. His words are on this page because they are the point of it. These sentences are the tenets themselves, the way the Rede’s couplet is — an earlier draft of this room named the concepts and sent you elsewhere for the words, which described the thing instead of showing it. Every quotation here names its author, its work and its year, and links to the edition. What is not here is the scene. The short lines above about storing things in other people come out of a long exchange between Miss Level and Tiffany that runs to several hundred words, and that stays where it belongs: quoted properly, at length and in context, on our own philosophy page, which is the better thing to read and is linked rather than raided. tools/make-covenstead.py holds this room to its own limit — wide enough for a defining sentence, not wide enough for a scene — and refuses any quotation that arrives without an author, a work and an edition to point at. The Rede and the Rule of Three belong to living religious traditions, and the second of them is argued about inside those traditions rather than settled. This page says which is which and declines to adjudicate, because a website assembling atmosphere out of somebody else’s faith is precisely the thing that would make this room not worth having. Read off the Wiccan Rede and the Rule of Three on 2026-09-22. Dead Tired Society

est. whenever you got here Peer support, by and for people who are burnt out and people on the far side of it. Nobody here is a professional, nobody is at the front, and nobody is going to fix you, because you are not the thing that broke. It is a room somebody has borrowed after hours, with the big lights switched off and the door left ajar — so that anybody can find it, anybody can leave by it, and nobody has to sit in the light. If tonight is worse than tired: our Help page is a set of doors, and Coping lists crisis lines and warmlines.
The standing orders

They are called standing orders. Nobody is standing. Nobody has to talk. Being here with your camera off and your mouth shut is being here. You may lie on the floor. Most of us already are. The meeting starts when you arrive and ends when you leave, and neither needs announcing. Minutes are not taken. Neither is attendance. Nobody asks how you are doing. If you say anyway, nobody tells you what to do about it — unless you ask, and asking is allowed. Nobody stands on the desks. Most of us have been told to stand up for ourselves quite enough. Nobody in here seizes anything, least of all the day. You can pass. Passing is a whole turn.
What we mean by dead tired
Having All of Your Internal Resources Exhausted Beyond Measure and Being Left with No Clean-Up Crew
The title of Dora M. Raymaker and others, Defining Autistic Burnout, Autism in Adulthood, 2020
What we mean by dead tired
Burnout therefore reflects a failure of relational ecology, not a lack of individual resilience.
Stimpunks, The Ecology of Neurodivergent Burnout
What we mean by dead tired

Not the tired a weekend fixes. Burnout, and autistic burnout in particular: the kind that comes from years of being asked to do more than you could, in places built for somebody else, with nowhere to recover in. The research that defined it was built out of interviews with autistic adults who had been through it, and the title the researchers gave their paper says it better than a definition does. This society is not a clean-up crew either. It is some of the others who were left without one, in the same dark room, which turns out to be a good deal of what a crew was ever for. And it puts the cause where our own writing puts it:
By the door, on the pegs

Everybody comes in carrying something, and there is a row of pegs by the door for it. What wore us out has names, and none of them is yours: every one below is a thing done to people, or asked of them, and not a flaw in the person carrying it. Each peg says what is hanging there, gives one line from somebody who has written about it, and adds one line of ours.
Masking
Masking is exhausting. Utterly utterly draining.
Finally Knowing Me: An Autistic Life, Wasting Energy, 2018
Masking

On the peg: A plain half-mask with nothing painted on it, hanging by its string. Hang it up. You may need it again on the way out, and nobody in here will pretend otherwise, because the street has not changed while you were sitting down. What nobody in here will do is ask you to put it back on. That is the whole of the difference, and for a great many of us it is the first room it has been true in. Masking, in our glossary →
Minority stress

Researchers hypothesize that decreased social standing leads to stigmatized minority groups being exposed to more stressful life situations, with simultaneously fewer resources to cope with these events.
Monique Botha and David M. Frost, Extending the Minority Stress Model to Understand Mental Health Problems Experienced by the Autistic Population, 2018
Minority stress

On the peg: A rucksack gone out of shape at the bottom, the way a bag does when it has been carried full for years. It is not one heavy thing. It is the stone somebody added this morning on top of every stone from before, carried by the people who were handed the fewest ways to set any of it down. Nobody in here asks why the bag is so heavy. Everybody in here already knows. Minority stress, in our glossary →
Epistemic injustice
Epistemic injustice refers to how people from marginalized communities are denied the opportunity to create knowledge and define their own meaning from their experiences. It’s about who is believed.
Sonny Jane Wise, a post on LinkedIn
Epistemic injustice

On the peg: A lanyard with a visitor's badge clipped to it, although the building was your own life. The badge says visitor. It has said visitor in every room where the subject under discussion was you. In here the expert on your life is the person living it, and the next most expert is anybody else on the floor who has lived something like it, which is what the word peer means and all that it means. Epistemic injustice, in our glossary →
Justice sensitivity
The world demands resilience. We are measured more often by our ability to take the hit and keep going rather than encouraged to stop the world from throwing punches.
NeuroHub Community Ltd, Justice Sensitivity And Autism: What Is It?, 2024
Justice sensitivity

On the peg: A whistle on a cord, worn smooth where somebody kept on blowing it. Noticing what is unfair and not being able to stop noticing is heavy to carry, and it gets described as a flaw in the person carrying it. Nobody in here thinks you are too much about it. You are also allowed to put the whistle down for an evening, which is not the same as agreeing with anything. Justice sensitivity, in our glossary →
Moral injury
No matter the profession, moral injury destroys the capacity for trust and creates an expectation of harm, which leaves few options for the individual to act.
Brianne Kramer, Denisha Jones and Clint Broadbent, The Intensification of Moral Injury in Teachers During the Pandemic, 2026
Moral injury

On the peg: A work apron with a name badge still pinned to the bib. This is the one that comes from being made to do the harm, or to stand beside it, by a place that told you it was your job: a classroom, a ward, a caseload, a helpline with a script. It is not the same thing as being tired, and it does not lift while the place that did it is still open tomorrow. Nobody in here will tell you it was not that bad. Moral injury, in our glossary →
Neuronormativity
Normal is merely a social construct that controls individuals by enforcing a right way to function, a right way to be, a right way to exist as a human.
Sonny Jane Wise, Normal Is A Social Construct
Neuronormativity

On the peg: A school blazer on a hanger, cut for somebody else, with the sleeves hanging down past where any hands would be. Behind every other peg on this wall is this one: the idea that there is one right way to have a mind, and that the rest of us are that way done badly. The blazer was never going to fit and it was not cut for you to grow into. Hang it up with the others. Neuronormativity, in our glossary → The wall is longer than this, and nobody has finished putting pegs up. Further along it: the double empathy problem, the disability double bind, affective injustice, spoon theory, shutdown and meltdown. All of them are in our glossary, argued by the people who carried them.
dts-turn-h
It has come round to you

In a circle like this a talking piece goes round, and whoever is holding it may speak or may pass. Passing is a whole turn, and nobody comes back to you afterwards to check whether you have thought of something. Say it here. It goes nowhere: nothing is sent, nothing is kept, and nobody reads it, us included.
What is not in this room

No advice nobody asked for, and no tips. Not one list of ways to get better. Advice is for when somebody asks, and asking is allowed. No resilience. Nobody here is going to congratulate you on how much you can take. That is how most of us got here. No timeline, and no before and after. Nobody is waiting for you to be better, and nothing in this room assumes you will go back to how you were. Nothing counted. No attendance, no days since, no streak, and no check-in that remembers you came. Nobody at the front. No facilitator with a clipboard and no professional in the corner. The only expertise in the room is having been there. No light you have to sit in. It stays in the corridor. The door is ajar so that it can find you if you want it, and so that you can leave by it if you do not.
Where the society actually meets

Not on this page. A web page cannot sit with anybody, and this one is the sign on the door rather than the room behind it. The people are in our community, by and for neurodivergent and disabled people, which is where our peer support lives. If what is wearing you out is money, mutual aid is the part of Stimpunks that exists because the systems failed us first. Further, and better than this page: Autistic Burnout: The Cost of Masking and Passing · The Ecology of Neurodivergent Burnout · Peer support · Peer respite · Rest

The name is a play on Dead Poets Society, the 1989 film directed by Peter Weir and written by Tom Schulman, about a group that meets away from a school built on conformity in order to resist it. We took the shape of the name and nothing else: no line, no scene, no character and no still. The poets in that title are dead. Everybody here is merely tired, and would like it on the record that merely tired is quite enough. Every line on a peg belongs to whoever wrote it, and is credited to them rather than to our glossary, which is where we found it: Finally Knowing Me, Monique Botha and David M. Laughingstock

Tonight: disabled comics, on their own terms Comedy is a form of knowledge. When disabled comedians take the stage, they bring a perspective shaped by daily navigation of a world that was not designed for them — and they do it on their own terms, in their own voice, controlling the frame. They make audiences do their own thinking. Disabled comedians are not inspiring for being on stage. They are comics who happen to be disabled. And these sets map the gap between how disability is publicly discussed and how disabled people actually live, laugh, and relate to their own bodies and communities. From our Campfire Learn Together, Being Disabled Can Be Pretty Funny, where the community watched Josh Blue and Tina Friml together and talked about what their work reveals about disability, identity, and the world.

Tina Friml has cerebral palsy. She frames herself as “the bisexuality of ability” — not fully committed to either side — and names three perks of being a disabled comic: she can never be a hack (“nothing about this is relatable”), CP is the most interesting thing about her (otherwise she is just “a liberal white girl from Vermont”), and nothing she does can fail, because an audience will file all of it under inspiration. ls-doing-h
What the laughs are doing

“I suffer from people” — not from cerebral palsy. That is the social model of disability in one sentence. Comedy delivers it where argument bounces off. Even bombing is treated as a TED Talk. Inspiration exploitation means disabled people cannot lose, and that is not a compliment: it removes disabled people from the possibility of being judged on their actual work. “Free play” is the same trap from another angle. It sounds like freedom. It is also a way of being taken out of ordinary life. “Nothing about this is relatable” is not a limitation. It is a position. Comedy from genuinely outside perspectives makes an audience aware of the frame it was inside without knowing it. Asking somebody’s companion “what will he have?” while the disabled person is sitting right there is not a rare failure of manners. It is a routine expression of the assumption that a disabled person at the table is not the one to address. The same person with the same walk gets read as a celebrity, a drunk, or a danger, depending on who is looking. Disability legibility is not neutral. It is shaped by race, gender, class and context. The disability community is the only minority group everyone will eventually join. If that is true, why is it still treated as other, and why is joining it coded as loss? Being around other disabled people — where your disability is the norm, not the exception — changes what you can say, how much energy you spend, and how you move through space. That kind of community is not a luxury. It is a need. From the takeaways of the same write-up, lightly trimmed.

For the bar afterwards

The Campfire ended with questions rather than answers. Three of them, to take home with you: What would it mean for a disabled person to just be bad at something — unremarkable, having a normal day? When have you seen humor do something that more direct advocacy couldn’t? And what are the costs of always having to be funny to be heard? There’s a difference between laughing with a comedian and laughing at the subject of their jokes. How do you read the difference in a room? The rest of them are in the write-up. On the bar: The Daily Tism

Not stand-up, and on the bar anyway. The Daily Tism is a satirical news site in the vein of The Onion, and every story in it is about being Autistic. Sara Gibbs and Elsa Williams founded it in 2024, and it is written by Autistic people for Autistic people — “and the people who like to laugh with us,” in their own words. It turns the usual coverage round the way the sets on the bill turn the usual frame round: Public warned to stop armchair diagnosing celebrities as neurotypical. It makes a sitcom, too. It’s a Superpower?? is an audio sitcom, which they call the first made by a team of Autistic creatives for an Autistic audience: five Autistic people meet at a support group, end up with magic powers they cannot control, and have to save the world from a neurotypical supervillain. The question marks are part of the title. It is made to be heard on headphones, and we think it is really good. Both are The Daily Tism’s and both live on their own site. Nothing on this page reaches it until you follow a link, and the sitcom plays there, from them.
ls-rules-h
House rules

There is no cover and no two-drink minimum, and nothing in here is for sale. The water on the stool is free. The way in is a ramp, and so is the way onto the stage. The mic comes down to whatever height the comic wants it at, and nobody has to sit on the stool. Nobody in the front row is made part of the act without asking to be. Sit wherever you like. Talk to the comic. Not to whoever came in with them. Bombing is allowed. A set that does not land is a set that did not land, and nobody here will turn it into a TED Talk. Nobody is called brave for getting up there. Tell them they were funny, or tell them they were not. Nobody headlines, either. The bill runs in the order the playlist keeps, and a place on it is not a rank. Laughter is loud and arrives without warning, which makes a comedy club one of the harder rooms on any street to be in. Nothing here plays until you press it, the volume is yours, and leaving in the middle of a set is not heckling. Laughingstock is the name of the club. It is nobody’s job.

The Lightbulb Picture House

Every screening is a relaxed screening. The house lights stay up. A lot of us found out who we were from a video. Somebody on a screen described a life that turned out to be ours — the textures, the plans that fell apart, the conversations that went sideways for no reason anybody would name — and something switched on. This picture house is named for that moment, and for the short film on its first screen that calls it a lightbulb moment. Most of what is showing here was made by the people it is about. Every screen is one of our own playlists, and every film on them has a card on a rack saying who made it, how long it runs and what is in it, before you press anything.

lph-rules-h
Every screening is a relaxed screening

The house lights stay up. Nobody sits in the dark who did not ask to. The captions are on. Every screen here asks for them before the film starts, and you can switch them off in the player. Nothing plays until you press it, nothing plays before the film you chose, and the volume is yours. Move, stim, rock, pace, flap, hum, sit on the floor, lie across three seats. Nobody shushes anybody. Bring your ear defenders, or borrow the pair hung on the seat in the second row. Come in late and leave early. You can walk out in the middle of a film and walk back in at the end of it, and nobody will ask why. Every film on a rack tells you what is in it before you press play — how long it runs, and anything you might want to know first, from a panic attack to a sponsor segment. Every screen has a rack under it, and every rack folds away if you would rather not scroll past it. Nothing in this building is blue. Every April, autism charities run by parents and professionals light landmarks up blue, and autistic people have been saying for years what they think of it — one of them, below, better than we could. The bulbs here are warm on purpose, there is no puzzle piece anywhere in the place, and the ornament over the screen is the gold infinity — Autistic UK’s, from Au, the chemical symbol for gold.

Samefood Cafe

Today’s special: your favourite. In the window: one divided plate, with pesto pasta in the big well on the left, nooch popcorn along the top right, cheese in the well below it, and the peanut butter in a small well of its own. On the right of the plate, a mug of coffee. On the left, the apple slices in a ramekin, to go with the peanut butter on the plate; on Ryan’s list they are one thing, and they meet when whoever is eating them decides they meet, and below them Ronan’s ketchup in its own ramekin, touching nothing, which is how Ronan has every red thing. Nothing on the table touches anything else, and every food on it is off a regular’s tray further down. A café for samefoods and safe foods, and for anybody whose plate has ever been treated as a problem somebody else had to solve. The kitchen knows its regulars: it keeps what each of them has, the way they have it, and it is ready for the day their samefood changes with the season, so the menu is whatever the regulars ask for and nothing on it changes unless somebody asks. Nobody here will ask you to try a bite of anything, nothing on your plate touches anything else unless you want it to, and the light over the table is the same at every hour, so that nothing on the plate ever looks different from last time.
House rules

We default to structure, separation and predictability, and every guest is accommodated individually. You are never regarded as fussy, picky or too much: you are quietly and professionally accommodated. The house fits itself to you, never the other way round, and nobody’s way of eating is anybody else’s rule. The same again is always on. Nobody asks whether you would like to try something different today. Samefoods have seasons. If yours changes, or you put one down for a while and come back to it years later, the kitchen still has it, and nobody asks why. Nothing touches unless you want it to. Every plate in here is divided for whoever needs it, every bowl is yours to fill the way you eat it, and every plate is the same plate and every bowl the same bowl. And if you do not mind your food touching, nobody here minds for you. Some of us need everything apart and some of us do not care at all, and both are the same again. Anything can come in a ramekin of its own, if you ask. Ronan, a Stimpunk, has every condiment that way and red things always, touching nothing else, so his ketchup comes in its own — and that is Ronan’s way, not the house’s, so nobody else’s ketchup has to. The same brand, the same shape, the same way. We can tell the difference as well, and nobody in here will tell you that you can’t. Nobody comments on your plate: not what is on it, not how much, and not how often you have had it. Nothing is hidden in anything. What it looks like is what it is, all the way through. Nobody has to eat with anybody. A table for one is a whole table. Nobody finishes your samefood without asking. Our glossary calls that a tragedy, and in here it is treated as one. Nobody in here is a picky eater. Selective, sensory, hypersensory, or simply somebody who knows exactly what they need: all of it is welcome, and none of it needs explaining.
On the menu
This café gets its menu from our glossary, and the menu is three words long. Each one is on a plate of its own.

Samefood

Eating the same food, often, sometimes for weeks or months at a time, made the same way every time and sometimes only one brand of it. It is how a great many of us eat, and plenty of us say it brings peace. Samefoods have seasons, too: one can carry you for months, get put down, and come back years later, and the kitchen here keeps every one of them. Nobody has an opinion about any of it. What is not on the menu

No calories, no nutrition labels, and no sorting of anybody’s food into good and bad. No ‘just one bite’, and no ‘they will eat when they get hungry enough’. Our Food Aversion entry says what that second one can do, and it is not nothing. Nothing smuggled into anything else. A plate you cannot trust is a plate you cannot eat from. No recipes and no tips about eating. There is a book on the counter by somebody who knows, and a menu that does not change. Nothing counted: not how many of us drink coffee, and not how many times anybody has had the same again. No surprise dish. A new one goes on the menu only when somebody asks for it — a regular, or somebody walking in for the first time — and the kitchen keeps it from then on, the way that person has it. Nothing is ever put in front of you that you did not order, and nothing comes off the menu because somebody else got bored of it.

A cabinet of our people’s collections. The house brings the furniture; the light is theirs. In the picture: the gallery from the doorway, dark, with the cabinets standing apart on the bare floor. House rules

Nobody asks how many. A collection is not a number, and nothing in here is counted: not the pens, not the plants, not the cabinets. Nothing is priced, valued or called rare. What a thing might fetch is none of our business, and a page that listed what people own with a price beside each thing would be a list for somebody else to shop from. Nothing is ranked. No best cabinet, no biggest collection, and nobody’s pens set against anybody else’s. Every cabinet has its own lamp, and no two lamps in here are alike. The owner chooses it. The house only ever guesses at the furniture. A collection can be anything somebody keeps on purpose. It can stop for years, sit in a drawer, and start again, and nobody asks why. Nobody explains their collection to anybody. “What is it for?” is not asked in here. The pictures are of things, never of people. A photograph with a person in it belongs on the polaroid wall, which has its own promises and its own consent record. Nothing in a picture says where you live. The location a phone writes into every photograph is stripped before a file comes anywhere near this site, and every frame is looked at for an address, a letter or a view out of a window before it goes up. Nothing is filtered or cropped. A photograph is made smaller so the page loads, and that is all that is done to it. The lamp’s colour goes round the picture and never over it. Everything comes down when you say so, one thing or the whole cabinet. It comes out of the repository too, and nobody asks whether you are sure.
put-something-in
Putting something in a cabinet

Send the photographs, and that is the whole job. Phone pictures are fine, badly lit is fine, the desk behind them is fine. You do not have to title anything, describe anything or caption anything: the house does the describing, and says it did. That is the opposite of the polaroid wall, on purpose. The wall asks you to write the words for a picture of yourself, because a description of a person is theirs to write and nobody else’s. A description of a pen is not a description of anybody. It is work, and work is exactly the thing that stops people sending a picture at all, so in here the house takes it. The describing is done by Claude, an AI, looking at each photograph, and every cabinet says so on its label. It writes only what it can see: colour, shape, what a thing is made of, what it is standing beside. It does not name a maker or a model from what a thing looks like, because a guess on a label reads as a fact. If a name is printed on the thing and can be read in the picture, it can go on the label; otherwise the name is yours to give, and yours wins over anything the house wrote. Reach us through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community, say whose collection it is and how you want to be named, and it goes in a cabinet. To take anything down, the same routes, and the word remove is enough.

Every collection belongs to the person whose name is on its cabinet, and so does every photograph of it. The photographs are not under this site’s Creative Commons licence and carry no licence onward at all, so that taking one down stays possible: a Creative Commons licence cannot be revoked, and “it comes down when you say so” would otherwise be a promise the licence contradicted. Every quotation belongs to whoever wrote it: C.L. Lynch at NeuroClastic, and Devon Price, whose book we have read only as far as our own glossary quotes it, and say so beside the line. Every quotation in this room is 30 words or fewer, names who said it, where and when, and says beside it how it was checked. tools/make-collection.py refuses a longer one; refuses a photograph that still carries any metadata, that nobody has described, or that nobody has looked at for a person or an address; refuses a maker’s name in words Claude wrote unless it can be read in the picture; refuses a filter on any photograph; and refuses two cabinets with the same lamp. Build your own bowl or wrap, or have one of ours. On the shelf over the counter, cut through the middle like everything else in here: scallions, with their white bulbs showing under the soil; cilantro, lacy and many-lobed; garlic, a whole bulb in the soil with its cloves drawn in; ginger, tall and narrow-leaved over a knobbly rhizome; a chili plant with its red chilies hanging; carrots, feathery on top and one orange root going down; red potatoes, three of them in the soil under the leaves; flat Italian parsley, broader-leaved than the cilantro; a leek, its white shaft half under the soil; and a small lemon tree with lemons on it. Everything in here is plants, and everything in here is drawn the way a cook sketches a dish to show what is in it: cut straight through the middle, so you can see every layer sitting on the one under it. Where the name comes from

This room was going to be called Ital Plant Livity, and both of those words are Rastafari’s. Ital comes from vital with the v taken off, so that the word begins with I, which Rastafari speech does to a great many words; livity is the life Rastafari hold is in everybody. Rastafari has been a big influence on Ryan, and the playlist on the stereo is still called Ital Plant Livity and is full of songs about Ital food. But this kitchen is not Ital, so it does not say it is. Many people who keep Ital avoid food with anything added to it, and some avoid added salt; this pantry has three kinds of salt, MSG, soy sauce and things out of packets. And how Ital is kept varies from one person to the next, which is not ours to settle from outside. So the name over the door says what it means in plain English, and the songs say the rest in their own words. Ital, on Wikipedia, which is where the lines above were checked.

vpl-rules-h
House rules

Everything in here is plants. Every bowl, every wrap, everything at the counter. Everything touches. The sauce runs into the rice and that is the idea. If you need your food kept apart, Samefood Cafe is a few doors along, and nothing on a plate in there touches anything. Vital means alive. Nobody in here will tell you what a bowl does for your body, and nothing on the board is good for you or bad for you. It is food. Nothing is weighed and nothing is counted: no portions, no numbers on anything, no favourite of the week. The builder keeps nothing and sends nothing. Copying puts your ticket on your own clipboard and nowhere else, and closing the page empties the bowl. No claims about anybody’s cooking. A flavour base is where a kitchen somewhere starts from; what you build on it is yours. Hot peppers, everything. Nooch, everything. Those two are Ryan’s, and they are on the house.
vpl-thanks-h
Whose these are

The pantry is Ryan’s, the list he cooks from for himself, written down as he gave it, including his names for its sections and his list of pairings, trinities and go-tos, which is where every flavour base in the builder comes from. Where a line of his held several things it is split into them, and a thing on his list twice is in the builder once. The combos, the notes on them and the drawings are ours. The words Ital and livity are Rastafari’s, and the songs on the stereo belong to the musicians named beside them. tools/make-vital.py builds this room out of one data file. It refuses a combo that brings in anything the pantry does not keep, and a combo that stands on no flavour base. It refuses the word Ital anywhere on the menu. It refuses the vocabulary of authenticity, of wellness and of counting in the room’s own voice. And it refuses a pot on the shelf that is not on the menu, and anything you can tick that the drawing of your bowl would not know how to draw. The type is Bagel Fat One, by Kyungwon Kim and JAMO, for the kitchen’s name and its headings, and Be Vietnam Pro, by Lâm Bảo, Tony Le and ViệtAnh Nguyễn, for everything you read: open, round-shouldered and easy going down a long list, which is most of this page. Both under the SIL Open Font License. More in the liner notes.

Community Center

CB sign-on at the front desk The street’s community center, at about ten in the morning. The sun comes in through the blinds, the chairs are stacked against the wall, and there is a radio on the front desk. The group chat is in the meeting hall, on Stoat, and this is where to find out how to get in. The radio is the CB, a chat channel patterned after citizens band radio, and this is the only place it is switched on. Sign on with a handle and the community password and it rides along in the corner of your screen, on every page of the street, until the password changes or you sign off. On the wall by the desk is the community service board: every way there is to give something to a room on this street, and how.
ctr-hall-h
The meeting hall

Our community’s group chat is a Stoat server of ours, and it is where the Stimpunks community meets for anything that has to be kept, or kept to the people in it. Stoat gives every member their own account and sign-in, and the server has channels, roles and permissions, so a conversation stays with the people it was meant for and is still there next week. The CB on the front desk is the opposite on purpose: one shared password, ten messages, and everything gone at midnight. The radio is for passing the time together on the street; the hall is for the conversations that matter enough to keep, and for anything you would not say in a room anybody with the password could walk into. Stoat is an open-source group chat app, the one that used to be called Revolt. It is free, it carries no ads, and it runs in a web browser and as an app on phones and computers. We are moving there from Discord, so for a while some of our pages on stimpunks.org will still say Discord where they mean the hall.
meeting-hall
Getting in

Fill in the join form on stimpunks.org. It takes a few minutes, and you share only what you are comfortable sharing. Our community page says what joining means. We email you an invite to the server. The form may still call it a Discord invite while we move; the invite you get is for Stoat. Make a Stoat account and follow the invite. The account is yours, with its own password, and it has nothing to do with the CB’s. Stoat’s own privacy policy says what it keeps. Already in? Open the meeting hall on Stoat. It only opens for members, and it opens in Stoat rather than on this page, because Stoat’s app does not let other sites put it inside theirs.
meeting-hall
What is inside

This is the shape of it, from our field guide’s page on team chat, which was written for Discord. The channels are moving across now, some names will change on the way, and this list will be brought up to date once the move is done. Information: a welcome, the rules, introductions, announcements, and a help desk for when something does not work. Community: the watering hole, for chatting about anything and sharing penguin pebbles; body doubling; coping, where everything said stays there; mutual aid, to give and get help; show your work; events; and work opportunities. Live rooms, with voice and video: a cave for quiet, a campfire, a watering hole, body doubling, and listening parties. Boards: infodumps, writing prompts, and a gallery for your art. Media and interests: what you are reading, watching, listening to and playing, and rooms for education, science and making, nature, and niche construction. Teams and projects: where the small teams that run Stimpunks do the work, editorial and operations among them, with room for anybody who wants to watch and learn. Caves, campfires and watering holes are David Thornburg’s primordial learning spaces: somewhere to be quiet on your own, somewhere to learn from somebody, and somewhere to learn with each other. The hall is laid out along those lines, and so is Cavendish Coworking upstairs from the street.
meeting-hall
How it goes

Our covenant applies, as it does in every Stimpunks space. Only members can see who is in the server. Be as visible or as quiet as you need to be; reading along without saying anything is a fine way to belong. Come when you can, and stay as long as you like. Nothing there needs an answer from you straight away. Nothing on the street reaches Stoat. This page links to it and that is all: nothing is sent there from here, and the CB and the hall do not talk to each other.
cb-signon-h
The front desk

A handle is whatever you type, up to 24 characters, except a moderator’s: those are on a list, and sign on only with the moderators’ password. The password is shared with the Stimpunks community, so ask for it there, in the meeting hall. It only changes if something goes wrong, and then everybody signs on again with the new one; if you are not in the community yet, joining is on stimpunks.org. Your handle The community password, or your own if you have claimed your username Forgotten the password for a username you claimed? Use the recovery code you were given when you claimed it, or a reset code from a moderator, and choose a new password. There is no email, so these codes are the only way back in. Your username The recovery code, or a moderator’s reset code A new password The same again You are on the channel as . Once you are on, Profile on the radio lets you claim your username with a password of your own, so nobody else can sign on as it. Signing on keeps your handle, a pass and where you put the radio in your own browser. What the channel keeps, for how long, and what it never keeps are all on the privacy page.
cb-how-h
How the radio works

Every button and switch on the radio, named the way the radio names it, is in the CB guide. These are the things worth knowing first. Open is on and closed is off. While the radio is open and the tab is in front of you, it listens to the channel every few seconds. Fold it away, or look at another tab, and it stops listening altogether. No alerts. No chimes, no notifications, no badges and no unread count, and nothing is saved up for when you come back. If you were not there when something was said, you missed it, and that is how it is meant to work. A picture can go with a message. Press Picture beside Transmit, pick a screenshot or a photo, and say what is in it if you like. The radio redraws it before it goes, which takes off where it was taken and anything else the camera wrote into it, and it goes when its message goes. Press a picture to see it larger, and Download keeps a copy on your own device; the same norm as a screenshot applies to passing it on. A message can be long. Up to 2,000 characters, and it keeps its lines: Enter sends and Shift and Enter starts a new line. The box grows as you type, and you can drag its corner to make it taller. A little Markdown works: **bold**, *italic*, `code`, three backticks on a line of their own round a block of code, > at the start of a line for a quote, and - or 1. for a list. A link’s words are always its address, so [words](an address) stays as you typed it. Copy on a message puts its words, as they were typed, on your own clipboard. Be seen here, if you like. In any room, Be seen here on the radio shows you, by your handle, to anybody else signed on who has switched it on in that room, and shows them to you, with the names of everybody in that room’s call, so you can see who is there before you join. Names only, and no count. It also puts you on Who’s online, beside World and This room, where anybody signed on can see who is around and which room they are in, and go there; typing @ in Teleport finds somebody the same way. While it is off you are on nobody’s list. Your browser remembers it until you switch it off. Three sizes. Size on the bar makes the radio Small, which is the bar and the newest message and still listening, Normal, or Large, which is wider and taller, for long messages and pictures. Ten messages, then midnight. The latest ten are all there is on the channel; an eleventh pushes the oldest off, and everything is deleted at midnight, Colorado time. The same sign-on writes on the chalkboard. Plural Mural has a chalkboard at the foot of its wall, Helen Edgar’s idea, and only people signed on here can chalk a note on it. It is not the channel: anybody walking past can read it, signed on or not, and a note stays up for seven days rather than until midnight. It sits in the bottom right corner. Drag it by its bar to put it somewhere else, or press Move and use the arrow keys; Home puts it back in the corner. It remembers where you left it. It reads aloud if you want it to. With the radio open, a screen reader hears new messages as they come in, and the switch New messages to a screen reader turns that off. Speak new messages aloud is for everybody else: switch it on and the radio reads each new message out, handle first, in your own device’s voice, with a burst of squelch as the station keys up and the tail as it lets go, like a voice coming over the air. At the Gentle setting you get the words without the static. It is off until you turn it on, it never reads what was already on the channel when you tuned in, and folding the radio away stops it. A screen reader user with both switches on will hear everything twice. There is one room it stays out of. The Healing Checkpoint, room 429, promises that it writes nothing down about you, and a radio that listens to a server and remembers where you put it would make that untrue. So the radio waits outside that door and is there again when you come out.
cb-norms-h
House norms

Our covenant is the floor. Everything in the Stimpunks Covenant applies on the channel, as it does in every Stimpunks space. A reaction names who pressed it. React on a message puts a heart, an otter, a penguin or any other emoji under it with your handle beside it, and pressing it again takes yours back. Nobody is shown a count, only names, so a reaction is a person saying something small, not a score. A handle is not proof of anybody. An unclaimed handle is whatever somebody typed, so do not borrow somebody else’s. A claimed username only signs on with its owner’s own password, so claim yours from Profile on the radio and nobody else can use it. The channel marks it: a message from a claimed username carries CLAIMED, which the sender cannot type or tick, only the server can put there. It says the message came from whoever holds that username’s password and nothing more, so a handle without it is still just what somebody typed. BASE is the other mark, and the one that means a moderator: only our moderators can send it, each under their own handle off the moderators’ list, which nobody else can sign on as. World, or this room. The radio hears one channel at a time. World is the one the whole street shares. This room is the room you are standing in, heard by whoever else is tuned to it there, and walking into another room tuned that way hears that room’s channel instead. Every channel keeps the same rules: ten messages, gone at midnight. Every room has a call. Join this room’s call opens voice and video for the room you are in, for people signed on to the CB. The rooms off the Town Hall for our directors, board and moderators are the base’s: anybody can walk in, and their channel and call are for the base alone. Camera and microphone start off, and camera off and microphone off is a fine way to be in a call. The base station moderates, and is the only one who can record a call or turn on transcription; before doing either, say so in the call, and a recording or transcript is shared only if everybody in it has said yes, the same as a screenshot of the channel. Anybody can share a YouTube video in the call for everybody to watch together; whoever shares it plays and pauses it for everybody, and while it plays with its sound on, Jitsi mutes your microphone, so unmute to talk over it. For watching at your own pace instead, use the room’s own players and the CB’s spots. Anybody in a call can share a screenshot or a photo there with Share file; it goes to 8x8, not to us, so share nothing with somebody else in it unless they have said yes, the same as a screenshot of the channel. It is a room, not a private line. Everybody with the community password can read the channel. Say what you would say in a room with people in it. What is said here stays here. That goes for pictures too. The channel forgets at midnight; do not carry it off in a screenshot or a repost unless everybody in it has said you can. That is the covenant’s own privacy norm, on the one channel of ours built to forget. Nobody has to answer. There are no alerts because nobody is waiting on you. A message into a quiet channel is fine, a quiet channel is fine, and you can leave without saying goodbye. Plain words are fine. Say ten-four and breaker-breaker if you like them. Nobody needs to know the codes. A room on the street is a link. Type # and the start of its name, like #den, pick it from the list, and everybody on the channel sees it as #The Den, linked. Arrow keys move through the list, Enter or Tab picks, and Escape leaves your # alone. A room’s full address works too, like stimpunks.world/the-den.html. An address on another site is a link that says it is leaving. Write it out with https:// and it opens in a new tab, with the site it goes to after it, like ↗ example.com. Check that name before you follow it: a handle proves nothing about who sent it. A link’s words are always its address, so [words](an address) stays as it was typed. A place in a film is a button. Watching something together, type @ and the time, like @34:12 or @1:02:03, or press Add my spot to put in where your film has got to, which film it is and which room you are in. Everybody sees it as a button that moves the film on their own page to that place, and the room as a link to go there. Following that link takes you to the film’s play button, ready to start at that place when you press it. If a spot names a room or a film, it only moves that film in that room, and anywhere else it tells you where that spot is instead. It does not press play, so anybody taking a break can catch up when they come back. A time without the @, like 7:30, stays words. Hosting is a beacon, not a remote. Press Host this film while you watch something, and everybody on the channel sees where you are in it and in which room, with a Catch up button if they are in the same room, and a Follow switch that keeps their film in step with yours, at their own volume. Nobody’s film moves unless they press one of those themselves, and pausing your own film stops following, so taking a break and coming back is always fine. One person hosts a room at a time. Keep the password inside the community. It only changes if there is a problem, and everybody is signed off when it does. If something is wrong, tell the base. Say so on the channel, or reach us privately. The base station can take a message off the air. If it keeps happening, the password changes, which signs everybody off at once, and that is the only other lever there is.
cb-covenant-h
The covenant

The Stimpunks Covenant is where our community norms live, and it is longer and better than anything this room could say about them. It starts from the Contributor Covenant, version 2.1, which every Stimpunk agrees to abide by, and adds what we have learned since: no proselytising, prosocial ways of settling conflict, and how to repair harm when it happens. Read it on stimpunks.org, where it is kept up to date, rather than here, where it would not be.
ctr-service-h
The community service board

The steel sorter on the wall by the desk has a slot for every room on the street that takes something in from our community. Each slot says what the room takes, what it asks of you and how to send it, and points at the room’s own words, where the full terms are. Nothing on this board sends anything, and neither does the CB: the radio forgets at midnight and everybody signed on can read it, which is the wrong place for somebody’s photograph. Everything here goes the way its own room says, and you do not need to be signed on to the radio for any of it.
slot-polaroid
A photograph of you

The Polaroid Wall, in Enid’s Room A photograph of you, for the wall in Enid’s Room. Say how you want to be named, and what you want said about the picture, or nothing at all. The yes has to be yours. A young person’s yes is their own, and a parent’s does not stand in for it. It goes up as you sent it: nobody crops it or filters it. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. How the wall takes one, and gives it back
slot-collection
Something you collect

The Collection Collection Photographs of something you collect, for a cabinet of your own under a lamp you choose. Choose the lamp, and say why it suits what it lights. No two lamps in there are alike. The house writes the titles and descriptions and says it did, so you do not have to. Nothing is counted, priced or called rare, and nothing in a photograph may say where you live. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. How to put something in a cabinet
slot-yell
Your yell

The Playhouse A recording of you yelling, badly, hoarsely, briefly, whatever comes out, for the yell button. Say how you want to be named, or stay anonymous. The room says whose yell it is out loud when it plays. A voice identifies you as surely as a face does, so it keeps the Polaroid Wall’s promises, and one message takes it down. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. The Playhouse’s own terms for a yell
slot-pebble
A pebble

The Pebble Board A song, a poem, a picture, a joke, a recipe: anything you would bring somebody because it made you think of them. The board is what one gathering brought each other, and a new edition goes up after the next one. Whoever keeps that edition decides what gets pinned. Bring it to a gathering in our community. What a pebble is
slot-quote
A quotation

The Zibaldone A short line for the commonplace book, for any state of mind. Thirty words at most, and never a song lyric. Say who said it, which printing it is in, and where you found it. The attribution slip in the room writes that out for you. Say what you are unsure of. It is checked against a printing before it goes in, and a line nobody can place stays out. Send it however you already talk to us: the contact page, our community, email, a text message. The attribution slip
slot-zine
A page for the zine

The Zine Table A page for the next issue, or an idea for one. One sheet, black and white, legible out of a bad printer. On paper, by photo, by voice note or by AAC: any way you have of getting a sentence out counts as writing. Your name goes on it the way you spell it. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. What the zine table asks for
slot-broadside
An idea for a broadside

The Broadsheet Broadside An idea for the press’s next sheet: a manifesto somebody on this street would want to pin up, or a memento of a room worth handing over. In words. Every sheet is written for the press, so an idea is an idea for a sheet rather than a sheet printed as it arrives. A sheet says what we hold and never what you must do. One sheet, both sides, and its credits and its licence on the paper. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. What the press takes
slot-samefood
Your samefoods

Samefood Cafe The foods that carry you right now, for a tray of your own. Written exactly as you give them, capitals and spelling and all. Nobody’s list is tidied, sorted or compared with anybody else’s. Say how you like it served, if you do. It comes down the moment you ask. Tell us in our community. The trays as they stand
slot-look
Your look

The Dopamine Dress-Up Den What you wear, in your own words, for a look on the peg with your name on it. Words, not a photograph: the pieces, the prints, the colours, and how they feel if you like. Your words go beside the look exactly as you give them. If something you wear is not on a rail yet, the house draws it and hangs it up. Say how you want to be named. Nothing is rated, and it comes down the moment you ask. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. How the Dress-Up Den takes a look
slot-mural
A mural

Plural Mural Something you would like painted on the end wall, in words, for the house to paint and put up in turn. Words, not a picture: what is on it, what it says if it says anything, and the colours. The house paints it. Nobody real is painted on the wall. Your words go beside the mural exactly as you give them. Say how you want to be named. Nothing is voted on, and it comes down the moment you ask. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. How Plural Mural takes a mural
slot-watch
Something to watch

The rooms with a screen in them A recommendation for a room with a screen in it. Laughingstock: a set by a Disabled comic, on their own terms. The Lightbulb Picture House: a film about being Autistic, ADHD or otherwise neurodivergent, best of all made by the people it is about. Looming Rocks: a whole concert played outdoors, filmed. The Live Room: a whole session played in a studio, filmed. Black Leather Lagoon: something spooky for the Halloween playlist on the drive-in screen. The Solarpunk Hermitage: a documentary for the campfire. Every one is checked before it goes up: that it plays, that it can be shown here, and how long it runs. A film for the Picture House is watched first, so its card can say what is in it before anybody presses play. A recommendation is a suggestion rather than a booking, and the choosing stays with whoever keeps that room’s list. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community.
slot-listen
Something to listen to

The rooms that keep a playlist A song for a room that keeps a list of them. Dance, Punks: something to dance to on the airstrip. Vital Plant Living: a song about food for the stereo. Club Chronic: a song for Chronic Neurodivergent Depressed Queer Punk, the playlist on the stage. Nothing musical is hosted here, so a song goes in as a link to where it already lives, and no lyrics go on any page. Every one is checked to see that it plays and can be shown here before it goes in. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community.
slot-poem
A poem for the scroll

The Doomscroll A poem of doom, for the scroll behind the Mopery’s library. Public domain everywhere, not only in the United States: its author has to have been dead more than seventy years. Say which printing it comes from, because poems change between printings. Send it however you already talk to us: the contact page, our community, email, a text message. The scroll and its rule
slot-room
A room of your own

Your Room An idea for the empty storefront with the keys in the door. One paragraph is plenty: what it is for, who walks into it, and what it looks like when they do. No form, no application, and no portfolio. A room here does not expire, and it comes down if you say so once. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. How to ask for Your Room
slot-street
A new shop, pitch or turning

The street, the campgrounds and the Outskirts An idea for somewhere new: a shopfront on the street, a pitch in the campgrounds past the treeline, or a turning off the Outskirts past the last streetlight. Say what it is for, and which way it goes. The campgrounds are for being somewhat apart, at peace, with the street still in reach. The Outskirts are for crowds, noise and staying out late, and for getting as far off as you can. Helen Edgar’s question helps: would it be just as happy on the campsite? Then it is probably a pitch. slot-wrong
Something we got wrong

Anywhere on the street A name spelled wrong, a credit missing, a quotation we cannot back up, a colour you cannot read, a button you cannot reach. Anything you cannot read, reach or press is a fault in the room, not in you. A correction is written up in the changelog and stays on the page it was made to, rather than being quietly swapped. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page. A security hole goes privately on GitHub instead. The changelog, where corrections go
slot-back
Taking something back

Anything with you in it Your photograph, your voice, your tray, your cabinet, your look, your page, your name in a credit. It comes down when you say so. One message, no reason needed. Coming down means gone, not hidden. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. What this site keeps about you
cb-whose-h
Whose this is

The CB was Ryan’s idea: a simple chat patterned after citizens band radio, one password shared with the community, no alerts, a short history cleared daily, and a radio that floats on the screen once you are on. It is the one thing on this street that talks to a server, and the only thing that sends anything anywhere, and the privacy page says in plain words what that server keeps. The type is Varela Round, by Joe Prince, for the letterboard, and Radio Canada, by Charles Daoud, Coppers and Brasses, Alexandre Saumier Demers and Jacques Le Bailly, for everything that is read, both under the SIL Open Font License and read off their own records rather than typed. The radio on the desk is ours. Everything is credited in the liner notes. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so.

The street’s town hall, at noon. The Fishbowl
A room for community Fishbowl Meetings for anyone with CB access.
fb-how-h
How a fishbowl goes

A fishbowl is a conversation for a lot of people that only a few hold at a time. A small circle in the middle talks. Everybody else sits in a wider circle round the outside and listens. One seat in the middle is always left empty, and anybody from the outside can come in and take it; when they do, somebody in the middle gets up and goes back out, so there is always a seat free. Nobody is called on, nobody is on a panel, and the circle is never closed. It suits a big group with one thing to talk through, because it keeps the talking small and the listening wide. James Carrier’s introduction at PeopleShift is where this room started, and it also says that some people find a format this loose and this level a little daunting. That is a fair thing to feel, and the outer circle is there for it.
fb-here-h
How it goes here

The middle is whoever has their microphone on. Everybody else is the outer circle, and listening there is a whole way to take part. There is always an empty seat. To come in, raise your hand in the call or say so in the chat, then unmute when there is room. When somebody comes in, somebody goes out. Stepping back is a thing you choose, and nobody needs a reason for it. Typing is talking. Something written in the call’s chat can be read into the middle, if you ask; you do not have to speak to be in the circle. Nobody is put on the spot. Nobody has to come into the middle, and nobody is asked to.

Executive Session
For those with the board role only.
es-what-h
What an executive session is

It is the board meeting without staff. A board closes the door for part of its meeting to talk through what cannot be talked through with everybody there: a review of the chief executive’s work, what staff are paid, a concern about somebody’s conduct, a conversation with the auditor. Sometimes the chief executive is asked to stay for part of it, and sometimes an adviser is asked in for one item. BoardSource’s guide to executive sessions, which this room is built on, recommends: Holding one at the end of every regular board meeting, so that having one never has to mean something is wrong. A written policy for when the board goes into session and who stays. A confidential record of who was there, what was decided and how the vote went. Telling the chief executive what was concluded, if they were not in the room. Ending the session once its business is done, and not holding closed sessions for what belongs in the open meeting. Those are BoardSource’s recommendations, not a Stimpunks policy. What our board has adopted is on our accountability pages.

Dopamine Dress-Up Den

Mix it, layer it, clash it. Nothing here comes in a size. Dopamine dressing is wearing what makes you glad to have it on: colours, textures and styles chosen for how they make you feel rather than for how well they help you blend in. Our glossary sets it beside unmasking, and it is often what happens when somebody stops dressing to pass. This is a shop on the street for it. There is a wooden valet stand in the middle of the floor and rails of clothes round the walls: put something on your head, something over the top, something underneath, the bottom half and your feet, in any print and any colours, and nothing has to go with anything.

a-look-of-your-own
A look of your own

If you would like a look on the peg with your name on it, tell us what you wear, in your own words, and the house will put it on the stand. Words, not a photograph. Say what the pieces are, the prints and the colours, and how they feel, if you like. Nobody’s body goes on the stand, yours included, so there is nothing to send a picture of. Your words go beside the look exactly as you give them. The house picks the prints and colours off the rails to match what you say, and says so on the look. If something you wear is not on a rail yet, the house draws it and hangs it up, with a line saying how it feels and how it comes off, for anybody to wear. Say how you want to be named, or be somebody in our community. Nothing is rated, and the looks go up in the order they arrive. It comes down the moment you ask, and down means gone rather than hidden. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. It is on the Community Center’s service board too, beside everything else the street takes in.
dd-rules-h
House rules

There is no dress code. Our Dress Codes entry is about what dress codes do to people, and it has a school in it that banned black clothing on the grounds of mental health. So nothing in here is required and nothing is turned away, and black is a colour in here too: every rail comes in all black, and choosing it is as much dopamine dressing as choosing all the colours there are. Nothing comes in a size, and nobody is measured. Nothing here is sold. The clothes hang on a stand rather than on a drawing of a person, because a drawing of a person is a body, with one shape and one skin and one gender, handed to everybody who walks in. Whoever is wearing these is you. No rail is for men or for women. A gown hangs on the same rail as a T-shirt, and a big wig beside a beanie. All the colours there are is borrowed from the title of our course, Neurodiversity and Gender: You Hit So Hard With All the Colors That There Are. How it feels counts as much as how it looks. Every garment on the rails says how it feels and how it goes on and comes off. Ryan wears Thai fisherman pants for sensory and comfort reasons first, and his own field guide says all of his outerwear has a means of escape, so every jacket in here says how you get out of it; it also says the knot on the pants is not accessible to everybody, so every other bottom half does up without one. Our Why Sheet for a hoodie makes the same argument to a school. Nothing has to go with anything. This street says on its front door that clashing is not the same as illegible, and in here that is the whole shop. Florals on patchwork on stripes is an outfit. Nothing is too much and nothing is too little. The dial never takes anything off the rails. The sequins, the boa and the big wig are all here at Gentle. The dial changes how much the room moves, which in here is only the rainbows on the wall, and only at MAX GLITTER; nothing flashes, and nothing sparkles on its own. Nothing is rated, kept or sent. No score, no like button, no best-dressed. The rails keep nothing, and the copy button puts what is on the stand on your own clipboard, for you to take wherever you want it: a shopping list, a message, nowhere. Closing the page empties the stand. Dopamine is in the name because that is what people call it. Nothing in here claims a colour does anything to anybody’s brain chemistry. It is a word for a feeling you already know, and the only one who can say what gives you it is you.

The room and its name are Helen Edgar’s idea. She suggested a Dopamine Dress-Up Den for the next shopfront, and the rails are the brief Ryan wrote from it: his own wardrobe first, which is Thai fisherman pants in bold florals, bold blocks and patchwork, button-down shirts in all sorts of colours, a haori over the top, and beanies and slouchy beanies in a staggering array; then Helen’s cardigans and flowing dresses; and then the rest of our community, some of whom take it further, with a veritable drag show of colour and variety. Helen’s look was relayed by Ryan rather than given by her, the witchy prints on it are the house’s guess, and she has the final say on it. The haori and the pants are named plainly. A haori is a Japanese jacket worn over a kimono, usually tied at the front with two short cords, and Thai fisherman pants are made so wide in the waist that one pair fits anybody, wrapped round and tied. Both were read off Wikipedia rather than remembered, and neither is anybody’s costume. tools/make-dressup.py builds this room out of one data file, and it refuses rather than guesses. It will not build a garment that does not say how it feels and how it comes off, a garment or a print it cannot draw, a set of colours with no all-black one in it, or a look with somebody’s name on it and not their own words. And it sweeps the room’s own copy, so that nobody can add a word here about anybody’s body, a rail for one gender, a rule about what goes together, a claim about brain chemistry, a word that turns somebody’s clothes into a costume, or a way of rating an outfit. The type is DynaPuff, by Toshi Omagari and Jennifer Daniel, for the sign and the headings, and Plus Jakarta Sans, by Tokotype, for everything you read, both under the SIL Open Font License and read off their own records rather than typed. Plural Mural

The street is Danny’s, and Danny repaints On the wall now: Queer without fear. A rainbow in six broad bands, red through violet, arching up from the foot of the wall on a navy ground scattered with small cream stars, and across the top a cream banner with its ends notched, painted in navy capitals: QUEER WITHOUT FEAR. This is the end wall of a building on the street, and it is never painted the same way twice. The street is Danny’s, and Danny rearranges what is on them for whoever turns up, so one day the wall is a rainbow and the next it is a hillside with its roots showing. At MAX GLITTER the wall repaints itself every three minutes, one mural dissolving into the next, and you can keep the one you like up for as long as you stay. At Gentle and Regular it holds still until you turn it over yourself. Every mural is on the list below at every setting, in words, with a button to put it up.
pm-chalk-h
The chalkboard

Leaning against the foot of the wall, on the pavement and not on the paint, there is a chalkboard for leaving a note to whoever comes by next. It is Helen Edgar’s idea, after the board at her floatation tank place. The chalkboard needs scripts to read it. A note, chalked up as Anybody who walks past can read this board, signed on to the CB or not, for seven days. Write what you would write on a board in the street. Writing on the board takes a CB handle and the community password: sign on at the Community Center, then come back. Reading it takes nothing. Anybody can read it, and only people signed on to the CB can write on it. That is what keeps the chalk in the community’s hands: the password is shared in our community and only changes if something goes wrong. A handle is whatever somebody typed, so a name on the board is not proof of who wrote it. A note is rubbed out seven days after it goes up, and the board holds thirty, so a full board loses its oldest note to make room. There is no archive and no copy. Search engines are asked not to keep it. The base station can rub a note out sooner, and so can we if you ask: what the board keeps. Nothing on it is counted or ranked. It is a board, not a feed: a note is there, and then it is not.

A mural of your own

If there is something you would like painted on this wall, tell us, and the house will paint it and put it up in turn with the rest. Words, not a picture. A person on it is nobody in particular, because a face is somebody’s own, and a mural of a real person would be putting them up on a street they never asked to be on. How the wall works

The wall turns over by itself at MAX GLITTER and nowhere else. A picture that changes without being asked is something moving on the page, and at Gentle and Regular nothing moves until you ask it to. Community Library

Knowledge is infrastructure. Access to it is mutual aid. This is our library, with the doors open and the sky in the windows. Books of the edges, zine walls, music, bookmarks, and things you can borrow and have, made by and for neurodivergent and disabled people. Nothing requires a card. You do not have to buy anything to be here, or explain yourself, or be social correctly. Libraries are already the most radical institution most people use without thinking about it: you borrow something, you give it back, and somebody else borrows it. No one owns it. Everyone benefits. At the library you are a patron, not a customer.
It asks nothing of you

Third places are the places between home and work that belong to everyone and ask nothing of you except that you turn up. No transaction, and no role to perform. Libraries are the third place, and especially for neurodivergent people, who get pushed out of so many other rooms: quiet corners for deep focus, tables for gathering, open floors for wandering, and nobody checking whether you are doing any of it properly. You can be there without performing being there. That is third places in our glossary, and it is Cavendish Space too: caves, campfires and watering holes, under one roof. We wrote about what makes one work for us in Neurodivergent Libraries.

The front desk

Librarians are doing the work the rest of our institutions walked away from. A palace for the people

Libraries are infrastructure, and not as a figure of speech. They hold a town together the way its roads and its water do, except that what they carry is knowledge, and safety, and the chance of walking out as somebody different from who walked in. Eric Klinenberg calls them social infrastructure in Palaces for the People, and we think that undersells them. Built with public money. Open to everyone. No dress code and no cover charge. They are worth defending.

Books are for use. Every person his or her book. Every book its reader. Save the time of the reader. A library is a growing organism.
— S. R. Ranganathan, The Five Laws of Library Science , 1931

cl-economy-h
The library economy

Borrowing is not only a way of running a building full of books. It is an ethic: a way of sharing what sustains a life that needs neither wealth, nor competition, nor owning anything for ever. Murray Bookchin named the principles under it usufruct, the freedom to use what is held in common without using it up; the irreducible minimum, the level of living nobody falls below whatever they put in; and complementarity, differences without a ladder in them, each of us a small part of something bigger than the sum. We call it the library economy, and tool libraries, clothing libraries and seed libraries are already running on it. What if we ran more of the world this way? Ours is the Things Library.

L-Space
