L-Space

Mass distorts space. Enough books distort it into something you can walk along. A library is not just a building full of books. It is a place in L-space: every library, everywhere, joined to every other through the sheer weight of what is in them. Knowledge is power, power is energy, energy is matter, and matter is mass, which is Terry Pratchett’s arithmetic, from the Discworld books, and mass bends the space around it. Enough books bend it into something you can walk through. What you need to find your way is not a map. It is a ball of string. — Terry Pratchett, Guards! Guards! , 1989 Read off our Library page, which quotes the passage it comes out of at length. Not checked against the book.

— Terry Pratchett, Guards! Guards! , 1989 Read off our Library page, which quotes the passage it comes out of at length. Not checked against the book. That is how we think about a library. Not a catalogue. Not a curriculum. A space you move through by following a thread, finding what you need on the way to something else, and getting home again because you tied one end to the door. A monotropic mind walks L-space whether or not there is a library in it: one thread, followed all the way in, and the rest of the building bends round it. The name for that from the inside is a rabbit hole, and there is one of those on the street too. — Terry Pratchett, Guards! Guards! , 1989 Read off our Library page, which credits it to Guards! lsp-unread-h
Have you really read all these?

People ask it about a big shelf of books as if it were an accusation. They have misunderstood what a library is for. An unread book is not a failure. It is a resource, a future you got ready for, and the books you have not read yet are the most honest part of any collection: the part that says there is more to know. That is the anti-library. Neurodivergent people often build our libraries this way. We follow threads, we collect ahead of a hyperfocus that has not arrived yet, and we buy the book because something in us knew it before the moment to read it came. That is not disorganisation. It is monotropism working across time, and in L-space it is how the shelves get so heavy. — John Waters Read off our Library page, WHICH GIVES IT NO SOURCE, and we could not trace it from here. It is here on that page's word, and it says so under the quotation.

Books of the Edges

We call our reading lists Books of the Edges because of where we live. Disabled and neurodivergent people are always the edge cases. The middle of the world is built for some people, with its neat categories and its smooth timelines, and real life happens at the edges: in the breaks, the mismatches and the overlaps, where systems fail to account for how complicated people are and where new worlds come from. The name is from Octavia E. Butler, whose disabled narrator in Parable of the Sower calls her philosophy Earthseed: The Book of the Living, after the Books of the Dead. L-space is the one place where every edge of every library meets every other.

Oook.
Not many people these days remarked upon the fact that he was an ape.

Oook.

A Discworld homage, from a library that finds him relatable Our library has a guide. He lives in the stacks of Unseen University, climbs the shelves with prehensile hands and feet, and communicates mainly in Oook. He was transformed by a magical accident and refused to be changed back. He kept his job because he was the only one who knew where all the books were. We find him relatable. He is Terry Pratchett’s, from the Discworld books, and this room is a thank-you note. — Terry Pratchett, Guards! Guards! , 1989 Read off our Library page, which quotes the whole passage and gives it as pages 3 and 4. Not checked against the book.
ook-why-h
Why we find him relatable

Not the ape. The rest of it. His body changed, suddenly and not by his choice, and he found the new one suited the work better than the old one had: shelves are easier to climb with four hands, and a librarian who can sort books with his feet is ahead of one who cannot. So he declined to be put back. Every offer to fix him was an offer to take away something that worked, made by people who assumed they knew what he ought to want. Nobody else got to decide that. And he kept his job because he was the expert: the only one who knew where everything was, which is a better reason to keep a job than most, and a reason an institution cannot argue with however much it might like to. On a Disabled people’s site that is not a joke about an animal. It is a librarian who was told what he should want to be, and said Oook.

Cavendish Coworking

every door shut, and not one of them locked Stimpunks is run in the open. Our team meetings are open to the world, because we default to open, and until now the only way into them was our Discord — which a great many people will not use, and that is their call to make rather than a thing to be talked out of. Open is not the same as an open-plan office. Nobody has to work in full view with every door propped, and nobody has to walk into a room to find out what is going on in it. So here the meetings are behind doors, the way a house has rooms: every one of them shut, every one saying on a note what is behind it and when, and none of them locked. The room our events meet in has a door here too, and up the stairs are rooms for just hanging out. You do not need the Discord, an account, or anybody’s say-so to knock and go in. Every note says when its room is in use before you open the door. The times are Central, as our events page gives them; where your browser will say, the note works out the same hour on your own clock underneath. The house in Bedford Square

Two of Henry Cavendish’s houses were kept for opposite things. At Clapham Common, then outside London, he worked: a red-brick house whose drawing room he made into a laboratory, with a forge in the room next to it, an observatory upstairs and an eighty-foot ship’s mast in the grounds for a telescope. Nobody needed to be let in to see that something was going on there: the mast alone told the neighbours that the new resident was different. In Bedford Square he kept his library, and he opened it for borrowing, at all seasons of the year, with a librarian to look after it. Anybody shown round it, his biographers write, would have concluded it was a house of knowledge. It was green throughout — green moreen curtains, green fire screens, green chair covers — and its mahogany blinds were lined with green transparent canvas: they could be down, and you could still see through them. It had rules, and the rules were his too. He signed the register for every book he took out of it to Clapham, like anybody else, and when the librarian died he gave a day a week to checking books out himself. That is the house this room is built after. A place can be open without being open-plan. What makes it open is that anybody can find out what is behind each door and when, that the rules on the door apply to the people who run the house, and that nothing is locked. Our meetings are where the Stimpunks team does its work, and the team goes in by the same doors you do. Everything on this page about Cavendish’s houses is from Christa Jungnickel and Russell McCormmach’s Cavendish: The Experimental Life, chapter 11, “Places” (second revised edition, 2016), read on 2026-09-25. The line about the librarian is their report of Thomas Young’s.

Why Cavendish

Cavendish Space is our name for psychologically and sensory safe space: caves for quiet reflection, campfires for learning together, watering holes for peer connection. We named it after Henry Cavendish, the eighteenth-century natural philosopher who discovered hydrogen, as Steve Silberman tells his life in NeuroTribes. Cavendish needed his cave. He also needed, now and then, a small set of his peers — the Royal Society’s Monday Club was his campfire — and he came to it on his own terms. A door is how you get to do that. Our page on Cavendish Space quotes Annie Murphy Paul on why a place to work needs doors: Here that authority is yours, on the doorstep. You decide whether to knock, and once you are in, the call will let you keep your microphone and camera off and stand off to the side, which is what the man the house is named after would have done. Next door in spirit: body doubling, which our Watering Hole Hangs welcome, and whose nature cams run up the street in the Jungle Room. The calendar with everything on it is on our events page.
On the other side of a door

Every door opens onto a room of its own, each with its call in it: the Events Room, the Operations Room and the Editorial Room for our meetings, and upstairs the Cave, the Campfire and the Watering Hole. Here is how the calls go: The meetings are open to anybody. Type the name you want to be called, and knock: you wait in the lobby until a moderator lets you in. No account, and nothing to install. The Hang Suites are for people signed on to the CB. Anybody can walk in and look round; to talk, and to be in the call, you need the CB, and the Community Center says how to get on it. Your microphone and camera start off, and staying that way is fine in every room. The calls are 8x8’s Jitsi as a Service, and the privacy page says what goes to 8x8 and that we keep nothing about a call. Nothing reaches a call until you join it. It opens in a window of its own on the room’s page, and leaving the page hangs up.
What is not in here

No open plan. Nobody is on show, and nothing is propped open to prove it. No lock and no list. Nothing to sign up for, and no Discord between you and the door. No register of you. Cavendish kept one for his books; this page keeps nothing and sends nothing. The hour on your own clock is worked out in your browser, from its own clock and time zone, and goes nowhere. No call inside the page. See above: it is behind the door, where calls go.

The Live Room

Sessions played in a studio rather than at a gig, and the band on the other side of the glass. A session is a band playing a room with nobody in it but the people making the recording — or a room with a small crowd in it, sitting down, that the band can see the faces of. A television studio, a radio station’s live room, somewhere with a desk and a sheet of glass. It is the nearest a record gets to being played in the room you are sitting in. That is why a room of them is worth having here. No queue, no crowd to stand in, no volume that somebody else chose, and you can stop in the middle and nobody sees you leave. On the desk so far: Austin City Limits, a television studio with a crowd in it, and two radio stations’ live rooms, KEXP’s and KCRW’s. Anybody else with a live room is welcome next.
lvr-rules-h
While the red light is on

Nothing plays until you press it. Nothing reaches YouTube until you press a strip, and pressing one plays that session and no other. Every strip says how long before you press it, and where and when the session was taped. Where a video is not the whole session, the strip says that too, because a runtime is only honest if you know what it is the runtime of. The desk is not a chart. Nothing here is ranked, rated or counted. The sessions are in the order they were patched in, and the order is not an argument about which is better. The red lamp is steady. It does not flash at any dial setting, and nothing else in the room does either. A light that can put somebody on the floor has no business in a room anybody is meant to enjoy. Nobody is drawn in the live room. The only people in there are the players, in their own sessions.
studio-acl-h
Austin City Limits Austin, Texas

A television studio with a crowd in it: the longest-running music series in American television, made by KLRU in Austin for PBS since 1974. Its first thirty-six seasons were taped in Studio 6A on the University of Texas campus, in front of a painted skyline of the city; since 2011 it has been taped at ACL Live at The Moody Theater, downtown. The Broadsheet Broadside

Manifestos and mementos, served across your bow. A broadside is two things. It is a large sheet of paper printed on one side and posted up where people will see it — proclamations, ballads, political views, advertisements — and it is the side of a warship, with every gun along it. Both definitions are Wikipedia’s, in print and at sea, read on 2026-09-25. This shopfront is the second, seen from a boat at the waterline, and what comes out of its ports is the first. Ours are printed on both sides, which strictly makes them broadsheets, and that is where the press gets its name. The form is the Stimpunks broadsides’, which whysheet.press prints: one sheet, made to be carried into a room and handed to somebody. Side A carries one thing you can read across the room, to pin up. Side B does the work, to hand over. And theirs is Alfie Kohn’s, whose Why Sheet was a single double-sided sheet laying out a case briskly.
bb-articles-h
The ship’s articles

One sheet, both sides. Every broadside prints to exactly one sheet, side A then side B, on a page that fits both A4 and US Letter, so it comes out of a printer in any country uncropped. Print this page, or press the button over a sheet, and nothing else comes out with it. Ink on white, on the screen as well. What you see here is a preview of the paper and not the paper, and it is drawn the way the paper will come out: white, because that is what comes out of a printer. Two inks to a sheet, and no two sheets share a pair. The pair is what tells two sheets apart face down in a stack. Every ink is measured on white before it goes on the press. Every address on a sheet is printed as the address. On paper a link is an underlined word that goes nowhere, so each one reads as the place it goes. Every sheet carries its credits and its licence on the paper, because a printed sheet is the one place a credit cannot be a link somebody follows later. The sheets are CC0: print a stack and give them away. A shot across the bow is meant to miss. A broadside here says what we hold and never what you must do. It makes you look, and that is all it is for. No gun is drawn on this ship, and nothing on it is aimed at anybody.

The Doom Scoop

Daily news, usually bad. Every morning a timer reads the channels Ryan keeps an eye on and fills a tub in the cabinet with what they put out between five the morning before and five that morning. That is the morning edition. The newest stands at the front with the scoop in it; the six mornings before it are behind it, each a flavour of its own and each a little more scraped out than the last. A week, and then it is gone. The eighth morning is not kept, not archived and not moved to a back page. It goes, and it is still on the channel that posted it. Up the street is the Doomscroll, whose whole shape is a roll with no end to it. This one has a bottom, and you can see it from the door.

Behind the counter

Nothing plays until you press it. Nothing reaches YouTube until you press a scoop, and pressing one plays that video and no other. Every tub has a screen of its own at the top. Any video in that tub plays where it is, or goes up on the screen, bigger, with the second button under it. Taking it off leaves the screen empty again. Every scoop says how long it runs before you press it, when it went up and whose channel it is on. A short is the shape of a phone, because that is the shape it plays in. Nobody here watched any of it before it went up. A timer filled the cabinet. What it asked about every video is whether it plays, whether it can be shown on this site and how long it runs. A video whose channel will not let it be shown on another site, or that YouTube shows only to signed-in adults, is a door out to YouTube rather than a screen in here, and it says which. The headlines are the channels’ own, word for word and capital for capital, and some of them shout. Rewriting somebody’s headline would be putting words in their mouth. Nothing is ranked and nothing is counted. No views, no likes, nothing trending and no most-watched. The sources are in the groups Ryan put them in and the order he listed them, and each one’s scoops are in the order they went up. A feed only reaches so far back. A channel’s feed carries its newest uploads and nothing older, so a channel that posts a great deal between two mornings has the earliest of them left off. Where that has happened, the tub says so on that channel rather than looking complete. Every time is Mountain time, the street’s own clock.

The MUD Room

Take your boots off, or put them on. The Slake is out the back door. A MUD is a multi-user dungeon: a world made of words that people walk around in together, typing where to go and what to look at. The first one was written by Roy Trubshaw and Richard Bartle at the University of Essex in the autumn of 1978. This one is the kind with nothing in it to fight. Out the back door of this room is the Slake, a tidal estuary with a marsh, a mill, a hut full of things people found in the mud, and an island you can walk to while the tide is out. There is nobody to fight and nothing is counted. You go where you like and look at what you like, and the people who live out there tell you what they are doing and what our glossary calls it. Everything is words first and picture second, so a screen reader plays it as well as a pointer does.

mud-whose-h
Whose this is

The Slake is ours. Every place, thing and person on it was invented for this room, and it takes nothing from any other game except the idea of one. The brief was Ryan’s: a non-violent graphical MUD set in Stimpunks.World, for exploring and learning, with Majuular’s Ultima Online Retrospective | The Last Hurrah as its inspiration. Ultima Online was released by Origin Systems in 1997. The games it comes after. Richard Bartle’s own history dates the first MUD to the autumn of 1978, when Roy Trubshaw wrote its first version at Essex. Paul Dourish’s introduction to MUDs says that when Jim Aspnes wrote TinyMUD in 1989 he set out to discard combat altogether, which is the Slake’s first rule thirty-odd years early. Lucasfilm’s Habitat, by Chip Morningstar and Randy Farmer with Aric Wilmunder and Janet Hunter, went into beta in 1986 as the first graphical virtual world. And Amy Bruckman’s MOOSE Crossing, from 1996, was a MOO for children aged nine to thirteen who learned to program by building things in it, which our glossary would call constructionism. The name. Wiktionary gives slake as a tidal wetland, and its 1868 quotation calls slakes common in Northumberland. The Slake is not any of them. Checked 2026-09-27 against sources read that day rather than remembered, and the page says so where it uses them. A tide mill's pond fills through a one-way gate on the rising tide and is let out through the wheel once the tide has fallen (Wikipedia, Tide mill). Common reed spreads mainly by rhizomes and stolons once established (North Carolina DEQ). Glasswort, which is samphire, grows on saltmarshes and is a pioneer on intertidal mud (Wildlife Trusts; JNCC). Grey herons may stand motionless in the shallows waiting for prey, and curlews feed by probing soft mud with a very long curved bill (Wikipedia). The Thames foreshore is littered with clay pipes, mostly fragments of stems (London Museum). A day beacon is an unlighted sea mark, and its daymark is the part made to be seen in daylight (Wikipedia). 'Slake' is a tidal wetland in Wiktionary, and its 1868 quotation calls slakes common in Northumberland. The Slake’s map and the view from the back step are drawn for this room. The type is credited in the liner notes, with every resident and the entry in our glossary they point at.

Pando Calrissian

Water it, and it spreads A hillside of aspen after sunset, with the root under it. Drawing the grove, and reading how much it has been watered, needs scripts. Watering the tree takes a CB handle and the community password: sign on at the Community Center, then come back. Looking at it takes nothing. This is one tree, and it is everybody’s. Every time somebody waters it, another stem comes up from the root, and the stems already up grow taller, reaching into what is left of the light. It is after the grow-a-tree game in our Discord’s Collaborative Nonsense channels, planted on the street so that it grows whoever is looking after it. It is named for Pando, an aspen in Utah that looks like a forest and is one tree, and for Lando Calrissian, because the name was too good to leave alone.
pdo-how-h
How the tree grows

Every watering sends up one sucker from the root. Each one grows over the waterings that come after it, and when a stem is old it falls and others come up around it, which is what the real one does. The root keeps spreading along the hill. There is no size it is growing towards and nothing happens at any number: it is never finished, because there is nothing to finish. Anybody can look at it, and only people signed on to the CB can water it. The password is shared in our community, which is what keeps the can in the community’s hands. The ground soaks for a minute after every watering, from anybody, before it will take more. If you arrive while it is still wet the tree says how long it has left. It is the whole tree’s wait and not yours, so nobody is timed. It counts the water and never who poured it. Watering sends your CB pass, so the tree knows somebody signed on is holding the can, and the pass is checked and forgotten. Pando is a stand of quaking aspen on the Fishlake National Forest in Utah, about 106 acres of it, and on the evidence of its DNA it is one tree: the Forest Service says it is “thought to be the largest organism in the world”. Every stem in it comes up from one root system, more than forty thousand of them, and its name is Latin for I spread. It was first described and studied in the 1970s. It is declining, and the Forest Service and scientists are working out why. Utah’s Division of State History says no one cause explains it, and that if one had to be named it would be browsing by deer, elk and livestock, which eat the young stems before they can replace the old ones; fenced enclosures have shown promising signs of it coming back. Watering this one does nothing for that one, and nothing on this page is a way of helping it. It is the idea we borrowed: a lot of stems that turn out to be one living thing. Bullet Journaling + Junk Journaling + Interstitial Journaling

My journaling is a mix of bullet journaling + junk journaling + interstitial journaling. This is a joyful and achievable mix for me that doesn’t feel like work, though it assists work. I keep my notebook open next to me as a regulatory artifact and as working memory.
onb-bujo
Bullet Journaling

Bullet journaling (BuJo) is an analog organizational system created by Ryder Carroll, designed to be a customizable, flexible method for tracking the past, organizing the present, and planning for the future — all in a single notebook. The core of bullet journaling is rapid logging: capturing information in short, scannable bullets using a simple symbol system. actions/tasks get a dot (•), events get a circle (○), notes get a dash (–), moods get an equal sign (=), and actions can be migrated (›), scheduled (‹), or marked done (×). NAME = Notes, Actions, Moods, Events. This quick notation means you spend less time writing and more time doing. Key components: Index — a running table of contents at the front of the notebook, so you can always find what you need. Future Log — a bird’s-eye view of the months ahead for long-range events and goals. Monthly Log — a two-page spread with a calendar view and a task list for the month. Daily Log — where most of the action happens: a running stream of tasks, events, notes, and thoughts for the day. Collections — any custom spread you add: habit trackers, reading lists, project pages, brain dumps, reference pages. These are where BuJo gets personal and powerful. Migration is a key ritual in bullet journaling. At the end of a week or period, you review your undone tasks and decide: Do this now? Move it forward? Strike it because it no longer matters? Migration creates natural checkpoints for reflection and intentionality, and it’s surprisingly clarifying to ask, “Is this actually worth migrating, or am I just hoarding tasks?” Bullet journaling is particularly compatible with ADHD and neurodivergent ways of thinking because it externalizes working memory, makes priorities visible, and is endlessly adaptable. There are no rules about what it has to look like. Minimal BuJo and elaborate BuJo are both valid. onb-junk
Junk Journaling

Junk journaling is a tactile, creative practice of making and keeping journals (or journal pages) from found, repurposed, and “junk” materials: ephemera, paper scraps, packaging, old book pages, envelopes, fabric, washi tape, stamps, tags, stickers, and whatever else comes to hand. Where bullet journaling is about organization and intentionality, junk journaling is about play, texture, and self-expression without pressure. There is no wrong way to do it. Pages don’t have to be beautiful, cohesive, or finished. The act of making is the point. What goes into junk journaling: Collage and mixed media: layering torn paper, magazine clippings, old receipts, maps, packaging Pockets and envelopes sewn or glued in for storing notes, cards, or small treasures Handwriting, doodles, and stamps alongside printed imagery Washi tape, twine, ribbon, and other found embellishments Lists, words, phrases, poetry, or stream-of-consciousness writing embedded in the visual Memorabilia: ticket stubs, dried flowers, candy wrappers, labels Junk journaling has deep roots in scrapbooking and art journaling, and it’s having a sustained revival in online craft communities. Its ethos is inherently anti-perfectionist. Because the materials are “junk,” there’s nothing precious to protect. You can glue that piece of packaging without overthinking it. This makes junk journaling a low-stakes, high-sensory creative outlet. For neurodivergent and sensory-seeking folks, junk journaling can be especially grounding. The physical handling of materials, layering textures, and making visual choices provides a kind of productive stim. It engages the hands and eyes while the mind wanders or rests, making it a natural accompaniment to listening, thinking, or decompressing. Junk journaling is also archival in its own way. Pages become a record of moments and moods through the things you saved: a bus ticket, a note someone wrote you, the label from something that made you happy. onb-interstitial
Interstitial Journaling

Interstitial journaling, developed by Tony Stubblebine, is the practice of writing short, timestamped journal entries in the transitions between tasks, in the interstitial moments when you finish one thing and before you start the next. Instead of a separate journaling session at the start or end of the day, interstitial journaling is woven throughout the day itself. Each time you shift your attention — finishing a meeting, completing a task, taking a break, returning from lunch — you pause to write a brief entry. You note the time, reflect on what just happened, capture any stray thoughts, and then set a small intention for what comes next. A typical interstitial entry might include: What you just did or what just happened How you’re feeling, your energy level, or any friction you encountered Things you want to remember or follow up on Distractions that arose and what you did with them What you’re going to do next and why Why it works: Interstitial journaling acts as a context reset. One of the biggest sources of distraction and lost time is the mental residue left over from the previous task bleeding into the next one. By writing at the transition, you close the loop on what just happened, offload anything lingering in working memory onto the page, and create a clear mental starting point for the next thing. For ADHD brains in particular, this is powerful. ADHD creates significant challenges with task-switching. The old context can hijack attention long into the new task. Interstitial journaling gives the brain a structured moment to “land” from one thing and deliberately “launch” into the next. It replaces chaotic mental drift with a brief, intentional ritual. It also creates a running log of the actual shape of your day — not the idealized plan, but what really happened, how it felt, and what got in the way. This is invaluable for self-knowledge and for adjusting systems over time. Cognitive offloading: Interstitial journaling is a form of cognitive offloading: the practice of transferring information from internal working memory onto an external medium to reduce mental load. Working memory is limited, and for many neurodivergent people it is more constrained and less reliable than average, making the cost of holding things mentally quite high. Every unresolved task, pending thought, half-finished idea, or nagging “don’t forget” sitting in working memory is competing for cognitive resources that could otherwise go toward the thing in front of you. Writing it down moves it out of the mind and into the page, where it will wait without consuming attention. The notebook becomes a trusted external memory system — and, crucially, it only works as a trust-builder if you actually look at what you wrote. Interstitial journaling builds that habit naturally, because each transition is also a moment to glance back at the previous entry and confirm that what was offloaded is still held. Over time, this creates a feedback loop: the more reliably the notebook catches things, the more easily the mind lets them go. Interstitial journaling and distraction: When a distracting thought arises mid-task — something you remembered, an urge to check something, an idea — interstitial journaling gives you somewhere to put it. Rather than acting on it and losing your thread, or suppressing it and losing it entirely, you write it down. It’s held. You can return to it at the next transition. Resources: Interstitial Journaling: What It Is and How to Do It - TinkeringProd Migrated to the collection: the videos this part points at are on the Interstitial Journaling shelf.
onb-mix
Why This Mix Works

Bullet journaling provides structure and captures tasks and plans. Junk journaling provides sensory engagement, play, and a pressure-free creative outlet. Interstitial journaling provides in-the-moment grounding and transition support throughout the day. Together, they address different needs: the organizational brain, the expressive body, and the transitioning self. None of them require perfection. All of them work with how the mind actually moves, rather than demanding it behave differently. Keeping the notebook open next to you — not put away, not closed — means it’s always available as an external brain. It holds what working memory can’t always hold. It absorbs the things that would otherwise scatter. It witnesses the day as it happens. This is journaling as tool, as companion, and as practice rather than as performance.

Journaling Reflection Questions

Opening What does your current relationship with journaling look like? Is it something you do, something you’ve tried and abandoned, or something that’s always felt out of reach? Ryan describes keeping a notebook open next to him as a “regulatory artifact and as working memory.” Do you have something that plays that role for you — analog or digital? Bullet Journaling The NAME system (Notes, Actions, Moods, Events) and rapid logging are designed to reduce friction. What gets in the way of capturing things for you — too much to write, decision fatigue, forgetting the system, something else? Migration asks: “Is this actually worth migrating, or am I just hoarding tasks?” What would it feel like to give yourself permission to drop a task rather than carry it forward? Bullet journaling is described as compatible with neurodivergent ways of thinking because it externalizes working memory. Where in your life do you notice the cost of keeping things in your head instead of somewhere external? Junk Journaling Junk journaling’s ethos is anti-perfectionist — because the materials are “junk,” there’s nothing precious to protect. Is there a creative practice in your life where the stakes feel low enough to just make something? What makes it feel safe? The post describes junk journaling as “a natural accompaniment to listening, thinking, or decompressing.” What do your hands need to be doing when your mind is processing something difficult or drifting? What ephemera or “junk” do you already accumulate that might want to go somewhere? Interstitial Journaling The transition between tasks is described as a moment of “mental residue” — the previous context bleeding into the next thing. Where do you notice this happening in your day? Interstitial journaling is a form of cognitive offloading: moving things from working memory onto the page so your mind can let them go. What are you currently carrying in your head that you haven’t written down? When a distracting thought arises mid-task, the practice offers a third option between acting on it and suppressing it: write it down and return to it at the next transition. How does that land for you? The Mix The three practices together are described as addressing “the organizational brain, the expressive body, and the transitioning self.” Which of those feels most unmet for you right now? Ryan says this is “journaling as tool, as companion, and as practice rather than as performance.” What would journaling as performance look like — and what would it take to step away from that? What’s one small experiment you might try this week?
Star Stuff Reflection Questions

The star stuff framing does a lot of work because it positions the writer as ancient, cosmic, made of real matter. Some writing or speaking prompt directions that fit the ethos: “You are made of exploded stars. What are you made of, emotionally, today?” “What in you feels elemental right now — fire, water, pressure, light?” “Name something you’re carrying that’s older than you.” “What part of you is still forming?” “Where did you come from, and where are you going?” As a prompt structure L★S could be an acronym that doubles as a journaling framework: L Look back what just happened / how you got here ★ The still point what’s true right now, underneath everything S Set forward what you’re moving toward

Our glossary has an entry for the spiky profile: strengths and difficulties further apart than most people’s, so that a graph of them comes out as peaks and troughs rather than a flat line. It is a description and not a verdict. Not in the same way, and not for the same reasons: a person’s profile is a life, and a model’s is its training data and the system somebody built around it. Hey, Good Cookin’

No one is turned away at our kitchen. A hall with every pot on, on a cold day. The steam off the line has fogged the windows from one end to the other, so the daylight comes in soft along that whole wall and lands on nothing in particular. The only sharp light in here is where a drop has run down the glass and cleared a line you can see the day through. There is no lamp over the food: the pans on the line sit in hot water, which is what keeps them warm, and where all that steam comes from.
hgc-welcome-h
Come in

Come to the community kitchen if you’re hungry. Come if you’re curious about cooking. Whether hungry for food or hungry for knowledge, no one is turned away at our kitchen. Here, you are fed with no strings attached. You don’t have to pay. You don’t have to volunteer. You can just come and eat and be. Cafeteria style self-service, with sit-down restaurant-style seating so you can sit alone, together with friends, or together with strangers who might become friends. Seat yourself. Just look for the communication badge placards at each table. — Ryan Boren, for the kitchen
hgc-index-h
In the hall

hgc-strings-h
No strings

Nothing is asked of you here: not money, not an hour at the sink, not your name, not a reason. There is no jar by the trays and no rota on the wall, and nobody asks whether you really need it. Eat, sit as long as you like, and go when you are ready. The other place on this street where nothing costs anything is Nothing For Sale, out on the road past the last streetlight: a free market in a lay-by, where everything on the tables is free to take.
hgc-seat-h
Seat yourself

The placards are the interaction badges our community already wears at events, set on a table instead of pinned to a shirt. Each one says how open the table is to company, so nobody at it has to say so out loud, again and again, to everybody who walks up. Colour is never alone: every placard carries a shape and a word as well, so it reads in grey, in bad light, and for anybody who does not see colour the way it was printed. Green · circle open community seating where strangers are welcome, you don’t have to ask, just sit wherever there’s a space Yellow · triangle if you know one of the folks already seated, you can ask to join Red · square please don’t sit here, I want to be alone And the rules for them, in Ryan’s words too: If a table doesn’t have a placard, pick one up at the station at the front, and sit it on the table. If you’re last to leave a table, return the placard to the placard station. Please don’t red placard a large table. They are for 2-top and 4-top tables. Fill the 2-top tables first. A table with no placard on it is a table nobody is at yet. A placard is about that table at that meal, never about the person behind it, and it can change: swap it at the station whenever you like, and nobody needs to know why.
hgc-line-h
The line

Cafeteria style: take a tray from the shelf at the start, slide it along, help yourself, and seat yourself. Every card says what is in the dish, whether it is vegan or vegetarian or which animal it came from, and which of the nine major food allergens it has in it: the nine the FDA names, which are milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soy and sesame. Gluten is on the card too, because barley and rye carry it as well as wheat. Nothing here is certified halal or kosher. Every dish with meat in it says which animal, so you can choose, and pork is only ever in a pan that says pork. Everything is cooked in one kitchen, so a dish that does not list an allergen may still have been near one: if an allergy is serious, say so at the line, and somebody will tell you what has been near what. Every cheese in a vegetarian dish is made with a rennet that came from no animal. There are no calorie counts, and nothing on a card says what a dish will do for you. Food is food. Nobody here says picky, and nobody is told to finish anything. Anybody who needs their food kept further apart than the plain things below is welcome at Samefood Cafe, a few doors along, and anybody who would rather build their own bowl out of a plant-based pantry, at Vital Plant Living.
hgc-shelf-h
The shelf at the start of the line

Take what you need from it. Nobody asks why. Trays, plates, bowls and cutlery, at the height of a seat as well as a standing hand. Cutlery with fat handles, and cutlery with weight in it. Plates with a raised edge to push food up against. Cups with lids, and bendy straws, paper and plastic. A tray with a lip all round, to carry across your knees.

hgc-chair-h
The line from a chair

The line and every table are built to work from a wheelchair. Every number here is out of the 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design, as the U.S. Access Board publishes them, and each one links to its section there. The tray slide runs the whole length of the line, with its top between 28 and 34 inches (710 and 865 mm) off the floor, so a tray slides along at the height of a seat. ADA 904 Every pan, shelf and dispenser on the line is in reach from a seat: nothing higher than 48 inches (1220 mm) and nothing lower than 15 inches (380 mm). The standard asks this of at least half of each kind of self-service shelf. Here it is all of them. ADA 308, ADA 227 Every table top is between 28 and 34 inches (710 and 865 mm) high, with clear space under it up to 27 inches (685 mm) and at least 30 inches (760 mm) wide, for knees and a wheelchair. ADA 902, ADA 306 Every aisle is at least 36 inches (915 mm) wide. ADA 403 There is room to turn a wheelchair right round, a circle 60 inches (1525 mm) across, at both ends of the line and by the placard station. ADA 304 The standard asks for at least one seat in twenty at a dining surface to be built this way. Here it is every seat, so there is no wheelchair table, and nobody has to sit wherever the wheelchair seat happens to be. ADA 226 And what no standard measures: Help on the line is offered, never assumed. Ask for a hand with a tray, a ladle or a lid, and somebody gives it; nobody takes your tray off you to be kind. If the line is more than you have in you today — standing, waiting, carrying, choosing quickly — sit down anywhere and say so, and somebody brings the week’s board, and then the plate. At every table one place has no chair in it, and every chair lifts out, so anybody can sit anywhere. The whole week is on this page, so you can choose before you arrive rather than at the counter with people waiting behind you.
hgc-classes-h
The teaching kitchen

Hungry for knowledge counts too. The teaching kitchen is at the back: a counter at table height with room under it for knees and a wheelchair, a mirror angled over it so everybody can see the cook’s hands, and a screen beside the mirror. There is no sign-up, and nobody takes a register. Every class is written here in full, to follow at your own pace, in here or at home. Each one says how long it takes before you start, what it sounds and smells like, and that all of it can be done sitting down. Nothing is graded, and nothing ends in a certificate.
hgc-class-knife-h
Hold a knife, or don’t

An onion, a carrot and a pepper cut small, which is how most things start Hands on 15 to 20 minutes In all 15 to 20 minutes Sitting down All of it. The teaching counter is at table height, with room under it for knees and a wheelchair. What it is like The knife on the board, a steady knock. Cut onion stings the eyes and nose for a few minutes; goggles hang on a hook by the counter, and nobody says a word about them. You need: A cutting board on a damp cloth, and a sharp knife: a blunt one needs more force, and force is what makes a knife slip. Or kitchen scissors, or a chopper you press down on. What goes in: An onion, a carrot, a pepper. Put the board on a damp cloth so it stays where you put it. Cut the onion in half from the root to the tip and peel off the papery skin. Lay each half flat side down: anything lying on a flat side cannot roll. Curl the fingertips of the hand holding it under, knuckles forward, so the flat of the blade rests against your knuckles and your fingertips are behind them. That is the claw. Cut by pushing the knife forward and down, and move the claw back a little after every cut. For something round, like a carrot, cut a thin slice off one side first, so it lies flat. Then do the same. If a knife is not for you today, kitchen scissors cut spring onions, herbs and peppers well, and a chopper you press down on does an onion in seconds. Frozen chopped onion and bags of cut vegetables count as cooking. Nobody checks.
hgc-class-rice-beans-h
A pot of rice, and a pot of beans

Plain rice for four, and black beans from a tin or from dry Hands on 10 minutes In all rice in 30 minutes; beans from dry take a night’s soak and 1 to 2 hours more Sitting down All of it. The teaching counter is at table height, with room under it for knees and a wheelchair. What it is like A quiet one. A lid that rattles means the heat is too high, which is the pot telling you to turn it down. You need: A pot with a lid that fits, a sieve, and a fork. What goes in: 1 cup of long-grain white rice, 1½ cups of water, salt. A tin of black beans, or a cup of dried ones. Oil, garlic, cumin. Rinse the rice in a sieve under the tap until the water runs nearly clear. Put it in the pot with the water and a pinch of salt, and bring it to the boil. Turn the heat to its lowest, put the lid on, and leave it for 15 minutes without lifting the lid. Take it off the heat and leave it covered for 10 minutes more, then loosen it with a fork. Brown rice wants more water and about twice as long; its bag says how much. Beans from a tin: drain and rinse them, and warm them in a pot with a splash of water, a little oil, salt, a crushed clove of garlic and a pinch of cumin. Beans from dry: soak them overnight in plenty of water, drain them, cover them with fresh water by a couple of inches, and simmer them until they are soft all the way through, which takes 1 to 2 hours depending on the bean. Salt them near the end.
hgc-class-soup-h
Soup out of what is there

A big pot of vegetable soup, about six bowls Hands on 20 minutes In all 50 minutes Sitting down All of it. The teaching counter is at table height, with room under it for knees and a wheelchair. What it is like Onions in oil hiss, then go quiet and sweet-smelling. The blender at the end is loud for about a minute; skip it and the soup is a chunky one, which is also soup. You need: A big pot, a wooden spoon, and a stick blender if you want it smooth. What goes in: 2 tablespoons of oil, an onion, 2 carrots, 2 sticks of celery, 2 cloves of garlic, 2 potatoes, a tin of chopped tomatoes, 4 cups (1 litre) of vegetable stock, salt and pepper, and whatever else is in the drawer. Chop the onion, carrots and celery small, and cook them in the oil over a medium heat with a pinch of salt for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring now and then, until they are soft but not brown. Add the garlic, chopped, and cook it for a minute. Add the potatoes in small cubes, the tomatoes and the stock. Bring it to the boil, then turn it down and simmer it for 20 to 25 minutes, until a piece of potato is soft when you poke it. Taste it. A soup tastes flat until it has enough salt: add a little, stir, taste, and add again. Blend it, or don’t. Soup keeps in the fridge for a few days. Reheat it until it is steaming hot all the way through. Another way: With chicken: stir in cooked chicken at the end and heat the soup until it is steaming hot all the way through, to 165°F (74°C). Safe temperatures, from FoodSafety.gov: Leftovers, of any kind: 165°F (74°C); Chicken, turkey and other poultry, all of it: 165°F (74°C).
hgc-class-one-tray-h
One tray, one oven, and a chair

Roast vegetables with chickpeas, or with chicken thighs, for two to four Hands on 15 minutes In all 45 minutes Sitting down All of it. The teaching counter is at table height, with room under it for knees and a wheelchair. What it is like The oven ticks as it heats, and the tray spits a little. It smells of roasting from about twenty minutes in. Oven gloves that cover the forearm hang on the hook by the oven. You need: A big baking tray, oven gloves, and a food thermometer for the chicken. What goes in: 4 potatoes or sweet potatoes, 3 carrots, 2 peppers, an onion, a tin of chickpeas, 3 tablespoons of oil, salt, pepper, and paprika or cumin. Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Cut the vegetables into pieces about the same size as each other, so they are done at the same time. Toss them on the tray with the oil, salt and spice, and spread them out in one layer. Piled up, they steam instead of browning. Roast them for 20 minutes. Drain the chickpeas, pat them dry, and scatter them over. Turn everything over with a spatula, and roast it for 15 to 20 minutes more, until the edges are brown and the potatoes are soft. Most of this is waiting, and all the waiting can be done sitting down. Another way: With chicken: leave out the chickpeas and lay 4 chicken thighs on the vegetables from the start, skin side up. They are done when a thermometer in the thickest part says 165°F (74°C), which is FoodSafety.gov’s number for chicken. Safe temperatures, from FoodSafety.gov: Chicken, turkey and other poultry, all of it: 165°F (74°C).
hgc-class-eggs-h
Eggs, and a scramble without them

Scrambled eggs, or a tofu scramble, for one or two Hands on 10 minutes In all 10 minutes Sitting down All of it. The teaching counter is at table height, with room under it for knees and a wheelchair. What it is like A quiet one. The butter or the oil sizzles softly; if it spits, the pan is too hot. You need: A non-stick pan and a flat spatula. What goes in: 3 eggs, a knob of butter or a spoon of oil, salt. Or a block of firm tofu, half an onion, a pinch of turmeric, salt and pepper, and black salt if you have it. Beat the eggs in a bowl with a pinch of salt. Melt the butter in the pan over a low to medium heat, and pour the eggs in. Push them slowly from the edges into the middle with the spatula, and keep going until there is no runny egg left: FoodSafety.gov says to cook eggs until the yolk and the white are firm. For the scramble without eggs: soften the chopped onion in the oil, crumble the tofu in with your hands, and add the turmeric, which is for colour, and salt and pepper. Cook it for 5 to 8 minutes, stirring, until it is hot and catching a little at the edges. A pinch of black salt at the end makes it smell of eggs, if that is what you want. Safe temperatures, from FoodSafety.gov: Eggs: Cook until the yolk and the white are firm. The temperatures the kitchen cooks to, off FoodSafety.gov’s chart What Inside, at the thickest part Chicken, turkey and other poultry, all of it 165°F (74°C) Ground meat and sausage 160°F (71°C) Beef, pork, lamb and veal steaks, roasts and chops 145°F (63°C), then rest 3 minutes Fish 145°F (63°C), or cook until the flesh is no longer translucent and separates easily with a fork Eggs Cook until the yolk and the white are firm Egg dishes, such as a frittata or a quiche 160°F (71°C) Leftovers, of any kind 165°F (74°C) Every hot dish on the line is cooked to these too, and leftovers are heated to 165°F (74°C) before they go back out.
hgc-screen-h
The teaching screen

The screen beside the mirror over the teaching counter. Every video on the rack plays where it hangs, or goes up here with the button under it. hgc-rack-h
The rack

The last month from cooking channels Ryan chose, in the order he listed them: their videos and their shorts, newest first under each. hgc-keeps-h
What the kitchen keeps

Nobody is turned away, and nobody is asked for anything: not money, not work, not a name, not a reason. Nobody is counted. No tally of meals, no count of who came, and nothing that remembers you were here. Every dish says what is in it before you take it, and which animal, if it has one. hgc-credits-h
Whose it is

pkp-cats-h
The cats

Every cat in here came from Rescue A Cat, the shelter on the street, and every one of them is waiting for a home. The café keeps no list of its own: each time it opens it reads the shelter’s, so a cat adopted this morning has already gone home, and a cat brought in an hour ago is already here, finding somewhere to sit. Press a cat to meet them: their name, what they are like, where they were found and when they came in, all in the shelter’s own words. Adopting happens at the shelter. Every cat’s card has a link to that cat’s own card there, where anybody signed on to the CB can adopt them. The café is not told who adopted whom, and does not ask. Where a cat goes is up to the cat. The shelter wrote down each cat’s mood when they came in, and that is all the café goes by: a cat who watches everything from the top of the cupboard stays up high, a cat who is only interested in food stays down on the floor and the chairs, where the crumbs are, a cat who went straight for a lap stays near the tables, and a cat who fell asleep before the door shut finds somewhere soft. Three legs, one eye, a kink in the tail: none of it decides where a cat may go. A cat with three legs gets to the top of the tree like anybody else. You can pick a cat up and put them on your lap, unless they want to be left alone, which is allowed. The shelter wrote that down too, and the café keeps to it: those cats have no button for picking them up. Sit near them instead. One cat to a lap: picking up another means the first hops down and goes somewhere they like. Look down and you see your lap under the café’s blanket, which it lends to anybody with a cat on them, because claws, and your table with whatever you asked for from the menu. At MAX GLITTER the cats wander about by themselves, now and then, one at a time, the way cats do. At Gentle and Regular they stay where they are until something moves them: wave the feather wand, roll the crinkle ball or put down a box, and whoever is interested goes after it. A cat who is asleep, or wants to be left alone, is not interested, which is allowed as well. The words say who went where at every setting; only the moving changes.

The telly

A telly hangs by the hatch, and the rack under it holds films from other cat cafés, most of them in Japan, picked by Ryan, in his order. Each one plays where it hangs, or goes up on the telly with the button under it. Nothing loads from YouTube until you press play, and every button says how long the film runs before you press it. The titles are the channels’ own, as they wrote them; none of the channels is ours or affiliated with Stimpunks. The telly. Nothing is on it. A Quiet Pint

A pint, something from the stove, and a table that fits you. Made like McAnally’s, in Jim Butcher’s Dresden Files. A pub a few steps down from the street, with a ramp beside the steps as wide as they are. The only light in here is the street’s. It comes in at the top of the walls, through thirteen small windows set at the level of the pavement, and most of it reaches the tables by way of thirteen old mirrors, each hung at its own height and tipped its own way. So it lands in patches, none the same shape and none in a row, a little dimmer and a little green, which is what old mirror glass gives back. Nothing in here is lit warm: the stove is shut, and nobody lights a lamp. Thirteen of everything, and no two alike: thirteen tables of thirteen heights, thirteen stools along a bar that meanders, thirteen carved columns standing where they stand, and thirteen ceiling fans. There is no television, no games machine and no jukebox, only a player piano. Nobody has to order anything to sit down.

The columns are wooden, each a different thickness, standing where they stand, and each is carved with a nursery tale. They break the room up, and they never block it: the plan above walks every way between them. The Twelve Dancing Princesses: a row of shoes, every pair worn through. The Enormous Turnip: a turnip as big as a barrel, and a line of everybody pulling at it, down to a mouse. The Golden Goose: a goose, and a line of people stuck to it and to each other. Jack and the Beanstalk: a beanstalk, climbing the whole of the column to the ceiling. Stone Soup: a pot over a fire, with hands round it, each holding something to put in. The Bremen Town Musicians: a donkey, a dog, a cat and a rooster, standing on each other's backs. Tables 1 and 4 are by it. The Princess and the Pea: a stack of mattresses all the way up the column, and one pea under the bottom of them. Table 3 is by it. Goldilocks and the Three Bears: three chairs, three bowls and three beds, no two of them the same size. The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse: two mice at a table, one of them putting on a coat to go home where it is quiet. Rapunzel: a tower, which is the column itself, with a window at the top and hair let down from it. The Fisherman and His Wife: a fish in a rough sea, and a hut on the shore. Tables 8 and 9 are by it. The sign over this door says neutral ground, and means it the way our own Third Places page does, where it is the first thing on a list: The characteristics of third places, from What Our Cities Are Missing, a video on YouTube, as quoted on our own Third Places page, which is where we read them. The same video, quoted on the same page. The term third place is Ray Oldenburg’s, from his book The Great Good Place , of 1989, and bars are among the first examples Wikipedia gives of one. What our page adds is the radical part, and the radical part is what this room is for.
aqp-rules-h
House rules

Neutral ground. Nobody in here has to be anybody’s host or anybody’s guest, and nobody starts anything. You never have to order anything to sit down, and nothing on the board has a price. Every pint says how strong it is before you order it, and the alcohol-free one comes first, in the same glass, at the same size. Nobody buys a round for anybody, and nobody asks what is in your glass. Fetch your order from the bar, or say so and it is brought to you. Nobody asks why. Sit where you like, and as long as you like. Nothing behind the bar has a screen. The piano is a player piano, and it plays only when somebody presses a roll, one roll at a time. Nothing in the pub moves, at any setting, the fans included. Nobody is counted: not the pints, not the rounds, and not you.
aqp-keeps-h
What the pub keeps

Nothing about you. The table you sit at and what is on it live in this page and are gone when you leave it. The pub’s own scripts store nothing in your browser and send nothing anywhere. Every card says what is in it before you order it, and every pint how strong it is. Nothing plays until you press a roll, and nothing is fetched from Wikimedia Commons until then. Every roll says how long it runs first.
aqp-credits-h
Whose it is

The brief is Ryan Boren’s, of 2026-10-05, and so is the name. The pub it is made like is Jim Butcher’s: McAnally’s, Mac and everything else in The Dresden Files are his, and nothing here is affiliated with him or his publishers. Ryan’s brief pointed at the Dresden Files fan wiki’s page for McAnally’s, and nothing here is drawn from it: the room is built from the books’ own passages, which Ryan quoted from his copies, and every quotation names its book. The tales on the columns are old and nobody’s; what is carved on each, and every word on the board, are ours. The piano’s rolls are recordings on Wikimedia Commons, each public domain on its own page and named on its card. The measurements are the 2010 ADA Standards’, read on the Access Board’s page. The drawings are Claude’s, written as code. Set in Amarante and Brygada 1918. Where each thing was read is in the liner notes. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so — and in this pub, nothing moves even then.

← BACK TO THE STREET
Your Room

There is a storefront on this street with nothing in it, and it is empty on purpose. It is not scenery and it is not “coming soon” — it is a room we are not going to decorate, because it is not ours to decorate.
THE OFFER, PLAINLY

One Disabled, Autistic, neurodivergent or otherwise stimpunk person gets a page on this street. You get: A room of your own at stimpunks.world/<your-room>, linked from the front door beside all the others. Your own stylesheet. Not a theme, not a template with your colours swapped in — a blank CSS file and a room that is allowed to contradict every other room on the street. That is the whole architecture here. Your name on it, spelled and pronounced how you say, linked where you want it linked. Help building it if you want help, and none if you don’t. Describe the room and we will build it; or take the files and do it yourself; or anything between.
What we keep

Four things, and they are the same four every room here already honours. They are not editorial control — nobody is going to tell you the room is too much. What every room on this street keeps, and why none of it is negotiable The rule Why it is not negotiable The dial works Gentle mode has to turn your room down without taking any of it away. It is the promise the whole street makes at the front door. Text clears 4.5:1 Clashing is not the same as illegible. Be as ugly as you like; be readable while you do it. Nothing autoplays Sound, video, motion: on press, never on arrival. No exceptions, including for a very good song. Credit what you didn’t write Attribution is a licence, not a house style. Quote anything; name whose it is.
conventions
What the street brings in

Some things turn up in every room on the street: the dial, the sign-off at the foot of the page, a job marker on the floor, the CB bar in the corner. As new ones develop, they arrive in your room too, without us asking first. That is part of being a citizen here. They are the street’s furniture and not a redesign: your room’s look, its drawings and its words stay yours. If you don’t like one, bring it to the Town Hall, where the street’s conventions are talked over from time to time and can change.
What we are not going to do

Edit your room for tone. Ask you to be more positive, or more palatable, or more professional. Take it down because somebody complained that it was weird. If we would not say it to Enid, we are not saying it to you.
how-to-ask
How to ask

Tell us what the room is. One paragraph is plenty — what it is for, who walks into it, and what it looks like when they do. There is no form and no application, and you do not need a portfolio or a reason to deserve it. Reach us however is easiest: through the Stimpunks contact page, or in our community.
with-your-ai
Build it with your AI, if you like

You can also design your room in conversation with Claude, or whichever AI you use, and send us what it makes. Copy the prompt below into a new chat. It asks you about the room first, then builds it as one web page you can look at and keep changing until it is right. Claude calls that page an artifact, and other AIs have their own names for it. When you are happy with it, send us the file or a share link, the same way as above. We take it from there. We bring the room onto the street, give it a share card and a place on the map, measure it against the four rules above, and fix anything that falls short with you rather than around you. Then we credit you, and say the room was built with an AI, the same way How this site is made says how we use one ourselves. That page is also the best short account of how rooms here work, if you or your AI want to read it first. You do not need an AI, and the room is yours either way. The prompt tells the AI to use your own words for anything about you and not to write your story for you. One thing to know first: whatever you tell an AI goes to the company that runs it, so tell it only what you are happy for that company to have. Nothing on this page sends anything anywhere. The prompt is text you copy.
The prompt

I'd like your help designing my own room on Stimpunks.World (https://stimpunks.world), a website run by Stimpunks, a Disabled people's organisation. The site is a street of rooms, and no two rooms look alike: every room is its own visual world with its own colours, typefaces and light. How the site works is explained at https://stimpunks.world/design.html, and the offer I'm answering is at https://stimpunks.world/your-room.html. If you can read web pages, read both. Make my room look like nothing else on that street. FIRST, ASK ME ABOUT THE ROOM. Ask a few questions at a time and let me skip any of them: - what the room is for, and who walks into it - what it looks like when they do, and where its light comes from (a lamp, a window, a screen, the floor, nowhere at all). Rooms on this street are told apart mostly by their light, so let that decide the palette. - what should be in it: words, drawings, songs or videos, anything to press - what it must never do - my name as I want it credited, how to say it, my pronouns if I want them shown, and where my name should link Use my own words for anything about me. Don't write my story for me. If you draft words, show them to me as drafts I can change. If I don't know an answer yet, pick something and let me react to it. THEN BUILD IT as a single self-contained HTML page I can preview and we can keep changing together. HOW THE PAGE HAS TO BE BUILT, so the street can bring it in: 1. One HTML file with lang="en", a that is the room's name, a <meta name="description"> of one short sentence saying what the room is (it goes on the room's door and its share card, so keep it under 200 characters), one <h1>, and headings in order. Put class="room-SLUG" on <body>, where SLUG is a short name for the room in lowercase with hyphens. Everything the room shows goes inside <main>. 2. All the CSS goes in one <style> element. Every selector starts with .room-SLUG, apart from :root. Every class name starts with a short prefix of two or three letters followed by a hyphen (for example "xy-"), and so does every @keyframes name. Declare every solid colour once, as a hex custom property on :root that uses the same prefix (for example --xy-ground), and use var() everywhere else, in the CSS and in any SVG fill or stroke. A translucent colour for a shadow can be written as rgba(). Set the room's ground (background-color) and text colour on .room-SLUG itself, and a link colour on .room-SLUG a: the street's own furniture (the way back to the street, the loudness dial and the sign-off at the foot) sits in your room and takes those. 3. Typefaces from Google Fonts only, under the SIL Open Font License or the Apache License 2.0. You may load them from Google Fonts for the preview; the street hosts its own copies. 4. No other external files at all: no scripts, stylesheets, images, trackers or embeds from anywhere else, and no <img>. Draw pictures as inline SVG or CSS. Don't use an image generator: nothing on this street comes from one. If I want a photograph in the room, leave a clearly marked space for it: an element with data-photo="a-short-name", role="img" and an aria-label describing the photograph, and list its name under Photographs in the notes. I'll send the photo separately, named to match, and only one I took myself, with the say-so of anybody in it. The street puts it in that space. 5. THE DIAL. The street sets data-intensity="gentle", "regular" or "max" on <html>, and the room has to honour all three: - gentle: nothing moves. No animation, no transition, no rotation or skew. Every word and every thing is still there. Gentle turns the room down and never takes anything away. - regular: motion only on hover or keyboard focus. - max: ambient motion is allowed. At every setting, nothing flashes or strobes (never more than three flashes a second). Until the street sets the attribute, follow prefers-reduced-motion. Add a small preview dial with three buttons so I can try all three settings. Put its markup, its styles and its script each in their own element marked data-preview-only, so the street can remove it cleanly and put its own dial where yours was. 6. CONTRAST. Every piece of text must reach at least 4.5:1 against the colour actually behind it. Put text on flat colour, never directly on a gradient, pattern or picture. Choose a link colour for every ground a link sits on, and make the keyboard focus ring clearly visible on each of those grounds. Next to each colour in the CSS, note in a comment which colours it is used with and the ratio. 7. NOTHING PLAYS BY ITSELF. No <audio>, no <video>, no iframes. For each YouTube video I want, put a <button type="button" data-media="LINK"> saying what it is, who made it and how long it runs (like 3:45). The street turns those into its own press-to-play players. Anything that isn't a single YouTube video, just link to it. 8. NOTHING IS SENT OR KEPT. No forms, no fetch, no cookies, no localStorage, no analytics. Any script is small, plain JavaScript in one <script> at the end of the page, with no onclick-style attributes, and the room still reads completely with scripts switched off. Anything meant to be found is reachable by keyboard and by a screen reader. Nothing is hidden with display:none or shrunk to a tiny target to make it a secret. 9. It works at 360 pixels wide with no sideways scrolling. Every meaningful picture has alt text, and decoration is aria-hidden. 10. CREDITS. Add a section at the foot of the room under a heading with the word Credits in it. Name every quotation (who, which work, which year, and a link), every typeface and who designed it, every song, and anything else borrowed. Don't quote anything you can't source. If you're unsure of a source, say so rather than guessing. Say in the credits that the room was built with your help, and name which AI you are. LAST, put this comment at the very top of the file, filled in in exactly this shape: one "Key: value" to a line, each item of a list on its own line starting with "- ", and "none" wherever there is nothing. The street's import tool reads it. <!-- FOR THE STREET Name: my name as I want it credited Link: where my name links, or none Pronouns: as I want them shown, or none Say it: how to say my name, or none Slug: the same SLUG as in room-SLUG Prefix: the two or three letters every class and colour starts with Light: where the room's light comes from, in one sentence Typefaces: - each family, exactly as Google Fonts names it Media: - title | who made it | link | how long it runs Photographs: none, or a line about them - the data-photo name of each space a photograph goes in Words: which words are mine and which you drafted Built with: which AI you are, and who makes you Could not do: anything I asked for that these rules did not allow, or none --> Keep improving the page with me until I say it's done.
A note on what happens if it goes quiet

A room here does not expire and does not need maintaining. If you stop updating it, it stays up exactly as you left it, with your name on it. If you want it taken down, say so once and it comes down, no conversation required. A gift with conditions attached is not a gift. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so.

A pebble is anything you bring somebody because it made you think of them. Gentoo penguins do it with stones; we do it with songs, art, poems, quotes, photographs, recipes, and whatever else was in our hands that day. We share artifacts of our constructionism. We share joy, sorrow, anger and pride, the silly and the serious, our truth and our lived experience. We share to remember and we share to forget.
