The Garden

Stimpunks is not one website. It is a knowledge garden, and this is the part of it you can walk out into: one bed for every site we publish, the path going wherever you like, and a gate at the bottom back onto the street.
What a knowledge garden is

Ideas spread sideways rather than down. A filing system runs subjects, then categories, then articles, which is exactly right for an encyclopedia and wrong for us. Our own page about the garden grows the other way instead: experiences first, then concepts, a glossary, patterns, recipes, environments, systems — each layer out of the one underneath it. Autistic Rhizome is the shape that describes, and it is a term in the glossary it describes. Nothing needs to be read in order. Skimming, skipping and stopping partway are all fine here. That sentence is on the garden’s own page and it is not a courtesy; a knowledge base that only works if you start at the top is a knowledge base for people who are not tired. It grows unevenly, and some of it lies fallow. The glossary and the pattern language have years in them; other regions are sparse, and a few are left alone for a season while the work moves elsewhere. A garden with no fallow ground is a catalogue — our words, on that page, and worth repeating in a room that could easily pretend every bed is thriving. When an idea outgrows a page it gets a site of its own. Which is what this room is a list of. Every bed below links straight out, because each of those is already somewhere, and a shopfront on this street promising a room you never arrive in would be a lie about the architecture. The working library behind it is not public, and the garden is. That shelf holds our own copies of other people’s work — things we can cite and cannot redistribute — next to private notes. What gets published is the writing that grows out of the shelf rather than the shelf. Everything linked from this page is open to anybody, with no account and no paywall. Nothing in here is ranked, counted or scored. No bed is the biggest, the best or the busiest, and no bed says how much its site holds. A number like that is wrong within the week and looks authoritative in the meantime, and a garden measured by volume is an inventory. tools/make-garden.py refuses both, so this stays true after we have forgotten we meant it. How the whole thing is actually tended is written up in three places, each answering a different question: the field guide to the system opens with what happens to everything we know when the person holding it is unavailable; the garden as curriculum reads it as a course of study rather than a filing cabinet; and start your own knowledge garden is the version written for you instead of for us. That last one is down the path.
The beds

One per site, in the order our own feeds page puts them in, which is not a decision this room gets to make. Beside each bed is the habit of growth it keeps, and every habit is different: that is what tells the drawings apart, rather than a colour of their own. Some of these were made with other people, and every bed says so on its face.
Stimpunks Foundation

stimpunks.org The garden itself, and the one the others were built to take weight off: a glossary kept in public, a pattern language grown out of lived experience, recipes for the environments those patterns ask for, and the frameworks that came out of all three. Its own page about the garden says nothing there needs to be read in order, and means it. What is growing here: A rhizome, running sideways under the bed and coming up in several places at once. That is the shape our own page gives this knowledge, and Autistic Rhizome is a term in the glossary it comes up in. Grown with Stimpunks Foundation, and everybody whose writing the glossary credits by name.
Star Stuff

starstuff.earth Zines, field guides and broadsides that start from something settled in physics, cosmology, chemistry or biology and let it carry an argument about belonging — not as loose metaphor, but as the same pattern showing up at more than one scale. Its about page calls itself the public flowering of this garden, which is its phrase and not ours. What is growing here: An umbel coming into flower: one stem, and every ray of it opening at the same height. It is the bed in flower because that site said it was. Grown with A collaboration between Stimpunks and More Realms, where a great deal of it was grown from seed.
Queering.Earth

queering.earth A cabinet of mounted sheets on queerness, illness and the natural world, with an accession register that publishes its own corrections rather than quietly fixing them. One of the sheets in it is about Monotropa uniflora, the ghost pipe, which makes no chlorophyll of its own and lives by what it is connected to underground. What is growing here: That plant, which is why this is the one bed in the garden with no green in it at all. It is carried by its outline and by the threads running out of it, the way the things in it are. Grown with Built with Helen Edgar of Autistic Realms, who is named on the sheets she wrote rather than folded into our “we”, and with contributions credited on the cabinet's own pages.
Cavendish Space

cavendish.space Caves, campfires, watering holes, the library of what we have worked out, and the habitat that holds all four — plus the Cavendish Cards deck, which lets somebody point at a picture instead of explaining, and the room sheets for working out which zones a real room can already hold. Everything there is free and CC0. What is growing here: The one bed with something built over it, because that site is about the structure: a frame changes what a bed can grow, which is the whole argument for zoning a room rather than telling somebody to cope in it. Grown with Stimpunks Foundation. The three primordial spaces are David Thornburg's, from From the Campfire to the Holodeck; the name comes from Henry Cavendish by way of Steve Silberman's NeuroTribes; and Ira Socol's home of opportunity is on that site's origin page beside them.
Penguin Pebbling

penguinpebbling.app A card game about bringing somebody a small thing for no reason, and about what that does. No winners, no pressure to perform, and you can leave whenever you need to. There is a cabinet in our arcade built on the same practice that deliberately takes nothing from that deck — the deck is the better thing and it is here. What is growing here: Runners: the plant reaches sideways and puts a new plant down beside itself, roots and all, without being asked for anything back. That is pebbling rather than trading. Grown with Helen Edgar of Autistic Realms and Ryan Boren of Stimpunks, together. The locution the practice is described in is Amythest Schaber's.
The Why Sheet Press

whysheet.press One-page arguments, openly licensed and editable, made to be printed and carried into a room where somebody is about to be talked over. You tick the sheets you need and the press hands back a single correctly paginated PDF with the citations intact. Nothing is uploaded and no account is kept. What is growing here: A seed head gone dry, which is the only bed here whose point is that you take it away. What it grows into somewhere we will never see is the intended outcome rather than a side effect. Grown with Stimpunks Foundation, and the researchers, lawyers and self-advocates each sheet cites on its own face.
Stimpunks.World

stimpunks.world The street you are standing on, and the loud half of the same lung. No single design system, no two rooms alike, credits scrawled in the margins, and a dial that lets you decide how much of it happens. The street is that way and the liner notes say where everything in it came from. What is growing here: A scramble: nasturtiums over the edges of the bed, out onto the path and up whatever is standing near them. Nothing in this bed has been kept in its row. Grown with Stimpunks Foundation, with a pitch in the campgrounds that is Helen Edgar's own room and a community board kept by Norah Hobbs.
Map of Monotropic Experiences

monotropicmap.org Twenty places a monotropic person goes, drawn as an island you can walk — attention tunnels, rabbit holes of research, infodump canyon, burnout whirlpools, the forest of joy, awe and wonder — with a second tool for drawing your own. Some of those places are where the good work happens and some are weather that other people make. What is growing here: A tendril: the stem puts out a feeler, finds something, and holds on. Tendril Theory is one of the places on that island, which is why this bed grows the thing the theory is named after. Grown with Helen Edgar's map of her own Autistic and ADHD experience, published with Stimpunks. Monotropism is Dinah Murray, Wenn Lawson and Mike Lesser's.
The garden next door

Through the ivy at the side, and not ours. Both of these are Helen Edgar’s — the grounded one, and the wilder ground beyond it — and they are here because so many of the beds above have her hands in them that a garden pointing only at itself would be a courtyard. Nothing over there is tended by us, nothing over there is on our feeds page, and neither of them is a bed: tools/make-garden.py refuses a plot that turns up on our own roster exactly as firmly as it refuses a bed that does not. You can see as far as the ivy and no further, which is why every drawing here stops where the ivy runs. That line was a woven fence for an afternoon, and Helen asked for ivy and stars instead. She was right about more than the picture: a fence says kept out, and ivy says this is as far as we can see. What it marks is the edge of what we know, never the edge of where anybody may go — which is the opposite reading, and the right one on a page about somebody else’s work.
Autistic Realms

autisticrealms.com Helen Edgar's own site, and the grounded one: neuro-affirming resources, reading lists, glossaries of the language to use and the language to avoid, and signposting for families, educators and Autistic people who have arrived without the words yet. Her own page sets out what the work is for as being, belonging and becoming, in that order, and she writes as an Autistic advocate, author and consultant who spent twenty years teaching in SEND early years and primary settings before any of this. Monotropism, flow and burnout are where she goes deepest. What is growing there: A nurse tree, which is planted to take the weather off whatever is growing under it until that can stand in its own light. The shelter is the work and it is not the same work as the growing — which is her argument rather than our metaphor: her page says young Autistic people need to feel accepted and understood first, and that the conditions come before the flourishing. Tended by Helen Edgar, who is a colleague and not a corpus. Her site is hers, her name is on her own writing there, and nothing of hers is folded into our “we” on this street either. What of it is already in this garden: She built Queering.Earth with us and is named on the sheets she wrote; Penguin Pebbling is hers and Ryan Boren's together; the Map of Monotropic Experiences is her own map of her own Autistic and ADHD experience, published with us. There is a yurt pitched in our campgrounds that is her room rather than ours, down to the colours.
More Realms

morerealms.com The wilder ground past it, and hers as well. Its own landing page says you have arrived beyond Autistic Realms and that things here are “looser, weirder, more speculative” — not a place of conclusions or answers but somewhere to wander, think sideways and dwell. Spiral time, liminal embodiment, neuroqueer and post-humanist reading, written monotropically. Its phrase and not ours: “there is no map, but there are threads, glimmers, and soft, weird spaces to explore”. What is growing there: A fern's crozier, still coiled. It opens from the inside outwards, slowly, and is the only thing in either garden that grows by unwinding rather than by reaching. Spiral time is that site's own phrase for how it moves, and a frond keeps the turn in it long after it has opened. Tended by Helen Edgar again — one gardener, and this is the plot she keeps for the work that does not have to arrive anywhere. What of it is already in this garden: Star Stuff and Queering.Earth are both Stimpunks and More Realms, which is how her own pages about them describe the arrangement — a collaboration between Helen Edgar and Ryan Boren — rather than how we have decided to describe it here.
The Garden Spider

There is a spider in this garden that will answer questions about it. It is grounded in the garden itself — the glossary, the patterns, the frameworks — so the words it reaches for are the ones we planted: monotropism, the double empathy problem, spiky profiles. That matters most for somebody who does not have the word yet, because you cannot search for monotropism if nobody has ever told you it exists. It can also be wrong. Generative AI can misstate, confuse, and confidently produce things we did not say, and scoping it to our own garden reduces the source of the distortion rather than the possibility of it. So every trail it puts you on ends at a page a person wrote: follow the link, read laterally, and treat what it says as a starting point rather than as us. A spider is a guide to the garden and never a replacement for it, and its best answer is an entrance. Those are our own sentences, from the page it lives on, and how we hold that line is written up at AI Collaboration and AI, Disability Justice, and the Ethics of Making. If you need a human read on something — anything that touches your situation, your community, or a decision that matters — say so to us directly. We are here. Ask the garden →
Start a garden of your own

None of this needs our budget, our tools or our people. The steps below are the short version of Start Your Own Knowledge Garden, and they degrade gracefully: most of the value is in the first one, which needs no software at all, and each later one only adds convenience on top of something that already worked. Stop wherever it stops being useful. A half-built garden is a garden, not a failure — and the opposite framing is how these things die, because a tool that only pays off once you have finished configuring it gets abandoned during configuration, on a bad day, by exactly the person who needed it.
Make a garden. No tools required.

One folder. Everything you read, save or write goes in it, untouched. One index file, listing what is in the folder with a line about why each thing is there. A habit of adding to both. That is a garden — no app, no subscription, no AI — and the line about why this is here is a small act of synthesis repeated hundreds of times, which is where the learning actually shows.
Never edit your own sources.

Not to tidy a filename, not to fix a typo. Every derived thing — summaries, categories, indexes — lives somewhere else and points back at the original. That single rule is the difference between provenance you can cite and a pile you have been quietly rewriting.
Put it in git, for mercy.

Not for collaboration and not really for backup. Once every version of your thinking is recoverable you stop being careful with your own work in the way that stops you working. Version control is mercy, made structural. The template arrives as a repository already, so check with git status before running git init anywhere — and check which folder you are standing in first, which is the one mistake on that page with real consequences.
Let something else write the index.

Past a few dozen files, keeping an index by hand stops being fun. The template ships a script that walks your originals and writes it for you. The index is disposable and the sources are not: if it comes out wrong, change the configuration and run it again, and never hand-edit a generated page, because your edits get silently overwritten — which is worse than being refused.
Make it searchable, when filenames stop being enough.

A library you cannot search is half a library, and a filename is a terrible index of meaning. The payoff is finding things by what they mean: somebody in distress does not arrive knowing your vocabulary, they arrive saying it hurts. Filling the Garden is the one-click version of the whole thing, including clipping an article into your library with its source and date intact, and it needs no terminal either.
Why the garden is off the street

None of it was planned as a system. It accumulated, the way a garden does, and then we went back and named what had grown — which is also the honest account of this street. The difference is that every bed out here belongs to a site that had to leave: an idea gets big enough that a page cannot hold it, somebody builds it somewhere of its own, and what stays behind is a label saying where it went. The gate at the bottom of the hedge is the one you came in by. The street is back through there, and it is a great deal louder than this. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes or plays until you say so — and out here the only thing that moves at all is the leaf shadow.

The Run

An open field, a row of trees, a porch to sit on, and every dog from the shelter out for a run. A field of grass with a row of trees along the back of it, a fence all round, and a covered porch on the near side with two swings, two rocking chairs and plush beds on the boards. It is a bright day with clouds going over, and each cloud’s shadow lies on the grass under it. The Run is painted in the colours a dog can see, which are blues and yellows and greys: there is no red here and no green, the grass is the yellow a dog sees it as, and the ball is blue.

Out on the Run

The dogs are at Rescue A Dog, the shelter on the street. The Run reads who is there each time it opens, and needs scripts to do it. A dog
Adopt them at Rescue A Dog → Adopting happens at the shelter, by anybody signed on to the CB, and the Run is never told who.
run-dogs-h
The dogs

Every dog on the Run came from Rescue A Dog, the shelter on the street, and every one of them is waiting for a home. The Run keeps no list of its own: each time it opens it reads the shelter’s, so a dog adopted this morning has already gone home, and a dog brought in an hour ago is already out on the grass. Where a dog goes is the shelter’s word for its mood, and nothing else. A dog who wagged the whole way in is out on the grass waiting for the ball; a dog who leans on everybody is on the porch, near the chairs; a dog who went straight for the radiator is flat out in a patch of sun; a dog who fell asleep before the door shut is on a bed, or in the shade. A dog with three legs gets to the far end of the field like anybody else. And a dog who wants to be left alone is left alone: nobody calls that dog over, and there is no button for it. Press a dog to meet them: their name, what they are like, where they were found and when they came in, all in the shelter’s own words. Adopting happens at the shelter. Every dog’s card has a link to that dog’s own card there, where anybody signed on to the CB can adopt them, and the Run is not told who adopted whom. Nobody gives a command on the Run. Nobody is told to sit, nobody is trained, and nobody is a good boy or a bad dog. A dog who brings the ball back is playing, and a dog who does not is also playing.
run-colours-h
In a dog’s colours

Most people have three kinds of cone in the eye. Dogs have two, which is what Jay Neitz, Timothy Geist and Gerald Jacobs found in 1989, and it means a dog sees in blues and yellows and greys. In 2017 Marcello Siniscalchi and his colleagues tested dogs themselves rather than their eyes, and the dogs could not tell red from green. Stanley Coren’s account of what that looks like is that green, yellow and orange all come out yellowish, blue and violet come out blue, blue-green comes out grey, and red comes out a very dark brownish grey. So everything the Run paints itself is a blue, a yellow or a grey, and the tool that builds the room reads every one of its colours to make sure. The grass is the yellow a dog sees it as. The sky is blue, which is one of the colours a dog has. The porch roof is slate and the boards are straw. The shadows are not blue: they are the grass’s own yellow, darker, because this is summer grass under clouds going over and not snow. The dogs are the one thing on the Run not drawn in a dog’s colours. A dog here is the same dog it is at the shelter and in the Profile of whoever adopts them, drawn by the same file in its own coat, chocolate and golden and brindle and all. The ball is blue, because on green grass a dog can find a blue ball and loses a red one. That is Marcello Siniscalchi’s own advice, given to Live Science when the 2017 paper came out, rather than something the paper tested, and we would rather say which it is. And the commonest colour blindness in people is red-green, the same pair a dog cannot tell apart, so on the Run nobody who has it is missing anything the room has put there.
run-tin-h
The treat tin

The tin on the porch is filled from the treat truck at the Truck Stop next door, out of the same list, so the two lots cannot disagree about what a dog is given. Shaking it brings the dogs who are only interested in food up onto the porch, hopefully. Nothing in the tin is on the ASPCA’s list of people foods to keep from pets, and the tool that builds the Run reads every bag against that list: no chocolate, coffee or caffeine, no xylitol, no grapes or raisins, no onion, garlic or chives, no milk, no nuts, no avocado, no citrus, no salt to speak of, no yeast dough or alcohol, and nothing raw.

A covered porch along the clubhouse wall, out of the sun and out of the rain, with two swings and two rocking chairs on it and plush beds on the boards for whoever wants one. A small television on the clubhouse wall, hung low, at about a dog’s eye level. It has nothing of its own on it. The rack holds Ryan’s pick of television made for dogs: dogs at daycare, dogs at play, a walk through the woods filmed from a dog’s height, and one channel that is live all day. The titles are the channels’ own, quoted as they wrote them, and some of them say what a film will do for a dog; that is theirs to say, and nothing of ours on this page says it. The dog telly. run-next-h
Next door

The Run is the first of the lots side by side where the buildings stop. Through the double gate on the far side of the field, one gate shut behind you before the next one opens, is the Truck Stop, where the trucks are, and the treat truck among them. Past that are the Green and the Pile.
run-rules-h
House rules

Shut one gate before you open the other. That is what the pen between them is for. Nobody gives a command, and nobody is trained, on the Run. Leave a dog who wants to be left alone to the shade. Every treat is from the tin, and the tin is from the treat truck, and nothing from your own pocket. Nobody is counted: not the dogs, not the throws, and not you.
run-keeps-h
What the Run keeps

Nothing about you. Who sat with you and which dogs you met live in this page and nowhere else, and are gone when you leave it. The Run’s own scripts store nothing in your browser and send nothing anywhere; the one thing they ask for is the shelter’s list. A film on the dog telly loads from YouTube only when you press it. Nothing about the dogs that the shelter did not write down, and nothing about who adopts them. Nothing plays until you press play, and every film says how long it runs first.
run-credits-h
Whose it is

The brief is Ryan Boren’s, of 2026-10-05, and so is the name. The dogs are Rescue A Dog’s, drawn by the same file that draws them there. What a dog sees was read in Neitz, Geist and Jacobs’ paper, in Siniscalchi and his colleagues’, and in Stanley Coren’s account of them; the blue ball is Siniscalchi’s, to Live Science; the list of foods to keep from a dog is the ASPCA’s. The films on the rack are their channels’, and Ryan’s pick. The type is Lilita One, by Juan Montoreano, and Mukta, by Ek Type, both under the SIL Open Font Licence. Every source is in the liner notes. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so — and on the Run, the dogs only wander off by themselves at MAX GLITTER.

Truckin’ Food Court

Five trucks round a covered porch, each doing one thing several ways, and nothing with a price on it. A lot of pale concrete in the sun, and a covered porch in the middle of it with picnic tables under the roof. Five trucks stand round it with their awnings out, and the sun comes through every awning in its stripes, so the colour at the Truck Stop is all under the awnings: laid across each counter and the ground in front of each hatch, a different two colours at every truck, and plain sun everywhere between. Everybody calls it the Truck Stop. It sits between the Run and the Green and serves both of them.
tks-court-h
At the Truck Stop
The court is wider than a phone: scroll the picture sideways to see all of it.
tks-trucks-h
The trucks

Every truck does one thing, several ways, and leads with a vegan way of doing it, the same size as the rest. Every item says what is in it before you ask for it, whether it is vegan or vegetarian or which animal it came from, and which of the nine major food allergens the FDA names it has, and gluten, worked out from what is in it. Every drink says how much caffeine it has. Each truck is its own kitchen, so if an allergy is serious, say so at the hatch, and somebody will tell you what has been near what. Nothing is certified halal or kosher; every dish with meat in it says which animal. Every truck has a low counter at the side of its hatch, no higher than 36 inches and at least 36 inches long, the 2010 ADA Standards’ figure for a service counter, and the tables on the porch are between 28 and 34 inches high, with room under them for a chair or a wheelchair.
tks-tacos-h
Tacos

Every taco is on two corn tortillas warmed on the plancha, with lime and both salsas on the side: a red one of tomato and chile de árbol, and a green one of tomatillo, serrano chilli and coriander. A taco is a Mexican dish: a small tortilla, corn or wheat, folded round a filling, in the words of Wikipedia's article on it. Mushroom al pastor Vegan In it: oyster mushrooms marinated in achiote, guajillo chilli and pineapple juice, grilled, with pineapple, white onion and coriander, on two corn tortillas None of the nine, and no gluten. Potato and black bean Vegan In it: crisp potato, black beans refried in olive oil, pickled red onion and green salsa, on two corn tortillas None of the nine, and no gluten. Al pastor Pork In it: pork shoulder marinated in achiote, guajillo chilli and pineapple juice, cooked on an upright spit and shaved, with pineapple, white onion and coriander, on two corn tortillas None of the nine, and no gluten. Cooked on an upright spit, the way shawarma is: Wikipedia's taco article traces al pastor to Mexico's Lebanese immigrants. Carnitas Pork In it: pork shoulder braised and crisped in lard, green salsa, white onion and coriander, on two corn tortillas None of the nine, and no gluten. Chicken tinga Chicken In it: chicken stewed with chipotle chilli and tomato, shredded lettuce and sour cream, on two corn tortillas Contains milk. No gluten. Fish, the Baja way Fish In it: cod in a batter of wheat flour and sparkling water, fried, with shredded cabbage, pico de gallo and lime mayonnaise, on two corn tortillas Contains eggs, fish, wheat and gluten. Fish tacos come from Baja California, Wikipedia's taco article says. Quesabirria Beef In it: beef stewed with guajillo and ancho chillies, folded with melted Oaxaca cheese and crisped on the plancha, with a cup of the broth for dipping, on two corn tortillas Contains milk. No gluten. Birria comes from Jalisco, where it is often goat; quesabirria, with the cheese and the broth to dip it in, from Tijuana. Wikipedia's articles on them say so. This one is beef.
tks-banh-mi-h
Bánh mì

Every bánh mì is a Vietnamese baguette, thin in the crust and light in the middle, with đồ chua, the pickled carrot and daikon, and cucumber, coriander and fresh chilli in it as well as what it is named for. The baguette came to Vietnam under French rule from the 1860s, and the sandwich became what it is in Saigon in the 1950s, Wikipedia's article on it says. The bread may be made with rice flour as well as wheat. Bánh mì chay Vegan In it: lemongrass tofu, mushroom pâté, eggless mayonnaise and soy sauce, with đồ chua, cucumber, coriander and chilli, in a baguette Contains wheat, soy and gluten. Chay is vegetarian. This one is vegan all the way down, the mayonnaise included. Bánh mì nấm Vegan In it: oyster mushrooms grilled with lemongrass and soy sauce, eggless mayonnaise, đồ chua, cucumber, coriander and chilli, in a baguette Contains wheat, soy and gluten. Nấm is mushroom. Bánh mì đặc biệt Pork In it: pork liver pâté, chả lụa pork roll, sliced roast pork, mayonnaise and soy sauce, with đồ chua, cucumber, coriander and chilli, in a baguette Contains eggs, wheat, soy and gluten. Đặc biệt is the special, with a bit of everything from the pork side of the board. Bánh mì thịt nướng Pork In it: pork grilled with lemongrass and fish sauce, mayonnaise, đồ chua, cucumber, coriander and chilli, in a baguette Contains eggs, fish, wheat and gluten. Thịt nướng is grilled meat. Bánh mì gà Chicken In it: chicken grilled with lemongrass, mayonnaise, đồ chua, cucumber, coriander and chilli, in a baguette Contains eggs, wheat and gluten. Gà is chicken. Bánh mì trứng Vegetarian In it: two fried eggs, soy sauce and mayonnaise, with đồ chua, cucumber, coriander and chilli, in a baguette Contains eggs, wheat, soy and gluten. Trứng is egg. Bánh mì xíu mại Pork In it: pork meatballs simmered in tomato sauce, with đồ chua, cucumber, coriander and chilli, in a baguette Contains wheat and gluten. Xíu mại is a meatball sandwich, Wikipedia says, and these are pork.
tks-ramen-h
Ramen

Every bowl is wheat noodles made with kansui, the alkaline water that makes them springy and a little yellow, in a broth flavoured with its tare. Wikipedia calls ramen a Japanese-Chinese fusion noodle dish, made with Chinese-style alkaline wheat noodles. Tare is the sauce that flavours the broth: shio, salt, is the oldest of the four kinds, and miso ramen comes from Sapporo. Miso, on kombu Vegan In it: ramen noodles of wheat, water and kansui, in a broth of kombu and dried shiitake with white miso tare, with fried tofu, sweetcorn, bean sprouts, spring onion and toasted sesame Contains wheat, soy, sesame and gluten. Vegetable shio Vegan In it: ramen noodles of wheat, water and kansui, in a clear broth of kombu and vegetables with salt tare, with bok choy, bamboo shoots, nori and spring onion Contains wheat and gluten. Spicy sesame Vegan In it: ramen noodles of wheat, water and kansui, in a broth of soy milk and kombu with sesame paste and chilli oil, with minced shiitake and bok choy Contains wheat, soy, sesame and gluten. Shōyu Chicken In it: ramen noodles of wheat, water and kansui, in chicken broth with soy sauce tare, with roast chicken, bamboo shoots, nori and spring onion Contains wheat, soy and gluten. Tonkotsu Pork In it: ramen noodles of wheat, water and kansui, in pork bone broth simmered for hours, with chashu pork belly, a soft-boiled egg, wood ear mushroom, nori and spring onion Contains eggs, wheat and gluten. Tonkotsu is pork bone, and the broth is the cloudy kind that takes all day. Sapporo miso Chicken and pork In it: ramen noodles of wheat, water and kansui, in chicken broth with red miso tare, with minced pork, sweetcorn, a pat of butter, bean sprouts and spring onion Contains milk, wheat, soy and gluten.
tks-treats-h
Treats

Everything on this truck is for a dog, and it says so on every bag. Take one across to the Run next door, where the dogs from the shelter are out, or to a dog of your own. Nothing on this truck is on the ASPCA's list of people foods to keep from pets: no chocolate, coffee or caffeine, no xylitol, no grapes or raisins, no onion, garlic or chives, no milk, no nuts, no avocado, no citrus, no salt to speak of, no yeast dough or alcohol, and nothing raw. The tool that builds this board checks every bag against that list. Pumpkin and oat biscuits Vegan For dogs. In it: pumpkin, oat flour and plain peanut butter, baked hard For anybody handling it: contains peanuts. No gluten. The peanut butter is peanuts and nothing else. Sweet potato chews Vegan For dogs. In it: sweet potato, sliced and dried slowly For anybody handling it: none of the nine, and no gluten. Banana and peanut butter licks Vegan For dogs. In it: banana and plain peanut butter, blended with water and frozen in a paper cup For anybody handling it: contains peanuts. No gluten. The peanut butter is peanuts and nothing else. Chicken jerky Chicken For dogs. In it: chicken breast, cooked and dried, and nothing else For anybody handling it: none of the nine, and no gluten. Beef liver bites Beef For dogs. In it: beef liver, baked dry and cut small For anybody handling it: none of the nine, and no gluten. Salmon and sweet potato bites Fish For dogs. In it: cooked salmon, sweet potato and oat flour, baked For anybody handling it: contains fish. No gluten.
tks-cooler-h
The Cooler

Everything cold to drink, and plenty of ice. Every cup says what is in it and how much caffeine. Agua fresca is fruit, flowers, seeds or grains blended with sugar and water, Wikipedia's article on it says, and jamaica, made with hibiscus, is one of the commonest. Shaved ice is a raspado in Mexico, kakigōri in Japan and shave ice in Hawaii. Iced water Vegan In it: filtered water, over ice None of the nine, and no gluten. No caffeine. Sparkling, if you ask. Iced tea Vegan In it: black tea brewed strong and poured over ice, with a wedge of lemon None of the nine, and no gluten. Has caffeine. Sweet, if you ask. Lemonade Vegan In it: lemon juice, sugar and water, over ice None of the nine, and no gluten. No caffeine. Agua de jamaica Vegan In it: hibiscus flowers steeped and chilled, sweetened with sugar, over ice None of the nine, and no gluten. No caffeine. Hibiscus tea is made from the calyces of the roselle flower. Agua fresca de sandía Vegan In it: watermelon blended with water and lime juice, over ice None of the nine, and no gluten. No caffeine. Brown sugar milk tea, with boba Vegan In it: black tea, oat milk, brown sugar syrup and tapioca pearls, over ice None of the nine, and no gluten. Has caffeine. Dairy milk, if you ask. Bubble tea comes from Taiwan, in the 1980s, Wikipedia says, and the pearls are tapioca, which is cassava. Jasmine milk tea, with boba Vegan In it: jasmine green tea, oat milk, cane sugar syrup and tapioca pearls, over ice None of the nine, and no gluten. Has caffeine. Dairy milk, if you ask. Raspado Vegan In it: ice shaved fine, with mango syrup, chamoy and a pinch of chilli and lime salt None of the nine, and no gluten. No caffeine. Chamoy is a sauce of pickled fruit and chilli. Oral rehydration solution Vegan In it: water with sodium chloride, glucose, potassium chloride and trisodium citrate, in the World Health Organization's amounts None of the nine, and no gluten. No caffeine. The WHO's recipe, per litre of water: 2.6 g of sodium chloride, 13.5 g of glucose, 1.5 g of potassium chloride and 2.9 g of trisodium citrate. Plain, or with a splash of orange. Nobody at the hatch asks why you want it. Coconut water Vegan In it: the water from inside young coconuts, chilled None of the nine, and no gluten. No caffeine. Salted lime soda Vegan In it: preserved salted limes, sugar and sparkling water, over ice None of the nine, and no gluten. No caffeine.
tks-free-h
Nothing has a price

The trucks hand things out. There is no price on any board, no till, no jar and nothing to sign; take what you want, as many times as you want, and nobody asks who you are or why you are hungry. Our own entry on third places asks where you are when you are not at home or at work or school but at a place that provides community without being required to buy stuff, and this is one of the answers.
tks-screen-h
The screen on the Cooler

The drinks truck has a screen on the side facing the porch. It has nothing of its own on it. The rack holds Ryan’s pick of films about the three things the other trucks make, on three shelves: bánh mì, tacos and ramen, made by people who know how and eaten by people who came a long way to. Every film says how long it runs before you press it. The titles are the channels’ own, quoted as they wrote them, and some of them rank things; nothing of ours on this page calls any taco, truck or bowl the best of anything. The screen on the side of the Cooler. Nothing is on it. Any film on the rack can go up here with the button under it, and nothing loads until you press one. tks-next-h
Next door

The Truck Stop is the second of the lots side by side where the buildings stop, and it serves both its neighbours. Through the gate at the left-hand end of the back fence is the Run, where the dogs from the shelter are out: its treat tin is filled from the treat truck here. Through the gate at the right-hand end is the Green, with a porch of its own to carry a cold drink to. Past the Green is the Pile.
tks-rules-h
House rules

Everything is free, and nobody keeps count of how many times you came back. Sit anywhere on the porch, for as long as you like. Nobody clears a table that somebody is still at. The treats are for dogs, and every bag says so. Nobody at a hatch asks why you want what you asked for. Nothing is counted: not the tacos, not the cups, and not you.
tks-keeps-h
What the Truck Stop keeps

Nothing about you. What is on your table lives in this page and nowhere else, and is gone when you leave it. The Truck Stop’s own scripts store nothing in your browser and send nothing anywhere. A film on the screen loads from YouTube only when you press it. Every card says what is in it before you ask for it, and every cup says its caffeine. Nothing plays until you press play, and every film says how long it runs first.
tks-credits-h
Whose it is

The brief is Ryan Boren’s, of 2026-10-05, and so is the name, which borrows a word that has been doing this a long time: Robert Crumb’s cartoon Keep On Truckin’, in the first Zap Comix in 1968, and the Grateful Dead’s song Truckin’, on American Beauty in 1970, with words by Robert Hunter. None of the song is quoted here. Where each dish comes from was read on Wikipedia’s article on it, named on its truck’s board; the oral rehydration solution is the World Health Organization’s recipe; the allergen line is worked out by the same engine as Hey, Good Cookin’, the caffeine line with Pekoe and Purrs’ words, and every dog treat is checked against the ASPCA’s list, which the Run holds. The films on the rack are their channels’, and Ryan’s pick. The type is Sansita, by Omnibus-Type, and Familjen Grotesk, by Familjen STHLM AB, both under the SIL Open Font Licence. Every source is in the liner notes. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so — and at the Truck Stop, nothing moves even then.

The Green

A wood, a pond, and a boardwalk round it, just after the rain. It has just stopped raining. There is no sun on the Green, so nothing casts a shadow, and everything that is wet holds a line of the pale sky along its top edge: every leaf, every board, every rail, the rim of every bed. A wood stands all round, there is a pond in the middle with the last of the rain still putting rings on it, and a wooden boardwalk goes round the pond in a meandering loop, built so anybody can go round it, with beds of herbs and flowers and vegetables all along it. It starts and ends at the covered porch, where you are.
grn-walk-h
Walk the trail

The boardwalk goes from the porch, round the pond, and back, and every stop on it has a resting place beside the boards. Here is every stop, in the order you come to them. Nothing on the trail is counted: not your steps, not the laps, and not how long you take.
grn-stop-porch
The porch

Where the trail starts and ends, under a roof, with the rain still running off its edge in a line of drops. The trailhead sign is on the post by the steps, and the steps have a ramp beside them as wide as they are. You might notice: The drip off the gutter, and the smell of the wet boards.
grn-stop-herbs
The herb bed

A raised bed at the first turn of the boardwalk, its rim at the height of a seat, planted with things that smell when you touch them. Planted: rosemary, thyme, sage, lavender, chives, mint, in a pot of its own, because mint runs. You might notice: Brush the rosemary and your hand smells of it for an hour. The lavender is heavy with water and bent over the rim.
grn-stop-vegetables
The vegetable beds

Three long raised beds along the boardwalk, every one 27 inches high, the height the University of Minnesota's extension service gives as comfortable for gardening from a wheelchair. Everything in them was planted to be eaten, and anybody may pick what is ripe. Planted: tomatoes, runner beans up canes, courgettes, kale, chard, peppers, lettuce, strawberries along the edge. You might notice: Wet tomato leaves, which smell green, and beads of water standing on the kale.
grn-stop-pond
The pond's edge

A wide landing over the water, with a rail along the edge at the height of somebody sitting. The last of the rain is still putting rings on the pond, and there are lily pads at this end. You might notice: Frogs, now that it has stopped. The rings spreading and crossing each other.
grn-stop-bridge
The bridge

Where the boardwalk crosses the pond's outflow, a little stream that runs into the trees. The bridge rises one inch in every twenty on each side, the steepest the trail ever gets. You might notice: Water going over stones, louder than usual after the rain.
grn-stop-rain-garden
The rain garden

A shallow dip below the boardwalk where the water off the boards and the porch roof runs to, planted with things that like their feet wet. It is full now, and will be dry again by tomorrow. Planted: rushes, sedges, irises, marsh marigolds, ferns at the shady end. You might notice: Standing water with the sky in it, and the rushes bent over by the rain and straightening.
grn-stop-pollinators
The pollinator bed

A long bed on the far side of the pond, planted for bees and butterflies. Nothing is flying yet: they wait for it to dry. Planted: coneflowers, bee balm, black-eyed Susans, asters, goldenrod, milkweed. You might notice: The coneflowers' heads full of water, and the bee balm bowed over under the rain it is still holding.
grn-stop-ferns
The fern bed

Where the boardwalk goes back in under the trees, a bed of things that grow in shade, and the softest things on the Green to touch. Planted: ferns, hostas, moss, wild ginger, foamflower. You might notice: Every leaf over you still dripping. The moss is cold and soaked through.
grn-stop-bench
The bench in the wood

A bench with a back and arms, on a resting place beside the boards, with room beside it for a wheelchair. You can see the porch from here, and the pond through the trees. You might notice: The quiet, which is mostly the drip.
grn-sign-h
The trailhead sign

On the post by the porch steps. The boardwalk is built to the U.S. Access Board’s standard for trails, section 1017 of the Architectural Barriers Act standards, and section 1017.10 asks a sign at the start of a trail for exactly these, so that somebody can decide before they set off. Everything on it is true of every part of the trail. Length 1,100 feet, one loop, back to the porch Surface boards laid across the way you walk, with gaps no wider than half an inch, and a strip of grit on every board, because they are wet Tread width 60 inches all the way round, and never less than 60 Running slope 1:48 usually, and 1:20 at the steepest, on the bridge Cross slope 1:60 usually, and 1:48 at the most Resting places a resting place at every stop, 60 inches long, beside the boards, with a bench that has a back and arms and room for a wheelchair beside it
grn-beds-h
The beds

Every bed along the boardwalk is raised, with its rim at the height of a seat, so nobody has to kneel in the wet to reach it. The vegetable beds are 27 inches high, which the University of Minnesota’s extension service gives as a comfortable height for gardening from a wheelchair. Everything in them was planted to be eaten, and anybody may pick what is ripe; nobody minds, and nobody keeps count. Every plant here is named by its common name only. A Latin name typed from memory reads as if somebody had looked, and nothing on this page was looked up in a key. Everything that is eaten on the Green was planted in a bed to be eaten, and that is the only thing on this page about eating anything.
grn-porch-h
The porch
A covered porch – allowing learning to stay outdoors in any weather – was essential.
Ira David Socol, Pam Moran and Chad Ratliff, Timeless Learning (2018), writing about William Alcott's schools in the 1830s, as quoted on our own Nature page.
grn-porch-h
The porch

A covered porch at the start and the end of the trail, which is where you stayed while it rained. Our own page about nature quotes a book about schools on why there should be one: Ira David Socol, Pam Moran and Chad Ratliff, Timeless Learning (2018), writing about William Alcott's schools in the 1830s, as quoted on our own Nature page. There are benches along the back wall, a rail along the front with the rain standing on it in beads, and a screen under the roof. Anything from the Truck Stop next door can be carried through the gate and up onto the porch: the Cooler’s drinks come over here more than anything.
grn-rain-h
After the rain
petrichor, the delicious earthy scent after rainfall, when oil from plants is released into the air.
Lucy Jones, Losing Eden (2020), as quoted on our own Nature page.
grn-rain-h
After the rain

The smell on the Green just now has a name, petrichor, which Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Thomas coined in the journal Nature in 1964, out of the Greek for stone and for the fluid in the veins of the gods. Our page about nature has it as Lucy Jones, Losing Eden (2020), as quoted on our own Nature page. The rain garden on the far side is full, and will be dry again by tomorrow. Nothing is flying in the pollinator bed yet. Everything is dripping, and nothing on the Green moves at any setting: the rings on the pond are drawn as they lie.
grn-screen-h
The screen under the porch roof

It has nothing of its own on it. Two racks stand under it. The first holds Ryan’s pick of films about cities and towns making room for green: wildlife corridors, mini forests, an edible garden city, a river with the concrete taken out of it, and cities built to take a flood. The second is the newest of the same, as YouTube’s search finds it, refilled every morning and chosen by nobody. Everything on both says how long it runs before you press it. The titles are the channels’ own, quoted as they wrote them, and some of them list what green space does for people; that is theirs to say, and nothing of ours on this page says it. The screen under the porch roof. Nothing is on it. Any video on either rack can go up here with the button under it, and nothing loads until you press one. Next door

The Green is the third of the lots side by side where the buildings stop. Through the gate on the left is the Truck Stop, and past it the Run; through the gate on the right, past the bench in the wood, is the Pile.

The Pile

Pallets, plywood, rope, an old piano, a slide off a playground that closed, and a den roofed in bubble wrap. Everything on it is whatever you say it is. A lot of sand with a big tree at one end and a heap of everything on it: pallets, plywood, tree stumps, an old upright piano, a metal slide, buckets, shovels, ropes, old chairs, fabric, duct tape, and pots of tempera paint, which has got on most of it. pil-history-h
Where junk playgrounds come from

The idea is a Danish landscape architect's, Carl Theodor Sørensen's, who wrote in 1931 about a junk playground where children could make their own world out of what was lying about. (Adventure playground, Wikipedia) The first was set up in Emdrup, in Denmark, during the German occupation. Wikipedia's article on adventure playgrounds says 1943, and its article on Sørensen says 1940; we have not read anything that settles it. (Adventure playground, Wikipedia) Lady Allen of Hurtwood, a landscape architect, brought the idea to Britain after the war, to the bomb sites, in a book of 1946 called Why Not Use Our Bomb Sites Like This? There the name changed from junk playground to adventure playground, to make it easier for councils to say yes to. (Adventure playground, Wikipedia) They are staffed by playworkers, and playwork, in Wikipedia's words, is the work of creating and maintaining spaces for children to play. (Playwork, Wikipedia) The one at the Berkeley Marina opened in 1979 and is still there. (Adventure Playground, the City of Berkeley) The Land, at Plas Madoc in Wales, seven miles south of Wrexham, has been open since 2011, and Erin Davis made a film about it, The Land, in 2015. (The Land (adventure playground), Wikipedia, and Erin Davis's page for her film The Land (2015)) The Yard, on Governors Island, is New York's only adventure playground, and grown-ups stay outside the main area so the children can play their own way. (The Yard, play:groundNYC) The idea under all of them has a name, the theory of loose parts, from the artist Simon Nicholson in 1971. (Simon Nicholson, Wikipedia) Simon Nicholson’s sentence is the one the theory is quoted by: Simon Nicholson, in How NOT to Cheat Children: The Theory of Loose Parts, Landscape Architecture 62, 1971, as Wikipedia's article on him gives it: Simon Nicholson. The Pile is for anybody, at any age. Nothing on it has been made safe, and nothing has been made dangerous on purpose: how high you climb is yours to decide.

The Campgrounds

Not everybody wants a shopfront. The street is a row of them shoulder to shoulder under a marquee that shouts at you, and some of us would rather be out at the edge of town with a stream going past. So the street stops here and the field starts, and the field has pitches on it.
WHAT THE FIELD IS

Nothing out here moves. Not at Gentle, not at Regular, not at MAX GLITTER. The dial still works and it still governs every pitch, because each pitch is its own world and sets its own noise — but this field has nothing for it to turn up. An area that exists for people who want quiet cannot have a loud setting and mean it. You can arrive and leave without telling anybody. There is nothing to sign, nothing to join, and nothing that notices you came. Read the sign before you go in. A pitch is somebody’s own place and it looks like them, not like this field and not like the street. The signs below say what is inside so that walking in is a decision rather than a surprise. The stream is the boundary. Past it is woodland and we have not drawn a map of it. That is on purpose too.

The Solarpunk Hermitage

A wood cabin on wheels at the far end of the field, bristling with panels, with sunflowers taller than the door and an aerial going up out of the quiet. This is my place, parked at the far end of the campgrounds where the field runs out. It is always morning here. The panels on the roof are soaking it up, the sunflowers are taller than the door, and the aerial on top keeps a thread running back to the street for whenever I want it. Inside there is a cave to read in, a campfire with a television and a stereo, and a watering hole with other people’s work left out on the benches. Come in, pick a corner, put something on or don’t. Nothing in here will ask you to say hello, and you can leave without saying goodbye. — Ryan
Solitude with the wire still attached

Every other room on this street is a dark ground with light put on it. This one is the morning. That is not a mood — a cabin that runs on the sun and reads as midnight would be an argument against itself, and the panels on that roof are the reason the reading lamp inside never gutters. The pitch is the furthest one from the street, which for some people is the whole specification. Betsy Selvam calls it lone wolfing — being alone well, rather than being left out — and the distinction this place is built on is hers: the aerial is up, the laptop is on, and nobody out here is unreachable. They chose the reach. Solarpunk, as our own glossary has it, is the future with humanity put back in: slower, more intentional, tied closely to the natural world. A future with a human face and dirt behind its ears.

The watering hole

A workshop with three tables on the go — a herbarium, a solar bench, and a table of Star Stuff. Where you learn from the people next to you. Pull up a stool → Those three are not decoration and they are not ours. They are the primordial learning spaces David Thornburg named in From the Campfire to the Holodeck — the cave where you learn from yourself, the campfire where you learn from a storyteller, the watering hole where you learn from peers — which our own glossary documents at Caves, Campfires, and Watering Holes. There is a fourth, Life, where you go and make something out of what the other three gave you. It is not a room in here. It is the door you came in by.

The shelves

Parable of the Sower Octavia E. Butler A girl with an unbearable gift for other people's pain walks north out of a collapsing California and writes a religion on the way. It is on this shelf because the cabin outside is the optimistic version of the same question — what do you build when the arrangements stop working — and because Butler refuses to let the answer be one clever person. Borrow or read it → On this shelf because we argue from it on Octavia Butler on Positive Obsession. The Fire Next Time James Baldwin A letter to a nephew and a long essay about what a country does to the people it will not look at. Baldwin is on more of our pages than almost anybody, usually in the sentence where an argument stops being comfortable, and a reading room of ours that did not have him in it would be a reading room that had been tidied. Borrow or read it → On this shelf because we argue from it on Allyship. From the Campfire to the Holodeck David Thornburg Where the cave, the campfire and the watering hole come from — the three primordial learning spaces this cabin is laid out around, plus a fourth, Life, which is where you make something out of what the other three gave you. The room you are standing in is named out of this book and says so. Borrow or read it → On this shelf because we argue from it on Caves, Campfires, and Watering Holes. Emergent Strategy adrienne maree brown Change as something you practise at the scale you actually have, borrowing its shapes from ferns, starlings and mushrooms rather than from strategy decks. Read it next to the sunflowers outside, which are doing the same thing without the book. Borrow or read it → On this shelf because we argue from it on Resilience. Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution Peter Kropotkin An anarchist geographer goes looking for nature red in tooth and claw, finds beetles and horses and villages cooperating instead, and spends a book saying so. It is the oldest thing on this shelf and the reason a hermitage is not a bunker. Borrow or read it → On this shelf because we argue from it on Mutual Aid. Care Work: Dreaming Disability Justice Leah Lakshmi Piepzna-Samarasinha Care as infrastructure built by sick and Disabled people for each other, on no budget, mostly without being asked. The book that makes it impossible to describe solitude as self-sufficiency, which is the mistake a cabin in a field invites. Borrow or read it → Buy it from a bookshop → On this shelf because we argue from it on Care Web. Empire of Normality Robert Chapman A history of how the normal was invented, who it was invented for, and what it costs to be measured against it. The book behind a lot of our glossary, and the argument for why a person might want a field between themselves and a street. Borrow or read it → On this shelf because we argue from it on Empire of Normality. Wild Therapy Nick Totton What happens to therapy if you stop treating the outdoors as scenery and the human as separate from it. The most solarpunk book on this shelf: technology and nature are not opposites here, they are the same argument with the fence taken down. Borrow or read it → On this shelf because we argue from it on Wild. NeuroTribes Steve Silberman The long, badly-behaved history of autism and the people it was done to, told with the autistic people put back in as its subject. Where a lot of readers first hear that there was a story before the diagnosis. Borrow or read it → On this shelf because we argue from it on Cavendish Space. Memory Craft Lynne Kelly Memory palaces, songlines and the physical memory techniques of oral cultures — methods older than writing, tried out by somebody who actually learned to use them. On the shelf because a hermitage full of books should also hold the case for not needing them. Borrow or read it → Buy it from a bookshop → On this shelf because we argue from it on Spaced Repetition.

The Outskirts

The street has lights on it and somebody sweeping it. This does not. Keep going past the last lamp, past the point where the kerb gives up and becomes a verge, and there are premises out here too — the mystical, the eldritch, and whatever else keeps its own hours. It is always dark in The Outskirts. That is not a mood we are setting. It is the hours.
What is out here

You can only see as far as your headlights. Everything on this road is lit from one low, level direction and goes black an inch past the beam, which is why the signs below have a bright face and no back. It is also why this page tells you what is down each turning rather than showing you: out here, a sign is the honest thing and a picture would be a claim. A sign with no road behind it is still a sign. Some of what is named here is not built. Those ones are lit and say so, plainly, on their own board — because an area that quietly listed rooms you cannot get into would be the street lying about its own architecture, and a website pretending it has no unfinished edges is doing something every actual outskirts knows better than. Each premises is its own world and shares nothing with this road. The verge is cold and dead and painted by hand. What is down the turning is not, and the sign says what you are walking into so that walking in is a decision rather than a surprise. Nobody was sent out here. Our town is stimpunks.world, which accepts everybody, so it has no outside to push anybody to — this road is a direction and not a verdict. What is down these turnings is here because this is where it is: a fort stands in a field, a screen stands in water, and neither of them is in exile. Out is not the same as out of favour. Nothing out here moves on its own. The dial still works and each premises sets its own noise, but the road itself has no ambient layer at any setting. Headlights that swept would be a car going past, and there is no other car.

An appreciation of The Cramps

Two people met in Sacramento in 1972 over a shared devotion to collecting records, decided that the obvious next step was to form a band, and then spent thirty-three years refusing every single opportunity to become a different one. That is the whole story, and it is a better model for a life than most of the ones we were handed. They moved to Akron, then to New York in 1975, and turned up in the early scene at CBGB alongside the Ramones, Blondie, Television, Patti Smith and Suicide. Lux Interior sang. Poison Ivy played guitar, and wrote, arranged and produced a great deal of what the band actually sounds like — which is worth saying at the top rather than in a footnote, because the singer is the one who gets remembered and the guitarist is the one who built it. The lineup around the two of them changed constantly. The two of them never did. The band was formed in 1976 and was active until 2009, when Lux died and Ivy did not carry on without him. There was no bass player. Not for years, and not by accident: two guitars, a drum kit, and a deliberate hole where the bottom end goes, which is why an early Cramps record sounds like something coming through a wall rather than out of a stage. It is one of the great examples of a limitation chosen on purpose and then defended for a decade, and if you have ever been told that the thing you do without is the thing you need, it is a useful noise to have in your ears. What they made out of that is usually filed as psychobilly — they are credited as the progenitors of it — and the recipe is simpler than the label: 1950s rockabilly, played at punk volume, about monster movies, with no wink anywhere. That last part is the part everybody gets wrong. The Cramps are funny, but they are never ironic. Nobody in these records is standing outside the material being clever about it. They loved the drive-in, they loved the cheap single nobody bought, they loved the rubber suit, and they played all of it absolutely straight, for decades, at cost. Sincerity about disreputable things is a much harder position to hold than a joke, and it is the reason this band has outlasted most of their contemporaries. And they were archaeologists. Half of Psychedelic Jungle is other people’s forgotten singles, dug out of a collection and handed back to an audience that had no idea they existed — a garage record from Texas, a novelty side from 1962, a rockabilly cut nobody had reissued. Their real argument, underneath the rubber masks, was that the good stuff had already been made and then dropped on the floor, and that somebody ought to go and pick it up. This street is largely built out of that same conviction, so we owe them the acknowledgement.
The Napa show, and how it usually gets told

In June 1978 the band played a free concert for patients at the state mental hospital in Napa, California. It was filmed by the San Francisco video collective Target Video on a portable camera and later released as a live tape, and it is one of the most-circulated pieces of footage they ever appeared in. There is no stage to speak of. The audience is right up against the band, people take the microphone, and nobody is managing the room. It is almost always told as a joke, and the joke is at the patients’ expense. The standard line — you will find some version of it wherever that tape is written about — is that you cannot tell the lunatics from the band. That framing is very old, it is extremely easy to repeat, and it is the exact thing this organisation exists to refuse: psychiatric patients used as the punchline that certifies how wild somebody else is. We are a Disabled people’s organisation. Some of us have been the people in that room. So here is the version we will stand behind, which requires no joke at all: a band went to a locked institution and played for people who do not get played for, for free, with the barrier between performer and audience removed rather than reinforced, and let those people do whatever they wanted for the duration. That is a booking decision, and it is a good one. Whether anybody in that room had a good evening is not ours to narrate — we were not there, they were not asked on camera, and every account in circulation is somebody else’s. We will not speak for them, and we would rather leave the gap visible than fill it with a nice sentence.
The door policy at the water’s edge

Nothing plays until you press play. Same rule as every other room on this street. No request reaches YouTube before you press something, and every record on a post says how long it runs before you do. The screen is the one control here that cannot say, because it is a playlist we keep adding to — so it says that instead. Nothing here flickers, at any setting. A drive-in screen is a flickering object; that is practically its defining feature, and building one without the flicker took more work than building one with it. It has none, at Gentle, Regular or MAX GLITTER, for the reason the punk club three doors up has no strobe: a light that can put somebody on the floor has no business in a room whose whole argument is come as you are. The dial governs everything else out here. There is simply nothing in this room for it to flash. None of these words are theirs. Every note on every post is ours, about what the record does. Not one line of any song is on this page, here or anywhere else on the street, and the tool that builds this room refuses a note shaped like verse. A room built on one band, whose words are half of why anybody loves them, is exactly where that rule would have been broken affectionately. Nothing is ranked. There is no best, no greatest, no countdown, no essential nine. They are in the order they were made, 1978 at the top and 2003 at the bottom, and that is the only ordering principle in the room. Not a costume you have to keep on. It is always Halloween here, which means you may arrive as anything and nobody asks what you came as or when you are taking it off.

Sithen

A hillock inhabited by fairies A ring of earth and whitethorn standing in a field, which you can walk all the way round and will not be going into. That is not coyness and it is not an unfinished room. The outside is the part of a fairy fort that anybody has ever actually seen. The inside is the part the stories are careful never to show you, and a page that flung the door open would be making up the one thing the tradition declines to.
What the name is, and whose it is not

Sithen is a real word and it was checked rather than assumed. Scottish Gaelic sìthean — a hillock inhabited by fairies — from sìth, fairy, with the diminutive ending; there is a dictionary behind it rather than a vibe. The Irish is sídhe, in the reformed spelling sí, which is the mound itself, and is where aos sí — the people of the mound — comes from. This mattered enough to look up. Two novel series are what sent us here, and one of them uses this exact spelling for the fae court, so a room taking the name while claiming to owe those books nothing would be advertising a debt it does not otherwise have. It turns out the word is older than both. It is said here so that nobody has to assume either way.
The ground, which is documented

This half is earthworks and a motorway, and it is kept apart from the folklore below on purpose, because the two are not the same kind of claim and a reader should not have to tell them apart by tone. A fairy fort is a ringfort: lios or rath, a circular earth bank, sometimes a ditch, sometimes stone. People built them from possibly the late Iron Age into early Christian times, and because the buildings inside were not durable, what is usually left in a field now is a vague circular mark and whatever has grown on it. As of 1991 there were between thirty and forty thousand identifiable fairy forts in the Irish countryside. The oldest of them possibly date back as early as 600 BCE. This is not a rare or sacred handful of sites. It is an ordinary feature of the landscape, in enormous numbers, that people have declined to plough. Believers in the fairies did not alter them, and even cutting the whitethorn growing on one was reputed to be the death of whoever did it. The tradition is specific about the thorn. Sceach, whitethorn, hawthorn: the tree of the ring, and the one you leave. In 1999 a whitethorn at Latoon in County Clare stopped a motorway. The folklorist Eddie Lenihan campaigned to save the tree from being cut down for the M18, calling it a meeting place for the supernatural forces of the region. It was spared in May 1999 and still grows there, on a strip of land between the motorway and a slip road.
A country that routes around a tree

Hold those together for a second, because it is the most interesting thing on this page. Tens of thousands of these rings are sitting in fields, and people decline to plough them. A motorway was rerouted around a single thorn bush. The stated reason is the Good People, and the actual mechanism is that leaving it alone matters to people and the paperwork required for that is a shrug. We are usually asked for a diagnosis, a letter and a business case before anybody will move a desk. There is no version of this room that does not notice the difference. A whole culture can make an enormous, expensive, permanent accommodation on the strength of this matters and I am not going to justify it to you — and the same culture will ask a Disabled person to evidence a chair.
The rules, which nobody will say out loud

Everything in the left-hand half of these is traditional and says where it comes from. Everything under what it is like is ours, written for this room, and is not claimed to be in the folklore. That split is the whole page: these taboos are a catalogue of consequential rules that nobody will state, where breaking one is punished and no one explains — which is the ordinary weather of neurotypical convention for a great many of us. Nothing here tells you how to behave. There is no advice, because a page about unwritten rules that ended in tips for following them would be a social skills curriculum with thorns on it. 01
Do not eat the food.

Accept a meal inside the hill and you may not be able to leave it. Traditional · A standard motif of the Otherworld visit in Irish and Scottish fairy tradition. What it is like: The invitation that cannot be declined without a cost. The coffee, the team lunch, the quick chat that is not quick and was never optional. Hospitality is the mechanism, not the kindness: once you have taken it you are inside an arrangement you did not read. 02
Do not say thank you.

Thanks implies the debt is settled, which is an insult, and a slight from a mortal is not taken lightly. Traditional · A widespread motif in fairy etiquette across Irish and Scottish tradition. What it is like: The rule where the polite thing is the wrong thing. Every autistic person has been punished for a courtesy delivered correctly, in good faith, to somebody who wanted a different courtesy and would not say which. There is no version of this you can work out from first principles, which is the entire complaint. 03
Do not give your true name.

A name is a handle. Give the real one and it can be used to call you, bind you, or hold you. Traditional · The power of the true name is a widespread motif in European fairy tradition. What it is like: Disclosure. Tell an employer what you are and you have handed over something that can be used to help you or to manage you out, and you will not find out which until afterwards. This is why so many of us are careful about the word, and why nobody should be told they are being paranoid about it. 04
Do not accept a gift you cannot return.

An unanswered gift is a debt, and the debt is collected at a time of the giver's choosing. Traditional · Reciprocity and its dangers are a recurring feature of fairy dealings in the tradition. What it is like: The favour economy, which is most workplaces. Being helped puts you in a ledger nobody shows you, and the entry is called in later as though it had been agreed. An accommodation offered as a favour rather than as a right is this exactly. 05
The bargain is kept to the letter.

What was agreed is delivered precisely, and precisely is not what you meant. Traditional · The literal-minded bargain is one of the oldest and most consistent motifs in fairy tradition. What it is like: The accommodation granted on paper. Yes, you may have the software. No, not the training, the licence, the time, or the colleague who stops scheduling meetings in it. Every word of the agreement was honoured. None of it worked, and the record shows you were given what you asked for. 06
Do not cut the thorn.

The tree on the ring is left standing, and no one is obliged to explain why. Traditional · Documented tradition; the whitethorn taboo is specific and is still observed. What it is like: The accommodation with no justification attached. A whole country routes around a tree because leaving it alone matters to people, and the paperwork for that is a shrug. We are usually asked for a diagnosis, a letter and a business case before anybody will move a desk. 07
Time is different inside.

A night of dancing, and everybody you knew is old or gone. Traditional · The supernatural lapse of time is a central motif of the Otherworld visit. What it is like: Burnout, and any long illness. You go in for what you are told is a short thing and you come out having missed a stretch of your own life, with everybody else further along the road and nobody quite able to say where it went. Nothing was stolen from you. It is simply gone.
Why the door is not opened

Every other warm underground place on this street is an interior with one small flame in it — a burrow with a lamp, a candlelit tent, panelling, a curtained cave. There is no interior here and there is no flame. Staying outside is what keeps this from being those rooms again with thorns on, and it is also the honest shape of the thing: a fairy fort is an outdoor object, and its whole character is that it is bounded, visible, and not entered. And it suits the argument. Half the rules above are about hospitality as a trap — the meal, the gift, the debt, the bargain honoured to the letter. A room that then insisted you come inside and accept what is offered would be doing the thing it spent the page describing. You are not obliged to go in anywhere. You can stand on the bank in the cold and look, and leave, and nothing about that is a failure to engage. If a door is ever opened here it becomes its own world behind this one, the way the Jungle Room grew a den, with its own light and its own rules. It does not become this page with rooms added to it.
What pointed us here, and what is not in this room

Laurell K. Hamilton’s Merry Gentry books and Seanan McGuire’s October Daye books are why this turning exists, and they are named here rather than quietly absorbed. Nothing in this room is drawn from either of them. Not a court, not a character, not a politics, not a cosmology, not a line. Those are invented worlds belonging to living authors, and the difference between being pointed somewhere and helping yourself is the whole of what this site means by attribution. That refusal is enforced rather than remembered: tools/make-sithen.py will not build this page if a rule’s source names either series or either author. The friendly edit here is a real one and it will arrive — the folklore is thin in exactly the places a novel is rich, so the most useful material lying around is the one thing this room may not pick up. Looming Rocks Amphitheatre

Two rock faces, a stage between them, and a great deal of very old stone that was here long before the stage was. Set amidst towering rock faces, Looming Rocks impose with their immense solidity. They give off an ancient and alive aura. Some say the rocks are sentient and full of lore from centuries of hosting storytellers and stages. They possess an unknowable intelligence that long pre-dates the humans drawn to them. The rocks saw the Sithen emerge, eons ago.
Why the rocks glow

The rocks are covered in lichen. In modern times, folks discovered that UV light made them fluoresce in a dazzling display. Charged during the day by a solar array with batteries, the stage production at Looming Rocks includes UV spots and floods that make the rocks glow at night. The floods stand on the ground and point upwards, which is why everything out here is brightest at its foot and goes dark towards the top, and why there is nothing overhead at all. The lamps are violet. What comes back is not.

The door policy at the foot of the rocks

Tuning is not playing. While the stage is dark, previous and next are silent — the screen names the act and its runtime and nothing is fetched. You can walk the whole bill without a single request going to YouTube. Once something is on, the desk changes the picture instead. Every control says how long before you press it, and the desk names the act it is about to move to as well. The shortest thing here is nearly an hour. Nobody should find out the length of a thing after committing to it. The bill is a list and not a verdict. Nothing here is ranked, rated or counted. The shows are in an order, and the order is not an argument about which is better. Nothing in the rig flashes or strobes, at any dial setting. A venue is exactly the kind of room that would grow a lighting effect, and this street settled that question in the punk club: a light that can put somebody on the floor has no business in a room anybody is meant to enjoy. The rocks glow steadily or not at all. You are allowed to sit down and you are allowed to leave. There is no standing, no queue and no crowd here, which is the one thing a web page can genuinely offer that the real venue cannot — and the reason a room like this is worth having on a Disabled people’s site rather than being a poster of somewhere most of us would struggle to get round.
Whose this all is

The real venue is Red Rocks Amphitheatre, an open-air amphitheatre near Morrison, Colorado, about ten miles south-west of Denver, owned and operated by the city of Denver. It is formed by two enormous sandstone monoliths — they have names: Ship Rock and Creation Rock, with the smaller Stage Rock between them — and it seats 9,525. Read off Wikipedia’s article on it on 2026-09-22. The room started there and is for outdoor music anywhere now, so the bill says where each show was played, and every one of them was played outdoors. Austin City Limits Music Festival is held in Zilker Park in Austin, Texas, and is a different thing from the television series it is named after, which is taped indoors — those sessions are on the desk in The Live Room, the street’s room for music played in a studio. Looming Rocks is not Red Rocks, or any other real place. It is a room on a made-up street that is extremely fond of the real ones — our executive director goes to Red Rocks whenever she can — and Stimpunks has no connection to any of these venues or festivals, is not endorsed by them, and is not describing them. The amphitheatre in Colorado is a real thing that belongs to a city; this one is a room on a street that rearranges itself for whoever turns up. None of these artists, their labels or the channels hosting these recordings is affiliated with Stimpunks, and none of them endorses us. The full running order with channels and links is in the liner notes.
