Dance, Punks

A silent disco on the old airstrip. Three channels, one crate, a headset each, and the volume in your own hand. The quietest thing on this road is also the biggest crowd on it. Out past the last streetlight there is an airstrip nobody lands on any more, long and flat and wide enough for everybody, and on it a great many people are dancing to three different things at once without a sound reaching the verge. From the road you see a field of small coloured lights bobbing about in the dark. That is the whole party, and it is lit by the headsets and nothing else.
The loudest room you can turn down

A silent disco hands everybody their own music, on their own headset, at their own volume. The dancefloor is still a crowd — you can see everybody, move with everybody, be right in the middle of it — but the sound only goes where somebody asked for it. Take the headset off and the runway is quiet: tarmac, somebody laughing, the wind. Nobody on this airstrip can make anybody else’s night louder. That is the dial this whole street runs on, built as a venue. Everywhere else here, how loud it gets is something the visitor holds rather than a property of the page. Out here it is something the dancer holds rather than a property of the room. A loud room is an access barrier, as Club Chronic says about itself on the street, and a silent disco is one of the ways a crowd gets round that without anybody having to leave it. Some of us dance to the same song forty times in a row — stim listening, one song or one list over and over, which is what our playlists are for. And some of us move because joy has to go somewhere. Our Autistic Joy entry quotes Authentically Emily on what it can feel like, and one line on that list is needing to move and stim to release the feeling. A runway is a lot of room to release it in.
dp-put-on
Put a headset on

Three channels, and they are one crate started in three places. The crate is Dance, Punks, a playlist Stimpunks keeps on YouTube. Each channel opens on a different song in it and plays on in order from there. A real silent disco has a DJ on every channel; this one has a starting point on every channel, and the room would rather say so than borrow a word for something it is not doing. It is not shuffle either. The player has no such button. Nothing is fetched from YouTube until you put the headset on. While it is off, choosing a channel only changes the colour of the band and what the headset says it will open on — you can try all three without a single request going to YouTube. Once it is on, changing channel changes the music, because by then you have asked for a headset. No channel says how long it runs, because the crate is a list we keep adding to and today’s total would be wrong next week. It runs until you take the headset off, and the volume is on the player, where nobody else can reach it. THE HEADSET IS OFF CH 1 · Blue Opens on Daft Punk Is Playing at My House by LCD Soundsystem, and plays on through the crate from there. The top of the crate, where the playlist itself begins. A song about a party that got out of hand, which is the one kind of party this runway cannot have: nobody here can hear anybody else's music. or open channel 1 on YouTube → CH 2 · Orange Opens on Wild Child by Shopping, and plays on through the crate from there. About a third of the way down the crate. Somebody on the Blue channel will not reach this song until they have danced through everything above it, and nobody on this channel has to. or open channel 2 on YouTube → CH 3 · White Opens on Starstruck by Sorry, and plays on through the crate from there. About two thirds of the way down, and the palest headset on the runway, which makes it the easiest one to find across a dark field. That is a perfectly good reason to be on it. or open channel 3 on YouTube →
The rules on the runway

Nothing strobes, flashes or pulses, at any dial setting. No lasers, no smoke, no mirrorball swinging a beam across anybody’s eyes. The headsets glow steadily or not at all. A dancefloor is the room on this road most likely to grow a light show, and a light that can put somebody on the floor has no business at a party anybody is meant to enjoy — the punk club on the street settled that first. The channels are told apart by more than their colour. Every headset says its number and its name, and the three colours are at least 1.5 to 1 apart in brightness from each other, so they stay three different headsets in greyscale and to anybody who does not see those colours as different. That bar is ours rather than a standard’s, and make-dance-punks.py refuses a channel under it. Take the headset off whenever you like. The runway is quiet underneath the music, and standing in a silent crowd watching everybody dance is a perfectly good way to be at this party. Nobody has to dance. Sit on the tarmac, lie on it and look up, walk the centre line out to the far end and back. There are no seats because there is nowhere you are supposed to be. Nothing is counted. Not songs heard, not time on the floor, not which channel is most popular. Nobody is keeping a list of who danced. Come on your own. Most of the crowd did. That is what a crowd on different channels looks like from the road.
Whose this all is

The crate is ours and the music is not. Dance, Punks is a playlist Stimpunks Foundation keeps on YouTube, read off its own page on 2026-09-23. Every song on it belongs to the people who made it and is on somebody else’s channel. Nothing is hosted by us, and none of those artists, their labels or the channels carrying them is affiliated with Stimpunks or endorses us. The three opening songs, who made them and whose channel each is on, are in the liner notes. The crate takes suggestions. If a song gets you moving, send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. It goes in as a link to wherever it already lives, because nothing musical is hosted here, and it is checked first to see that it plays and can be shown on this page. No lyrics go on this page either way. The airstrip is invented. Silent discos are not, and neither are the headsets that glow the colour of the channel they are on.

The Small Hours

An all-night diner for bodies that keep other hours. It is open, and nobody is going to ask why you are up. Open whatever time it is where you are. This is the last lit thing on the road. You see it a long way off: one long low building with a band of window all down its side, bright as a lamp, and the light from it lying out across the car park in pale rectangles. Out here you are standing in the dark looking in. Everybody in there is in the light, and nobody in there is looking out at you. The door is the one on the right, and it is not locked.
The clock over the counter has no hands
Rather than bend disabled bodies and minds to meet the clock, crip time bends the clock to meet disabled bodies and minds.
Alison Kafer, Feminist, Queer, Crip, as our Crip Time entry quotes it
The clock over the counter has no hands
Crip time is time travel.
Ellen Samuels, Six Ways of Looking at Crip Time, as our Crip Time entry quotes it
The clock over the counter has no hands

Nobody in here is late and nobody is early. A great many of us are awake when the town is not — because a body takes its sleep when it can get it rather than when a day has room for it, because the rhythm it runs on is not the one a work week was drawn around, because it is the only quiet time there is, or because it simply is. Our Crip Time entry has the best sentence about this that anybody has written, and it is Alison Kafer’s: That is what the diner is. It does not ask you to arrive at a sensible hour; it has no sensible hour. It has a counter, some booths, a kettle that is always hot and a clock that does not tell anybody anything. The same entry quotes Ellen Samuels saying something shorter, which is written on the wall under the clock:
Nobody asks why you are up
The sleep-wake cycles of Autistic adults also differ, on average, from the circadian rhythms of neurotypicals, and many of us experience sleep disorders.
Devon Price, Unmasking Autism, as our Sleep entry quotes it
Nobody asks why you are up
sleep facilitating factors are in a direct contrast to the sleep hygiene recommendations
Georgia Pavlopoulou, A Good Night’s Sleep: Learning About Sleep From Autistic Adolescents’ Personal Accounts, as our Sleep entry quotes it
Nobody asks why you are up

Not the person behind the counter, not the menu, not the sign. Being awake at this hour is not a symptom anybody here is going to take an interest in. Our Sleep entry quotes Devon Price on how ordinary it is: And there is no sleep advice in this building. Not a tip, not a routine, not a leaflet by the till. The same entry quotes a study in which Autistic teenagers described what actually helped them sleep, and what they described was the opposite of the advice they were usually handed. Georgia Pavlopoulou, who wrote it up, put it in one line: So the diner keeps its opinions to itself and keeps the kettle on.
The menu
they’d sit me at the small table they’d put next to their bed and hand me some crayons so that I could blissfully colour while they watched over me in semi-consciousness.
Sarah Kurchak, I Overcame My Autism and All I Got Was This Lousy Anxiety Disorder, as our Sleep entry quotes it
The menu

Written on the board behind the counter. There are no prices, because this is a website and a price would be the one thing on it that was certainly made up. Breakfast, whenever it is for you Eggs any way and toast cut however you like it, at any hour. It is breakfast because it is the first thing you have eaten since you woke up, and that is the only clock the kitchen goes by. The same as last time Say it and it arrives exactly as it did before, down to where things sit on the plate. Nobody suggests you try something new. A safe food is a perfectly good reason to come back. Our Safe Food entry. A booth to yourself For as long as you like. Nobody is waiting for the table, and nobody will stand near it looking as if they are. Something warm in a heavy mug Refilled without asking, or never refilled at all, whichever you said when you sat down. Either is remembered until you leave and not a minute after. Crayons and a paper placemat On every table, for the reason quoted under the menu, and there is one waiting in the window below. Colouring at a small table while somebody keeps you company is a thing the small hours have been for since long before this diner. The quiet end of the counter Furthest from the kitchen and the door. The stools down there do not spin; the ones at the other end do, for the people who asked for that instead. Nothing at all You can sit here without ordering anything. Nobody brings the bill over to make a point. About the crayons. Our Sleep entry opens with Sarah Kurchak remembering the nights she did not sleep as a child, and what her parents did about it:
sh-mat-h
A placemat and some crayons

Every table has one: a paper placemat printed in one colour, and a paper sleeve of crayons beside it. Pick a crayon, then press a shape to colour it in, or switch to scribbling and draw wherever you like. Over the lines is fine. Nobody here minds. Every part of the placemat can also be coloured in by name, from the list underneath it, with a keyboard or a screen reader; scribbling needs a pointer or a finger. The red is the booths’ vinyl, the teal is the counter’s formica, and the white does next to nothing on white paper, the way it does in every box. The crayons red orange yellow teal blue purple brown black white What a press on the placemat does Colour in: press a shape and it fills Scribble: draw wherever you like Colour it in by name, one part at a time Nothing on it is marked and nothing is kept. When you leave, the placemat goes in the bin and nobody looks at it first. If you want it, take it home: that saves a picture of it to your own device and sends it nowhere else.
sh-record-h
Up All Night
Insomnia is a research priority for autistic communities. At Stimpunks, we keep the hour-of-the-wolf.
Our post, The Neurodivergent Experience in Josephmooon’s “So Far So Good”

Up All Night

Josephmooon · lyrics by Ronan Boren, a Stimpunk There is one record in the jukebox that everybody in here puts on sooner or later, because it is about them. “Up All Night” is a song about Autistic insomnia, from Josephmooon’s first album, and its words are Ronan Boren’s. When we wrote about that album in 2021, we said this about it: Track 4 of So Far So Good · runs 2:41 Ronan Boren all lyrics Bill Paige vocals, guitar Ronnie Nice guitars, keyboards, bass, drums, programming Ian Nice piano, keyboards, backing vocals
The words
The whole album is on the jukebox below and on its own page on the band’s site.

The jukebox

Both of Josephmooon’s albums, every track, played from the band’s own site. Nothing loads until you press something, every button says how long the song runs before you press it, and only one song plays at a time: starting another pauses the one before. The rules of the house

It does not close. There are no last orders and no time you are expected to leave by. The sign does not read your clock, either: a diner for people up at odd hours is the last place that should be keeping an eye on the time. Nobody asks why you are up, and nobody gives you advice about it. The tubes do not flicker and do not hum. A fluorescent light that buzzes and stutters is the sound of half the waiting rooms we have ever sat in, and it is gone from this one. You can sit without ordering, stay as long as you like, sit in a booth on your own or at the counter next to somebody you have never met and not say a word. Nothing is counted and nothing is kept. Not what time you came in, not how often, not how long you stayed, and not your placemat unless you take it home yourself. Nobody here is keeping a record of how many nights you were awake.
Whose this all is

Every quotation here names who wrote it and is linked to the page of ours that quotes it. Each was read word for word off that page, and every author was checked against a library record rather than remembered — which is how the crayons passage got its right author: our Sleep entry links the book without naming who wrote it, and the name this room was nearly given from memory belonged to somebody else. The full list is in the liner notes. The diner is invented. Crip time is not, and neither is being up at an hour a town has decided is for sleeping.

The Repeater

A radio mast on the ridge, as far from everything as the road goes, and the easiest place on it to be reached. At the very end of the road a track goes up, and at the top of it there is a ridge with a mast on it and a hut at the foot of the mast. Nothing up here is lit. The cloud above is, a little, from underneath: every lit thing on this road and the whole town past the last streetlight throws a glow up onto it, so from the ridge you see the mast, the hut and the hill as black shapes against a sky the colour of somewhere else’s light. Two small red lamps on the mast are the only lights of its own, and they do not blink. A repeater is a radio station that listens on one frequency and sends what it hears straight back out on another, louder and from higher up, so that two people who could never reach each other directly can talk. It stands where nobody lives because that is where it can hear everybody.
Signal is a place too
The mode of connection carried by signal rather than proximity — a voice note, a thread, a call left open in the background, a message typed and read across distance.
Our Shared-Signal Space entry
Signal is a place too
No mode sits at the top.
Our Shared-Signal Space entry
Signal is a place too

This road has turnings for crowds and turnings for staying out late, and it has this one for wanting to be as far off as you can get. Far off is not the same as cut off. Our Shared-Signal Space entry names what a lot of us already live in: For a great many Autistic, ADHD and otherwise neurodivergent people that is where connection comes easiest — away from the masking and the noise a room asks for — and the entry is careful to say it is not a stand-in for being in the same room. It is a mode in its own right, beside shared-air space rather than under it. The written word is a channel, not a lesser one; in the study our entry cites, by Howard and Sedgewick, phone calls came last among Autistic adults’ preferences and written channels came near the top. AAC is real communication, and so is a message that took a long time to send. The shape of it has a name: the Autistic Rhizome, which DGH Neurodivergent Consultancy gave to the network of Autistic communities growing on Discord, and which Helen Edgar has written about at Autistic Realms. Connection that spreads sideways, with no single origin and no correct path, and online spaces that work like watering holes, where turning up is enough. Our entry puts the whole argument in six words, and they are painted on the door of the hut:
rp-line-h
Leave the line open

One of the things on that entry’s list is a call kept open in the background while two people just exist near each other. So the hut has a line you can open and leave open. There is nobody on the other end. It is the quiet hiss of an open line and nothing else, made in your browser when you press the button, for keeping you company while you get on with something else. The line fetches nothing, sends nothing and listens to nothing: the page never asks for your microphone and could not use one if it had it. THE LINE IS CLOSED How loud A steady noise with no tone in it. It does not beep, pulse, fade in and out, or change on its own. The slider only goes as loud as a line left open in the background should.
The log

Radio operators send each other a card to confirm a contact happened. The log in this hut confirms that every kind of contact counts, and it keeps no count of any of them — no totals, no awards for how many, no list of who reached whom. These are the kinds it has cards for: VOICE NOTE Contact confirmed Left for later and played back twice. The breath in it arrived as well as the words. THREAD Contact confirmed Picked up again days afterwards, mid-sentence, and nobody asked where anybody had been. OPEN LINE Contact confirmed A call nobody hung up. Two people getting on with separate things, near each other, saying nothing for an hour. TYPED Contact confirmed Drafted, read back, rewritten and only then sent, so what arrived was what was meant. LETTERBOARD Contact confirmed Spelled out one letter at a time. It took longer to arrive and it is no less a voice for that. LURKING Contact confirmed Read everything and said nothing for months. That was being there the whole time. ONE REPLY Contact confirmed A single answer after a long quiet. It counts the same as a conversation.
The rules on the ridge

The lamps are steady. A lot of the lights on masts flash, and these are the kind that do not. Nothing on this page blinks, pulses or moves on its own at any dial setting. Nothing here sends anything anywhere. There is no form, no message box, no call-in, and nothing that listens. The line you can open is made where you are and stays there. Nobody has to talk. Listening counts. Reading and saying nothing counts. So does coming back after a long time away without an explanation. Nothing is counted. Not contacts, not time on the line, not who turned up. A place for being reached should not be keeping score of who reached it. If you want the real watering holes rather than a hut on a made-up hill, the Stimpunks community is where ours are, and our online space page says how they are built.
Whose this all is

The argument is our own Shared-Signal Space entry, and the two lines quoted from it are ours. The Autistic Rhizome was named by DGH Neurodivergent Consultancy and has been written about by Helen Edgar at Autistic Realms; neither is folded into our “we”. The study on communication preferences is Howard and Sedgewick’s. Details are in the liner notes. The ridge and the mast are invented. Radio repeaters are not: they stand on hills all over the world, passing on the signals of people who could not otherwise reach each other.

Nothing For Sale

A ring of cars in a lay-by with their headlights on, and everything laid out in the middle is free. Take what you need, leave what you can, and nobody is counting either. The Outskirts is lit by your headlights. This turning is lit by everybody’s. Nobody who came out here brought enough light on their own, so everybody pulled into the lay-by in a ring, nose in, and left their lamps on, and the middle is as bright as a room. No two of those lamps match — an old estate on halogen, a newer van on LEDs, a hatchback running on one yellow fog lamp — so everything laid out in the middle throws a whole fan of shadows, one for every car, each with a slightly different colour at its edge. Everything on the tables is free. It is the only free market on the road, and the only one where the word means that.
Solidarity, not charity
Mutual aid is not charity. It is not a handout or an act of pity. It is a profound, ongoing, messy practice of loving each other into the future.
Sparrow, Mutual Aid: How We Survive, How We Transform, as our Mutual Aid entry quotes it
Solidarity, not charity
showing up for each other, laterally, with no proof of worthiness required.
Our Mutual Aid page
Solidarity, not charity

That phrase is the mutual aid movement’s rather than ours, and our Mutual Aid entry quotes it from a talk about Autistic mutual aid. The difference it names is the whole of this lay-by. Charity comes down, from somebody who has to somebody who has been judged to deserve it, and it wants to know you deserve it first. Mutual aid goes sideways. Sparrow, writing at Unstrange Mind, puts it like this: And our own Mutual Aid page ends its opening on the thing that actually helps:
On the tables
Knowledge is infrastructure. Access to it is mutual aid.
Our Library page
On the tables

Everything laid out here is ours, and every one of them is free by its own page’s account, which was checked table by table before anything went on one. Our library says why the tables are here at all: BOOKS
Our library

Books from the edges, music, bookmarks, and reading lists by and for neurodivergent and disabled people. First table, because the library page is where the argument for all the others is written down. START HERE
The Autism and Neurodiversity Starter Pack
A download: foundational ideas, why so many of us are burnt out, and ways forward. By David Gray-Hammond and Helen Edgar. LEARN
Our courses

Zine walls

Walls of declarations: short lines, one idea each, made to be read fast by somebody who has not got long. Two things of ours are not on a table, on purpose. Our mutual aid grants are not take-what-you-need: they have an application, limits on who can apply and a waiting list, and a lay-by that suggested otherwise would be promising something they cannot do. They are on our Mutual Aid page, which also says why they exist. And our Things Library argues for a library economy — tools, clothes, furniture, everything held in common — without yet listing anything to borrow, so there is nothing of it to lay out.
The rules of the lay-by

Nothing here is for sale, and nothing is a swap. Taking something does not put you in anybody’s debt, and nobody will ask for anything back. Out at Sithen there is a whole page about the old rule that eating what the fair folk offer leaves you theirs; this lay-by is that rule turned inside out, on purpose. Nobody asks what it is for. No form, no proof, and no question about whether you need it enough. Leave what you can, and nothing is a perfectly good amount. Nothing is counted. Not what anybody took, not what anybody left, not who came. Leave your headlights on if you have them. If you walked, there is light enough. That is what a ring is for.
Whose this all is

Every table is ours, and every quotation names who wrote it. The starter pack is David Gray-Hammond’s and Helen Edgar’s. The line about mutual aid not being charity is Sparrow’s, at Unstrange Mind. Solidarity, not charity belongs to the movement. Details are in the liner notes. The lay-by is invented. Free shops, free tables and mutual aid networks are not, and they are mostly run by the people who need them.

Rebellion Rave Room

Peak Sensory Seek That Goes to Eleven An aircraft hangar at the end of the airstrip road, taken over by the sensory seekers in our community who wanted somewhere to stim loudly and brightly. The ceiling is a very long way up, the walls are scaffolding, tier on tier of it, and the rig is bolted to every deck. This is the one place on the street where you will see a strobe: switched on by you, twice over, and off again the moment you say.
rr-ante-h
The ante-chamber
You come in through a small room first, with the hangar doors shut behind it. It is lit plainly and evenly, and everything you need to decide is on its walls before you open them.
rr-warning
Strobe and laser warning

The hangar’s rig has a strobe in it: flashes of bright white light, from one to eleven a second. Flashing light can cause seizures in people with photosensitive epilepsy, and it can bring on migraine, dizziness, nausea or disorientation in people without it. Every rate the knob has is inside the range that can trigger a seizure. The Epilepsy Society says flashing between 3 and 30 times a second is the common range, varying from person to person, and 16 to 25 a second the most likely. It also says the UK’s Health and Safety Executive recommends that a strobe in a club or at a public performance flashes no more than four times a second. The knob starts at four. Everything above four is faster than that recommendation, and the knob says so as you turn it. It is off, and it stays off until you switch it on and then say yes to a second question, which tells you the rate before you answer. Nothing on the rig starts by itself, and nothing is remembered: it is off again every time you come in. Escape switches everything off at once, and so do the Stop buttons, going to another tab, and leaving the page. The festival films on the big screen have their own lighting in them, strobe and lasers included. The rig cannot reach inside somebody else’s video, so none of its limits apply there.
House rules

You hold the rig. The lasers and the strobe are two separate switches, the rate is a knob, and you choose whether the rig stays in its picture or takes the whole screen. The dial does not switch any of it on or off: nothing on the rig runs until you ask, at any setting, and it stops when you ask, at any setting. It goes to eleven, and it stops there. Eleven is a joke about amplifiers, and it is also where the knob ends. There is no twelve. Seekers and avoiders share the floor. Nobody has to switch anything on, and nobody on this floor is too much. Leave the rig off and dance to the screen, or just sit at the edge. Ask before you touch anybody. A dance floor is shared and a body is not. You can leave whenever you like. The Cooldown Room is through the other door in here, and the rig does not reach it. Nothing is counted. No number on the door, no streak of nights, and no board of who went to eleven.
The hydration station

Water, cold or at room temperature, in paper cups or into your own bottle, free and as much as you like. Beside it, a basket of foam earplugs, a hook of ear defenders, and a box of dark glasses for anybody who wants the dance floor without the rig in their eyes. Through the other door: The Cooldown Room →
Through the doors: the hangar

The ceiling goes up and keeps going. It is all open floor, with tables and chairs round the edges and nothing in the middle but room. The DJ booth stands two floors up on its own tower at the back. Scaffold decks climb every wall, with the rig bolted to them: moving heads, speaker stacks and laser heads. The lift in the corner stops at every deck, so the stair beside the booth is not the only way up. The light in here is light you can see in the air. The haze catches every beam along its whole length, so a laser is a line drawn across the room rather than a spot on a wall, and the strobe is light in time rather than in space: all of it, then none of it.
rr-rig-h
The rig
Two switches and a knob. Nothing here runs until you press it, and everything stops on Escape. Strobe rate 4 flashes a second
On the big screen

On the shared screen over the floor: three films that play on into YouTube’s own mix and one playlist somebody keeps. Nothing is fetched from YouTube until you press something. While the screen is dark, previous and next move along the channel list without loading anything at all. Once something is on, they change the picture, because by then you have asked for a screen. The Cooldown Room

Somewhere small and soft to come down in. A room the size of a living room, through the wall from one the size of a hangar. Couches, armchairs, floor cushions and low tables everywhere, the doors shut on the noise, cold water on tap, and a vending machine along one wall where everything is free and made by people from round here.
The light in here

Most of the light comes out of the front of the vending machine: one tall, steady, pale panel at the side of the room, at about the height of your head. Every couch has a pale edge on the side that faces it and soft shade on the side that does not, and there is a pool of it on the floor in front of the glass. It is the same light all night, and nothing in here is switched. Next door the light is yours to set going. In here there is nothing to set.
The machine

Press a slot and it drops into the tray. Everything in it is free, and you can take as many as you like: it does not run out and it does not ask. Every slot says what is in it and how it feels before you press, because crunch, cold and sour matter more than usual in a room like this one.
Water

A cooler by the machine, with cold water and water at room temperature, paper cups and a tap low enough to fill a bottle at. A bowl of ice beside it. Free, like everything else in here, and as much as you like.
House rules

Stay as long as you like. Nobody asks why you are in here and nobody asks when you are going back. You do not have to go back. The rig does not reach in here. Nothing next door can flash, sweep or sound in this room. The walls are thick and the doors shut. Nothing in here moves and nothing makes a sound, at any dial setting. The machine drops a snack and says so in words. Nothing is counted and nothing is kept. Nobody writes down what you took or how often you came in. The tray empties when you leave. Lie down if you want to. The floor cushions are for exactly that, and so are the couches.
Whose this all is

The snacks and the people who make them belong to this road: the orchard off the verge, the crisp fryer behind the old control tower, the overnight bakers by the fuel pumps, the sweet shed, the pretzel oven, the lolly van and the Tuesday jam club. Arlesglad Caverns

Under the street there is rock nobody dug, and a way down into it that anybody can take. The weather stops at the top of the shaft. The daylight stops too, and the clock is up there with it. What is down here is here because it needs things to stay the same, and down here they do. We are glad of it, which is half the name.
What is down here

The deeper you go, the steadier it gets. A cave keeps its weather out. At the real Carlsbad Caverns, the National Park Service measures the Big Room at an average of 56°F (13°C), moving a little with the seasons, and the lowest point at a constant 68°F (20°C) with the air close to saturated all year. So everything down here needs something to hold still: a cellar, a crop that grows in the dark, a light that only shows without one, warm water that holds you up, and a room at the bottom that is simply the steady part. The only light is the handrail. It runs at hand height along the one route, from the lift to every door, and the rock is lit where the path goes and nowhere else. There is no sky down here and no lamp overhead. Down here the only colour is the light; each room brings its own. The lift is the ordinary way down. The stair comes down beside the shaft, and every landing has the same names painted on it as the lift’s panel, so neither one is the other’s alternative. If you came down in the lift, you came the usual way. Nobody was sent down here. Underground, here, is a direction and not a place to keep things out of sight. A cellar is under the street because a cellar is always under the street; a mushroom farm is in a cave because that is where mushrooms have always been grown. Down is not the same as hidden. Nothing down here moves on its own. The dial still works and each room sets its own noise, but the passage has no ambient layer at any setting. The rail does not flicker, because it is the one thing you are holding.

Where the name comes from

Arlesglad is a play on Carlsbad Caverns, with a glad spin, and with ARLES in the middle of it: the Stimpunks Design Method, whose ladder starts at the bottom, where a person actually is, and works outward to the room and the systems around it. Carlsbad Caverns is a real place, a national park in New Mexico looked after by the National Park Service. This is not it. What the strengths mean

A percentage is how much of the drink is alcohol, by volume. It is on every pour, before you take it, the way every button on this street says how long it runs before you press it. Alcohol-free, for a beer or a wine, means under 0.05%. That is the same drink with the alcohol taken out after it was made, and a brewed drink with the alcohol taken out can keep the faintest trace of it. If you need none at all, the kombucha’s alcohol-free pours have none. Kombucha is never quite zero, and ours says so. It is fermented, so there is always a little alcohol in it, and how much varies from one batch to the next. So its fermented pour gives the most it can be, under 0.5%, rather than a number that would be wrong half the time. Its alcohol-free pour is the same tea and fruit, not fermented.
House rules

Nobody here asks why you are not drinking, or whether you are sure, or whether you want to try a little of the other one. Nothing here counts how many you have had. No rounds, no games, nobody keeping up with anybody. The pours with alcohol in them are for adults. Everything else in the cellar is for everybody. Nothing here is good for you, and nothing is bad for you either. None of it is a remedy or a supplement, kombucha included. It is something to drink. The vessels are glass and steel on bare rock, lit from behind, so the light comes through the drink. There is no wood in here. The house styles, their names and every word about them are ours. Why a mushroom farm

Because of a post of ours. We once spent a Campfire Learn Together on the way fungi grow, break things down and make something new of what is left, and one line of it is the whole reason this room is under the street: A mushroom is the fruit. The part that does the growing is the mycelium, the pale threads that run all the way through a block of straw or sawdust and that nobody ever sees on a plate. When a block has given all the mushrooms it is going to, it goes out of the farm as compost. Mushrooms are fungi, not plants, which is also why this is not the plant kitchen upstairs.

How long a glow lasts

Down here a glow lasts seconds, not the hours a real one can, so that you can watch one go from start to finish. Green lasts longest, and red and orange go first, which is true of the real pigments. Green glow is the brightest and longest-lasting there is. Red and orange are the dimmest: partly because the pigments that glow those colours are weaker, and partly because your eyes are least sensitive to red in the dark. The order of the colours in between is ours, not measured. The glow stick is the odd one out. It is not charged by light at all: bending it cracks a capsule inside, two liquids mix, and they glow until they are spent. It only goes once, so ours glows until you leave.
House rules

Nothing here is for sale. Trinkets or not, you play with them on the page. Every colour glow comes in is on these shelves, blue included. Nothing flickers or flashes, at any setting. Nothing in here is radioactive. Glow pigment stores light you give it; it does not make its own. Nothing is counted and nothing is kept. The shelves do not remember which toys you charged. Stay Frosty

A quiet place to chill, literally. Chill as in calm, not cold. Down here the temperature is the one thing you never have to think about, because it never moves, and nothing else in the room moves either. 68°F20°C All year, at the bottom. It said this before you came in and it will say it after you leave. Read off the National Park Service’s weather page for Carlsbad Caverns on 2026-09-26.
Why it is always the same down here

The caverns are named after Carlsbad, so this room keeps Carlsbad’s number. The National Park Service’s own words for the lowest point of Carlsbad Cavern are that “this lowest point remains a more constant and warmer 68°F (20ºC) and closer to 100% relative humidity”. The rooms above move a little with the seasons. This is where the moving stops. The air down here is close to saturated, so the rock is damp, and the only light that gets this far is the handrail’s. It does not arrive as a lamp. It arrives as a small point in every bead of damp on the wall, and that is all the light there is.
Who it is for

Anybody whose body does not keep the temperature a building assumes it will. Plenty of us run hot, run cold, or only find out we were too warm once it is already too much. Our own Interoception entry lists temperature among the signals from inside the body, and says that when our attention is taken over we may not notice them at all. In here there is nothing to notice. It is the same on the way in, the same while you are here, and the same when you leave. That is the whole of it. This room is not treatment and it is not a test of anything. Nobody here is going to tell you what it will do for your bodymind.
What never changes in here

The temperature. 68°F (20°C) , and it was that before you came in. Nothing moves, at any setting. The dial on this page still works, and it changes nothing in this room, because there is nothing here for it to change. Nothing in the room makes a sound, and nothing is waiting to play. The CB stays upstairs: if you are signed on to it, the radio does not come down this far. There is no clock. Nothing on this page knows what time it is or how long you have been here. There is nothing to press. No button in the room at all: only links out, and the guild’s marker on the floor if you want it. The room counts nothing and keeps nothing. Not your visits, not your time, not that you came. It is not for anything. Not a cold plunge, not a reset, not somewhere to recharge. You do not have to come out better than you went in. Through the door at the back: Stay Breezy → A hall full of fans, for anybody who loves moving air and the noise it makes. The fans in there make a sound when you switch them on. Nothing in here does. The temperature is the National Park Service’s, and the room says where it came from on the thermometer. Carlsbad Caverns is a real national park and not affiliated with Stimpunks. Credits are in the liner notes.

House rules

Nothing makes a sound until you switch it on, and every fan says what it sounds like first, in words. Every ceiling fan’s lamp hangs below its blades, so the blades never pass between you and the light. Nothing in here flickers or flashes, at any setting. The dial keeps its promise and the fans keep theirs. At Gentle the blades stay still and the fan keeps running, because the sound is the thing you asked for. At Regular they turn once you switch a fan on. At MAX GLITTER the ribbons on the fans flutter too. No fan here is named for who made it. They are named for what they are. Your usual is kept in your own browser, and nowhere else. The speed you last set on each fan, which fan is on your table, and which fans you last had on. It never switches anything on by itself: your speeds come back when you arrive, and the fans only start when you press Switch on my usual. Forget my usual clears it. Nothing is counted, and the sound is made here and sent nowhere. You do not need a reason to love a fan. None of these is a sleep aid or a way to get more done. They are fans. Ryan’s words are his own. The fans are ours, drawn and made in the browser; none of them is a recording. Credits are in the liner notes.

Covenstead

A meeting place, and a shopfront on the street: a kitchen in the afternoon with one window open and the good china out, not one cup matching the next. That mismatch is the subject of the room sitting on the table, because a covenstead is where a group meets — several people who do not entirely agree, meeting on purpose anyway. It began as turning 03 in The Outskirts and was moved. Ryan’s call, 2026-09-22, and the reasoning is about what each area is for: the campgrounds are for people who want to be somewhat apart from each other, at peace in nature, with the street still in reach; the road out of town is for night revelry and for being as far off as you can get. A covenstead is neither — it is a group that meets regularly, which wants a premises with a door on a street where people already are. Helen Edgar’s observation sharpened the split: that everything out on that road could sit on the campsite if it had planning permission, which turns out to be a useful test for anything placed in either area. It changed worlds when it moved rather than being relocated with the same paint on it. Out there it was a dark room lit by several lamps that did not match — the only room on the street lit by more than one source. Here it is daylit, warm and domestic, and the argument moved with it: the thing carrying several people who do not match, meeting anyway is now the china. That device is load bearing, and if the crockery is ever made to match, the room has lost its subject and kept its wallpaper. Terry Pratchett’s words are on that page, and they are the point of it. First Sight and Second Thoughts are his, named in the Discworld books, and the sentences that define them are the tenets — the way the Rede’s couplet is. An earlier draft named the concepts and linked out for the words; it described the thing instead of showing it, and it gutted the room. Ryan’s call, 2026-09-22. Every quotation names its author, its work and its year and links to the edition, which is the habit this site keeps when it drops all the others. What is not there is the scene. The lines about storing things in other people come out of a long exchange running to several hundred words, and that stays quoted properly, at length and in context, on our own philosophy page — the better thing to read, linked rather than raided. tools/make-covenstead.py sets its own cap rather than borrowing the Zibaldone’s: thirty words is right for a quote bank, where the danger is drift, and wrong for a room quoting a handful of named passages it is actually about. Sixty fits a defining sentence and refuses a scene. The Rule of Three is argued about inside the tradition, and the room says so instead of settling it. It is not a universal article of faith: there are Wiccans who read it as an over-elaboration on the Rede and others who consider it a modern innovation built on Christian morality, with a possible prototype in a 1949 novel of Gerald Gardner’s. A page stating it flat, as the witch law, would be deciding a live argument inside somebody else’s religion on their behalf, from the outside, in passing, for atmosphere — and the flattened version is always the one that travels. The tool refuses a tenet marked contested that does not say what is contested about it. Rede means counsel, not commandment, which is the hinge the room turns on: Middle English for advice, first publicly recorded in its best-known couplet in a 1964 speech by Doreen Valiente, and still counsel sixty years later rather than a code somebody can be expelled for breaking. make-covenstead.py refuses a tenet written as an order — which is the opposite of the rule one turning up the road, where make-sithen.py refuses advice outright. Two rooms in one area holding opposite rules about the same vocabulary, for the same underlying reason, and they must not be made to agree. Nobody is initiated and nothing is counted. No degrees, no levels, no test at the door, no record of how often you came. The Wiccan material is somebody else’s religion, treated as such, and read off the Rede and the Rule of Three on 2026-09-22. Peer support by and for people in burnout and people on the far side of it, and a shopfront on the street: a borrowed room after hours with the big lights off and the door left ajar. The name is a play on Dead Poets Society (1989, directed by Peter Weir, written by Tom Schulman; read off Wikipedia’s summary on 2026-09-23), a film about a group resisting the conformity of the school it meets in. The room takes the shape of the name and nothing else — no line, no scene, no character, no still, no motto — and tools/make-dead-tired.py refuses the film’s characters, its school and its two famous lines anywhere on the page, because the most famous parts of somebody else’s screenplay are exactly the parts most tempting to borrow for atmosphere. The light comes from outside the room, and nobody sits in it. The only light is a corridor’s strip lights through the gap in a door, lying across the floor as one hard wedge, and every word on that page stays in the shade on purpose: masking is performing under a light, and this is the room where nothing has to. The drawing places everything — a beanbag, a mug, a chair with a coat over it, a mattress, a pair of shoes, an armchair — outside that wedge, and draws nobody at all, because nobody in there is on display. The corridor’s tubes do not flicker, at any setting, for Club Chronic’s reason. Every line on a peg is somebody else’s and says whose. Each was read off our own glossary entry for that peg on 2026-09-23 and is credited to the source the entry credits, never to the entry. Where an entry named only a title or only initials, the authors were resolved rather than guessed: Botha and Frost against Crossref’s record for their DOI, and Kramer, Jones and Broadbent against the journal’s own citation metadata, because Crossref has no record for that one. The definition of burnout at the top of the room is the title of Raymaker and others’ paper in Autism in Adulthood, 2020, also checked against Crossref. The line under each quotation is ours, written for this room. Nothing there gives advice nobody asked for, counts anything, or praises anybody for how much they can take. The tool refuses the vocabulary of all three in the room’s own voice, with a window so the room can still say it will not — and skips the quotations, because two of them are the sharpest things anybody has said against resilience, and a quotation criticising a word has to be allowed to contain it. The page is not a meeting and does not pretend to be one: it has no times, no sign-up and no facilitator, and it points at our community, where the people are, and at mutual aid. The type is Sorts Mill Goudy, Barry Schwartz’s revival of Goudy’s Oldstyle, for the society’s name and headings — set like a founding charter for a society whose members are lying on the floor — and Lexend, by Bonnie Shaver-Troup, Thomas Jockin, Santiago Orozco, Héctor Gómez and Superunion, for everything that is read. Lexend was drawn to reduce visual stress and ease reading fatigue, which is the whole reason a room for the dead tired sets it. Rebellion Rave Room

An old aircraft hangar by the airstrip, turning 08 in The Outskirts, Ryan’s brief of 2026-09-27: somewhere for the sensory seekers in our community to stim loudly and brightly. It is the one room on this street with a strobe in it, and that reverses a rule the street has held since Club Chronic, which every room with a light show in it has repeated since. The reversal is an opt-in and nothing else: the rig is off on every visit, the strobe takes two presses and the second answers a question that names the rate, and Escape, the Stop buttons, another tab or leaving the page switch everything off at once. tools/make-rave.py refuses the page if the warning moves below the rig, if the rig stops shipping hidden, if the knob goes past eleven or starts anywhere but four, if the flash has any colour in it, or if rave.js stores anything or can start without a press. The flash rates in the warning are the Epilepsy Society’s, read off its page on photosensitive epilepsy on 2026-09-27: 3 to 30 flashes a second the common range, 16 to 25 the most likely to trigger a seizure, and the Health and Safety Executive’s recommendation, which that page reports, that a strobe in a club flashes no more than four times a second. The knob starts at four and goes to eleven, and everything past four says so as you turn it. “Goes to eleven” is Nigel Tufnel’s amplifier in This Is Spinal Tap (1984), directed by Rob Reiner and written by Reiner with Christopher Guest, Michael McKean and Harry Shearer. A broadsheet press on the street, in the side of a ship: manifestos and mementos served across your bow. The third area, and the first one under the street rather than past an end of it: a cavern reached by a lift beside the stoop and the stair beside that, lit only by a strip in its handrail. Level B3 of Arlesglad Caverns: glow-in-the-dark toys and trinkets in every colour glow comes in, blue included, Ryan’s call. The toys, the drawings and every word about them are ours, and nothing is for sale. Every toy starts dark, is charged by being held up to the rail, and gives the light back; down here that takes seconds rather than hours, so it can be watched. What the room says about how long each colour lasts was checked, and it says which half was. Green glow pigment is the brightest and longest-lasting, with afterglow reported in hours by pigment makers such as Techno Glow’s notes on strontium aluminate. Red and orange are the dimmest and first to go: the pigments are weaker, and the eye is least sensitive to red in the dark, which the introduction to a study of red afterglow phosphors sets out. The order of the colours in between is the room’s own, and tools/make-glow.py refuses a green that does not last longest and a red or orange that is not among the first to fade. Looming Rocks Amphitheatre

An open-air stage at the foot of enormous rock faces, turning 03 in The Outskirts. The real venue is Red Rocks Amphitheatre, near Morrison, Colorado, owned and operated by the city of Denver, formed by two sandstone monoliths named Ship Rock and Creation Rock with the smaller Stage Rock between them, seating 9,525 — read off Wikipedia on 2026-09-22. The room started there and is for outdoor music anywhere now (Ryan’s call, 2026-09-25): every act says where it was played, and tools/make-looming.py refuses one that was not played outdoors. That rule arrived the same day as ten Austin City Limits videos, nine of them taped for the television series in a studio, so only the festival set, in Zilker Park, is on this bill, and the other nine are on the desk in The Live Room, which refuses a set played outside. Looming Rocks is not Red Rocks, or any other real place: it is a room on a made-up street that is fond of the real ones, Stimpunks has no connection to any of these venues or festivals and is not endorsed by them, and the sentient rocks, the solar array and the ultraviolet rig are this street’s own invention. The lichen is real and the room says so without making a lesson of it. Fluorescence under ultraviolet light is a genuine property of many lichens and a genuine field technique for telling species apart. An earlier draft split the page into what is real and what is invented, and Ryan cut it — this is a street named after a genderqueer, shape-shifting road, and a disclaimer explaining that the sentient rocks are fiction is a page apologising for being the thing it is. What still needs saying is the part about somebody else’s property, which is a different job and lives in the credits. The guard stayed even though the paragraph went. tools/make-looming.py refuses anything shaped like a species name anywhere in the file: the room must never say which lichen glows which colour, because nobody here has checked and a confident binomial beside a colour is the format most likely to be believed. That is the herbarium’s refusal arriving in a light rig — but not the herbarium’s check, which does not survive the move. A bare shape test works on a page of short labels and matches the start of nearly every sentence in prose; its first run here refused “Rocks that”, “Once something” and “Ferrell sings”. It is a shape in a place now: sentence starts are ignored, and it only reads sentences that are about lichen at all. Verified in both directions — a real binomial in a lichen sentence is caught, and a band name in a note is not. Every id was checked on its own watch page before it went up — status, playableInEmbed and length — and the runtimes below are measured rather than typed. That matters more here than anywhere else on the street: these are full concerts, none of them under the hour and the longest over two, so a wrong number in front of a press breaks the street’s promise at the largest scale it can. Nothing is hosted by us and every act names the channel it is on — most of them the artist’s or the band’s own, which is the most durable shape of upload this site carries. The count and the range printed in the room are generated from this same file, because both were typed by hand at first and both were wrong within a day. The stage is the Hermitage’s set on a rock face, and it keeps that set’s promises because they are the street’s rather than that room’s: while the stage is dark, tuning is silent and nothing is fetched; once something is playing, tuning changes the picture. looming.js is a separate file from hermitage.js on purpose — the two sets look alike and are not the same object, and a shared widget would be the harmonising instinct arriving through a script tag. What is shared is love-embed.js, still the only thing on this site that builds a YouTube iframe. The running order is a <details> and opens and closes with no script at all. A fairy fort seen from the outside, turning 02 in The Outskirts. Two novel series are what pointed us at it and nothing in the room is drawn from either: Laurell K. Hamilton’s Merry Gentry books and Seanan McGuire’s October Daye books are named and linked in the room as the reason it exists, and not one court, character, politics or cosmology of either is used. Those are invented worlds belonging to living authors, and the difference between being pointed somewhere and helping yourself is the whole of what this site means by attribution. The refusal is enforced rather than remembered — tools/make-sithen.py will not build the page if a rule’s source names either series or either author. The name was checked rather than assumed. Scottish Gaelic sìthean, a hillock inhabited by fairies, from sìth plus the diminutive — cited to Colin Mark’s Gaelic–English Dictionary (Routledge, 2003, p. 530) by way of Wiktionary, read 2026-09-22. That mattered because one of those two series uses this exact spelling for the fae court, and a room taking the name while claiming to owe the books nothing would have been advertising a debt it does not otherwise have. The word is older than both. The documented half is kept apart from the folklore on purpose, because they are not the same kind of claim and a reader should not have to tell them apart by tone. Ringforts, the thirty-to-forty thousand of them identifiable in 1991, the whitethorn taboo and the 1999 campaign that saved a thorn bush from the M18 at Latoon in County Clare were read off Wikipedia’s article on fairy forts and its article on the Latoon fairy bush. The rules are traditional and the readings beside them are ours. Every taboo says where it comes from; every line under what it is like was written for this room and is not claimed to be in the folklore. Nothing on that page tells anybody how to behave, and the tool refuses the vocabulary of advice, because a page about unwritten rules that ended in tips for following them would be a social skills curriculum with thorns on it. The Raven is Edgar Allan Poe’s, first published in the Evening Mirror, New York, 29 January 1845, and out of copyright everywhere. Where each one sits is our decision and the room says so: that edition printed the poem straight through and the plates after it, and here each plate stands at the lines its own caption quotes. A separate facsimile of the poem in Poe’s own hand is linked and not copied, at the Library of Congress: that printing was made in 1949 and carries a reproduction notice on its own first leaf, and this site does not relicense other people’s assets by copying them. One explicit licence and one notice saying no; the room shows the first and points at the second. The borrowed names

The rooms named after things other people made. None of these people or estates are affiliated with Stimpunks, and none of them endorse us. The rooms are homage, not licence — we took the shape of the idea and wrote our own words in it. Danny the Street A character from DC Comics’ Doom Patrol, created by Grant Morrison and Richard Case, first published in August 1990. A sentient street who turns up wherever somebody needs shelter and rearranges what is on them to suit whoever has arrived. The whole architecture of this site is stolen from Danny, and we would like that on the record — which is why the credit is no longer only in a scrolling marquee that a screen reader never reaches. There is a page about it now: where the name came from, what Danny has been since, the television version, and why the Danny in our marquee uses they/them. Nothing of DC’s is reproduced there; every drawing on it is of a road. Pee-Wee’s Playhouse Created by Paul Reubens. Where the idea of a room in which every object is alive and clickable comes from, and the Playhouse’s secret word too: whenever anybody said it, everybody screamed, and in our room when a toy says it the room screams. The secret word did not start there: Groucho Marx had one on You Bet Your Life, where a duck came down instead, and crediting only the most recent hand is how an idea’s history gets shorter every time it is retold. Pink Pony Club, and Chappell Roan A song by Chappell Roan, and now also a subroom of thirteen videos from the same catalogue. Both take the shape of the work and none of the words — not because a lyric is untouchable, but because this room never needed one to make its point. Where we do quote a song we follow how we quote: a line or two, never the chorus on its own, and the songwriter named separately from the performer. The smial, and J.R.R. Tolkien The Latibulum is drawn as a hobbit-hole — round door, brass knob in the middle of it, thick walls, lamplight, a hill on top — and that shape is Tolkien’s. Smial is his word for it too, which is why it is in this list rather than in a comment. The Tolkien Estate is not affiliated with Stimpunks and does not endorse us. What the room takes is the silhouette and the argument that a hole in the ground is a good place to live; no name, character, place or line of his is used, and the room is named in Latin for that reason. The room checks the sense against Lewis and Short rather than restating the post, so that the two can be read against each other. Enid Sinclair A character in Netflix’s Wednesday. Colorful goth, and the patron saint of not matching the house. Riot grrrl A movement rather than an author. The zine table takes its form — xerox, ransom note, staples, free — and none of its text. Penguin pebbling — Amythest Schaber Not borrowed and not ours either. Penguin pebbling is one of the Five Neurodivergent Love Locutions, coined by Amythest Schaber (Neurowonderful) and documented by Stimpunks in 2022. The line most people meet it through is @brainsandspoons’: “I thought about you today. I remembered this thing about you. Here’s something I want to share with you specifically.” Helen Edgar wrote it up at Autistic Realms in 2023 — a pebble, a twig, a flower, a photograph from a walk, and explicitly not spending money. The cabinet is built on the locution and on nothing else. Penguin Pebbling, the card game — Helen Edgar & Ryan Boren There is already a Penguin Pebbling game and the cabinet here is not it. Penguin Pebbling: A Game of Creating Belonging, Building Connection and Understanding Autistic Identity is thirty cards across all five locutions, by Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms) and Ryan Boren (Stimpunks), 2026, with Helen’s artwork. Go and play that one — it is the better thing and you can print it. The cabinet takes nothing from it: no cards, no prompts, no artwork, no five-locution structure. The reason is a licence rather than modesty. The deck is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and this site is CC BY-SA 4.0; an adaptation would carry the non-commercial clause onto a page that cannot hold it, and share-alike means that is not a thing we could quietly absorb. Relicensing is not ours alone to do either — half the authorship and all the artwork are Helen’s. What the penguins are actually doing Adélie and gentoo penguins build nests out of stones, carry them about, and steal them from each other. The tidy romance is the popular retelling — one penguin choosing the perfect pebble and presenting it to its beloved — rather than the finding, and the cabinet says so on its own face. The locution is named after the image and is not weakened by that: a metaphor does not have to be a finding. Otterly Adorbs, and the otters — Helen Edgar Not borrowed either, and here for the same reason. The Stimpunks Solidarity Session leaves an otter cam running every Saturday while the conversation drifts in and out, and Helen Edgar wrote down what that was doing for her in Stimpunks Solidarity and Otters (Autistic Realms, 2026) — the otters as parallel play, a cave and a watering hole in one animal. Otterly Adorbs is built on her reading, and it is hers: credited to her by name and not folded into our “we”. Helen is at Autistic Realms. What the otters are actually doing The mechanics come from The Stone You Keep (Star Stuff No. 58), which took Helen’s reading to the primary literature and sources every finding. The three the cabinet states on its own face: Tinker, Bentall & Estes, PNAS 105(2) 560–565 (2008), on individual dietary specialisation — there is no standard otter; Hall & Schaller, Journal of Mammalogy 45(2) 287–298 (1964), Point Lobos, thirty instances over six days, a mussel taking a mean 35.5 blows with a range of 6 to 88; and Law et al., Science (2024), 196 tagged otters, tool use varying enormously between individuals and the users showing less tooth damage. One thing the zine corrects and this cabinet follows: the lifelong favourite rock kept in a pouch under the arm is a popular retelling, not a finding. The primary supports a stone kept and reused across successive food items within a bout of feeding, and that is all the game does with it. Quill Drift’s one rule That a porcupine cannot shoot, throw or fire a quill is the correction on card No. 3 of the Quillery, which sources it to Uldis Roze, Porcupines: The Animal Answer Guide (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2012). It is the cabinet’s whole mechanic and not a note at the bottom of it.

The Feed

The object is somebody else’s: a split-flap indicator board is a Solari di Udine machine, the kind that stood in railway stations and airports for decades and the reason a particular clacking noise still means something has changed. The one in that room is drawn from nothing in CSS, is not one of theirs, and makes no sound. Solari are not affiliated with Stimpunks and do not endorse us. What is on the board One wire per site, read off each site’s own RSS feed by tools/pull-arrivals.py into data/arrivals.json, and drawn by tools/make-arrivals.py. Which feed belongs to which site was read off each sibling repository’s own feed.xml — the self link its generator writes — rather than guessed from the domain. Two of those sites publish more than one feed, so which one a wire carries is a decision recorded in the data file, named on the board and linked. Whose words they are The room holds none of them. A row is a title, a date and a link, and there are no summaries, excerpts or opening paragraphs anywhere on that page — make-arrivals.py refuses a row carrying one. Every title belongs to whoever wrote the page it points at. Several of those sites were built with Helen Edgar of Autistic Realms, who is named rather than folded into our “we”; Penguin Pebbling is hers and Ryan Boren’s together. The running order Not ours to choose. It is the order our sites appear in on stimpunks.org’s own feeds page, which is the one place they are already collected by somebody deciding. Re-sorting them here — alphabetically, or by which wire had something newest — would be this room overruling a decision made somewhere else, which is the rule the Jungle Room keeps about its cams. Why it says the minute it was set None of those hosts sends a browser the header that would let our page read its feed, so the board cannot be live, and the ways round that are a proxy we do not run and a third-party reader we would be handing visitors to without asking. So it is a snapshot and it says so: every plate carries the minute its own wire was read, the hall carries the minute the whole board was set, and both numbers are generated from the same file the rows come out of. This is make-jungle.py’s refused runtime upside down — a live camera has no length to give, and a board has a time it was set. Nothing is ranked No busiest, no quietest, no rows-per-week, nothing saying which of our sites has been getting on with it. make-arrivals.py refuses the vocabulary in the room’s own copy. A board that showed that would turn publishing into a race between our own people, most of whom are Disabled and several of whom are one person. The typefaces Michroma sets the room’s name and the nameboard over each machine and nothing else — a very wide squared face is what machined signage looks like and what a paragraph must never be. Space Mono sets every row, date and plate, because a flap board is a grid of cells with one character in each. Both are under the SIL Open Font License. The prose is the street’s ordinary sans, so only the machine has an accent. This street is on its own board stimpunks.world’s changelog feed is fetched over the network like every other wire rather than lifted out of the file next door, which means the board can be out of date about this site too. the-garden
The Garden

The knowledge garden is stimpunks.org’s own idea and its own page, and the argument this room is built on — that ideas spread sideways, that nothing needs to be read in order, and that a garden with no fallow ground is a catalogue — is that page’s. What is ours here is the drawing of it. The Garden. One bed per site we publish, built from data/garden.json by tools/make-garden.py. Which sites are in it is not decided in either of those files: the roster and the running order are read out of data/arrivals.json, whose order is the one our sites appear in on stimpunks.org’s own feeds page — the same list The Feed runs on, and the same reason: re-sorting it here would be this room overruling a decision made somewhere else. What each site is was read off that site’s own pages, and where one of them describes itself in a phrase worth keeping, the phrase is attributed to it rather than absorbed — Star Stuff calls itself the public flowering of this garden, which is its sentence and not ours. The notes here are written for this room: The Feed says what has arrived from a site and this says what grows there, because two rooms holding one paragraph is one room with two doors. Every bed says whose hands are in it, on the face of the bed. Half of these sites were made with Helen Edgar of Autistic Realms; Star Stuff is a collaboration with More Realms; the Cavendish model is David Thornburg’s three primordial spaces by way of Steve Silberman’s NeuroTribes; monotropism is Dinah Murray, Wenn Lawson and Mike Lesser’s; the pebbling locution is Amythest Schaber’s. A credit filed only here and not in the room is a credit nobody reads, so the generator refuses a bed with nobody on it. The garden next door is Helen Edgar’s and is not a bed. Autistic Realms and More Realms are hers, so the only way to plant them would have been to write them into the roster above — which would put them on The Feed as our own wires and claim her work as ours in the one file this room is not allowed to invent anything in. They are through the ivy instead, and the grammar inverts to say so before the words do: a bed shows its soil and most of them show what is under it, and a plot stops where the ivy runs, because we do not get to draw the ground of somebody else’s garden. Nothing over there casts a shadow either — the sun has not moved, the floor is past the ivy. What each of them is was read off its own pages, and the phrases in quotation marks are theirs. It was a woven fence for an afternoon, and Helen asked for ivy and stars instead. Her call, on a drawing of her own gardens, and she was right about more than the picture: a fence says kept out and ivy says this is as far as we can see. What that line marks is the edge of what we know and never the edge of where anybody may go, which is the opposite reading and the correct one on a page about somebody else’s work. The stars are glimmers caught in the ivy rather than a sky — this room is still midday, nothing is lit by them and nothing was added to the page — and threads, glimmers, and soft, weird spaces is More Realms’ own line about itself, which is where the word comes from. They are limewash white carried by an outline, because white on this path measures 1.07 and what has to separate is the edge: the ghost pipe’s answer in Queering.Earth’s bed, in a star. The drawings are ours, and each one is a different habit of growth — a rhizome, an umbel, a plant with no chlorophyll in it, a frame with seedlings under glass, a runner, a dry seed head, a scramble, a tendril. That is the campground’s grammar inverted on purpose: out in the field each pitch gets one lit colour of its own, and there are not many kinds of light. Every habit is also written out in a sentence beside its bed, because the drawings are decoration a screen reader never reaches and the habit is the argument. The Garden Spider is ours too, and it is an orb weaver rather than anybody’s mascot. The spider’s own words are stimpunks.org’s. That a spider is a guide to the garden and never a replacement for it, and that its best answer is an entrance, are lines from our Ask page, quoted from ourselves rather than paraphrased into something softer. The typefaces are Faustina and Mulish, both under the SIL Open Font License, and this is the one room on the street that sets no display face at all.
the-zibaldone
The Zibaldone

The object is nobody’s invention of ours. A zibaldone is a notebook people have been keeping since the fourteenth century, the English word for it is a commonplace book, and our own glossary has had an entry for one since 2022. The room was asked for by somebody in our community — a quote bank, quotes for any state of mind. What is ours is the desk, the drawings and the rules. The good lines belong to the people who wrote them, which is the entire point of the room and the reason its generator refuses so much. The Zibaldone. Built from data/zibaldone.json by tools/make-zibaldone.py, which refuses more than any other generator here: a quotation over its word limit, a song, a line naming a title but no printing, one with no record of how it was checked, a public domain claim that does not clear for the translator as well as the author, a margin note carrying a second quotation, and the vocabulary of ranking. Nothing in that room is ranked, counted or voted on. Every quotation names its printing, and the room prints how it was checked. The public domain lines were read out of the transcriptions named on each card rather than recalled — which is how the Dickinson turned out to be in the second series and not the first, and how the Thoreau kept the sentence he actually wrote instead of the one everybody quotes. The contemporary lines were read off our own published pages. Karen Barad, Helen Edgar, Montaigne, Whitman, Dickinson, Thoreau and Marcus Aurelius by way of Meric Casaubon’s 1634 English — because a translation is a copyrightable work of its own and has to be out of copyright too. The room quotes lightly and refuses songs. The word limit is a number in the generator and the page prints it; a quote bank is the shape of thing that becomes a book one entry at a time. No song lyrics at all, refused by the tool rather than by care, because nothing musical is hosted on this street and this is where that promise would have been broken in the way that looked most harmless. The typefaces are EB Garamond, Newsreader and Lora for the quotations and Kalam for the hand, all under the SIL Open Font License, and the tool refuses a quotation set in the hand. The drawings are ours, one pressed thing per leaf, and each is described in a sentence beside it because a drawing is decoration a screen reader never reaches. The attribution slip copies to your clipboard and sends nothing anywhere — its fields are Creative Commons’ TASL with the three a quotation also needs.
the-rabbit-hole
The Rabbit Hole

Seven more facades and six engravings, down the shaft at the end of the street, and a fifth data file because they came from a fifth place: our own glossary entry, Rabbit Hole. Every video below is one of that page’s own embeds, in that page’s order, which interleaves them with the quotations they sit under — so the running order is an argument somebody made and not a list to re-sort. Titles, channels and runtimes were read off YouTube’s own watch pages on 22 September 2026, along with whether each one plays and whether its owner allows it to be embedded; none of them was written from memory. Three are published by a rights holder and four are re-uploads on individuals’ channels, which the room says on every plate, because that changes how long a link lasts. Not one second of it is hosted by us. The words to White Rabbit are not on that page and will not be. Our glossary entry prints them; this one does not. Song lyric reproduction is a minefield in the United States in a way prose is not — music publishing enforces on quotation where prose publishing shrugs, the licensing is separate from the recording, and one line is a far larger fraction of a song than of a novel — which is the same reasoning that makes the Zibaldone refuse a song outright. So the recordings are offered, Grace Slick’s own published account of writing it is quoted, and tools/make-rabbit-hole.py refuses a lyric field and any value shaped like verse rather than leaving that to anybody’s care. The two headings on that page that are her phrases are credited to her where they stand. The engravings are John Tenniel’s, cut for the first edition of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland in 1865. Tenniel was born in 1820 and died in 1914, so they are out of copyright everywhere; each scan below is one that Wikimedia Commons carries an explicit public domain statement for, which is exactly what the Mopery’s Library of Congress facsimile did not have and the reason that one is linked rather than shown. Every file was re-encoded to greyscale here and written out with no metadata carried over. Nothing was cropped, tinted or filtered. Which engraving sits beside which paragraph is our reading — the 1865 edition captioned none of them — and the room states that rather than letting a reader assume they are looking at the book’s own arrangement. The Healing Checkpoint

Room 429 is built out of one page of ours: the glossary entry for Rest, read out of the Knowledge System mirror on 22 September 2026 rather than fetched live, because on stimpunks.org a 301 is a failure and not a pass. Three lines are quoted from it, each under the thirty-word limit tools/make-checkpoint.py enforces and the room prints, and each one names the page it came from and the day it was checked. Two things on that page are named here and deliberately not copied onto this street — a poem, and three illustrations of Disabled people resting — because a page built out of somebody else’s page should say what it did not take rather than leave it to be noticed. Nothing in that room says what rest is for, and that is a refusal in a tool rather than a habit. Star Stuff’s zine No. 58 spends a spread refusing “rest so you can produce”; otterly.js already holds that line for one cabinet, where floating fills nothing. This is the room where the whole street says it, so the generator sweeps its own data and the published page for the vocabulary of rent — earn, deserve, recharge, productive, bounce back, so you can — with a negation window, so the room can still say out loud that it will not. The friendly edit here arrives from somebody being kind, because every wellness page on the internet is written the other way round, and one sentence of encouragement would turn rest from a thing owed into an investment. Nothing in it is counted and nothing is stored. No total, no streak, no visits, no local storage, no server — which is the pebbling cabinet’s refusal of a tally arriving where a counter is the most obvious improvement anybody could propose, and one floor above a job board that does keep a list in your own browser. A checkpoint that remembered you would be keeping a record of how often you needed one. The Retry-After slips send nothing anywhere: each one is a <details> that works with scripts off, and checkpoint.js only adds a copy button that ships hidden — the Zibaldone’s slip and the guild marker’s arrangement, in a room that cannot afford a dead control. The status code is the joke and it is load-bearing. 429 Too Many Requests was added to HTTP by Mark Nottingham and Roy Fielding in RFC 6585, April 2012, and it says the rate is wrong rather than that the sender is. The room quotes it because a rate is a property of a situation and not of a person. The bed, the alcove and the light in the floor are ours; the trope is TV Tropes’ name for a thing games have always had, and belongs to nobody. The typefaces are Quicksand and Rubik, both under the SIL Open Font License, and they are the only two rounded faces in the room because it is the only room on the street with no hard edge in it.
