What the street is for

I could not live in any of the worlds offered to me – the world of my parents, the world of war, the world of politics. I had to create a world of my own, like a climate, a country, an atmosphere in which I could breathe, reign, and recreate myself when destroyed by living. — Anaïs Nin,
The Diary of Anaïs Nin, Vol. 5: 1947–1955
What the street is for

As neurodivergent and Disabled people, we’re often told we live in our own worlds. We said why not and built Stimpunks.World. It’s infused with fantasy and hopeful longing, but also rimed with hard lessons in hard reality. You don’t have to explain reality to us. We live closest to it. We’ve found better ways, and present them here. Read off the front page of stimpunks.org, which quotes it, and not checked against the Diary from here. That page’s copy prints the pronoun as a vertical bar, a slip from reading the words off an image; it is an I here. What follows is the street’s mission. Every aim names the page where it is already being kept, and the failure that would show we had quietly stopped, because a list of values you cannot check against the work is only a list. The argument underneath it is the manifesto, Ribald Songing, printed as a broadside you can pin up. Last updated 2026-09-30. Every change to it is dated in the changelog.
THE WHOLE OF IT, IN ONE SENTENCE

Stimpunks.World is the Stimpunks Foundation getting wild, wacky and loose on purpose: a street of rooms that share nothing but a dial and a set of promises, built so that difference is the layout rather than the exception, and so that nobody has to earn the right to walk in.
claiming
What we are claiming

Belonging comes before anything else. The street is Danny’s, and it rearranges itself for whoever turns up, so it has no wrong side and no outside to push anybody to. Even the road past the last streetlight, The Outskirts, is a direction and not a verdict. We would have stopped the day a page calls any corner of the street the place where the people who do not fit end up. No two rooms alike. Every room brings its own light, its own type and its own colours, even where they argue with the room next door, and that repetition of ideas in different clothes is the product. How this site is made says why. We would have stopped the day two rooms share a palette because it was tidier.
owed
What we owe whoever walks in

How loud it gets is yours to hold. Every page carries the dial, and Gentle takes away the wobble, never the words. A checker renders every page at every setting to hold us to it. We would have stopped the day Gentle shows somebody less, or anything moves before they asked. Nothing from anybody else plays or loads until you press it, and every play button says, before the press, how long the thing runs or that it runs until you stop it. We would have stopped the day a video frame loads on arrival. Clashing is not the same as illegible. The colour under every word is measured, and a pair that fails stops the build. We would have stopped the day a colour ships because it looked fine. Rest is owed, not earned. The Healing Checkpoint and Stay Frosty are for it, and neither says what rest will do for you afterwards. We would have stopped the day a room calls rest a way to recharge for more work. Nobody is counted, ranked or scored. No tally in the pebbling cabinet, no score on the Adventurer’s Guild’s board, no headliner on any bill. The numbers on the street belong to nobody: Pando Calrissian’s, how many times we have watered one tree together, and Count Me In’s, the step we have climbed to together and the highest it has reached. None of them says who. We would have stopped the day anybody on the street has a total of their own, or anything grows a progress bar. Your face and your voice stay yours. A photograph goes up only with its subject’s own consent, stays outside the site’s licence, and is deleted when they say so, as Enid’s wall promises. A recording of a voice says whose it is on the press. We would have stopped the day a photograph is still up after somebody said no. We keep as little about you as we can, and the privacy page says exactly what that is. We would have stopped the day something is kept that the page does not name.
work
How we work

The credits get louder, not quieter. Every writer, printing, typeface and drawing hand is named, in the room and in the liner notes, because attribution is the one careful habit this street kept when it dropped the others. We would have stopped the day a quotation goes up without the printing it came from, or a song without its writers. In the open, errors included. Ryan Boren and Helen Edgar build the street, and either of them can change anything in it. Changes are dated in the changelog, and a correction to something we published stays on its page, where the person who read the mistake will see it. We would have stopped the day a mistake is quietly swapped for the right answer.

What a street has to do with Stimpunks

Stimpunks builds accessible infrastructure and public tools that support disabled and neurodivergent people to live with dignity, challenge dehumanizing systems, and design environments that honor difference as strength. — We, Stimpunks, Mission
stimpunks
What a street has to do with Stimpunks

The Stimpunks Foundation is created by and for neurodivergent and Disabled people, and its mission begins with direct support and mutual aid. It also says this: This street is the last part of that sentence, built rather than argued: an environment where difference is the architecture. It is also the only one of our sites that gets to be loud, and it was built to show that loud and accessible are not opposites.

The limit, said plainly

This street is not mutual aid. It pays no rent, buys no groceries and gives no grant. The foundation does those things, and the street says so and sends people there. A page of loud rooms that let anybody blur the two would be doing the thing we exist to name. It also does not speak for every Disabled or neurodivergent person, and it is not finished: the street keeps growing, and if the rooms stop matching this page, the page is what is wrong.

How this site is made

Every other Stimpunks site has a design system. This one has a street instead, and every room on it refuses to look like the one next door. This page says what is shared, what is not, what gets checked, and who makes it, including how we use AI. Last updated 2026-10-04. Every change to it is dated in the changelog.
THE SHORT VERSION

No design system, on purpose. Every room is its own visual world, and no two are alike. One thing every room shares is the dial, so how loud the street gets is up to you. Loud is allowed. Illegible is not. Contrast is measured on every page. Nothing from anybody else plays or loads until you press it. The credits are loud, because attribution is the one careful habit this street kept. Most of the building is done by Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, working to briefs from Ryan Boren and Helen Edgar. What that means is below.
no-design-system
No design system, on purpose

Queering Earth is drawn as a herbarium sheet in daylight. Star Stuff has a design system page with a palette you can copy. Both are careful, and so is every other site we run. This one started from Ryan’s brief of 2026-09-19: “All of our sites are so careful. Careful color palettes, careful fact checking, careful sourcing, careful attribution. I wanna get wild and wacky and loose.” So here the street is the system and the rooms refuse to share one. Each room brings its own ground, its own typefaces and its own palette. What does the most work is that each one is lit differently. The Faery Yurt is candlelight in canvas. The Latibulum has one low lamp in a burrow. The Community Center gets morning sun through a venetian blind. The Healing Checkpoint is lit from under the floor. The Outskirts has nothing but headlights, and the Adventurer’s Guild is lit like a photocopy, from nowhere at all. When two rooms are about the same feeling, something structural keeps them apart: where the light comes from, what the room is built of, which way round the words sit. A nudge to a colour will not do it. The instinct to tidy all that up, with one type scale, one palette and shared components, is the right instinct on every other site we make. Here it would delete the thing the street is for. The rule we work to is short: if a change would make two rooms look more alike, it is probably wrong. You will not find a count of the rooms anywhere on this site. The street keeps growing, and a total written into a dozen places goes out of date in eleven of them the day a room opens. A small checker refuses any sentence that states one.
shared
What every room shares

One stylesheet, love.css, holds the whole street. It opens with a small shared base: the typefaces, a few ground rules every page needs (the skip link, the focus ring, making sure a hidden thing stays hidden), the dial, and some shared furniture. That furniture is the press-to-play plate, the job marker from the Adventurer’s Guild, the fractal window and the sign-off at the foot of every page. It carries layout and no colour of its own, so it turns up in each room wearing that room’s ink. After the base, every room gets a section of its own, free to contradict all the others. Those sections duplicate each other’s ideas in different clothes, and that duplication is the point. The pages that have a job to do and no room to be, like this one, Privacy, the liner notes and the changelog, share one quiet look and otherwise get out of the way.
the-dial
The dial

Every page has a dial with Gentle, Regular and MAX GLITTER on it. It starts wherever your device says about reduced motion, and once you pick a setting your browser remembers it (that is love-intensity on the privacy page). Gentle stills everything. Regular moves things when you hover over them or focus them. MAX GLITTER turns on the ambient layers, like the mirrorball over the dancefloor and the sparks at the guild. Gentle takes away the wobble, never the words. No content is kept behind a louder setting, and nothing you can read at MAX is missing at Gentle. A checker loads every page at all three settings and measures both halves of that. Games keep a speed control of their own, separate from the dial, so Gentle never hands anybody a lesser game. Nothing on the street flashes or strobes, with one exception. The Rebellion Rave Room has a strobe for the people who stim with one, and it sits behind a warning and two presses. This is a Disabled people’s organisation. A glitter-maximalist site that overwhelmed the people it is for would be the kind of self-own we exist to name. We did not fix that by toning the site down. We made loudness something the visitor holds. Access is the premise of this design, not the brake on it.
contrast
Loud, not illegible

Clashing is not the same as illegible. All text on the street is held to WCAG AA contrast against every ground it sits on, and two different checkers do the holding. The first is a list of every text colour and ground somebody chose, each with its ratio and the reason beside it. The second renders every page in a browser and measures each piece of text against the colour actually behind it, because the colour that renders is not always the colour that was written down. Each checker has caught failures the other could not see. Decoration that carries no words is listed with its measurement rather than ignored, and every room chooses its own focus ring, because a ring picked for a dark street disappears on a pale one. The one change this repository made to Helen Edgar’s design for the Faery Yurt was a single grey, which failed contrast on every ground it sat on. That change is written up in the liner notes and the changelog rather than left in a diff.
press-to-play
Nothing plays until you press it

Every video and player on the street is a plate standing in for the real thing. Until you press it, this site has made no request to that service for you. Every plate says how long it runs before you press it. A live camera or a playlist has no length to give, so its plate says that instead. Every typeface, script, stylesheet and image is served from this site, so opening a page talks to nobody but our host. The full account is on the privacy page.
type
Type

Every typeface is self-hosted, and a room only downloads the faces it sets. The Foundry holds every face on the street, with who drew it, what licence it travels under and which rooms set it, all read from each family’s own record in Google Fonts’ public repository rather than typed in. Most are under the SIL Open Font License and a few are under Apache 2.0. We know that because a tool read those records and found our own credits saying every face was OFL.
cards
Share cards

Every page has a share card, the picture that shows up when somebody posts a link. Each one is rendered in a headless browser from the page’s own markup and stylesheet, with a design for each room rather than one template, and none is written without alt text. A new room will not build until it has a card of its own. A room with somebody else’s face on its card would be the street tidying itself up somewhere nobody looks.
built
How it is built

The site is plain HTML files, one stylesheet and some small scripts, with no framework and nothing to compile before it can be served. Next to them sits a workshop of Python tools. Some generate the parts of a page that have to agree with a data file: a jukebox’s track list, a credit, the sitemap, a share card. Others check things we have got wrong before: a page left out of the sitemap, a photograph still carrying its location, a colour nobody measured, a quotation longer than a room allows, a credit with nobody’s name on it. The tools refuse rather than guess, and when one refuses, we fix the cause and leave the tool alone. It is hosted on Netlify. The only code that runs on a server is the CB radio, together with its chalkboard, its pebble bowls and the Slake. Everything else is files. The source and its whole history are on GitHub. Architecture has the code and the hosting in full: the deploy, the generators and checkers, the CB’s server side, the morning timers and every outside service. Our words and design are under CC BY-SA 4.0. Photographs, recorded voices, songs, typefaces and borrowed names keep their own terms, the broadside sheets are given away under CC0, and the licence file says which is which.
ai
Who makes it, and how we use AI

Ryan Boren and Helen Edgar make this street. They decide what each room is, what it argues, what it refuses and where on the street it goes. They write the briefs that the rooms quote, and they correct the rooms when they are wrong. The Faery Yurt is Helen’s own design, from a mockup she built. Most of the building is done by Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, in Claude Code sessions that Ryan or Helen directs. Claude writes nearly all of the code: the pages, the stylesheet, the scripts, and the generators and checkers described above. It also drafts most of the words in the rooms, working from the briefs, from our own pages on stimpunks.org, and from the sources each room credits. Nearly every change in the site’s public history names Claude as a co-author, so you can see which parts it wrote. Some specifics, so nothing here has to be guessed at: The drawings are code. The pictures you see in the rooms, from the shopfronts to the chairs, are SVG shapes and CSS, and Claude writes that code to a brief. No image generator made any picture on this street. Stimpunks does not use generative AI for art on stimpunks.org. These drawings are made by a language model writing code, and we would rather say that plainly than call them hand-drawn. The photographs and the old engravings are not AI-made. The photographs are of real people and real things, published with consent and credited. The engravings and plates are public domain scans, each one credited to its artist. In the Collection Collection, Claude describes the photographs by looking at each one, so that nobody has to write a title, a description and a caption before they can send in a picture. Every cabinet says so on its label. No voice on this site was made by an AI. Every recorded voice belongs to the person named beside it. When the CB reads messages aloud, it uses your own device’s voice. Nothing you do here is sent to an AI. No page on this street calls an AI service. The Garden’s spider links out to Ask, the generative search on stimpunks.org, and says what that is before you go. What an AI gets wrong, and how this site catches it. A language model’s most common mistakes are exactly the ones this site’s tools are built to refuse: a quotation, a credit or a number written from memory, a book link that points at a different book, a framing borrowed because it sounded right. Many of those mistakes were Claude’s, and many are written up in the changelog along with how they were found. Quotations are checked against a source, and each one says how it was checked. Where one could not be checked, the page says that too. Checkers catch what can be checked. People looking at the page catch the rest, and several faults on this street were found by Ryan simply pressing the buttons. Stimpunks’ policy on all of this is AI Collaboration at Stimpunks, and the thinking behind it is at AI at Stimpunks and AI, Disability Justice, and the Ethics of Making. Those pages name the tensions honestly, the energy and water costs included, and we carry the same tensions here. Generative AI is built from knowledge taken from communities, so what we make with it goes back to the commons. That is one reason everything we write here is under an open licence.

hosting
Hosting and deploy

Netlify serves the repository root as it is, and a push to main is a deploy: live in a minute or two, with no staging step and no review. There is no build command, no bundler and no fingerprinting. The HTML in the repository is what you are reading. Domain. stimpunks.world since 2026-09-23. stimpunks.love (2026-09-19 to 2026-09-23) and stimpunks-love.netlify.app stay registered and send you here, path for path, with a 301. Functions. Netlify bundles netlify/functions/*.mjs on deploy and installs the one dependency in package.json, @netlify/blobs. Nothing else is installed or built. Storage. One Netlify Blobs store named cb, opened with strong consistency. It is the only thing the site keeps on a server. Rate limits. Each function declares Netlify’s own limiter in its config. The limiter counts addresses itself, so no IP address ever reaches our code or our storage. Every pass is an HMAC keyed by it, so changing it and redeploying signs everybody off. CB_MOD_PASSWORD The base station’s password, for moderators CB_MODS Which handles hold which roles. Missing or unreadable, it fails closed. CB_JAAS_KID, CB_JAAS_KEY The 8x8 key id and private key that sign call tokens CB_JAAS_EVENTS_SECRET Checks 8x8’s webhook saying who is in a call CB_JAAS_HOOK_SECRET An optional check on 8x8’s settings webhook The local server is not the site. npx serve sends no headers, so a policy failure only shows on the live host. It drops a query string on its clean-URL redirect, which Netlify does not. It runs no functions, so /cb/* answers 404 there; the CB runs under netlify dev after npm install, or live.
front-end
The front end

Every page is a hand-written HTML file at the repository root, complete before any script arrives, styled by one shared stylesheet and plain scripts with no framework and no dependencies. There is deliberately no design system: each room is its own visual world, and the code is arranged so that stays true. A page. Its <body> class names the room, and that class is the hook for the room’s section of love.css and for its share card. The <head> carries, in order: the pre-paint snippet, the same on every page byte for byte, which sets the dial from localStorage or prefers-reduced-motion before first paint; its sha256 is in the security policy; the canonical address, the description and the Open Graph tags, with the share card written by make-og.py; structured data from tools/structured.py, built from the page’s own title, description and address; love.js, plus whatever scripts that room needs, all deferred. love.css is one file in numbered sections. §1 is the self-hosted typefaces, with fonts/_sources.json recording where each came from. §2 is ground rules: every colour as a custom property on :root, and a global rule that keeps a hidden thing hidden. §3 is the intensity dial. §4 is shared furniture that is layout and never colour: the back link, the sign-off, the press-to-play plate, the job marker. Then each room, area or piece of street furniture gets a self-contained section, duplicating ideas in its own clothes on purpose. Small screens and print close the file. check-classes.py refuses a class claimed by two rooms, a custom property declared twice, and a section number out of order. The dial. Gentle, Regular and MAX change motion and sparkle only, never content. §3’s reset carries !important, and rooms scope their own tilts with :where() so the reset can win. check-gentle.py measures every page at all three settings. Script Loaded Job love.js every page The dial, the Playhouse toys and the superposition panel, and two loaders: the radio and the fractal window love-embed.js pages with something to press The only code that builds a frame or an audio player. It holds the lists of origins it will frame and play from, and the call’s. rack.js rooms with a rack A rack’s screen and each card’s second button, found by data-rack-* attributes and never by class quest.js every page with a job marker The Adventurer’s Guild’s markers. The markers themselves are <details> and work without it. finder.js the front page and the map only Search over room names, descriptions and search-index.json cb.js and cb.css only once signed on to the CB The radio, in a shadow root so no room’s styles reach it guest.js not signed on The radio’s bar folded shut: the teleporter and the way on. It knows nothing about the channel. call.js, callroom.js on a press A room’s 8x8 call window, and the mover the radio shares fractal.js on a press The sign-off’s fractal window, limited so it cannot flash a room’s own script that room’s page only Its game, toys or machine: arcade.js, mud.js, stay-breezy.js and the rest Press to play. A play button is a <button class="facade"> that names the thing and how long it runs. Nothing reaches a third party until it is pressed. Then love-embed.js checks the address against its list and swaps the button for a youtube-nocookie.com frame, or another origin on the list. A room styles the pressed state on the container, because the button’s classes do not survive the swap. What your browser keeps. Only localStorage, and only in your browser: love-intensity (the dial), love-cb (your CB pass and handle), love-cb-guest (the guest panel left open), love-quests (the Guild’s list), love-rescues (animals you rescued) and love-breezy (Stay Breezy’s usual fans). Privacy says the same. Every read and write is wrapped so a private window still works. Machine-readable files, all generated: sitemap.xml, llms.txt, feed.xml (from the changelog), cb-rooms.json, search-index.json, /.well-known/security.txt, /.well-known/api-catalog and the agent skill under /.well-known/agent-skills/.

cb
Server side: the CB

The CB, a chat channel patterned after citizens band radio, is the only server-side code on the site: Netlify Functions in netlify/functions/ sharing one library, netlify/cb/lib.mjs, and one Netlify Blobs store. Every promise on Privacy is kept in that library. How it runs. Each function is a JavaScript module whose config gives its address and a Netlify rate limit. A request carries the pass from the browser, readPass() checks it, and a change is written only if the stored copy has not changed since it was read, so people writing at once never lose a message. One scheduled function, cb-midnight, runs every hour and sweeps whatever has expired. It runs hourly because midnight in Colorado moves between 06:00 and 07:00 UTC. The radio only asks while it is open and in front. One function in cb.js decides; folded, or in a background tab, the radio sends nothing. Open, it listens every four seconds. Tuned to World it says nothing about where it is; tuned to a room it names that room. Area Addresses What is kept, and for how long Signing on /cb/signon, /cb/account, /cb/account/recover, /cb/account/admin A pass is an HMAC keyed by the password, kept only in your browser. A claimed username is a salted scrypt hash, a version and a lock, filed under a hash of the name. No email, and no list of accounts. The channels /cb/channel, /cb/transmit, /cb/moderate, /cb/react, /cb/image Ten messages per channel (World, or one per room), gone at midnight Colorado time. Pictures are redrawn in your browser, refused if they still carry metadata, and deleted with their message. Being seen, and watching together /cb/here, /cb/here/leave, /cb/online, /cb/beacon One record per visit, shown for 30 seconds after its last check; Who’s online is read from those records and nothing records who looked. A host’s beacon is replaced, never added to. Calls /cb/call, /cb/call-events, /cb/call-settings Nothing about a call. It signs an 8x8 token for one handle and one room, and reads 8x8’s webhooks for who is in a call. Boards /cb/chalk*, /cb/pebbles*, /cb/brass*, /brass-tacks.xml The chalkboard and the pebble bowls: a week. The Brass Tacks Board: until a moderator takes a post down. Shared games /cb/pando*, /cb/fridge*, /cb/stair*, /cb/shelter*, /cb/pets*, /cb/adopted A tree’s count, finished sentences and a stair’s step, kept with no name in them. Adopted pets, under a hash of the handle, until Forget Me. The Slake /cb/mud/here, /cb/mud/say, /cb/mud/leave, /cb/mud/moderate Presence per visit, replaced on moving. Each place’s talk is gone at midnight. The sweep cb-midnight, scheduled Deletes what has expired across all of the above Never stored: an IP address (Netlify’s limiter counts them and never hands them over), anything a person types in a log line, an email address, or a list of who has signed on. Who’s online is worked out from the thirty-second records Be seen here keeps, each time somebody asks. Roles. CB_MODS says which handles hold which roles, and it is read on every request. The server decides who may enter each private room in the Town Hall, in one function. A page that hides its radio from the wrong person is only keeping quiet; it is not the lock. Calls are 8x8’s Jitsi as a Service. The CB signs a token with CB_JAAS_KEY for one room, and nobody joins without one. Guests get a token, never a moderator’s, only for the rooms Cavendish Coworking keeps open to the world. love-embed.js builds the call’s frame, and 8x8 is the only origin given the camera, microphone and screen.
timers
Scheduled jobs

The rooms that show other sites’ feeds are snapshots refreshed by Ryan’s laptop each morning, not live pages. None of those hosts lets a page read its feed from another site, and the alternatives were a proxy we do not run or a third-party reader. Each room prints when it was last set, so a missed morning leaves an honest page rather than a wrong one. The task. A Claude Code scheduled task, arrivals-board-daily, runs at 06:10 local time on Ryan’s machine. Its instructions are tracked in .claude/scheduled-tasks/arrivals-board-daily/SKILL.md, and tools/install-scheduled-task.sh installs that copy and reports drift. The schedule itself lives in the scheduler, not the repository. Each script does the same five things. It refuses unless the tree is on main and its own files are clean. It pulls, which is the only network step; redraws its room; runs the fast offline checkers as a gate; then commits only its own files under a fixed subject and pushes. A failed push is left for a person. The scripts never rebase or force. Third parties

A page load contacts nobody but stimpunks.world. The security policy makes that a property of the site rather than a habit: default-src, script-src, font-src, img-src and connect-src are all 'self', so there is no analytics, no CDN and no third-party script to remove. Every outside origin below is reached only after somebody presses something. working
Working on it

Ryan Boren and Helen Edgar both commit straight to main, one at a time, each working through their own Claude, and they agree outside the repository whose turn it is. A push is a deploy and nothing reviews it, so the routine is the safeguard: Pull before touching anything; the morning task will have pushed. Run tools/check-all.sh before every commit. Files it changes are generated files catching up with a source, and they go in with the change that caused them. Commit and push when you stop. Uncommitted work blocks the other person and the morning task, which refuses to run over anybody’s edits. Never hand-merge a generated file. Take either side, fix the source and run the build again. A new changelog entry goes at the top with its own id, because the id is the feed item’s permanent address. Privacy
What this site knows about you is very little, and this page is all of it. Last updated 2026-10-07. Every change to it is dated in the changelog.
THE SHORT VERSION

No cookies. This site sets none, on any page. No advertising, no trackers, nothing sold, and no email. There is nothing to sign up for and nobody to sell anything to. The CB asks for a handle and a shared password. An account is optional: signed on, you can claim your username with a password of your own, and that account is the username, its password and nothing else. More below. A few things are kept in your own browser, each because you asked for it. Only one of them is ever sent anywhere, and only to us, and only by the CB: the radio, the chalkboard, the pebble bowls, Pando Calrissian’s tree and its fence, the Fridge of Sighs, Count Me In’s stair, the cat and dog shelters and Profile, and the Slake. The CB is the one thing on this site that sends anything, and only while you have it open. What is said on it is kept for the day, ten messages at most, and then deleted. A room’s call is run by 8x8, and only people signed on to the CB can join one, except the three public calls behind Cavendish Coworking’s meeting doors, which a guest joins under a name they type. While somebody is in a call we keep their name in it, from 8x8, and it goes when they leave. More below. You can choose to be seen. Signed on, Be seen here puts your handle and the room you are in on the radio’s Who’s online list, for anybody signed on to the CB, and shows you and anybody else seen in the same room to each other, with who is in its call. Nobody who has not chosen it is shown, and nothing is counted. In a room that keeps to itself, being seen shows you only to people seen there, and never on Who’s online. More below. Hosting a film is the CB too. If you press Host this film, everybody signed on sees which film you are watching, in which room, and where it has got to, until you stop. More below. The chalkboard on Plural Mural is the CB’s too, and it is public. Only people signed on to the CB can write on it, anybody at all can read it, and every note is rubbed out after seven days. Pando Calrissian’s tree is the CB’s too. Signed on, you can water it. It keeps how many times it has been watered, for good, and never who watered it. The fence beside it holds notes on the chalkboard’s rules. More below. The Fridge of Sighs is the CB’s too. Signed on, you can put up one word of a sentence. Finished sentences are kept for good and no word says who put it up. More below. Count Me In’s stair is the CB’s too. Signed on, you can take the next step, by number or by the lift. It keeps the step it is on and the highest it has reached, for good, and never who took any step. More below. Rescue A Cat, Rescue A Dog and Rescue Small Animals are the CB’s too. Signed on, you can rescue an animal and name it, and adopt one into Profile on your radio. The shelters and the list of everybody adopted never say who rescued or adopted anybody. Your pets are the one thing the street keeps under a person, filed under a scrambled form of your handle, and Forget me in Profile deletes them. More below. The Slake, out the back of the MUD Room, is the CB too. Signed on, you can choose to be seen out there, on each visit, and only then does it send anything: where you are and what you say. You meet people in the place you are in; nobody gets a list of who is out there, and nothing is counted. Nothing from anybody else loads until you press it. Every video and player on the street waits for a press. Our host keeps ordinary server logs, the way every web server does.

What our host sees

This site is served by Netlify. Like any web server, it receives what every browser sends with every request — your IP address, your browser’s user-agent string, the address you asked for and the time — and it keeps logs of that under Netlify’s own privacy policy, which also says how long. We need that to run and secure a website, which is the legal basis for it (legitimate interests). We have not switched on Netlify’s analytics, we do not add anything to those logs, and we do not use them to find out who anybody is. Every typeface, script, stylesheet and image on this site is served from this site, so opening a page makes no request to anybody but Netlify.
search
Searching the street

The search box on the street and on the Map does its searching in your browser. The first time you type in it, it fetches two files from this site, the list of rooms and the words on every page, and nothing else. When you press play

The jukeboxes, screens and players on the street are press-to-play: until you press one, this site has made no request to that service on your behalf. When you press, your browser loads that service’s player, and from then on the service receives what any website receives from you — your IP address, your browser details, and that you came from stimpunks.world (the site’s address only, not the page) — and may set its own cookies. What it does with that is covered by its own policy, not ours: The services a press-to-play control loads, and their privacy policies Service Where on the street Its privacy policy YouTube, through youtube-nocookie.com Most of the videos, songs and live cameras Google’s privacy policy Spotify Club Chronic’s stage Spotify’s privacy policy Apple Music Club Chronic’s stage Apple’s privacy policy VideoPress Swaying Sweetgrass Automattic’s privacy policy 8x8, whose Jitsi as a Service runs the calls A room’s call, opened from the CB’s radio by people signed on to it. More below. 8x8’s privacy notice Wikimedia Commons A Quiet Pint’s player piano, which plays its rolls from where each recording is kept The Wikimedia Foundation’s privacy policy Josephmooon’s own site, on WordPress.com The Small Hours’ jukebox, which plays the band’s recordings from where the band keeps them Automattic’s privacy policy The recordings in Hear Queer Here, the Faery Yurt and the Playhouse are served from this site, and none of them loads until you press it either.
When you follow a link away

A lot of this site is links to other places. When you follow one, the site you arrive at learns that you came from stimpunks.world — the address of the site, never the page you were on — and from then on you are covered by that site’s policy.
People on these pages

Some pages carry photographs of people, recordings of people’s voices, and the names of the people we credit. Every photograph of somebody, and every recording of somebody’s voice, is published with that person’s consent, recorded in our files with a date — the readings in Hear Queer Here included — and it comes down when the person in it says so: one message, no reason needed. A young person who is doing the work and has said yes themselves is published and credited like anybody else; a parent’s yes does not stand in for theirs, and a child too young to give that consent is not published at all. The whole of that is on the Polaroid Wall’s page. The photographs are excluded from this site’s CC BY-SA licence precisely so that taking one down is something we can actually do.
cb
The CB

The CB is a chat channel, patterned after citizens band radio. You sign on at the Community Center with a handle you make up and a password we share with the community and change from time to time. Until you sign on, the radio is not on any page and nothing is sent. Before you sign on. A folded bar in the corner of each page, with a teleporter and a way to find out how to get on the CB. It is not the radio: it sends nothing to the channel, knows nothing about who is on it, and shows nothing that is said. Opening the teleporter fetches this site’s list of rooms, from this site, and nothing else is fetched. If you leave its panel open, your browser remembers that under love-cb-guest, and folding it away deletes it. You can sign on from it too, if you know the password: that sends exactly what the front desk sends, only when you press Sign on, and then the radio takes its place. What it sends. While the radio is open on your screen and the tab is in front of you, it asks this site for the latest messages every few seconds, and the first time it does, or the first time you open its teleporter, it also fetches the list of rooms on the street, so that a room named with a # can be shown as a link and the teleporter knows where it can take you; that request carries nothing about you. Teleporting to a room is an ordinary link on this site: it sends nothing to the channel and tells nobody where you went. Typing an @ into it asks us who is online, once, and narrows that list in your browser, so what you type after the @ is not sent. More below. Closed, folded down, or in a tab you are not looking at, it sends nothing. When you transmit, your handle and your words come to us. World, or this room. The radio hears one channel at a time. World is the one everybody shares, and listening to it tells us nothing about where you are on the street. This room is the room’s own channel, and to hear it the radio has to tell us which room it is, each time it asks. We do not keep that: nothing records who listened to which room. The radio starts on World, and it remembers which you chose, in your own browser. A place in a film. Somebody can put a place like @34:12 in a message, and on every radio it is a button that moves the film on your page to that place. It never presses play, and nobody else can move your film: only your own press does. Add my spot reads where the film on your page has got to, and the film’s title and the room you are in, and writes them into your message box. The room’s name in a spot links to that room with the spot on the end of the address, after a #, which your browser never sends to any server, ours included; arriving that way gets that film’s play button ready to start at the spot, and nothing plays until you press it. The radio and the film talk to each other inside your browser. That sends nothing, to us or to YouTube, until you transmit it like anything else you type. What we keep. The latest ten messages on each channel, World and every room’s, each with its handle, its words, the time it was sent, whether it came from the base station or from a claimed username, the picture sent with it, if there was one, and its description, and the sticker, if it was one: a copy of what one of your pets looks like and is called, taken when you sent it. Reactions are kept on the message they were pressed on: which reaction and the handle that pressed it, shown to everybody on that channel by handle and never as a number, and deleted with the message. An eleventh pushes the oldest off, picture and all. Everything on every channel is deleted every day at midnight, Colorado time, and a moderator can delete a message sooner. There is no archive, no backup and no copy. A picture. A screenshot or a photo sent on the channel is redrawn in your own browser before it leaves it, which takes off everything a camera or a phone writes into the file, where it was taken first of all; this site refuses a file that still carries any of it. It is kept only with its message and deleted when the message goes, and one that was never sent is deleted within the hour. It has no public address: only a radio signed on to that channel can fetch it, and a picture sent in one of the Town Hall’s private rooms only by the people that room is for. Download saves the copy your radio already holds onto your own device, which is yours; it asks us for nothing more. A link to another site. An address on another site in a message is a link that opens in a new tab and says which site it goes to. Following it sends that site nothing from here: no referrer, so it is not told which page of ours you came from, and nothing about the channel. What it does once you are there is up to that site. Copy. Copy on a message puts its words on your own clipboard, in your browser. It sends nothing, to us or anybody. What we do not keep. Your IP address is not stored with a message or anywhere else by us, and we do not write handles or messages into any log. We keep no list of who has signed on. Where it is kept. Netlify, our host, stores the channel for us and runs the small program that answers the radio, under Netlify’s privacy policy. Netlify’s ordinary logs record that the radio made a request, the same as for any page. Netlify also limits how often one address can try the password; it does that itself, without handing the address to us. Who can read it. Anybody signed on, which means anybody who has the current password. That makes it a room full of people rather than a private line, so say on it what you would say in a room. An unclaimed handle is not checked, so a handle is not proof of who somebody is, except a moderator’s: our moderators’ handles, and which of them hold the board, director or administrator role, are on a short list kept in the site’s settings on Netlify and not published. A handle on it signs on only with the moderators’ password, and is refused with the community one. The list is read each time a pass is checked and never written to by the radio, and the only thing a radio is told about it is its own roles, so that it can keep out of the Town Hall’s rooms it cannot use. What it does not do. No notifications, no chimes, no badges, no unread count. If the radio is closed, nothing reaches you and nothing is saved up for later. Speaking aloud. If you switch on Speak new messages aloud, the radio reads each new message out, handle first, using a voice built into your own device. It only uses voices your device says are on the device itself, so the words are not sent to a speech service anywhere else; some browsers also offer voices that are, and the radio will not use those. If your device has no voice of its own, nothing is spoken. Each message comes with a burst of radio static before it and the tail of static after, made in the page and not fetched from anywhere; at the Gentle setting the words come without it, and there is no static without a message being spoken. It is off until you switch it on, it only reads what arrives while the radio is open, and folding the radio away stops it mid-word. We keep a message because you sent it for other people on the channel to read, and keeping it for the day is what that takes. Transmitting is your consent to it, and you can take that back by asking us to delete what you said.
hosting
Hosting a film

Anybody signed on to the CB can host the film they are watching, with Host this film on the radio, so that everybody else on the channel can see where it has got to and catch up. It is off until you press it, it is never remembered, and a new page starts with nobody hosting. What it sends, and when. Your pass, your handle, the room you are in, the film’s title, its YouTube id and how long it runs, the place in it and whether it is playing. The id is what lets everybody else’s radio find that film’s own play button on the page, when several films have nearly the same name, and how long it runs is what a play button says when a radio has to put one up (below). It goes when you start hosting, when the film plays, pauses, jumps or changes, and every half minute besides, and only while the radio is open and the tab is in front of you. Put the tab behind another and it stops sending until you come back; fold the radio away or leave the page and you stop hosting. What we keep. One record for each room somebody is hosting, holding exactly that and the time it was last heard. Every update replaces it rather than adding to it, so there is no history of what you watched or where you were in it. It is deleted the moment you stop hosting. If you go quiet instead, by folding the radio or leaving, it is shown to nobody seventy-five seconds after it was last heard, and it is gone for good at the next update from any host or at the hourly sweep, whichever comes first. There is no archive, no backup and no copy. Who can see it. Anybody signed on, on every page: their radio shows who is hosting which film in which room, and where it has got to. Everybody’s radio is sent every host on the street with the channel, so nobody’s radio has to tell us which room they are in to find the host for theirs. A room that keeps to itself is the exception: its host is sent only to radios tuned to that room’s own channel, and to nobody else. What it does not do. It moves nobody’s film. Catch up is a button on each person’s own radio, and only their press moves their film, the same as a place in a message. Follow, beside it, keeps your film in step with the host’s, playing, pausing and moving with it, but only once you have pressed it yourself; it sends nothing, it is never remembered, and your own pause ends it. One person hosts a room at a time, and only the base station can take a room over. A moderator’s own video. A moderator can paste the address of one YouTube video into Screen a video on the radio, and it goes up on the first screen of the page they are on. It plays on their page and nowhere else, and nothing is sent to us until they host it. If they do, pressing Catch up or Follow beside them puts that video’s play button on the first screen of your page, in place of what it had, saying how long it runs and who put it there. Nothing reaches YouTube until you press it, and the screen’s own controls put back what was there. On a set you tune, like the Solarpunk Hermitage’s television, Looming Rocks’ stage or the Rebellion Rave Room’s big screen, it is tuned on the set, which stays off until you press play. Only a moderator’s hosting can do this, and our server, not their radio, says whose hosting is a moderator’s. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, and no list of who watched. We keep that you are hosting because you pressed Host this film so that other people could see where you are, and keeping it while you are hosting is what that takes. Pressing it again takes that back.
seen
Being seen in a room

Signed on to the CB, the radio has a switch, Be seen here, in every room on the street. It is off until you press it, and once pressed your browser remembers it, so you are seen in each room you open with the radio until you switch it off. Since 2026-10-07, being seen puts you on the radio’s Who’s online list, for anybody signed on to the CB, with the room you are in. Before that it showed you only to people seen in the same room. If you switched it on before then, it now does more than it did when you pressed it, and switching it off takes you off the list at once. What it sends, and when. Only while you are seen, the radio is open, and the tab is in front of you: every few seconds, your pass, which room this page is, and a random number the page makes up for this visit, which nobody else is shown. Switch it off, fold the radio away, put the tab behind another or leave the page, and it tells us you have gone and sends nothing more. Who can see you. Anybody signed on to the CB, seen or not, on Who’s online: your handle, whether it is a claimed username or the base station, and the room you are in. Anybody else seen in the same room sees you there too, and only they are shown who is in that room’s call. Names come in alphabetical order and nobody is shown a number. A room the base keeps is named only to the people it is for, and somebody seen only there is on nobody else’s list. A room that keeps to itself is named to nobody: being seen there shows you only to people seen there. An unclaimed handle is not checked, so a name without CLAIMED beside it is not proof of who somebody is. What we keep. While you are seen, one record: your handle, whether you are the base station, whether your handle is a claimed username, which room, the time of your last check and the visit’s number. Opening another room replaces it rather than adding to it, so which rooms you have been in is not kept. It is shown to nobody thirty seconds after your last check, and deleted when you stop being seen, or within two minutes by anybody else’s check, or by the hourly sweep at the latest. We keep that you are in a room because you chose to be seen there, and keeping it for as long as you are is what that takes. Pressing Be seen here is your consent to it, and pressing it again takes that back.
online
Who’s online

Who’s online, beside World and This room on the radio, lists everybody seen in a room and which room, with a link to go there, except a room that keeps to itself, which is never on it. While its panel is open, the radio is open and the tab is in front of you, it asks us every few seconds, sending your pass and nothing else. Typing an @ in the teleporter asks the same once and narrows the list in your browser, so the letters you type are not sent. Nothing records who looked, or when.
calls
A room’s call

People signed on to the CB can join a voice and video call for the room they are in, with Join this room’s call on the radio, and in the rooms behind Cavendish Coworking’s doors from the room itself. Three of those calls are open to anybody; see below. The rooms off the Town Hall for our directors, our board and our moderators are the other way round: anybody can walk in, and their channel, their call and any film hosted in them are handed to the base and to nobody else, so nobody else’s radio hears anything about them. The call is run by 8x8’s Jitsi as a Service, not by us, and it opens in a window of its own at the foot of the page. What we send, and to whom. Pressing the button asks this site for a pass into that room’s call, which carries your handle and, if you are the base station, that you are. We sign it and send it back; your browser hands it to 8x8 when the call opens. 8x8 sees your handle, as your name in the call, an id we make from your handle so that 8x8 counts one person once, and which room it is. What 8x8 gets. Whatever any video call gets: your IP address and browser details, and, once you join and switch them on, your camera, your microphone, what you type in the call’s own chat and any screen you share. What 8x8 does with that is covered by 8x8’s privacy notice, not by this page. Camera and microphone. Both start off. Opening the window may make your browser ask about them, so the call’s first screen can show you a preview; nothing goes to the call until you join on that screen. The call is the only thing on this site allowed to ask for a camera, a microphone or a shared screen, and our pages never ask for any of the three themselves. Sharing a YouTube video in a call. Anybody in a call can share a YouTube video for everybody in it to watch together, from the call’s own menu. That is Jitsi’s feature, and when somebody uses it, Jitsi loads the video from YouTube itself (youtube.com, not the no-cookie address our own players use) in the call window of everybody in the call, so YouTube gets what it gets from any of its players, and may set its cookies, under Google’s privacy policy. Jitsi’s analytics, its avatar lookups and its animated-picture search stay switched off. The public calls, and guests. The calls in the rooms behind Cavendish Coworking’s Events, Operations and Editorial doors are open to anybody, not only people signed on to the CB. Somebody who is not signed on types the name they want to be called, and that name comes to us with the room, is signed into their pass and sent back, and goes to 8x8 as their name in the call; we do not keep it. 8x8 also gets an id we make from that name, so that 8x8 counts one person once. A guest knocks and waits in the lobby until a moderator lets them in, and so does everybody else who is not a moderator. Before each of those meetings 8x8 asks us whether it has a lobby, and all we answer is yes or no. Recording and transcripts. The base station can record a call or turn on live transcription, and nobody else can. Jitsi shows everybody in the call when either is on. A recording or transcript is kept by 8x8, under its notice. Sharing a file. Anybody in a call, guests included, can share a file there, a screenshot or a photo, from the call’s own Share file. The file goes to 8x8 and to the people in the call, never to us, and we keep nothing about it. 8x8 does not publish how long it keeps a file shared in a call, so share nothing there you would not want kept, and nothing with somebody else in it who has not said yes. For anything to be kept, or kept to the people it is for, our group chat on Stoat is the place: see the meeting hall. The CB’s own channel forgets everything at midnight. Who is in a call is shown before anybody joins. 8x8 tells us when somebody joins or leaves a room’s call, and when the call opens and closes, and the radio of anybody signed on who has chosen to be seen in that room shows the names of everybody in its call: handles, and the names guests typed, in alphabetical order, with no number. A room the base keeps shows its call only to the people it is for. What 8x8 sends is checked against a secret we share with 8x8, and what does not match is not believed. What we keep. While you are in a call, one record: your name in the call, whether you are a moderator, the time you joined, and 8x8’s id for you, scrambled so it cannot be looked up. No email, and nothing else 8x8 sends. It is deleted when you leave, when the call closes, or by the hourly sweep once it is older than a pass into a call can be. Somebody’s leaving is remembered, without their name, for an hour, so that a late message from 8x8 cannot put them back. We do not keep who was in a call once they have left, when they joined before, or for how long. The pass is signed and handed back, and not stored. Leaving. Leave the call, or leaving the page, hangs up.
the-chalkboard
The chalkboard

Plural Mural has a chalkboard leaning against the foot of its wall, for leaving a note to whoever comes by next. It was Helen Edgar’s idea. It is part of the CB and runs on the same rules, with two differences, both written above the box you write in: anybody can read it, and a note stays up for seven days rather than until midnight. Who can write on it. Only people signed on to the CB. Writing sends your handle, your note and your pass to us, the same as transmitting on the radio. Who can read it. Anybody who opens Plural Mural, signed on or not. That makes it a board in the street rather than a room, so write on it what you would write on a board in the street. An unclaimed handle is not checked, so a name on the board is not proof of who wrote it. The board’s answers ask search engines not to index or archive it; that is a request they honour rather than a lock. What we keep. The latest thirty notes, each with its handle, its words and the time it went up. A thirty-first rubs out the oldest. Every note is deleted seven days after it was written, and the base station can rub one out sooner. There is no archive, no backup and no copy. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, and no list of who wrote or who read. Where it is kept. Beside the channel, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy. We keep a note because you chalked it up for passers-by to read, and keeping it for the week is what that takes. Writing it is your consent to that, and you can take it back by asking us to rub it out.
the-pebble-bowls
The pebble bowls

The Solarpunk Hermitage and the Faery Yurt each have a bowl by the door for leaving a pebble: a line of your own, and a link if the thing is somewhere else. It was Helen Edgar’s idea. Each bowl is part of the CB and runs on the chalkboard’s rules: anybody can see what is in it, and a pebble stays for seven days. The basket beside it, of things the host has put out to take, is part of the page and sends nothing: taking one is following a link, and nothing records that you did. Who can leave a pebble. Only people signed on to the CB. Leaving one sends your handle, your words, the link if you gave one, which room it is for, and your pass to us, the same as transmitting on the radio. Who can see it. Anybody who opens that room, signed on or not, so leave in it what you would leave by a door somebody else walks through. An unclaimed handle is not checked, so a name in the bowl is not proof of who left it. The bowls’ answers ask search engines not to index or archive them. What we keep. For each room, the latest thirty pebbles, each with its handle, its words, its link and the time it was left. Every pebble is deleted seven days after it was left, a thirty-first lets the oldest go, and the base station can lift one out sooner. There is no archive, no backup and no copy. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, no list of who left or who looked, and nothing about what anybody took from a basket. Where it is kept. Beside the channel and the chalkboard, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy. We keep a pebble because you left it for whoever comes to that door, and keeping it for the week is what that takes. Leaving it is your consent to that, and you can take it back by asking us to lift it out.
the-tree
Pando Calrissian’s tree

Pando Calrissian has one tree on a hillside, which anybody signed on to the CB can water, and a fence beside it for notes. Both are part of the CB. The tree is kept for good, and what it keeps is a number. Who can water it. Only people signed on to the CB. Watering sends your pass to us, so the tree knows somebody signed on is holding the can. The pass is checked and not kept, and nothing about who watered is written down: not your handle, not when you watered, not how often. What the tree keeps. How many times it has been watered, and the time of the last watering, so it can tell everybody when the ground will take more. Nothing else. That number never expires and is never reset. It is not personal information about anybody, because it cannot be traced to anybody. The fence. The chalkboard’s rules exactly. Only people signed on can pin a note, which sends your handle, your words and your pass to us; anybody who opens the room can read it; the latest thirty are kept, each with its handle, its words and the time; every note is deleted seven days after it went up, and the base station can take one down sooner. An unclaimed handle is not checked, so a name on the fence is not proof of who wrote it. Its answers ask search engines not to index or archive it. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, no list of who watered, who pinned a note or who looked, and no copy or backup of the tree or the fence. Where it is kept. Beside the channel and the chalkboard, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy. We keep a note because you pinned it up for whoever comes up the hill, and keeping it for the week is what that takes; pinning it is your consent to that, and you can take it back by asking us to take it down. The tree’s number is kept because it is the tree, and it holds nothing of yours.
the-fridge
The Fridge of Sighs

The Fridge of Sighs is a fridge door covered in word magnets, where a sentence is built one word at a time by whoever comes in. It is part of the CB. Finished sentences are kept for good, and that is only simple because none of them holds anything about who wrote it. Who can put up a word. Only people signed on to the CB. Putting one up sends the word and your pass to us. The pass is checked and not kept. The one thing kept about anybody. To stop anybody putting up two words in a row, the fridge keeps a mark saying the last word was yours: your handle, scrambled with the community password, so it cannot be looked up from a handle without that password. It is replaced by the very next word, from anybody, and it is never shown to anybody, sent to any page, or stored with a sentence. Nothing records who put up any other word. What the fridge keeps. The words on the line so far, the finished sentences, and the time each one was finished. The newest forty stay on the door, and older ones are filed by month into the drawer. They are kept for good, with no names in them, and the base station can take a word or a sentence down. Who can read it. Anybody who opens the room, signed on or not. Its answers ask search engines not to index or archive it. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, no list of who put up words or who looked. Where it is kept. Beside the channel and the chalkboard, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy. A word you put up is part of a sentence that belongs to everybody who added to it, which is why it is kept with no name on it. If something on the door should not be there, ask and we will take it down.
the-stair
Count Me In’s stair

Count Me In is a stairwell everybody climbs together, a number to a step, with a chairlift beside the stair. It is part of the CB, and what it keeps for good is two numbers. Who can take a step. Only people signed on to the CB. Taking a step sends your pass to us, and the number you typed; riding the lift sends your pass and no number. The pass is checked and not kept. The one thing kept about anybody. To stop anybody taking two steps in a row, the stair keeps a mark saying the last step was yours, the same kind of mark as the Fridge of Sighs: your handle scrambled with the community password. The very next step replaces it, and it is never shown to anybody or sent to any page. Nothing records who took any other step, or whether anybody came up by the stairs or the lift. What the stair keeps. The step it is on, the highest step it has reached, and where it had got to the last time it went back to one, with the time. The highest step is kept for good. None of it is personal information about anybody. Who can read it. Anybody who opens the room, signed on or not. Its answers ask search engines not to index or archive it. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, no list of who climbed or who looked, and nothing about who put the number that sent the stair back to one. Where it is kept. Beside the channel and the chalkboard, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy.
brass-tacks
The Brass Tacks Board

The Brass Tacks Board is for posts meant to last: news, notices, events and celebrations. Anybody can read it, and it has a feed of its own, so its posts reach feed readers and search engines may find them. Who can post. Only our moderators, signed on to the CB as moderators. Posting sends their pass, the title, the words and the picture, if there is one; the pass is checked and not kept. What we keep. Each post’s title, its words, the moderator’s username, when it went up and when it was last edited, and its picture and description. The username is public on the post, on purpose, so anybody can see who put it up. Posts are kept until a moderator takes them down; there is no other copy and no archive, and nothing about who reads the board is kept or counted. Pictures. A picture is redrawn in the moderator’s browser before it is sent, which takes off everything a camera writes into a file, where it was taken first, and the board refuses one that still carries any of it. It must have a description, and the moderator says that everybody recognisable in it has said yes to it being on the board. It is served to anybody from this site, and deleted when its post is taken down or its picture changed; one that never made it onto a post is deleted after a day. If you are in a picture on the board and want it down, ask any moderator, and they will take it down. Where it is kept. Beside the CB, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy.
accounts
Your username, if you claim it

On the CB, Profile on the radio lets you claim the handle you are signed on as, with a password of your own. It is optional, and only possible once you are signed on with the community password. Once claimed, the username signs on with its own password and nothing else: the community password stops working for it, so nobody else can sign on as you. What we keep. The username as you claimed it; your password and a recovery code, each only as a salted scrypt hash, from which neither can be read back; when you claimed it; a version number that moves whenever the password changes, so every other device is signed off; and a count of wrong passwords with the time the username is locked until after five of them. If a moderator gives you a reset code, its hash, for a day. No email, no other name, and nothing about what you do. It is filed under a scrambled form of the username, so the store does not list usernames, and there is no list of accounts for anybody to read, moderators included. Your password. We never see it again once you have typed it, cannot tell you what it is, and it is never logged. There is no email, so the ways back in are the recovery code you are shown, once, when you claim, and a reset code from a moderator, who will want to be sure it is you first. Either is used at the Community Center, and gives you a new recovery code. On the channel. A message you send from a claimed username is marked CLAIMED for everybody on that channel to see, until it goes at midnight. We put the mark there from your pass; nobody can set it on a message themselves. It tells people the username is claimed, and that is all it tells them. Your pets. Once you have claimed your username, the pets you adopt are kept under it, and only your password reaches them. Deleting it. Delete my account in Profile deletes the username, its password and your pets at once, and anybody can claim the name afterwards. A moderator can do the same, if you ask them to or if the covenant needs it. Your adopted animals stay on the list of everybody adopted, where nothing connected them to you. Moderators. A moderator can move onto a password of their own in the same way, from Profile while signed on with the moderators’ password, which every moderator knows. After that the moderators’ password no longer signs on as them. We keep exactly the same record for them as for anybody: which roles they hold is not in it, and is kept where it always was, on the moderators’ list. The desk will not reset or delete a moderator’s username. What moderators can do. Look up one username by typing it, give it a reset code, or delete it. That is all: they cannot read your password, and there is no list of everybody to browse. Where it is kept. Beside the channel, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy. We keep your account because you asked us to, so that your username is yours; claiming it is your consent, and deleting it takes that back.
the-shelter
The shelters, and your pets

Rescue A Cat, Rescue A Dog and Rescue Small Animals are shelters where animals turn up at random, and the first person signed on to the CB to press brings one in and can name them. Anybody signed on can adopt one, who then lives in the Profile on their radio. Both are part of the CB. Who can rescue or adopt. Only people signed on to the CB. Rescuing sends your pass, which animal, and the name you typed, if you typed one; adopting sends your pass and which animal. The pass is checked and not kept, and nothing records who rescued any animal. What each shelter keeps. The animals waiting for a home: each one’s looks, where they were found, their name and when they came in; and when the next animal is due, which is random and never sent to any page. An animal stays until somebody adopts them. The base station can take a name off an animal, wherever the animal is. The list of everybody adopted, kept for good. Each adopted animal’s looks, name, and when they came in and were adopted, and, once their person has renamed them, the name they came in under. It never says who adopted or renamed anybody, and anybody who opens the rooms can read it. Showing your pets, if you choose to. With a claimed username, Show my pets on the CB in Profile lets anybody signed on to the CB press your handle on the channel and see your pets: what they look like and what they are called, not when they came in or were adopted. It is off until you switch it on, and an unclaimed handle cannot switch it on, because it is anybody’s who signs on with it. We keep only that it is on, and when you switched it on; switching it off, Forget me and deleting your username delete that. Showing them lets people find them on the list of everybody adopted, which still says nothing itself. Pressing somebody’s handle sends your pass and their handle, and we keep neither. Stickers. Sticker on the radio sends a drawing of one of your own pets, with its name, to the channel you are tuned to. It is a message like any other, kept and deleted with the channel’s messages, and it says nothing more than the drawing and the name. Renaming. Once adopted, a pet can be renamed from Profile, as often as you like. That sends your pass, which pet and the new name; the name changes in your pets and on the list of everybody adopted, and the base station can take a name off there as it can in the shelter. Your pets, which with your username, if you claim it, is all the street keeps under a person. When you adopt, the animal is filed under your handle so that your Profile shows them on any device you sign on with. The record is filed under a scrambled form of your handle, not the handle itself, so the store does not list handles; it holds your pets’ looks, names and dates, and nothing else about you, and beside it, only if you switch it on, that your pets are shown. An unclaimed handle is not an account: anybody who signs on with the same handle sees the same pets, and can forget them, until you claim your username. Opening your Profile sends your pass to us, once, to fetch them. Forget me. The button in Profile, on your radio. It deletes your record there and then. Your animals stay on the list of everybody adopted, where nothing ever connected them to you. It cannot be undone. What your browser keeps. The animals you rescued, under love-rescues, as listed above. That is on your device and never sent to us. The cat café. Pekoe and Purrs reads Rescue A Cat’s list when it opens, the same way anybody opening the shelter does, with no pass. Its own script sends nothing and keeps nothing: the cat on your lap and what is on your table live in the page and are gone when you leave it. A film on its telly loads from YouTube only when you press it, like every film on the street. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, and no list of who rescued, who adopted or who looked. Where it is kept. Beside the channel and the chalkboard, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy. The shelters’ and the pets’ answers ask search engines not to index or archive them. We keep your pets because you adopted them and asked the street to remember, and keeping them is what that takes. Adopting is your consent to it, and Forget me takes it back.
the-slake
The Slake

The MUD Room has a world out its back door called the Slake, a multi-user dungeon with nobody to fight. Playing it on your own happens inside the page and sends nothing. Meeting other people on it is part of the CB and runs on the radio’s rules, with one switch of its own, Be seen out here, which is off every time you arrive and is never remembered. What it sends, and when. Only once you are signed on to the CB and have pressed Be seen out here, and only while the tab is in front of you. Then, every few seconds and whenever you move, it sends your pass, which place you are in, and a random number the page makes up for this visit, which nobody else is ever shown and which is how your visit moves and leaves without a list of visits anywhere. When you say something, your words come too. Switch it off, put the tab behind another or leave the page, and it tells us you have gone and sends nothing more. Who can see you. Anybody else who is signed on, has chosen to be seen, and is in the same place as you, by your handle. Being seen is also the only way to see: nobody can watch the Slake without being seen on it. Nobody is given a list of who is out there, or a number of people, and the map shows only you. An unclaimed handle is not checked, so a name out there is not proof of who somebody is. What we keep. While you are seen, one record: your handle, whether you signed on as the base station, which place you are in, the time of your last check, and the visit’s random number. Moving replaces it rather than adding to it, so where you have been is not kept. It is shown to nobody thirty seconds after your last check, and deleted when you stop being seen or leave, or within two minutes by anybody else’s check, or by the hourly sweep at the latest. What is said in a place is kept like the radio’s channel: the latest ten things said there, each with its handle, its words and its time, all of it deleted at midnight, Colorado time, and the base station can take one off sooner. There is no archive, no backup and no copy. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, no list of who was out there, and no record of where anybody went. Your tide, what you are carrying, the places you have found and the map stay in your page and are gone when you close it. Where it is kept. Beside the channel, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy. We keep that you are in a place because you chose to be seen there, and keeping it for as long as you are is what that takes. Pressing Be seen out here is your consent to it, and pressing it again takes that back. We keep what you say in a place for the day because you said it to whoever is there, the same as on the radio, and you can ask us to delete it sooner.
Things that look like forms

A few rooms have boxes you can type into, and none of them sends anything. The Guild’s hand-in box checks a code inside the page. The Zibaldone’s attribution slip puts a block of text on your own clipboard, and you decide where it goes. The Foundry sets the words you type in a typeface, in your browser. The MUD Room’s command line plays the game inside the page and sends nothing, except what you say while you are seen on the Slake. The CB is the one exception: its boxes, the chalkboard’s, the pebble bowls’, the fence’s on Pando Calrissian’s hill, the Fridge of Sighs’ and what you say on the Slake included, send what you type, to us, as written up above.
Your rights

Because we hold so little, most of what the law gives you a right to ask about is not here to ask about. What there is: Your photograph, your recording or your name in a credit: ask us to see it, correct it or take it down, and we will. What you said on the CB: ask us and we will delete it now rather than at midnight. After midnight there is nothing left to ask about. What you said on the Slake: ask us and we will delete it now rather than at midnight. Where you were is already gone. What you chalked on the board: ask us and we will rub it out now rather than at the end of its week. What you pinned on Pando Calrissian’s fence: ask us and we will take it down now rather than at the end of its week. Your waterings are not there to ask about: the tree never knew they were yours. Your pets: Forget me in Profile on your radio deletes them at once, or ask us and we will. Your username: Delete my account in Profile deletes it, its password and your pets at once. Ask a moderator if you cannot get in, and they can delete it for you. An animal’s name in a shelter or on the list of everybody adopted: tell us which animal and we will take the name off. Nothing says which ones were yours, so only you can tell us. A word on the Fridge of Sighs: nothing says which words were yours, so we cannot find them for you; but if a word or a sentence should not be there, tell us what it says and we will take it down. Our host’s logs: Netlify holds those. Ask us and we will ask on your behalf, or contact Netlify directly. What your browser keeps: it is on your device and yours to clear. We never keep a copy, the CB pass included. If you are in the EU or the UK, you also have the right to access, correct, erase, restrict, object to and move your personal data, and to complain to your data protection authority. We do not sell or share personal information for advertising, so a Global Privacy Control signal from your browser has nothing here to opt you out of — the answer is already no.
Reporting a security problem
If you have found a hole in this site, report it privately on GitHub; the policy is in SECURITY.md and security.txt. A report there is handled by GitHub under GitHub’s privacy statement.
When this page changes

If what this site does with your information changes, this page changes first, the date at the top moves, and the change is written up in the changelog on the day, where the feed will pick it up. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so.
