The CB guide

The CB is the street’s radio: a chat channel patterned after citizens band radio, in a panel in the corner of every page. This guide goes through it part by part, top to bottom, with every button named the way the radio names it. To get on, go to the front desk at the Community Center; the house norms are there too, and Privacy says what the CB keeps. Last updated 2026-10-04.
THE SHORT VERSION

Open is on, folded is off. Open, with the tab in front of you, the radio listens every four seconds. Folded, or behind another tab, it sends nothing. Ten messages a channel, gone at midnight, Colorado time. An eleventh pushes the oldest off. No alerts. No chime, no badge, no unread count, and the tab’s title never changes. Names, never numbers. A reaction says who pressed it, and Who’s online says who is around and where. Nothing shows a count. Nothing on it moves, at any setting of the dial, and it is the same radio in every room.
where
Where it is

The radio sits in the bottom right corner of every page. Two places do not have it. The Healing Checkpoint and Stay Frosty each promise something the radio would break, so it waits outside their doors. The private rooms off the Town Hall show it only to the moderators each room is for. The Community Center has its own front desk instead of the bar, and once you sign on there the radio appears in the corner.
guest
Before you sign on: the guest bar

Until you sign on, the corner holds a smaller bar. It is not the radio. It knows nothing about the channel and sends nothing to it, and the only thing it remembers is whether you left it open. Control What it does CB The radio’s name. Teleport Opens the teleporter, the same one the radio has. Get on the CB Opens a panel saying what the CB is and where the password comes from, with a form to sign on. It reads Fold away while the panel is open. Your handle The name you go by on the channel, up to 24 characters. The community password, or your own if you have claimed your username The community password is shared inside our community. Ask for it in the meeting hall. Sign on Checks the password and swaps this bar for the radio, on every page, until you sign off. The front desk at the Community Center has the same form, and one more: Forgotten the password for a username you claimed? It takes Your username, The recovery code, or a moderator’s reset code, A new password and The same again, then Set it and sign on.
bar
The bar

Signed on, the bar runs along the top of the radio. You can drag the radio by any part of the bar that is not a button. Control What it does When folded CB The radio’s name, and somewhere to drag it by. shown Teleport Opens the teleporter under the bar. hidden Move Drag the bar to put the radio somewhere else. Or press Move: it takes the keyboard and says how it works, and then the arrow keys move the radio 24 pixels a press and Home puts it back in the corner. The radio remembers where you left it. shown Size Opens a choice of Small, Normal and Large. Escape closes it. hidden Fold away Folds the radio down to its bar and stops it. It reads Switch on while folded, and that opens it again. reads Switch on
sizes
Sizes, and folded

State What you see Is it listening? Small The bar, the line saying what you are tuned to, and only the newest message. Good for keeping the radio on over a film. yes, and it still reads new messages to a screen reader Normal Everything, in a narrow panel. yes Large Everything, wider and taller, for long messages and pictures. yes Folded Only CB, Move and Switch on. no. It sends nothing, stops reading aloud, stops hosting and following a film, and stops you being seen. The radio is never wider or taller than your window. If it would cover a film’s play button when you are getting that film ready, it goes Small for the moment and says so; Size puts it back.
tuning
Tuning: World or this room

Under the bar, a line says On the channel as and your handle. Then two buttons choose what you hear, and a third shows who is around: Control What it does World The channel the whole street shares. A new radio starts here, and tuned to World the radio never says which room you are in. This room The channel of the room you are standing in. Walk into another room and you hear that room’s channel instead. Pages that are not rooms do not have one. Who’s online Not a channel. It opens a list of everybody who has switched on Be seen here, in alphabetical order, with BASE or CLAIMED beside a name the way the channel marks it, and the room each is in; a room’s name takes you there. A room that keeps to itself is never on it. Your own line says (you), and a line under the list says whether you are on it. While it is open it is redrawn every few seconds, quietly, and it never shows a number. A line above the messages says Tuned to World or Tuned to the room’s name. Every channel keeps the same rules: ten messages, gone at midnight. A quiet one says Nobody has said anything today.
seen
Be seen here

In a room, Be seen here puts you, by your handle, on Who’s online for anybody signed on, with the room you are in, and shows you and anybody else who has switched it on in the same room to each other. In a room that keeps to itself it shows you only to people seen there. While it is off you are on nobody’s list; you can still open Who’s online, but not see who else is in this room or in its call. Also seen here: lists the others, alphabetically, by handle. Nobody else here is seen. means just that. In this room’s call: lists everybody in the room’s call, so you can see who is there before you join. Names only, and never a count. The lines update quietly, without announcing themselves. Your browser remembers the switch. Folding the radio, leaving the page or putting the tab behind another takes you out of sight.
reading
Reading messages

Each message starts with a line: the sender’s handle, a mark if it has one, and the time it was sent, by your clock. Then come its words, a picture or sticker if it has one, and its reactions. Part What it means or does The handle A button. Press it to see that person’s pets, if they have chosen to show them. Close or Escape puts it away. CLAIMED Sent from a claimed username, which only signs on with its owner’s own password. Only the server can put this mark there. BASE Sent by one of our moderators. Only the server can put this mark there either. A handle with neither mark is whatever somebody typed. Copy Puts the message’s words on your own clipboard, as they were typed. It reads Copied for a moment. React Opens the reactions under the message. A picture Press it to see it larger, with Download and Close. Download under it keeps a copy on your device. A sticker A drawing of the sender’s pet, with its name. It goes when its message goes. Links in a message. An address on this street is an ordinary link. An address on another site, written with https://, opens in a new tab and has an arrow and the site’s name after it, like ↗ example.com, so you can see where it goes before you press it. A room written as #the-den shows as #The Den, linked. A time like @34:12 is a button that moves your own film to that place: see watching together. It never scrolls under you. If you have scrolled up to read, new messages wait at the bottom. The radio follows them only when you were already at the bottom, or when you have just transmitted.
react
Reactions

React opens a row of quick reactions: a heart, thumbs up, laughing, a party, eyes, sparkles, a penguin for a pebble, a dog, a cat, an otter, a rainbow, a unicorn, the sign of the horns, a hedgehog, a hugging face, people hugging, and a crying face. Under them, Or any emoji takes one emoji of your own from your system’s emoji picker (Control, Command and Space on a Mac, the emoji key on a phone, Windows and . on Windows), and its own React button sends it. Under the message, each reaction shows the handles of everybody who pressed it, alphabetically, and never a number. Press a reaction there to add yours, or to take yours back.
writing
Writing a message

Control What it does Your message The box. Up to 2,000 characters, and it keeps your lines. It grows as you type, and you can drag its corner to make it taller. Picture Adds a screenshot or a photo. See pictures. Sticker Shows your pets. Press one to send a sticker of them to the channel straight away; what is in the box stays there. No pets yet? Adopt one at Rescue A Cat or Rescue A Dog. Transmit Sends the message, with its picture if it has one. Keys in the box What they do Enter Transmits, unless the list of rooms is open. Shift and Enter Starts a new line. # and the start of a room’s name Opens a list of rooms. ↑ and ↓ move through it, Enter or Tab picks one, and Escape leaves your # as you typed it. Answers from the radio, like Transmitting… or No signal. That did not go out., appear in one line just above the box. If you send more than twelve messages in a minute it asks you to wait a moment.
markdown
Markdown

A little Markdown works, and the radio builds it into the page as text, never as code. Type You get **bold** bold *italic* or _italic_ italic. A single _ inside a word, as in snake_case, stays as typed. ~~struck~~ struck through `code` code, with nothing inside it changed Three backticks on a line of their own, before and after a block of code > at the start of a line a quote -, * or 1. at the start of a line a list A blank line a new paragraph There are no headings, images or HTML, and a link’s words are always its address, so [words](an address) stays exactly as you typed it.
pictures
Pictures

Press Picture and choose a screenshot or a photo. The radio redraws it in your browser before it goes, which takes off where it was taken and everything else the camera wrote into it. Then: Say what is in it, if you like is a description, up to 280 characters. It is offered, never required, and it is what a screen reader hears. Remove the picture takes it off the message. It goes with your next Transmit, with words or without. It is deleted when its message goes, and one you never send is deleted within the hour. Pictures on the channel have no public address. Only people signed on can see them, and the same norm as a screenshot applies to passing one on.
tools
The row of tools

Under the box is a row of buttons. Some only appear when they can do something. Control What it does Shown Add my spot Puts where your film has got to into your message, with the film’s title and the room. Nothing goes out until you transmit. once a film on the page has started Host this film Lets everybody on the channel see where you are in your film. See watching together. once a film on the page has started Screen a video Opens a box labelled A YouTube address, to put a video up on the page’s first screen with Put it up. See watching together. to moderators, on pages with a screen Join this room’s call Opens the room’s voice and video call. Press it again to leave. See calls. in rooms, when calls are switched on New messages to a screen reader: on New messages are announced to a screen reader as they arrive, at every size. Press to switch it off. always Speak new messages aloud: off Press to have the radio read each new message out in your own device’s voice, handle first, with a burst of static before and after; at the Gentle setting, the words without the static. It never reads your own messages or what was already there. when your device has a voice Profile Opens your username and your pets. always Sign off Signs you off and takes the radio away, on every page, until you sign on again. always With both New messages to a screen reader and Speak new messages aloud on, a screen reader user hears everything twice. At the foot of the radio are links to the house norms and to this guide.
teleport
The teleporter

Teleport opens a box labelled Teleport to a room, or to @somebody and a list of every room on the street, in walking order. The room you are in says you are here; the others show their #tag. Type to narrow it. It finds rooms whose names start with what you typed, then rooms with it inside a word of their name, so fire finds The Campfire, then rooms whose own description uses the word, with a few of those words shown. ↑ and ↓ move through the list, Enter goes to the room highlighted, and Escape puts the box away. Going is ordinary navigation. Nothing is sent to the channel, and nobody learns where you went. An @ looks for a person. Type @ and the list becomes the people on Who’s online, one line for each room they are in; type some of a handle to narrow it, and Enter goes to the room highlighted. Handles that start with what you typed come first. You are left out of it, and the letters you type are not sent anywhere. To search the words on every page rather than the rooms’ names, use the search box on the front page or the map.
films
Watching together

When people watch the same film in a room, each person plays their own copy and pauses when they like. These help everybody find the same place. Control What it does An @time in a message Type @ and a time, like @34:12 or @1:02:03. Everybody sees it as a button that moves the film on their own page to that place. It never presses play. If the spot names a film or a room, it only moves that film in that room; anywhere else it says where the spot is. A time without the @ stays words. Add my spot Writes the @time for you, with the film and the room. Host this film Everybody on the channel sees where you are in your film, whether it is playing, and in which room. In a room that keeps to itself, only radios tuned to that room’s channel see it. One person hosts a room at a time. Putting your tab behind another pauses it; folding the radio or leaving the page stops it. Catch up Beside a host in your room: moves your film to where they are now. Follow Beside a host in your room: keeps your film in step with theirs, at your own volume. Pausing your own film, or pressing Follow again, stops following, so a break is always fine. Screen a video For moderators. Paste the address of one YouTube video, from youtube.com or youtu.be, and press Put it up: it plays on the page’s first screen, from the time in the address if it has one, in place of what the screen had. It is on your page only. Press Host this film once it plays, and everybody who presses Catch up or Follow beside you gets its play button on their own screen, with how long it runs, waiting for their press. The button under the screen puts back what was there. On a set you tune, like the Solarpunk Hermitage’s television, Looming Rocks’ stage or the Rebellion Rave Room’s big screen, it is tuned on the set instead, which stays off until they press play, and the set’s own controls tune back to its listing. A playlist’s address is refused. A spot’s room is a link. Following it takes you to the film’s play button, ready to start at that place when you press it. Nobody’s film moves unless they press something themselves.
calls
Calls

Every room has a voice and video call, run by 8x8. Join this room’s call on the radio opens it, and some rooms have a panel of their own that says Join the call as and your handle. A few rooms at Cavendish Coworking also let in people who are not signed on: they type The name you want to be called in the call and press Knock on the door. The call opens in a window of its own in the bottom left corner. Control What it does CALL and the room’s name Which call this is. Move Drag the bar, or press Move and use the arrow keys; Home puts it back in its corner. Small, Large Make the window smaller or larger. Press again to go back to the middle size. Leave the call Hangs up. Leaving the page hangs up too. In the call now: Who is in the call, if you have Be seen here on and the radio open. Inside the window is 8x8’s own screen. Your browser may ask about your camera and microphone so it can show a preview, but both start off, and nothing goes to the call until you join there. Folding the radio leaves the call running.
profile
Profile
Profile opens a tray with two parts.
username
Your username

Claiming. An unclaimed handle can be used by anybody with the community password. Type A password of your own and The same again, then Claim and your handle. From then on only your own password signs on as it, and your messages carry CLAIMED. There is no email. The recovery code is shown once, when you claim. It is the way back in if you forget your password, at the front desk. Keep it, then press I have kept it. A moderator can also give you a reset code. Change my password asks for Your password now, A new password and The same again, then Change it. Every other device signed on as you is signed off. Delete my account asks for your password, then Yes, delete my account or Keep it. It cannot be undone. Five wrong passwords lock a claimed username for fifteen minutes.
pets
Your pets

Every pet you have adopted, with its drawing, its name and when you adopted it. Rename or Name them gives one a name; the name it came in under is kept on the list of everybody adopted. Show my pets on the CB lets anybody on the channel press your handle and see them. It needs a claimed username, and it starts off. Forget me deletes everything the street keeps under your handle: your pets and whether they are shown. It asks first, with Yes, forget me or Keep my pets. The animals stay on the list of everybody adopted, with nothing connecting them to you.
base
What moderators see

Our moderators sign on as the base station, and their messages carry BASE. They also have Take off on every message, which takes it off the air, and Clear the channel, which clears the channel they are tuned to. In a call, the base is the only one who can record or turn on transcription, and the house norms ask them to say so first. If something is wrong, tell the base.
keys
Keys at a glance

Where Keys Anywhere on the radio Tab moves between controls. Escape closes whatever panel is open and puts you back on the button that opened it. Move, on the radio or a call Press it, then the arrow keys move the window; Home puts it back in its corner. The message box Enter transmits; Shift and Enter starts a new line; # opens the list of rooms. A list of rooms ↑ and ↓ move; Enter picks or goes; Escape closes it. A large picture Escape or Close.
keeps
What it sends and keeps

In short: the radio asks this site, and nothing else, for the channel while it is open and in front of you. The channel keeps ten messages, until midnight. No IP address is stored, nothing anybody types is logged, and the only list of who is on is Who’s online, made from Be seen here and gone thirty seconds after somebody stops being seen. Your browser keeps your handle, your pass and where you put the radio. Privacy has the whole of it, and Architecture says how it is built. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so.

2026-10-07-call-devices
2026-10-07 — Calls can use your camera and microphone in Chrome

In Chrome, a room’s call could not switch on its camera, its microphone or a shared screen, and said you had refused them although nothing had ever asked you. That was this site’s fault, not 8x8’s and not yours: our security header gave those three to the call and deliberately not to our own pages, and a browser will only hand a frame what the page round it already has. So Chrome switched them off inside the call before it could ask. The header now gives them to our pages as well, so that the call can have them, and Chrome asks you the first time a call wants them. Because the call sits inside our page, Chrome’s question names stimpunks.world. This reverses the rule written down when calls arrived, that the page itself gets none of the three. That rule could not work. Our pages still never ask for any of the three themselves. The header used to keep that promise, and now the tool that writes the header does: it reads every script this site serves and refuses one that asks for a camera, a microphone or a screen. The privacy page’s sentence about it stays true, and Architecture now says how.

2026-10-07 — Find somebody by name with an @ in the teleporter

Type @ and somebody’s handle into the radio’s Teleport, press Enter, and it takes you to the room they are in. Helen Edgar asked for a way to find where people are, and Ryan suggested the teleporter. Nobody can be found until they choose to be. Be seen here only ever showed you to people in the same room, and that is what everybody who pressed it agreed to, so being found from anywhere is a second switch under it, Let people find me. It is off until you press it, your browser remembers it, and it only works while you are seen. Only a claimed username can be found, because an unclaimed handle is anybody’s who signs on with it, and somebody could sign on with your name and have people sent to them. Only somebody who can be found can look: the same one switch, both ways, that Be seen here and the Slake keep, and the street checks it, not only the radio. One whole handle, and never a list. Part of a handle finds nobody, and nothing offers names as you type, because a list of names to pick from would be a list of who is on. The answer is the room and nothing else; anybody who cannot be found, for any reason, is “nobody by that whole handle can be found right now”, and a room kept for the people it is for is never named to anybody else. 2026-10-05 — A Quiet Pint: a pub under the street, made like McAnally’s

A Quiet Pint is a new shopfront, at Ryan’s ask: a pub a few steps down from the street, made like McAnally’s in Jim Butcher’s Dresden Files. Thirteen tables, thirteen stools along a bar that meanders, thirteen carved columns, thirteen windows, thirteen mirrors and thirteen ceiling fans, as in the books, and no two of any of them alike. There is no television, no games machine and no jukebox, only a player piano. The only light is the street’s, through small windows at the level of the pavement, passed round the room by old mirrors, so it lands in patches, none the same shape, a little dimmer and a little green. Nobody lights a lamp and the stove is shut. Nothing in the pub moves, at any setting, the fans included. A table that fits you. The tables are all different heights, so the room has a plan of the floor and a list of every table in words, with boxes to tick for what you want: room under it for a wheelchair or your knees, a tall table, a low one with soft seats, your back to a wall, out of sight of the door, away from the bar, by the stove, in a patch of light or out of it. Every table can be reached from the door by a way at least 36 inches wide, and the room’s own tool walks the floor to make sure. Sit at a table, order from the bar, and look down to see your table. Where it parts from the books, and says so: a ramp beside the steps, as wide as they are; the ceiling still low, but the fans up between the beams; and your order fetched from the bar or brought to you, whichever you say, and nobody asks why. The measurements are the 2010 ADA Standards’, read on the Access Board’s page. Every pint comes alcohol-free first, in the same glass, at the same size, so nobody can tell from across the room which one anybody has. Ale at cellar temperature, never cold; lemonade with lemonade ice; a mushroom sandwich first and a steak sandwich after it, from the stove. Nothing has a price, and nobody has to order anything to sit down, which is our own Third Places page’s line. Butcher’s words are quoted, not retold: short passages, each naming its book and pages, held to a cap. McAnally’s, Mac and the Dresden Files are his; no wizard drinks here, and nothing is drawn from the fan wiki. Set in Amarante and Brygada 1918, read off their own records. Two shared tools changed for it. table.js can now say how an order reached you, which only this room uses. Big Steep Fermentables’ list of words that press somebody to drink refused the pub’s round tables on its first run, so “round” there now means the round somebody buys. love.css: section 100 is the pub; small screens and print are 101 and 102.

2026-10-04 — Hey, Good Cookin’

A community kitchen on the street, at Ryan’s ask and in his words: come if you’re hungry for food or for knowledge, no one is turned away, you don’t have to pay and you don’t have to volunteer. Under them come the sections of pages that hold every word you typed, each linked to the section rather than the top of the page, with a few lines round the first match, and the changelog after everything else. A quotation is never cut down in a result. A match inside a quotation shows who it is credited to and where it is, and not a trimmed piece of somebody else’s words. A snippet that would start or end inside a quotation in our own sentences is widened to hold all of it. It reads every page’s own words, written into search-index.json by a new tool each time the site is checked. It leaves out the parts the morning timers refill (the Doom Scoop’s cabinet, The Feed’s board, the kitchen telly and the Now Playing bill), the job markers, and the lyric printed in full at The Small Hours, which is there with permission and not under this site’s licence. Why not Pagefind, which one of our sites uses: it runs WebAssembly, which would loosen the part of this site’s security policy that decides what scripts may run; its index is a folder of many small files that would change in every morning’s commit; and both of the machines that publish here would need it installed. A file of our own words, searched in your browser, is how most of our sites do it. The file is fetched from this site the first time you type, and what you type never leaves your browser. The privacy page says so.

2026-09-30-pando-calrissian
2026-09-30 — Pando Calrissian, one tree that is all of us

A new shopfront on the street: Pando Calrissian, a gap between the shopfronts with a hillside of aspen behind it after sunset, and one tree on the hill that is everybody’s. It is after the grow-a-tree game in our Discord’s Collaborative Nonsense channels. Signed on to the CB, you water it, and every watering sends up another stem from the one root; the stems grow over the waterings after them, the old ones fall, and the root spreads along the hill. Named for Pando, the aspen in Utah that is one tree, and for Lando Calrissian, whose name is the only thing taken from Star Wars. The tree keeps a count, and it never expires. That reverses the Mission’s aim that nothing is counted, and it was narrowed rather than dropped: the Mission and Broadside No. 2 now say nobody is counted. The tree counts the water and never who poured it: it keeps the number and the time of the last watering and nothing else, so nobody has a total, and there is no leaderboard, no streak and no goal. The ground soaks for a minute after every watering, from anybody, before it takes more. It is the whole tree’s wait, which is how it can wait without a record of who watered when. A fence round the new growth holds notes, on the chalkboard’s rules: anybody reads it, the CB writes on it, and a note comes down after seven days. The privacy page changed first: a section on what the tree and the fence keep. Set in Averia Serif Libre and Averia Sans Libre, Dan Sayers’s type made by averaging every font Google Web Fonts carried in 2011. Four new CB functions, tested with fifteen waterers at once. A job marker, a share card, the map and a street door. Also: the Board room’s Governance & Ethics section was re-copied, because our Accountability page now says the Bylaws were adopted on 29 September 2026. Every morning’s tub in The Doom Scoop has a screen of its own at the top now. Any video in the tub plays where it is, as before, or goes up on the screen, bigger, with a second button that says how long it runs. A short goes up upright. The screen starts empty, because a morning is not one list you could put on whole, and it says so. Taking a video off leaves it empty again. Nothing loads from YouTube until you press. This is the same rack behaviour as the Lightbulb Picture House, Mycelium Munchies and Club Chronic, in the parlour’s own ink and frost.
2026-09-29-club-rack
2026-09-29 — Club Chronic’s records go up on the stage

Every record along the back wall of Club Chronic has a second button now, with its runtime on it, that puts it up on the stage’s YouTube deck in place of the playlist. Or play it where it hangs, as before. Taking it off puts the playlist back, and plays nothing until you press it. Each rack folds away, and each comes open. The second button is a strip of paste stuck to the sleeve, because in this room a black plate in a marker ring means it plays right there, and a dashed one is a door. The playlist still starts somewhere random after a record comes off the stage. Without a fix it would have gone back to the top: the part that picks the starting point listened on the old button, and putting the playlist back makes a new one.
2026-09-29-mycelium-rack
2026-09-29 — Mycelium Munchies’ rack plays on the big screen, and holds more

Derek Sarno’s rack in Mycelium Munchies works the way the Picture House’s racks do now. The masterclass plate is the room’s big screen, and every video has a second button, with its runtime on it, that puts it up on that screen in place of the whole masterclass. Or play it where it hangs, as before. Taking it off puts the masterclass plate back and plays nothing. Ten more of his videos are in the rack, from April 2025 back to December 2023: the next most recent by upload date, read off the playlist again today. Each was checked to be on his own channel, to play in a frame and not to ask anybody to sign in. The newest ten had not changed. The rack folds away, and it comes open. It is dressed in the kitchen’s own steel, cream and lamp red, and the behaviour is the shared rack.js. The masterclass now plays on the first press. Its button was missing the autoplay the room’s other buttons carry, so you had to press twice.
2026-09-30-conventions
2026-09-30 — The street’s conventions reach every room, and the guest bar signs you on

Everybody’s own space takes the street’s conventions as they develop, the dial, the sign-off, the job marker, the CB bar and whatever comes next, as part of being a citizen here, without being asked first. It never touches a room’s own look or words, and a convention somebody does not like is for the Town Hall. Ryan’s call, after Helen Edgar said yes to the guest bar in the Faery Yurt and said she does not need to approve future additions. Your Room says so. The guest bar is in the Faery Yurt now. You can sign on from the guest bar if you already know the community password: the front desk’s own two boxes, and the radio takes the bar’s place on the page you are on.
2026-09-30 — A CB bar for everybody not signed on

Every page now has a folded CB bar in the corner for visitors who are not signed on, with the teleporter to go to any room on the street, and Get on the CB, which says what the CB is, that the community password is asked for in the meeting hall, and where to sign on. It is also where a member who signed off will find the way back. It is not the radio: it sends nothing to the channel and shows nothing of it. It stays out of the rooms the radio stays out of, and out of the Faery Yurt until Helen Edgar says yes, because the yurt is hers. The privacy page lists the one thing it keeps, that you left its panel open.
2026-09-29-follow-ready
2026-09-29 — Follow and Catch up take you to the film

Follow, Catch up and a time in a message now get the film ready for you when it is not already playing: its rack opens, the page goes to it, its play button is marked and has the keyboard, and it will start at the right place when you press it, or press Enter. Before, they only wrote a sentence under the message box, which people missed, and left them to find the film on a rack full of similar names. A host’s film is found by its video, not only by its title, so a rack of lookalike names cannot send you to the wrong one. If the radio is in the way, it goes small for the moment and says so. The radio’s answers are under its readout now, beside the log and the host’s buttons, rather than under the message box.
2026-09-29-call-window-who
2026-09-29 — Who is in a call, in the call window too

The call window says who is in the call, under its own bar and just above 8x8’s Join button, for anybody signed on and seen in the room. The window’s note no longer says nothing about the call is kept.
2026-09-29-call-panel-who
2026-09-29 — Who is in a call, on the room’s own panel

A room’s call panel says who is in the call now, under the Join button, for anybody signed on who has chosen to be seen in that room, the same as the radio. The panels’ small print no longer says we keep nothing about a call, which stopped being true when the list arrived.
2026-09-29-be-seen-here
2026-09-29 — Be seen here, and who is in a call

The radio has a Be seen here switch in every room, the Slake’s own, at the community’s asking. Switched on, you are shown by your handle to anybody else who has switched it on in the same room, and they are shown to you: names only, in alphabetical order, and no count. It is one switch both ways, so while it is off nobody sees you and you see nobody. Your browser remembers it once you press it. Seen in a room, you can see who is in its call before you join: everybody in it, guests included, from 8x8. A guest’s notice on the public calls says so before they type a name, and the privacy page says what is kept, which is a name while somebody is in the call and nothing after.
2026-09-29-call-downloads
2026-09-29 — Downloading a file shared in a call

A file shared in a call downloads in Firefox and Safari now. The call said “Download started” and nothing arrived, because this site’s own security policy refused the way Jitsi hands a file to the browser; Chrome never asked, so it worked there. The policy allows it now, and still admits no other site.
2026-09-29-cb-links-away
2026-09-29 — Links to other sites on the CB

An address on another site in a CB message is a link now, where before only rooms on this street were. It opens in a new tab with the site it goes to written after it, like ↗ example.com, sends no referrer, and a link’s words are always its address. This reverses the street-only rule of 2026-09-25, at Ryan’s call, and the house norms and the privacy page say what it does.
2026-09-29-cb-long-messages
2026-09-29 — Longer messages on the CB

A CB message can run to 2,000 characters and keep its lines. The message box is a box of several lines now, which grows as you type and can be dragged taller: Enter sends, and Shift and Enter starts a new line. A little Markdown works: bold, italic, code, a block of code, a quote and a list. It is drawn by the radio as ordinary text, never as markup, and links are still only rooms on the street. Copy on every message puts its words, as they were typed, on your own clipboard. Size on the bar makes the radio Small, Normal or Large. Large is wider and taller, for long messages and pictures.
2026-09-29-cb-lightbox
2026-09-29 — A picture on the CB opens larger

Press a picture on the CB to see it as large as the window allows, with its description and a Download button; Escape or Close puts you back on the picture. Every picture also has a small Download link under it. A picture can no longer push the radio wider than its window, which was cutting off Transmit in Safari, and the Picture and Transmit buttons keep their full labels in Firefox.
2026-09-29-cb-pictures
2026-09-29 — Pictures on the CB

A message on the CB can carry a picture now: press Picture beside Transmit, pick a screenshot or a photo, and say what is in it if you like. The radio redraws it in your own browser before it goes, which takes off where it was taken and anything else a camera writes into a file. A picture goes when its message goes: pushed off by an eleventh, taken off by the base, or at midnight, and one that was never sent within the hour. It has no public address, and a picture sent in a private room is only for the people that room is for. The privacy page says the rest.
2026-09-29-call-files
2026-09-29 — Sharing files in a call

Everybody in a room’s call can share a file now, a screenshot or a photo, from the call’s own Share file button, which used to be greyed out. The file goes to 8x8, who run the calls, and never to us; the privacy page says what that means. The CB’s channel stays words only.
2026-09-29-executive-session
2026-09-29 — Executive Session, off the Town Hall

A new door off the Town Hall opens onto Executive Session: the board without staff, in a dark room lit only by the EXIT sign over its shut door, with what an executive session is, from BoardSource’s guide. Its radio and call are for the board role and nothing else. It is the one room the administrator key does not open, because an executive session is the board meeting without staff. Anybody can walk in and read it; the server keeps the rest.
2026-09-29-board-directors
2026-09-29 — Directors join the Board room

The Board room now takes moderators with the director role as well as the board role, because directors join board meetings. Its radio, its call and anything hosted in it follow, and the server checks, every time.
2026-09-29-mod-roles
2026-09-29 — Moderators have their own handles and roles

The moderators’ password now only works for a handle on the moderators’ list, and the community password refuses any handle on it, so nobody else can sign on as a moderator. The list is kept in the site’s settings and not published. The Town Hall’s rooms follow the roles on it. The Moderators’ room is for any moderator, the Board room for moderators with the board role, the Directors’ room for moderators with the director role, and administrators can go into all of them. The server checks, every time.
2026-09-29-moderators
2026-09-29 — The Moderators’ room, and every door off the Town Hall is open

The last door off the Town Hall opens onto the Moderators’ room: a room for Stimpunks Moderators to meet, above the street at night, lit only by the shopfronts’ own colours on its ceiling. It says what the base looks after and where to report a concern. Anybody can walk in; the radio and the call in there are for the base, and the server keeps it that way.
2026-09-29-board-agenda
2026-09-29 — Today’s board meeting, in the Board room

The Board room carries the outline of today’s board meeting: the decisions required, the order of business with its timings, and how to take part from somewhere else. The papers behind it go to the board.
2026-09-29 — The Board room, off the Town Hall

A door off the Town Hall opens onto the Board room: a room for Stimpunks Board Members to meet, at one long table with the same small lamp at every seat. It lists the board as our Board & Governance page does, and carries the Governance & Ethics section of our Accountability & Transparency page, word for word. Anybody can walk in; the radio and the call in there are for the base, and the server keeps it that way.
2026-09-29-directors
2026-09-29 — The Directors’ room, off the Town Hall

A door off the Town Hall opens onto the Directors’ room: a room for Stimpunks Directors to meet, lit only through the frosted pane in its door. It lists the directors as our About page does, each linked to their own section there. Anybody can walk in; the radio and the call in there are for the base, and the server keeps it that way.
2026-09-29-fishbowl
2026-09-29 — The Fishbowl, off the Town Hall

The first door off the Town Hall opens onto the Fishbowl: a room for community fishbowl meetings for anyone with CB access. A few people talk in the middle, everybody else listens round the outside, and one seat in the middle is always kept empty for whoever wants to step in. It is a glass bowl of water on a sunny sill, lit by the sun bent through the water into bright lines on the gravel, with a ring of stones inside that always has one gap in it. The call is for people signed on to the CB, and anybody can look round.
2026-09-29-town-hall
2026-09-29 — The Town Hall

A new shopfront on the street: the Town Hall, a round hall under a dome that is open to the sky, where the sun lies on the floor as one disc. Doors round its wall go to the Fishbowl, for community fishbowl meetings on the CB, and to rooms for our directors, our board and our moderators. The rooms behind the doors open one at a time. Those three rooms are the base’s. Anybody can walk into them; their channel, their call and any film hosted in them are handed to people signed on with the moderators’ password and to nobody else, by the server rather than only by the page, and the radio waits outside for everybody else.
2026-09-29-meeting-hall
2026-09-29 — The meeting hall, at the Community Center

The Community Center now starts with the meeting hall: our community’s group chat, which is moving from Discord to Stoat. It says what Stoat is, how to get an invite through the join form on stimpunks.org, what the channels are, and how the hall and the CB differ: the hall keeps things and has proper sign-in, and the CB forgets everything at midnight. The hall is a link, not part of this page. Stoat’s app does not let other sites frame it, and nothing on the street sends anything to Stoat.
2026-09-28-cavendish-cave
2026-09-28 — The Cave, upstairs at Cavendish, and Proton has gone

The Cave door at Cavendish Coworking opens onto the Cave: a tunnel in glacier ice, for quiet solo work with other people nearby. Nothing in it gives off light; the daylight comes through the ice itself, blue. Caves to leave on, chosen by Ryan from a shortlist: water dripping in a cave on Mount Cucco first, then sea caves, ice caves, cenotes and lava tubes, each with how long it runs. The call is for people signed on to the CB, and anybody can look round. Every door at Cavendish opens a room of ours now, and Proton Meet has gone from the site. 2026-09-28-cavendish-campfire
2026-09-28 — The Campfire, upstairs at Cavendish

The Campfire door at Cavendish Coworking opens onto the Campfire: a fire in a clearing at night with a ring of logs round it, for small groups working on something together or watching and listening together. The fire is the only light, so every shadow points away from it. Real campfires to leave burning: the fire in the middle is the playlist the fire pit at Swaying Sweetgrass keeps, and round it are fires from that playlist, each with how long it runs. 2026-09-28-cavendish-watering-hole
2026-09-28 — The Watering Hole, upstairs at Cavendish

The Watering Hole door at Cavendish Coworking opens onto the Watering Hole: a pan of water in the desert at noon, for come-and-go chat with no agenda, with every shadow straight under the thing that casts it. Its norms are on the wall. A rack of cams to leave on: the Jungle Room’s desert, otters and jellies, read out of that room’s own list. Each plays in its card or on the screen by the water. The call is for people signed on to the CB; anybody can come in and look round, and the room says how to get on the CB. It is the first of the Hang Suites to replace its Proton room. 2026-09-28-cavendish-editorial-room
2026-09-28 — The Editorial Room, behind Cavendish’s Editorial door

The Editorial door at Cavendish Coworking opens onto the Editorial Room: a designer’s light table in a dark studio, the proofs lit from underneath and the only light there is, where we work on the words, design and everything we put into the world. The meeting’s time is on the proof, in our events page’s own words, with the hour on your own clock. All three of our open meetings now have a room and a call of their own, open to anybody who knocks. The Hang Suites still open Proton until theirs are built.
2026-09-28-cavendish-operations-room
2026-09-28 — The Operations Room, behind Cavendish’s Operations door

The Operations door at Cavendish Coworking opens onto the Operations Room: a building’s plant room, where we run the thing, with every main painted the colour of what it carries and one caged lamp throwing its cage’s shadow across everything. The weekly task scrub’s time is on the log, in our events page’s own words, with the hour on your own clock. Its call is open to anybody, the same way as the Events Room’s: type the name you want to be called, knock, and wait in the lobby for a moderator.
2026-09-28-cavendish-events-room
2026-09-28 — The Events Room, behind Cavendish’s Events door

The Events door at Cavendish Coworking opens onto a room of its own now: the Events Room, a lighthouse keeper’s watch room, lit by one column of light from the lantern above. Our recurring events are its light list, in our events page’s own words, with the hour on your own clock under each one. Its call is open to anybody. If you are not signed on to the CB, type the name you want to be called and knock, and you wait in the lobby until a moderator lets you in. It is the first of the rooms that replace the Proton links, one door at a time; the other doors still open Proton until theirs are built.
2026-09-28-cb-follow-the-host
2026-09-28 — Follow the host

When somebody is hosting the film in your room, the CB’s radio has a Follow switch beside Catch up. Press it and your own film keeps pace with the host’s: it plays when they play, pauses when they pause, and moves when they jump, while its volume and captions stay yours. That is the thing Jitsi’s shared video cannot do, since only the person who shares one gets a volume. Pausing your own film stops following, which is how you take a break, and pressing Follow again picks up where the host is. It is off until you press it, it is never remembered, it sends nothing, and it stops when the host stops.
2026-09-28-cb-call-shared-video
2026-09-28 — Share a YouTube video in a call

A room’s call can share a YouTube video now, from the call’s own menu, for everybody in it to watch in step. It was missing because one setting of ours, which kept Jitsi from contacting anybody else, also switches that feature off. That setting is gone, and the three other things it covered (Jitsi’s analytics, its avatar lookups and its animated-picture search) are each switched off on their own instead. The person who shares a video plays and pauses it for everybody, and Jitsi mutes your microphone while it plays with the sound on. When somebody shares one, YouTube loads in everybody’s call window, and the privacy page says so.
2026-09-28-cb-answers-overlap
2026-09-28 — The radio’s answers no longer run under its buttons

A long answer on the CB’s radio, like the one Catch up gives when no film has been started, ran underneath the buttons below it on a full radio. Every part of the radio keeps its own height now, and the radio scrolls instead.
2026-09-28-cb-call-moves
2026-09-28 — A call moves like the radio

A room’s call can be moved anywhere on the screen, the way the radio can: drag its bar, or put the keyboard on its Move button and use the arrow keys, and Home puts it back in its corner. It never goes off the edge, and Large still fills the window and then goes back to where you had it. Where you put it is not remembered, because nothing about a call is kept.
2026-09-28-cb-call-small
2026-09-28 — A small size for a call

A room’s call has a Small size now, beside Large: a tile in the corner, so there is room to watch a film on the page while you are in the call. Changing size never interrupts the call. Small and Large each go back to the middle size when you press them again.
2026-09-28-cb-room-calls
2026-09-28 — A call for every room

Join this room’s call on the CB’s radio opens voice and video for the room you are in, in a window of its own at the foot of the page, for people signed on to the CB. It runs on 8x8’s Jitsi as a Service, and it replaces nothing: the channel and the Proton rooms are still there. Camera and microphone start off, and you arrive on a screen where you choose before joining. The base station moderates and is the only one who can record or transcribe a call. Leaving the page hangs up; folding the radio away does not. It is the first thing on this site allowed to ask for a camera or a microphone, and the only thing: our pages never ask for either themselves. The privacy page says what goes to 8x8, and that we keep nothing about a call.
2026-09-28-cb-fits-the-window
2026-09-28 — The radio fits the window

The CB radio is never taller than your window now. With a full channel, a host and the teleporter open, it could grow past the top of the screen and take its own Fold away and Small buttons with it. The bar along the top stays where it is and everything under it scrolls, and the radio moves back onto the screen whenever it grows, wherever you have put it. For the base station, Take off now sits at the end of each message’s name-and-time line instead of on a row of its own under every message, which roughly halves the height of a full channel. A screen reader still hears each new message’s words before the button.
2026-09-28-cb-room-channels
2026-09-28 — A channel for every room

The CB tunes to World or to this room. World is the channel it always had. Every room on the street now has a channel of its own too, with the same rules: ten messages, and gone at midnight, Colorado time. The radio hears one at a time, says which at the top of its readout, and remembers which you chose, so walking between rooms tuned to rooms hears each room’s channel in turn. Listening to World tells us nothing about where you are. Listening to a room’s channel has to say which room, and the privacy page says so. Nothing records who listened where.
2026-09-28-cb-host-beacon
2026-09-28 — Hosting a film on the CB

Host this film is on the radio once a film on your page has been started. Press it and everybody on the channel sees which film you are watching, in which room, and where it has got to, as it plays and pauses. In the same room, each radio has a Catch up button that moves that person’s own film to where the host is. Nobody else’s film moves, so anybody taking a break can catch up when they come back. From another room, the host’s room is a link that arrives with the film ready to start at the host’s place. One person hosts a room at a time. It is never remembered, it only sends while the radio is open and the tab is in front, and folding the radio away or leaving the page stops it. The radio never tells us which room you are in to find your room’s host: every radio is sent every host. The privacy page says exactly what is kept, and for how long.
2026-09-28-picture-house-big-screen-spot
2026-09-28 — A spot reaches the big screen

Arriving at the Lightbulb Picture House by a spot on the CB, the film starts at the spot whether you press its card or put it on the big screen, and the line under the screen says where it started from.
2026-09-28-cb-spot-link-arrives-ready
2026-09-28 — A spot’s room link takes you to the film, ready

Following the room’s name in a spot takes you to that room with the film’s play button ready to start at the spot. The keyboard lands on it, the radio says what it is, and nothing plays until you press it. If the film has no play button of its own there, because it is part of a whole programme, the radio says so and tells you what to do instead.
2026-09-28-cb-spot-names-film-room
2026-09-28 — A spot on the CB says which film and which room

Add my spot writes the film and the room now, like @34:12 in “An introduction to neurodiversity” at #lightbulb-picture-house. The room shows as its name, linked, so anybody can go there. Before this, a spot dropped from one room moved whatever happened to be playing in another. A spot that names a room or a film only moves that film in that room. Anywhere else, or with a different film playing, nothing moves, and the radio says where that spot is. A time typed bare, like @34:12, still moves whatever is playing on your page.
2026-09-28-cb-film-places
2026-09-28 — A place in a film is a button on the CB

@34:12 in a CB message is a button now. Pressing it moves the film on your own page to that place. It does not press play, so somebody back from a break can catch up with the room and still keep their own pace, their own volume and their own pauses. This replaces pasting timestamps into the channel by hand at a watch-together. A time without the @, like 7:30, stays words. Add my spot appears on the radio once a film on the page has been started. It writes where your film has got to into your message box, and sends nothing until you transmit. It works in every room with a YouTube player, and it does not load YouTube’s own script: the page asks the player it already framed. We tested that the player takes a jump before building anything. Live cameras are left out, because a place means nothing in a live picture. The privacy page and the house norms say how it works.
2026-09-28-picture-house-arday-card
2026-09-28 — One campfire film the playlist cannot hold

Jason Arday’s second talk, Things Can Only Get Better, is on the campfire rack at the Lightbulb Picture House and not in Screen Three’s programme, because YouTube would not let it be added to the playlist. It still plays, from its card or up on the screen from there, and the card says why the programme skips it. The two April campfires whose posts had not been tagged Campfire Learn Together on stimpunks.org are tagged now, so the tag page holds every campfire on the rack.
2026-09-28-picture-house-screen-two-rack
2026-09-28 — Screen Two’s rack, and racks that fold away

Screen Two at the Lightbulb Picture House has a rack now, like the others: a card for every film saying who made it, how long it runs, what it is about and what is in it before you press play, written from the films’ own captions. Each card can play its film in place or up on Screen Two. Every rack folds away. They start open, so nothing on the page is hidden until you choose to fold it, and folding one is a single press on its heading. It works without scripts.
2026-09-28-picture-house-big-screen
2026-09-28 — A card's film on the big screen

Every card on a rack at the Lightbulb Picture House can now put its film on that rack’s own screen, in place of the whole programme: Screen One for the first rack, Screen Three for the campfire rack. The button says how long the film runs before you press it, like every other press here. Pressing it takes you to the screen, which says what is now showing, so the film does not start somewhere you cannot see. Putting the programme back does not start it: the screen goes back to its own press-to-play plate and waits. Without scripts the button is not there at all, rather than being a button that does nothing, and every card still plays its film in place.
2026-09-28-picture-house-campfire
2026-09-28 — Screen Three at the Lightbulb Picture House: every campfire

The Lightbulb Picture House has a third screen, and on it is everything we have watched together at Campfire Learn Together, our Sunday watch-along, newest first. New campfires go on at the top. It has a rack like Screen One’s: a card for every film saying who made it, how long it runs, what it is about and what is in it before you press play, and which campfire it was watched at, with a link to the post we wrote for that campfire. The words are ours, written from each film’s captions rather than from its title; the few films with no captions are described from their own descriptions and from our posts, and the liner notes say which. Three campfires are listed under the rack and are not on the screen, because what we watched is on Vimeo or has since been made private on YouTube. Leaving them out would make the screen look like the whole record when it is not. Checked before it went up: every film plays and embeds, the whole playlist plays inside a frame on this site with captions on, and nothing reaches YouTube until you press play. The page no longer says how many screens it has.
2026-09-28-sweetgrass-fire
2026-09-28 — A fire in the fire pit at Swaying Sweetgrass

Swaying Sweetgrass had a fire pit with talks round it and no fire in it. Now it has one: a whole playlist of real campfires filmed in the forest by Norwegian Fireplace and Campfire, on one large screen the width of the clearing. You hear the crackle, the wind and birds. There is no voice and no music, and the channel says none of it is looped. Nothing loads until you press it. It is the one thing in the clearing that does not say how long it runs, because a playlist the channel keeps adding to has no length. The room says so beside it, and the sentence that said every label there gives a runtime has been rewritten to be true again. Everything told at the fire still says how long before you press. The screen shows no fire until you press it. Before that it is drawn in the meadow’s own colours, because the fire in this room is small and far off and is not what lights the page. The videos’ own titles sell them for sleep and focus. The room repeats none of that. Checked before it went up: the first video in the list plays and embeds, and the whole list plays inside a frame on this site. It is credited in the liner notes and is the first thing on the Now Playing poster for that room.
2026-09-28-import-room
2026-09-28 — A way in for rooms built with your own AI

A room somebody builds with their AI from Your Room’s prompt can now come onto the street through one tool, tools/import-room.py. It reads the note the prompt asks the AI to leave at the top of the page, checks everything it says against the page itself, and holds the room to the same promises every room here keeps. 2026-09-27-fractal-window
2026-09-27 — A fractal window in (almost) every room

Every page’s sign-off has a new switch: Switch on the fractal window. It opens a small window of its own in the corner of the screen with a slow fractal in it, drawn in your browser in that room’s own colours. No two rooms draw the same picture: Julia sets, the edge of the Mandelbrot set, Newton fractals, a fern, a dragon curve, a crystal. The window has its own speed control (Slow, Steady, Quick), moves between corners, goes full screen, and closes when you switch it off or leave the room. It is not synced to the music, and it says so before you press. Almost everything that plays here plays inside another site’s frame, and a page is not allowed to listen to another site’s frame. The one plain audio player streams from a host that does not let other sites read the sound. So the window is a picture that runs beside the music. It follows the Arcade, not the dial. It runs at every setting because the motion is the thing you switched on, and the dial is not wired to it. At Gentle it starts at Slow. It never flashes, and that is enforced in its code. Every frame, no pixel is allowed to change brightness, or redness, faster than a fixed rate. That keeps every spot well under the three flashes a second that the accessibility rule for seizures (WCAG 2.3.1) allows. Played without that limit, most rooms’ pictures would flash at Quick. A test counts flashes in what every room’s window actually paints, using its own arithmetic, before anything is published. Nothing is fetched until you press. The window’s script and stylesheet download on the first press and not before. It stores nothing and sends nothing. Two rooms do not have it yet, on purpose. Stay Frosty promises on its own page that there is nothing to press in it and nothing moves, so a switch there would make that false. And the Faery Yurt is Helen Edgar’s room: a picture in her colours changes how her room reads, which is hers to decide.

2026-09-23 — Lighter pictures, where that is measurably true

Fifty-six of the street’s JPEGs are WebP now, and the pictures on those pages weigh about 29% less — 2.4MB across the scans, prints, engravings, photographs and thumbnails. The biggest single waste went with it: the Pebble Board’s video thumbnails were stored 1280 pixels wide and are never drawn wider than 170, and they are 512 now, which still covers a phone screen at three times density. Twenty-four stayed JPEG, each for a reason written down. Every file was converted at the lowest quality that measured as faithful to its source, and swapped only if that saved at least a tenth. Most of Doré’s and Tenniel’s engravings did not clear that bar: fine hatching is the one thing lossy formats are worst at, and at the same fidelity WebP was no smaller than the JPEG, sometimes larger. Converting them anyway would have meant a heavier file or a softer engraving, chosen for the format’s sake. data/webp.json holds every decision and its numbers. The first attempt measured the wrong thing and was undone. It compared colour as well as detail, and WebP always stores colour at half resolution, as most JPEGs do — so on small, bright thumbnails it concluded no quality was good enough and left the oversized ones exactly as they were. It had deleted JPEGs under that rule, so everything went back to the last commit and ran again measuring detail, which is what the eye looks for. Nothing about the pages changed but the files. WebP goes into the same image tags, so no room’s layout moved; AVIF was often smaller still, but serving it safely means wrapping every picture in a new element, and at least one room’s layout depends on its images not being wrapped. The share cards and icons stay PNG, because link previews and home screens do not all read anything else. Every picture on the affected pages was loaded and checked afterwards, and the photographs still carry no location or device data. 2026-09-23 — Structured data, and a note for any agent reading the street

Every page describes itself in JSON-LD, the format search engines and agents treat as fact. Everything in it comes out of that page’s own head — its title, its description, its address — so it cannot say anything the page does not. The publisher is marked with the same identifier Star Stuff uses, so two of our sites describe one Stimpunks Foundation rather than two. The licence is on the site, not on each page, because the photographs of people are excluded from it. The missing-address page gets none: it has no address to describe. There is a skill for agents, at /.well-known/agent-skills/stimpunks-love/SKILL.md: how to read, quote and cite this site. It says where the indexes are, why the site gives no count of its rooms and what to do if you need one, that the rooms are different on purpose, that two of them must not be summarised as advice or a fortune, and what the licence covers — including that the photographs are not to be reused. The counting check reads it, so it obeys the site’s own rule. /.well-known/api-catalog lists every machine-readable resource (RFC 9727), and every response now points at it. It uses only link relations that are actually registered, which is why the sitemap and the skill are not in it under relations they do not have — Star Stuff found out the hard way and published the correction. Both files are generated: the skill’s sha256 is computed from its bytes on every run, and the catalogue refuses to name a file that does not exist. Both refusals were tested by breaking them. Turning 03 in The Outskirts is a venue. The Outskirts shipped carrying the ordinary real-world reading of an edge-of-town, and it was wrong here. Three lines: premises that were never going to get planning permission, a bullet saying out-of-town is where everything gets pushed that a town has decided is not respectable, and a fair amount of that is us, and a Covenstead described as a group the town would rather not think about. Ryan caught it. All three are gone. The objection is structural rather than a matter of taste. Our town is stimpunks.love and it accepts everybody, so it has no outside to push anybody to. A street named after a character who turns up wherever somebody needs shelter and rearranges himself for whoever has arrived cannot also have a wrong side of himself. The framing was imported from real towns, where it is perfectly true, into the one place on this site whose whole premise contradicts it. It got past everything because it arrived sounding sympathetic. This is where the disreputable ends up and we are the disreputable reads as solidarity, and on most pages it would be. Here it quietly builds a category of people this site would rather not look at, and then generously puts us in it — which is a thing to remember, because no checker on this street can see an argument that is wrong only in context. The road is a direction and not a verdict. 2026-09-22 — Danny the Street, and the credit that was only in a marquee

The street’s own name has a page: Danny the Street. Ryan’s brief — an about page for the character this site is built out of, its origin and its history in comics and on television, with our Danny taking they/them. Where the name came from, what Danny has been since, the television version, the pronoun question, and which parts of Danny are ours to take. The credit already existed and only sighted readers could get it. The front page has said DANNY IS THE STREET since it opened, in a marquee that is aria-hidden because it scrolls and is decoration — so the one place the architecture is credited was unreachable by a screen reader, on a site whose two surviving careful habits are contrast and attribution. There is now a paragraph under the loudness dial, in text, above the shopfronts it explains, and it declares its own link colour: the street has no base link rule at all, which is the hole The Doomscroll and the Playhouse both fell down. It is the road surface seen from directly above, under one sodium lamp, and the collapse to watch is the front page itself. A first: every earlier separation on this street was between two rooms, and this one is between a room and the page it hangs off. Both are a street at night. §5 is seen from the pavement, at eye level, looking into lit windows, with everything in it standing up and a typeface per shopfront. This is a plan — kerbs down both sides of the page, a broken centre line through the middle of it, nothing standing up anywhere, one typeface and one hue. One hue, because a sodium lamp has one wavelength in it. Low-pressure sodium is effectively monochromatic, so under it nothing has a colour of its own — only a brightness. That is what keeps this off the warm rooms, and by now the warm family has arrived seven times: the Faery Yurt, The Latibulum, The Den, the Hermitage’s cave, The Mopery and Swaying Sweetgrass are all lit by a flame or by the sun, and in every one of them things keep their own colours. Sodium takes colour away, and there is nothing in here to sit on. If a second hue ever appears in §33 the lamp has been changed for a different kind of lamp. The campgrounds is the other outdoor night, and the separation is the sky. The field is cold blue with the sky still on it. Under a lamp you cannot see up at all: the light is a lid and the dark past the kerb is absolute. The Rabbit Hole is the other hard grey and is cold, wet and vertical; this is warm, dry and flat. One new face, and it is the road’s own. Overpass, by Delve Withrington, Dave Bailey and Thomas Jockin for Red Hat, is drawn from the lettering on American highway signs — the only family on this street whose whole reason for existing is being painted onto or bolted above a road, read at speed, from a long way off, by somebody who is doing something else at the time. It sets the nameplate, the road legends and the dates. The prose is the base’s Space Grotesk, which makes this the only room here with a display face and no text face of its own — the exact inverse of the Garden, which has two text faces and no display face, because a garden has labels and no signage. Under the SIL Open Font License. Nothing on that page was written from memory, because half of what everybody remembers about Danny is somebody’s retelling. The debut issue and date, the creators, the pun on Danny La Rue, the Polari, the Men from N.O.W.H.E.R.E. and every later form were read rather than recalled; so were the air date, writer and director of “Danny Patrol”. The spelling of Dannyzens came off DC’s own page, because it varies everywhere else. And an unsourced origin story for the character that is still circulating was left off deliberately — the herbarium’s refusal to guess at a binomial, arriving in a fandom. The one quotation was chased to the original and the chase is published. Morrison’s line about genderqueer and non-binary not existing as words in the late 1980s is quoted from the Uproxx interview it was given to — but uproxx.com renders its article text through JavaScript and hands a fetch nothing but navigation, so it was read against the Internet Archive’s capture of 23 July 2025 and the page says so. Swaying Sweetgrass’s rule: do not let an unchecked quotation sit among checked ones looking identical. The pronouns are three different answers and the page keeps them apart. The comics write Danny as he, in 1990’s vocabulary; the television version is genderqueer and uses they/them; the Danny in our marquee uses they/them, which is a decision about this site rather than a correction of anybody’s canon. On a site run by and for neurodivergent and Disabled people, they is what we would default to for a person whose pronouns we had not been told. Nothing of DC’s is reproduced and the page says so where somebody will read it. No panels, no artwork, no dialogue: every drawing on that page and on its share card is of a road, which is a thing nobody owns. What the page is, is a namesake credit — the habit the liner notes keep for every song, typeface and borrowed phrase, applied to the borrowed thing holding the whole building up. No ambient layer at any setting, which is Club Chronic’s rule in the quietest room that has ever held it: the lamp is on at Gentle because it is the light in here rather than an effect, and nothing else moves, because nothing on a street at four in the morning does. There is no transform in §33 either — a painted road legend is stretched along the road, and a scale is exactly what check-gentle.py reads out of the computed matrix and cannot tell from a page tilting itself. The legends are letter-spaced and left alone, which is the call The Foundry made in the room where a slant is a control.
