2026-09-22-a-bold-that-was-there-all-along
2026-09-22 — One Space Grotesk, and a bold the bench had been hiding

Space Grotesk was stored three times over, byte for byte. Same sha256, same 22320 bytes, and fonts/_sources.json recorded the same gstatic URL for all three, because the family ships as a variable font and Google serves one file for every weight. On the shared base that every page on the street loads, that cost about 45KB. It is one file now, declared three times against the weight axis, the way §1 already handles Cabin, Karla and the rest. The Feed was preloading the copy that got deleted, which would have 404’d on a published page; it preloads the one that survives. And then the interesting half: identical bytes are not an absent bold. The obvious reading of three identical files is that a weight-700 declaration renders the same drawings as the 400 — and The Foundry had been built on exactly that reading since it opened, grouping each family’s variants by the sha of the file they point at and keeping one. It is the wrong question. A variable font carries a weight axis inside the file, and the browser instances it at every @font-face declaration: same bytes, genuinely different outlines. The rule was throwing away bolds that work. Measured rather than argued about, because the premise sounded right. Rendered out of one file at 64px: Cinzel’s 700 lays down 68% more ink than its 400, Work Sans’ 600 45%, Space Grotesk’s 700 41%, Nunito’s 39%. Not one pair on the shelves came out the same. Twelve families had a weight the street holds and the bench was keeping in a drawer — Cabin, Cinzel, EB Garamond, Faustina, Jost, Karla, Mulish, Nunito, Quicksand, Rubik, Space Grotesk and Vollkorn — and every one of them is offered now. tools/check-weights.py is the check the sha was standing in for. It renders the published picker — never the generator, which is check-quests.py’s rule — and refuses two offerings of one family that come out the same drawings, a weight love.css does not declare, and a declared weight the room does not offer. Advance width alone cannot decide it: Courier Prime and Space Mono are monospaced, so their 400 and 700 share an advance to the hundredth of a pixel while the bold lays down about 40% more ink. It measures ink and advance and calls two the same only when both match. It found a bug in itself on the first run, which is why it was broken on purpose first. @font-face is lazy, so nothing is downloaded until a page sets it — and a canvas asked to draw a font it has not got silently draws the fallback instead. The first draft measured before loading anything, so every face on the street would have measured identically and been reported as the same drawings. It loads, waits, then measures, and still asks whether each face actually arrived. Fed a static face declared at two weights, it correctly calls the second one a control that does nothing; that is the protection the sha was giving, and it is still there. Nunito’s bold was not in the record at all. love.css declares that one file at 400 and 700; fonts/_sources.json listed only the 400, and nothing compared the two. The new checker reads the stylesheet the browser actually obeys, so that class of drift now refuses rather than sitting there. Two things found and deliberately not changed. Jost is still stored twice — jost-400.woff2 and jost-500.woff2 are byte-identical, the same duplication Space Grotesk had — and it is logged here rather than swept into a commit about something else. And the campground sets its emphasis in Alfa Slab One because Bitter’s bold “was byte-identical to its regular”: that reasoning is the one corrected above, so the decision rests on a premise that turns out to be false. It is a room’s own design decision and not a bug, so it stays until somebody who owns that room says otherwise.
2026-09-22-the-foundry
2026-09-22 — The Foundry, and the first room whose content is the typefaces

A type foundry on the street: The Foundry. Ryan’s brief — a font play storefront, your own text or text out of The Playhouse, The Mopery and The Zibaldone, every setting the type has, and a way to print it. A grey iron workshop under a dirty roof with a bench in it. Every other room on this street uses a typeface; this is the one where they are the thing in the window. It is the first mid-grey ground here, and that is the whole separation. Every other world on the street is either a night ground with light applied to it or a sheet of paper with the room cropped away. This is the middle — the colour of the metal — and the only pale object in it is one proof lying on a bench. The four paper rooms are the obvious collapse and each one is held off by something structural: The Mopery is a cold building you stand up in whose type is impressed into the page, the guild is manila lit like a photocopy from nowhere, The Doomscroll is one unbroken roll of warm foxed newsprint, and The Zibaldone is bound leaves with a gutter and a fold. There is no fold in here and nothing is bound. It is the third daylit room, and north light is what a workshop was built for — the glazing faces away from the sun so the work has no glare on it, which means flat, cool, directionless daylight and no lit face on anything. The Hermitage has a low morning sun with long sideways shadows; the Garden’s light has come through leaves and tints every pale surface green. A furnace would have been the obvious build and would have made this the seventh warm room on a street that already has six. The only warm value in here is brass, and brass is a metal rather than a light. Nothing about any typeface was typed. tools/pull-foundry.py reads every family’s own record out of github.com/google/fonts — family name, designer, licence, copyright, repository, classification — and cross-checks the licence against which directory of that repository the family lives in. It refuses a family it cannot resolve rather than publishing a face with nobody’s name under it. It is kept out of the pre-deploy sequence with check-jukebox.py because it needs the network, and make-foundry.py needs nothing but the file it writes. Do not merge them. The first thing it found was that four of these families are not OFL, and three published pages said they were. Permanent Marker, Rock Salt, Special Elite and Ultra are under the Apache License 2.0. love.css’s §1 comment said “every family here is OFL-licensed”, the liner notes said “all are licensed under the SIL Open Font License” and again “the typefaces keep their own OFL licence”, and the Mopery’s generated credit line said it a fourth time. All four are corrected and every face now carries its own licence on the shelves. A licence nobody has checked since the file was added is a claim rather than a fact, which is the whole argument for a tool that goes and reads. The Mopery’s picker had quietly lost eighteen families, and tools/check-faces.py is why it cannot again. That room says in its own copy that the picker holds every typeface on this street and llms.txt says the poem can be set in any face on it; both had been false for a long time, because adding a file to fonts/ and adding an <option> in a room two doors away are two edits in two places and only one of them is obviously required. The picker is generated now, from the same record The Foundry’s shelves are built from — when something has to agree in several places, make the others read it rather than write it out again, which is love-embed.js’s ORIGINS lesson. The new checker reads both rooms’ published markup and never the generators, in both directions, and it was broken on purpose before being believed. An italic is not a slant, and the bench is built to show you rather than tell you. A real italic is a second alphabet, cut separately, with different letters in it. A machine slant is the upright pushed over by something that has no idea what it is looking at. Both are offered and both are labelled, and the italic is disabled where this site holds no italic file — because the browser answers a request for one it has not got by inventing it, nothing looks broken, and the room has told you a lie about somebody’s typeface. Measured rather than assumed: on Rye, a requested italic renders at the roman’s own advance widths; on Cardo, which has a real italic, oblique 12deg comes out at 399.65px against the italic’s 377.42px, so the slant really is the roman pushed over. The slant is a font setting and never a transform, deliberately. check-gentle.py reads rotation and skew out of the computed matrix and cannot tell a leaning page from a leaning letter, so a skewX() here would be reported — correctly — as this room’s decoration outranking somebody’s Gentle setting. There is no transform anywhere in §32, which is the call arcade.js made with left/top and the Oracle Deck made with its lozenge. A weight is offered only where the bytes differ. Seven of these families ship as variable fonts, so love.css declares one file against two or three weights — and a bold that renders the same drawings as the regular is a control that does nothing, which is make-chappell.py’s typo that never becomes a video arriving as a dropdown. The puller records a sha for every variant and the bench groups by it. Hashing the whole shelf also turned up Space Grotesk stored three times over, byte for byte, on the shared base that every page loads; that is logged separately rather than fixed in this commit. Four ink and paper pairs, each printing its own measured ratio on its own control, and the tool refuses one under 4.5:1. This is the one room on the street where somebody other than us picks the colour of the text, which makes it either the place contrast quietly stops being ours to keep or the place it becomes a thing you can watch being kept. There is no colour picker and there is not going to be one. The light moved rather than the palette. The north light was a fixed full-height wash to begin with, which composites the floor to #596267 — and against that the room’s link brass measures 3.14 and its fine print 3.34, both under the bar. Worse, fixed, that composite could arrive under any paragraph on the page depending on how far somebody had scrolled, which is the shape The Rabbit Hole’s scrolling ground already taught this stylesheet. It is 340px tall and absolute now: the light comes in at the top of the room and the page scrolls out from under it, which is also what happens in a building. A light that follows the viewport is not a light, it is a veil in front of the reader. The only words standing in it are the topline’s, and they are bone at 5.19 for that reason. The proof prints and the room does not, and what prints carries a colophon naming the family, the person who drew it, the licence and every setting it was pulled at — because printing somebody’s typeface is exactly where the credit should travel with it. It comes out black on white whatever pair is on the screen: paper colour is a screen decision and a printer would spend your toner on it. Measured rather than asserted: the rendered PDF is one page with two fonts embedded in it, the proof’s face and the colophon’s, which is how you can tell the shelves did not print. Nothing here describes a typeface, and that is a refusal rather than an omission. A line of appreciation beside every family on this street would mean inventing type history at scale in the format most likely to be believed — the herbarium’s refusal to name a pressed plant to species, arriving where there is one to write for every face. What the room says truthfully is who drew it, what licence it travels under and which room here sets it, and that last claim is checked against love.css: make-foundry.py refuses a line the stylesheet does not support. A derived version got it wrong on its first run, because the street letters each door in that room’s own face. Nothing is counted. Not the faces, not the proofs pulled, not the sizes tried, and there is no favourite and no ranking of one designer’s work against another’s. This is the room most likely to want to boast about how much type it holds, and the generator refuses the sentence as well as the habit. Two new faces. Stardos Stencil sets the nameplate and the headings and nothing else — a stencil letter is a hole rather than a mark, a shape cut out of metal so it can be used again, which is the idea of type arriving four centuries early and in the wrong material, and it is what gets painted on a workshop’s crates. Anton is the street’s other condensed display face and is Club Chronic’s: solid, on a black wall, under a marker. Work Sans is the prose and is a workhorse on purpose, because a room whose content is other people’s typefaces cannot have a voice that argues with the window. Both under the SIL Open Font License. New: foundry.html, foundry.js, data/foundry.json, data/foundry-faces.json, tools/pull-foundry.py, tools/make-foundry.py, tools/check-faces.py, §32 of love.css, Stardos Stencil and Work Sans self-hosted, a share card drawn as a galley with its letters mirrored the way cast type is, and a single sort lying on the workshop floor with a job on it. 2026-09-22-the-healing-checkpoint
2026-09-22 — The Healing Checkpoint, room 429, and the first room lit from the floor

The guild’s bed exists: The Healing Checkpoint, room 429. Ryan’s brief — a guest room for the Adventurer’s Guild, patterned after the Healing Checkpoint, leading with an appreciation of rest built out of our own Rest entry. A save room: an arched alcove with a spring in the floor, a bed in it, and nobody at the desk. It is a shopfront on the street AND a back stair out of the guild, and the two doors are the argument. A room saying rest is owed rather than earned cannot be reachable only by walking through the place that hands out the work — that would make it structurally something you get to after the jobs. So the front door is on the street, where anybody arrives at it having done nothing, and the guild’s unattended counter is the back way up. It is the first room here with two entrances. No job sends you to it; the one job that lives in it is a question about a status code. The light comes UP, and that one physical fact is the whole separation. Every other world on this street is lit from somewhere else and no two from the same place — the Jungle Room from above through leaves, the Zibaldone from one side at desk height, Swaying Sweetgrass from behind and a hundred feet off, The Feed through a mask in front of a lamp, The Garden from directly overhead, the guild from nowhere at all. Here it comes out of the floor: every top surface is dark, every underside carries a rim, the shadows run up the walls, and the room gets lighter towards your feet. The warm enclosed family is the collapse to watch and by now it has arrived six times. The Faery Yurt, The Latibulum, The Den, the Hermitage’s cave and The Mopery are every one of them lit by a flame you could put your hand over. There is no flame in here; the light is under water and you could put your hand in it. All five are brown, amber or candle-gold, and there is no warm ground anywhere in room 429 at all — only one warm ink, which is what pale stone looks like with a cold light on it. The guild is its other door and its exact opposite: manila, square, ruled, hairlined, lit like a photocopy from nowhere. There is not a straight edge in the checkpoint anywhere. A board and an inn share a building and nothing else. The generator refuses instrumental rest, which is a refusal nothing else here makes. tools/make-checkpoint.py sweeps its own data and the published page for the vocabulary of rent — earn, deserve, recharge, productive, bounce back, so you can — with a negation window so the room can still say out loud that it will not. Star Stuff’s zine No. 58 refuses rest so you can produce in as many words and otterly.js already holds that line for one cabinet; this is where the whole street says it. The friendly edit here arrives from somebody being kind, because every wellness page on the internet is written the other way round, and one encouraging sentence would turn rest from a thing owed into an investment. Nothing in it is counted and nothing is stored. No total, no streak, no visits, no local storage, no server — the pebbling cabinet’s refusal of a tally arriving where a counter is the most obvious improvement anybody could propose, and one link above a job board that does keep a list in your own browser. A checkpoint that remembered you would be keeping a record of how often you needed one. The trope’s other two promises are refused in the room’s own copy: it restores nothing, because you are not a health bar, and there is no hard part waiting on the other side. The tally check was copied wrong and its first run caught it. make-guild.py narrowed points years’ worth of care ago — “a book it points at” is the verb — and this file reproduced the flat version from the identical shortcut. What refused it was save point, which is what a healing checkpoint is. The narrowed pattern was taken over rather than the phrase excepted, which is check-counts.py’s first-run lesson arriving a fourth time. Every refusal was then broken on purpose before being believed — a long quotation, an off-site trail entry, an entity in a field, a missing checked date, and an instrumental sentence planted in the page itself. Five Retry-After slips, and they send nothing anywhere. 429 Too Many Requests is Nottingham and Fielding’s, RFC 6585, April 2012, and it says the rate is wrong rather than that the sender is, which is a thing a great many Disabled people have spent a great deal of energy trying to explain to somebody holding a deadline. Each slip is a <details> that works with scripts off; checkpoint.js only adds a copy button, which ships hidden so a page without JavaScript shows no dead control. It is the spoon drawer’s shape — it hands out the sentences and not the thing itself — and the Zibaldone’s clipboard, for the Zibaldone’s reason. The answer lands on the slip you pressed, not at the top of the page, which is the Playhouse’s lesson, and it was measured rendered at 653×28 rather than asserted from the DOM. Two new faces, and the crowding is written down rather than hoped about. Quicksand is display only — the third geometric sans here, kept apart from Jost and Josefin Sans by job and by its semicircular terminals, which is what lets it carry a room whose every corner is a long radius. Rubik is the text face, and The Latibulum is the collision: that room’s Nunito is a humanist rounded face paired with a slab, and this is a grotesque with eased corners and flat-cut terminals. Two warm-shaped text faces kept apart at the stroke, which is the only place they could be. Both under the SIL Open Font License. Nothing flashes at any setting, which is Club Chronic’s rule holding in the room whose entire subject is not being jolted. The steam over the water drifts at MAX with a translate and a scale — rotation and skew are all check-gentle.py can read — and is gone at Gentle. The light in the floor is not the dial’s and is on at every setting: it is not an effect, it is where the light in the room comes from, and a Gentle that unlit the room rather than quieting it would be the lite-version mistake with a torch. Two things on the Rest entry are named here and deliberately not copied onto this street: Kristina Daniele’s poem, and three illustrations of Disabled people resting by Jonathan Soren Davidson and Campbell Royales for Disabled And Here. A page built out of somebody else’s page should say what it did not take. The three lines it does quote are Fergus Murray’s and Tricia Hersey’s, each under the thirty-word limit the tool enforces and the room prints, each naming the page and the day it was read off the mirror. Tricia Hersey and The Nap Ministry are credited in the room’s own copy rather than in a footnote, which is what the guild promised when it said the bed was not built yet. 2026-09-22-ivy-not-a-fence
2026-09-22 — Ivy and stars instead of a fence, because Helen asked

The boundary in The Garden’s two plots was a woven fence this morning and is winding ivy with stars caught in it now. Helen Edgar’s call, on a drawing of her own gardens: my first thought is fenced in though. Her sites, her say — the same rule the Faery Yurt has kept since it was pitched. She was right about more than the picture. A fence says KEPT OUT. Ivy says THIS IS AS FAR AS WE CAN SEE. That line was never marking the edge of where anybody may go; it marks the edge of what we know, which is why the drawing stops there in the first place — we do not get to draw the roots of somebody else’s garden. The second reading is the only correct one on a page about somebody else’s work, and the picture had been quietly making the first one. The refusal underneath it is unchanged and still bites. below_the_fence() is below_the_ivy() and FENCE_Y is IVY_Y; the walker still refuses a coordinate past the line, re-broken on purpose with a frond pushed under it. The rename was scoped to the one section that owns those names — the fence in §20 of love.css belongs to another room and was left alone — which is the rule this repository has now written down three times and broken twice. The stars are glimmers and not a sky. This room is midday and stays midday: nothing is lit by them, no ambient layer was added to the page, and the street’s one daylit garden is not quietly turned into a night one. They are limewash white carried by an outline, because white on that path measures 1.07 and what has to separate is the edge — the ghost pipe’s answer in Queering.Earth’s bed, arriving in a star. No new colour anywhere in it. Threads, glimmers, and soft, weird spaces is More Realms’ own line about itself, which is where the word comes from; they are not the meadow’s fireflies, which are many small lights carrying a dark field. Every ivy leaf is turned by baked coordinates rather than by a transform, because check-gentle.py reads rotation out of a computed matrix and a room must not ask a checker to take its word for something — arcade.js’s call about its sprites and quest.js’s about its sparks, arriving in a leaf. The correction is written down in five places — make-garden.py, data/garden.json, the room’s own copy, the liner notes and here — for the reason the one colour of hers this repository ever changed is written in four. Except that this one runs the other way, from a contributor to us, and a correction in that direction is worth recording at least as loudly as one we made to her work.
2026-09-22-the-garden-next-door
2026-09-22 — The garden next door, which is not a bed and could not be made one

Autistic Realms and More Realms are in The Garden, over the fence. Ryan’s call. They are Helen Edgar’s own sites — the grounded one and the wilder ground beyond it — and they are named, linked and credited to her on the face of the page rather than in a footnote. A bed is a site WE publish, so neither of these could be one. The garden’s roster is data/arrivals.json, whose order is stimpunks.org’s own feeds page, and the only way to plant one of hers would have been to write it into that file — which would put it on The Feed as one of our wires and claim her work as ours in the one place this room may not invent anything. So the two refusals in make-garden.py now face each other: a bed that is not on the roster is refused, and a plot that is on it is refused, and no edit to the garden’s own data file can move a site across that fence. You can see over the fence and not into the ground, and the drawings say so before the words do. Every bed shows its soil and most of them show what is under it. A plot shows a woven hurdle across the foot of the frame and nothing below it, because we do not get to draw the roots of somebody else’s garden — the tool walks every coordinate and refuses one that reaches under, which is the soil-line walker with the ink filter taken off. It was broken on purpose first, with a frond pushed under the rail, a circle whose edge dipped below and a relative path that walked down; it caught all three. And nothing over there casts a shadow, although everything in the beds does: the sun has not moved, the floor a shadow would land on is on the far side of the fence. A plot must say what of it is already in this garden, and the tool refuses one that does not. Without that line the section is a list of a friend’s websites on a page about ours. With it, it is the other half of every with line in the beds above: those say who helped us, and this says whose garden that help walked out of. So the link rule widens by exactly our own roster — a plot may point at its own ground or at ours, and a third garden is still refused. A plot’s name is not on a limewashed board, and that is the whole visual difference. Every bed’s label is a stake driven into our own ground, and nobody gets to go and put a label in somebody else’s garden, so the name over there is simply written down. The rule under a plot is double where a bed’s is solid — two rails repeating the hurdle, as a bed’s heavy plank repeats the plank along its soil — and the plots stand as narrow columns side by side, which is the fourth geometry this site has for a list of places. No new colour anywhere in it; the fence, the plants and every word are in the room’s own inks on the room’s own path. One habit each, across the fence as well as along the path. Autistic Realms is a nurse tree, planted to take the weather off whatever is growing under it until that can stand in its own light — her argument rather than our metaphor, since her page puts feeling accepted and understood before the flourishing. More Realms is a crozier, a fern still coiled, the one thing in either garden that grows by unwinding rather than by reaching, after that site’s own phrase for how it moves. The drawing dedup now spans both sets, because two drawings alike is two drawings alike whichever side of the hurdle they stand on — which is also what keeps the crozier off the Monotropic Map’s tendril. What each of them is was read off its own pages, in the Knowledge System mirror rather than from memory, and the phrases in quotation marks are theirs and are marked as theirs. Counts, ranking and dates are refused in a plot exactly as in a bed, and the ranking refusal matters more here: ranking a neighbour’s garden against ours would be worse than ranking our own beds. 2026-09-22 — The Rabbit Hole, and the first room that carries a song without its words

A new storefront, and it is not a room: The Rabbit Hole. Ryan’s brief. Every other door on this street opens onto somewhere you can stand; this one opens onto a shaft with no floor at the bottom of it. It leads with our own glossary entry, Rabbit Hole, and the argument is that one: for monotropic minds the rabbit hole is not a detour, it is the destination, and three hours you did not mean to spend is not a failure of discipline. It carries all seven of that page’s embedded videos, six wood engravings from 1865, a feed your head section, and a trail out. The glossary entry prints the whole lyric and this room prints none of it, which is the one place a room here deliberately does less than the page it came from. Song lyric reproduction is a minefield in the United States in a way prose is not — music publishing enforces on quotation where prose publishing shrugs, the licensing is separate from the recording, and one line is a far larger fraction of a song than of a novel — which is the reasoning that already makes the Zibaldone refuse a song outright. The friendly edit here is real and it will arrive: a room whose spine is one song, whose source page has the words on it already, and whose section headings are phrases from it, reads thin without them, and whoever pastes them back will be right about the page and wrong about everything else. So tools/make-rabbit-hole.py refuses a lyric field and any value shaped like verse — several short hand-broken lines, which is what a lyric looks like in a JSON string and what a sentence never does. The recordings are offered instead, with Grace Slick’s own published account of writing it, and the two headings that are her phrases are credited to her where they stand. The Latibulum is the hardest collapse this street has had, harder than any subroom, because these two rooms are literally both holes in the ground. Every earlier version of the temptation came with a structural excuse attached — it is only a subroom, an area should look like an area, they are both cosy — and this one needs no excuse at all: the floor plan is the same. What keeps them apart is that the burrow is somewhere you arrive and the hole is somewhere you keep going. The burrow has a floor, walls, furniture, a lamp at knee height and a shelf; it is horizontal, it is at rest, and almost every word in it sits dark on lit plaster. This has no floor, no walls to lean on and no furniture whatsoever; it is vertical, the light is above and behind you and there is less of it the further down you read, and every word is pale on the dark. The burrow is earth and is brown. There is no brown in this room at all — it is wet slate — and if these greys ever warm up, the two rooms have become one and it is this one that moves. The ground darkens down the document, which is a shape of ground the contrast tools had not met. The Zibaldone’s rule is a flat background-color under the gradient, and its flat colour is the darker end; here it is the lightest end, because that room sets dark type on pale paper and this one sets pale type on a dark wall. In both cases the flat colour is the worse case for the type standing on it, which is the actual rule and is what makes the live checker’s answer the pessimistic one. And because the gradient runs the height of the document rather than of a sheet, the colour under a word depends on how far somebody has scrolled — so every block that carries text sits on a flat panel of its own and the wash carries nothing but the header’s lines. Two grounds, two link decisions, made at the room. Brass measures 6.74 and up on all three dark grounds and 1.83 on the paper mats the engravings sit on, so a single room-level link colour would have shipped an illegible provenance line under every plate. That is the hole The Doomscroll left and the Playhouse had been carrying since it opened — a colour nobody decided leaves no pair for check-contrast.py to hold — caught this time before the room shipped rather than by somebody looking at the page. Six engravings by John Tenniel, 1865, public domain, shown rather than linked because each scan says so. Tenniel was born in 1820 and died in 1914 and the book came out in 1865, so they are out of copyright everywhere, and every file used carries an explicit public domain statement on Wikimedia Commons — which is exactly what the Mopery’s Library of Congress facsimile did not have and the reason that one is still a door and not a window. The 1865 edition captioned none of its illustrations, so unlike that room’s Doré plates there is nothing printed to quote: every word beside an engraving here is ours, which engraving sits beside which paragraph is our reading and the room says so, and the generator refuses a plate with no sentence of ours, no rights page, or no file on disk. Nothing was cropped, tinted or filtered, and every file was re-encoded with no metadata carried over. One performer is not named on their own upload and the room does not guess. The trailer edit describes itself as an edited remix of the Jefferson Airplane recording and credits no remixer in its title, its description or on its channel, so the plate says what the upload says and says the hand is unnamed there — which is the herbarium’s refusal to guess at a binomial, applied to a credit. And the running order is the glossary page’s own, which interleaves the videos with the quotations they sit under, so it is an argument somebody made rather than a playlist to re-sort — the rule the Jungle Room keeps about its cams. Three of the seven are published by a rights holder and four are re-uploads on individuals’ channels; each plate says which, because that changes how long a link lasts, and the generator refuses a track that does not say. The room carries our own entry’s warning as well as its argument. Be wary of the holes you rabbit, and the reason: the appetite a recommendation engine farms is the same appetite, and what changes is who chose the next thing. So there is no autoplay in there, no next-up, and nothing that decides for you what comes after — seven things, all named, and nothing reaches YouTube until you press it. Nothing in that room moves at any setting, and it has no transform in it anywhere. Not a tilt, not a rotation, no flicker and no strobe; at MAX GLITTER the wash of daylight from the mouth of the hole is a little stronger and that is the whole of it. A rotation is indistinguishable from a tilt to check-gentle.py, which can only read the computed matrix, so a room with no transform in it cannot get that argument wrong — the call arcade.js and The Oracle Deck both already made. The trail’s stepping indent is a padding for the same reason. 2026-09-22 — The Zibaldone, and a quote bank that refuses to become a book

A new storefront, asked for by somebody in our community: The Zibaldone. The request was a quote bank — quotes for any state of mind and emotion, seeded by us and added to by anybody. It is built as a commonplace book, which our own glossary has had an entry for since 2022, and named for the Italian miscellany notebook: a zibaldone is a heap of things. Montaigne kept one and invented the essay out of it; the Meditations is one. A quote bank is the most dangerous shape of page this site has built, and the danger has no moment anybody could catch. Nobody decides to republish a book. They add one good line, then another, each individually reasonable, and a year later the page is the work instead of pointing at it. So tools/make-zibaldone.py refuses a quotation over thirty words, the number lives in the tool, and the room prints it — because “we quote lightly” is not something a page can promise and not enforce. Where the line is not enough, the book is linked. No song lyrics, refused structurally rather than by care. Ryan’s reply to the person who asked: song lyric reproduction is an intellectual property minefield in the US. Music publishing enforces on quotation where prose publishing shrugs, the licensing is separate from the recording, and one line is a far larger fraction of a song than of a novel. This street already says that nothing musical is hosted here, and a quote bank is exactly where that promise would have been broken in the way that looked most harmless. The first thing that check ever refused was a false positive — the word song matched Whitman’s Song of Myself — and the pattern was narrowed rather than the poem excepted, which is check-counts.py’s own first-run lesson happening for the third time. Every line names its printing, not its title, and says how it was checked and when. A title is not a source: these texts differ between printings, and a quotation nobody can trace is the thing The Doomscroll dropped a poem over. The Emily Dickinson is the proof it matters — it is in the Second Series of 1891, edited by Mabel Loomis Todd and T. W. Higginson, not the first, and the only thing that found that out was reading the title page above the poem instead of remembering it. The Thoreau is the other proof: the version everybody quotes has somebody marching to a beat, and he wrote neither word. The public domain lines were grepped out of the transcriptions each card names; the contemporary ones were read off our own published pages. A translated work has to clear the public domain twice — a trap this repository had not met before. make-doomscroll.py’s test is the author dead more than seventy years, everywhere rather than in one country; but a translation is a copyrightable work of its own, so a Roman emperor in a modern English is a modern book. The Meditations here is Meric Casaubon’s 1634, and he is credited on the card. Seneca is not in the room at all and the data file says why: our glossary quotes him on words becoming works, that wording is a modern translation the entry does not name, and the public domain one does not read that way. A gap somebody has already checked is worth more than a line nobody can place. There are no faces in that room, and that is the whole answer to “any state of mind”. The obvious build is a grid of moods you pick from, and the obvious drawing for a mood is a face — which on a Disabled people’s site is the emotion flashcard autistic people spend their childhoods being drilled with. The Playhouse settled this for its sound board and the answer is the same here: each card says what it is for in a sentence about a situation, and the tool refuses an emoji in that field. Nothing is ranked, counted or voted on either, checked with make-guild.py’s negation window so the room can still say so out loud. The quotations are set in type and only the margins are handwritten. The room varies the face per entry, which is what was asked for — EB Garamond for the oldest, Newsreader for the nineteenth century, Lora for the living — and Kalam is the hand and never carries a quotation, refused by the tool. A passage in a handwriting face is an access failure wearing atmosphere, which is the lesson The Doomscroll’s blackletter already carries one room over. The margin note on every card is ours, and the tool refuses a quotation mark in it, because margins that could hold quotations would quietly become a second uncited quote bank running down the side of the cited one. The room it could collapse into is every other paper room on this street, and the separation is that all of those are PRINTED. The Mopery is a cold building you stand up in, with type punched into the page by a press. The Doomscroll is one unbroken machine-set roll of cold grey newsprint with nothing cut and nothing rotated. The zine table is a photocopy made in a hundred copies to give away. This is one object at arm’s length, seen from above, written into by hand, and bound — there is a fold down the left of every sheet, and the fold is what makes it a book rather than a page. And where the guild is lit like a photocopy and the garden’s light has come through leaves, this is the one room lit by something in the room with you: a lamp on the left, at desk height, which is why the paper has a tooth and the fold has a shadow in it. The attribution slip is TASL plus the three fields a quotation also needs, and it sends nothing anywhere. Creative Commons’ Title, Author, Source, Licence is the right skeleton for a photograph, where the thing you point at is one file at one address; a quotation comes out of a work, in a printing, and the person copying it found it somewhere else again — and that last field is the one that catches a misquotation, because most of them are copied in good faith off something already wrong. There is no form action and no endpoint: the button writes a block of text to your clipboard and you send it however you already talk to us. Its fields are generated from the same list the cards are checked against, so the day somebody adds a field to an entry cannot be the day the form stops asking for it. A colour under the bar, and a tilt with no reset, both caught before it shipped. The pencil grey carried every citation, margin note and provenance line and measured 4.43 on a pasted leaf; check-contrast.py refuses a colour it has never seen, which is how it surfaced, and it was darkened. check-gentle.py then found all seven leaves still lying at their pasted angles at Gentle: :where() guarantees a tilt cannot be out-ranked but does not conjure a rule to outrank it, and §3’s reset names the shared tilt classes and nothing else. The room resets its own now, which is the fault that shipped on the Faery Yurt’s windowsill. 2026-09-22 — The Garden, and a palette that splits at the soil line

A gate in the wall, and a garden behind it: The Garden. Ryan’s brief. Our knowledge garden as a place you can walk: an intro to what knowledge gardening is and how this one is tended, one bed for every site we publish, the Garden Spider, and everything needed to start a garden of your own. Every bed links straight out, because each of those sites is already its own room — so it is not a door in the grid but an opening, and it is the one place on a night street where the sun is up. The roster is not in the garden’s own data file. Which sites exist, in what order, with what names and addresses, is read out of data/arrivals.json — the same list The Feed runs on, whose order is stimpunks.org’s own feeds page. So a bed cannot be invented, a site cannot be quietly left out, and re-sorting the garden would mean overruling a decision made somewhere else, which is the rule the Jungle Room keeps about its cams. data/garden.json holds nothing but our own writing about each site. The Feed is the room this one could collapse into, and both rooms list every site we run. So the division is structural rather than tonal: a board is a timetable — a title, a date, a destination and the minute it was set — and this is a planting plan: what a site is for, whose hands are in it, and nothing that changes when somebody publishes. Hence no network in tools/make-garden.py, no pull step beside it, and a refusal of dates in a bed, because that is the edit that would turn one room into the other. The drawings are told apart by FORM, which is the campground’s grammar inverted on purpose. Out in the field every pitch gets one lit colour of its own — the yurt emits, the hermitage catches, the meadow carries — and that runs out at about the fourth pitch, because there are not many kinds of light. There are as many kinds of growth as you like: a rhizome, an umbel in flower, a plant with no chlorophyll in it, a frame with seedlings under glass, a runner rooting a new plant beside itself, a dry seed head, a scramble over the path, a tendril. Each one says something true about its site, and every habit is also written out in a sentence beside its bed, because the drawings are decoration a screen reader never reaches and the habit is the argument. No bed says how much a site holds, and nothing is ranked. No glossary-term count, no sheet count, no biggest or busiest. A number like that is wrong within the week and authoritative-looking meanwhile — the fault The Feed spends a paragraph avoiding — and a garden measured by volume is an inventory. Both are refused in the generator, the ranking one with make-guild.py’s negation window so the room can still say that it does not rank anything. Green on that earth measures 1.38, and no brown can fix it. check-contrast.py put the two greens at 1.38 and 2.14 against the soil, and because they are only 1.55 apart from each other no soil colour clears 3:1 against both at once — so there was no palette fix available and the drawings changed instead. The palette splits at the soil line the way a plant does: green above it, pale below it, so every root, rhizome, mycelial thread, spilled seed and blanched shoot is drawn in the path’s own colour, which is also what a shoot looks like before it reaches the light. make-garden.py walks every coordinate of every green element and refuses one that crosses the line — broken on purpose first, with a stem pushed two pixels under and a leaf circle whose edge dipped below, and it caught both. The two rooms it could collapse into are the two other daylit ones, and the separation is physics. The Solarpunk Hermitage’s light lands on a warm plaster wall, with everything standing in front of it and the shadows falling sideways off a low sun. The Adventurer’s Guild has no light source at all, lit like a photocopy, with nothing casting anything. Here the sun is overhead and has come down through leaves: every pale surface is tinted green, and every shadow is small, hard and directly underneath the thing that made it. And the palest thing in the room is not the ground — a limewashed board is brighter than the path it lies on, where both neighbours put their panels darker than their paper. It sets no display face at all, which is the room’s one claim about type. Every other world here has something that shouts — a woodtype, a condensed grotesque, a fat slab, a blackletter, a pixel face — and a garden has no signage in it, only labels. So Faustina sets the garden’s own name and the label on every bed in the same breath, Mulish carries the notes, and the loud things in the room are the plants. Both are under the SIL Open Font License. The Garden Spider is an orb weaver and not a mascot, and its panel is careful in our own words rather than softer ones: a spider is a guide to the garden and never a replacement for it, its best answer is an entrance, it can be wrong, and every trail it puts you on ends at a page a person wrote. Those lines are from our Ask page, quoted from ourselves, with the ethics pages linked beside them and a way to reach a human instead. Every bed says whose hands are in it, on the face of the bed. Half of these sites were made with Helen Edgar of Autistic Realms; Star Stuff is a collaboration with More Realms; the Cavendish model is David Thornburg’s by way of Steve Silberman’s NeuroTribes; monotropism is Dinah Murray, Wenn Lawson and Mike Lesser’s; the pebbling locution is Amythest Schaber’s. The generator refuses a bed with nobody on it, and refuses a link inside a note that points somewhere that is neither ours nor that bed’s own site — make-hermitage.py’s rule about the Star Stuff table. The with line is the exemption, and that is the whole reason it exists. The leaf shadow is still at Gentle, drifts at Regular and drifts further at MAX. The light is never taken away, because the light is not the wobble — the campground’s own call about its grass. Both are keyframes, so §3 kills them at Gentle with !important; nothing flashes, pulses or strobes at any setting, which is Club Chronic’s rule holding in the brightest room on the street. New: data/garden.json, tools/make-garden.py, the-garden.html, §28 of love.css (Small screens and Print renumbered to §29 and §30), a gate on the street, Faustina and Mulish self-hosted, a share card whose row of labels is read off the beds, and a plant label lying on the path with a job on it.

2026-09-21 — a contrast checker that reads the page instead of the intention

check-contrast.py is a list of pairs somebody wrote down. tools/check-contrast-live.py is the page. It renders all 29 and walks every piece of text against the ground it actually sits on — what check-gentle.py already does for motion, and what nothing did for colour. It exists because the pair list was blind three times, each found by a person looking: a link colour nobody ever decided, a decided colour that lost the cascade, and three hexes that had never rendered at all. Same shape every time — the colour that renders is not the colour that was written down. It found the skip link unreadable in twenty-one rooms. .skip carries its own yellow ground and near-black ink at (0,1,0); every room sets .room-x a at (0,2,0). So the first control a keyboard user meets took each room’s link colour on a yellow box: 1.26 in the chapel, 1.10 in the arcade, 1.00 — yellow on yellow — on every plain room. Nobody had seen it because it sits off-screen until focus and nobody screenshots a focused skip link. It carries !important now, for the reason §2’s [hidden] guard does. And it found two of the Hermitage’s bean bags under the bar. The chairs take their colour inline out of data/hermitage.json; the checker had three lighter hexes in it that the page has never used, so every run passed while the magenta sat at 2.79 and the teal at 3.38 against the 4.5 their copy needs. The constants are read from the page’s own values now and the failure is written into the checker’s notes beside the Pink Pony Club’s, because which colours those chairs are is a choice about the room rather than a checker’s to make. Three dead custom properties came out of :root with it. --bag-1/2/3 were referenced by nothing — .bag reads var(--bag), singular, which only ever exists on the element. A dead declaration is not harmless when something else is checking against it, and the old checker’s own guard caught them the moment the constants were corrected. Its first run reported 314 failures and most of them were the tool’s fault, which is the point of breaking a checker before believing it. About a sixth of this site’s text stands on a linear-gradient with no background-colour under it — the Doomscroll’s newsprint, The Den’s shag — and walking up to the body reported 222 pieces of pale text as near-black on near-black. It declines rather than guesses now: a gradient in the chain makes a piece of text unmeasurable, counted and reported as such, and left to the hand-written list where those grounds are recorded with their measurements. It also unhides every [hidden] element and opens every <details> before measuring, because the bug it was written for was in a control that ships hidden. Both findings are fixed and the sweep is clean: 0 under the bar on 29 pages. The Hermitage’s magenta and teal chairs were lightened rather than re-coloured — hue and saturation untouched, all three now sitting together at 4.80 to 4.82. Taking the lighter palette the checker had been assuming would have put the teal at 7.34 and made one chair a different weight from its neighbours, in a room whose own comment says no two of them are the same colour because nobody furnishes a room like this by agreeing. The Pebble Board’s slug ink was darkened by four thousandths of lightness to clear 4.41. New: tools/check-contrast-live.py.
