Nothing is counted and nothing is deducted — the tool refuses the scoring vocabulary on every tile, because the stim box already says “nobody is counting” as a joke about counting and the joke does not survive a second toy repeating it straight. The double empathy telephone never says which account was right, because the idea it is wearing is that neither was wrong. Two handsets, one encounter, two honest reports of it; pick up both ends and the next press is a new call. Its tile is a <div> and the handsets are the buttons, since a button cannot be nested in a button and the alternative was one control pretending to be two. The off switch has no are-you-sure. It stops every sound on the page at once, closes the audio context so nothing the sound board has scheduled survives, and says so. A stop button that asks whether you meant it is not a stop button, and that room can now stack nine sound-board keys and two recorded yells with no single way out. An aria-live region does not announce text it already holds, and two of these toys exist to repeat themselves — the echo says the last thing again, the tin says the same sentence forever. Written the obvious way both are silent to the one reader who most needs them while looking perfectly correct on screen, which is a failure with no symptom for anybody watching. The region is cleared and set back on the next tick, which is what makes a repeat a change. An HTML entity is right in a blurb and wrong in a payload, and nothing in a data file shows which is which. The blurb is written into the markup as HTML; anything that becomes a data- attribute is written by the script with textContent, so “ there arrives on the page as five literal characters. The spoon drawer shipped its first draft that way. The tool refuses an entity in a payload field now. The generator caught a fill collision on its first run. The newcomer had taken .toy--violet, which the word clock has owned since the room opened, and two rules in one section would have settled it by source order in silence. That is check-classes.py’s collision arriving inside a section, where that tool deliberately does not look. The newcomer was renamed rather than out-specified. And that room had three live contrast failures nothing could see. .room-play a was yellow, which is right on the near-black boxes — and every link on the page sits either on the blue ground or inside a white card. The house-rules links measured 1.31, the quest marker’s hand-in link 3.88, on a page published since the street opened. check-contrast.py holds a pair for every colour somebody decided on, and an inherited colour was never decided, so there was nothing to hold a pair for — the exact hole the Doomscroll left, found again in an older room. The room decides at each ground it actually has now: white on the blue at 5.08, the room’s own blue on the white cards at 5.08. Every link in there was re-measured afterwards. Every toy makes a noise now, because six of them making none read as breakage. In a room where nine other things answer out loud, the quiet ones feel faulty rather than quiet — Ryan's report. Each one is its own short synthesised sound, no two alike and none alike to the sound board's keys: an echo of a blip, a line opening, one unchanging note for the safe food tin, a teaspoon against a mug, two notes down for the off switch, and a fast run for the infodump. make-toys.py refuses a toy without one. The off switch's noise comes after the silence, which is the only order that makes sense for that button, and its copy says so. And the echo plays the last sound back as well as the last words, which is Ryan's idea and makes the toy the thing its name says it is — including sounds made by the board next to it. The mechanism is that a toy's noise is a factory: called once to choose, handing back a function that plays that choice. The obvious version, calling the toy's noise again, silently advances anything that varies, so the echo of the stim box would be the next note up the scale and nothing would look wrong. Measured: two stim presses give 659 then 784, two echoes give 784 twice, and the next press resumes at 880; a recorded yell echoes as that person's yell rather than a fresh draw. Four of the new answer boxes were rendering near-black on near-black at 1.00:1, and three more between 1.28 and 1.48. .toy--orange span was written when a tile held one span; the readouts arrived later, also spans, and that rule is (0,2,0) against .toy__said at (0,1,0). Styling by element is a rule that cannot see what it will hit. The blurb has a name now and every fill rule is scoped to it. check-contrast.py passed the whole time, because it holds pairs somebody wrote down and not pairs that render — the pair was declared correctly and lost the cascade. That is the second time in a day the pair list was blind, after the inherited link colour, and both were found by a person looking at the page. The first attempt at that fix missed a tile, and so did the check on it. The rescope was a regex expecting one space before span; .toy--green span had two. The grep that verified the work carried the same assumption and reported clean. Break the check differently from the fix. And then the buttons looked broken, because the room answered somewhere nobody could see. Every press wrote into the one live region at the top of the page, which is off the screen by the time anybody has scrolled to the toys — let alone to the sound board underneath them. Ryan pressed the toys he had asked for an hour earlier and thought they were faulty. Nothing caught it because every check, ours included, was reading the box: the handler fired, the text was right, the live region updated, and the person pressing saw nothing. That is the 0×0 iframe again in a different shape — the DOM correct and the screen wrong. Every toy answers on the tile you pressed now, and the sound board in one strip under its keys, since a key is a hundred pixels wide and a sentence does not fit on one. One readout at a time, all of them aria-hidden with #playhouse-says still the only live region, and all of them shipping hidden so a page without scripts shows no empty boxes. Chairy’s blurb stopped being a hand-typed number. It said “one of twenty-eight things”, which had been right by luck since the day the sayings stopped being five; it is generated from data/chairy.json now. New: data/toys.json, tools/make-toys.py. The tool carries Chairy’s sayings and the yell button’s recordings across untouched, because a generator that silently empties another generator’s output is the _headers trap with two tools in it instead of one.
2026-09-21-sound-board
2026-09-21 — a sound board in the Playhouse, and a row of moods with no faces on it

The Playhouse has a sound board on the wall. Ryan’s brief: everything in that room is a button, so a three-by-three board of stimmy noise keys, with the bottom row holding mood keys that toggle between happy, sad and angry noises, and a different visual fanfare for each key at MAX GLITTER. A click, a pop, a rainstick, a chime, a purr and a squeak; then a hum, a spring and a drum with three moods each. The bottom row is not a feelings chart, and that is why there are no faces on it. A face is the first thing anybody sketches for a mood key, and a row of happy/sad/angry faces on a Disabled people’s site is the emotion flashcard — the thing autistic self-advocates spend their lives being drilled with. What a mood is here is the shape of a noise: a hum that lifts a third and stays up, the same hum sagging a tone and a half, two drones fourteen cents apart buzzing against each other. Each one is a word, a drawn waveform and a sound, and the room says so in its own copy rather than leaving the absence for somebody to helpfully fill in. It also says that a sad noise is a perfectly good thing to want, and that you can leave a key on angry and go and do something else. A mood key shows the mood it is about to play. Press it and you get that noise; the key then offers the next one. The face of a button should describe what pressing it does, which the alternative — naming what you just heard — does not. The flourish keeps the colour of the noise that just happened while the label has already moved on, which is why that button carries two attributes and not one. Every noise is synthesised in the browser and nothing is fetched, so the room’s own house rule stays true: it is silent when you walk in and silent if you never touch anything. Oscillators, filters and a buffer of white noise, built inside the click handler — the AudioContext cannot start without a gesture, which is the platform enforcing the promise rather than us making it. A bell is 880 and 2.76 times 880, which is the whole difference between a bell and a sine; a purr is a trill at twenty-two on the gain rather than on the pitch; a bubble goes up, which every first draft of that sound gets backwards. Every key says what it sounds like, in words, on the press. A board made of sounds is the one thing on this street that can lock somebody out completely, so the room’s live region gets the noise described rather than just its name — the Jungle Room’s rule that colour is never the only channel, in a room where the channel is audio. make-soundboard.py refuses a key without that line, and refuses two keys that claim to sound the same. Three files have to agree about every key and none of them is near the others, so the tool reads all three: the markup is in the page, the noise is a registered voice() in love.js, the colour and the flourish are rules in love.css. A key whose voice is missing is not an error anywhere — it is make-chappell.py’s typo that never becomes a video, arriving in a room where the press is the content. A key whose flourish is missing is quietly ordinary at MAX, which nobody would notice because nobody screenshots MAX. Both refuse now, along with two keys sharing a flourish, a mood key anywhere but the last row, and a mood set that is not the same three in the same order. Nothing on it is counted. No total, no streak, nothing kept between visits. A board of nine keys is exactly the shape of thing that grows a press counter, and the stim box one object over already counts its own presses as a joke about counting — a joke that does not survive being repeated by a second object with a straight face. The pebbling cabinet’s refusal of a tally, arriving a third time. Nine flourishes and no two alike, at MAX GLITTER only. Rings, bubbles, falling hairlines, a burst thrown eight ways, widening bars, darts, flat arcs off the bottom edge, a stretching coil, confetti — each clipped to its own key, so the flourish belongs to the button that made the noise. Everything moves with a translate or a scale and nothing rotates, which is arcade.js’s call and quest.js’s: rotation and skew are all check-gentle.py can read, and a checker must not be asked to take a room’s word for something. Nothing flashes and nothing strobes — Club Chronic’s rule, in the loudest room on the street. At Gentle nothing is built at all and the words are identical; measured at all three settings, along with the rendered boxes of the pieces themselves, because “the elements exist” is a question about the DOM and this was a question about paint. Red was the obvious colour for angry and it measures 3.06 on the mood keys’ near-black. Angry is orange at 8.03, sad is cyan at 10.7 and happy is yellow at 14.5. The mood ink is on the word as well as on the line, so these are body-text pairs rather than graphics ones. Seven new pairs. A media block written above the rules it overrides loses exactly the declarations the base rule also sets, and keeps the rest. A new failure shape here, and it renders as a layout nobody wrote: the phone block sat before .stimpad, so flex-flow and a font size lost to the base rule while a flex basis the base rule does not set went straight through. Half a breakpoint. It looked like a stale stylesheet and it was source order. And it is three across where there is room and one column on a phone. Held at three columns at 375px, a key gets about seventy pixels of text column and every blurb sets one word to a line. Hiding the blurbs to keep the grid would have been the lite-version mistake arriving through a breakpoint, so the grid gave way; the sentence describing the board’s shape is generated and carries its own caveat. New: data/soundboard.json, tools/make-soundboard.py.
2026-09-21-adventurers-guild
2026-09-21 — The Adventurer’s Guild, and the one tidy room

The Adventurer’s Guild has opened a shopfront on the street. Ryan’s brief: the trope with the inn and the job board, jobs ranked by difficulty class, sending people on quests across the rooms; a discreet clickable drawing in each room as the quest target; a code revealed at the target and redeemed at the board; hints; and fanfare that follows the HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? dial. The room is tidy, and that is its entire costume. On a street whose architecture is that nothing matches, somebody has come in and filed everything: manila, printer’s ink, hairline rules, ruled rows, a class in the margin, a stamp. Nothing in §26 has a gradient, a shadow, a rounded corner or a rotation in it. It is the second room you can read by daylight and it has no light source in it at all — the Hermitage has a sun in it, with a direction and shadows falling away from it; this is lit the way a photocopy of a document is lit, evenly, from nowhere. And it is the second pale ground on a dark street: the Doomscroll is one unbroken roll of foxed newsprint with nothing ruled on it, and this is made of rules. It states its own link colour, at the room, which is the hole the Doomscroll left the day before: that page declared a colour for one line and every other link fell through to the base stylesheet’s pink, at about 2.4 on paper, and the contrast checker had nothing to hold a pair for because nobody had decided anything. Every room on the street carries a marker, and no two markers are alike. A staple on the zine table, a token on the arcade carpet, a spindle adapter on the den floor, a tent peg in the field. make-guild.py holds one drawing per room and refuses a room it has no drawing for — make-og.py’s refusal, for make-og.py’s reason, because the failure mode of guessing is one shared glyph quietly appearing in every room on a street whose whole point is that the rooms share nothing. Each marker is drawn in its room’s own declared colours and every one is held against the floor it lies on at the body-text threshold, the Jungle Room’s quills rule: a marker you cannot pick out of the floor is a control you cannot use. The Playhouse lost that argument to its own floor — its yellow measures 3.88 on that blue, so the block is white at 5.08. The marker is a native <details>, and the way out of a question is another one. So the code, the hints and the “give me the answer” escape all work with JavaScript off; the scripted part is only the answer box, which ships hidden and is revealed by quest.js, so a page without scripts shows no dead control. Discreet means visually quiet and nothing else: every marker is a full-size target in the tab order with a real name on it, which is The Den’s door rule. And every marker is on the floor of its room, said out loud on the board, because scattering them at a different depth in each room would have made finding one a test of eyesight and of a mouse rather than a walk between rooms. The marker is never the play button, although the example in the brief starts from one. A facade is two elements and love-embed.js replaces the pressed <button> with a bare <div class="facade">, so anything it was wearing evaporates — the fault that shipped Swaying Sweetgrass’s players at 0×0 the day before. A play button that also does a second thing hands a popup to somebody who only wanted the song, and gating a quest behind a press would put it behind consenting to a third-party frame. So the George Jones job is a spindle adapter on the den floor and its question is what makes you read the tile: who wrote She Thinks I Still Care , which the room credits to Dickey Lee and Steve Duffy on the cut itself. Nothing is scored, and the tool refuses the vocabulary. No total, no percentage, no streak, no rank you climb, nothing that expires. A job board is exactly the shape of thing that grows a score, and a score beside a walking tour of a Disabled people’s site turns a wander into a workload — the pebbling cabinet’s refusal of a tally, in the room most likely to talk itself out of it. The difficulty class is how far you walk, enumerated in the tool and defined by geography, so it says nothing whatever about the person doing it. The first thing that tool ever refused was a false positive, and the pattern was narrowed rather than excepted. “A book it points at” is the verb, and a scoring pattern that cannot tell it from a points system is check-counts.py’s first draft refusing “no two rooms alike”. A point is only a point now when it is being awarded or counted. The fanfare follows the dial and the words never do. Gentle says its piece and adds nothing; Regular chimes; MAX chimes properly and throws sparks that rise once and fade. The sentences are identical at all three, and nothing flashes or strobes at any setting — Club Chronic’s rule. The sparks move with a translate rather than a rotation, deliberately, because rotation and skew are all check-gentle.py can read and a checker must not be asked to take a room’s word for something. A marker’s link carries its code to the board and stops there. It fills the box; the visitor still presses. That press is what the fanfare is consented by, and it is the accessible path for anybody who finds typing expensive, which is most of the reason it exists. The board holds a checksum of each code rather than a second copy, and the tool says out loud that this is a courtesy and not a lock. Every code is printed in plain text in the markup of a public page — that is the mechanism. What the checksum buys is that opening the source of the board is not a spoiler sheet for every room at once. check-quests.py reads the published HTML and never the data file. The generator writes both surfaces, so they cannot disagree the moment it runs; this is about every moment after that, when a generated line sitting in a committed file gets edited by hand. That is the frame-src shape exactly. It found a bug in itself on its first run: it sliced each marker at the next </details>, the marker’s own hints are <details>, and it reported eighteen missing escapes that were all present. It slices on the generator’s end marker now. check-classes.py caught this page wearing two of the street’s classes — pavement and masthead__dial — which is the tagline leak again, and the newcomer was renamed rather than out-specified. The guild ends in its own voice, like every other room. The marker does not print. It is a control whose whole content is a code to type into a page you cannot type into on paper, and the zine room’s one-sheet promise has been broken by a single paragraph twice. Pitch 01 got a marker and it is ours, not Helen Edgar’s. A candle stub on the Faery Yurt’s windowsill, drawn in her own declared colours, added on Ryan’s call so that her pitch is not the one room on the street with no job in it — and written into the liner notes beside the one colour of hers this repository has changed, because a change to a contributor’s room should be visible somewhere other than a diff. Helen has the final say on whether it stays. Two pages carry no marker, on purpose and by name in the tool. The changelog is a dated record and writing new furniture into a log is the same instinct as rewriting a September entry to satisfy a linter; the guild is where jobs are handed in, so a marker there would be a job that sends you to the room you are standing in. Everything else refuses to ship without one. Two faces nothing else here sets — Rye, a woodtype face for posted bills, and Public Sans, which was drawn for United States government forms, which is the room’s joke set twice. Thirty-five new contrast pairs and one measured ornament. New: data/quests.json, tools/make-guild.py, tools/check-quests.py, quest.js. love.css gains §26 and the two cross-cutting sections renumber to §27 and §28. Still to come: the bed. A guild is an inn as well as a board, and this one has no room over it yet. When it does it will be about rest as something owed rather than earned, which means it will owe a great deal to The Nap Ministry and Tricia Hersey and will say so in its own copy. The board says that out loud rather than leaving a gap.
2026-09-21-swaying-sweetgrass
2026-09-21 — Swaying Sweetgrass, and a book we are not going to serve

Swaying Sweetgrass is pitched on pitch 02, which had been open ground since the field opened. Ryan’s brief: a meadow of sweetgrass left alone, except for a natural-surface path a wheelchair can use, running to a clearing at the centre with a communal fire pit under open sky. The light is behind the grass, and that is the only thing keeping this out of a family it would otherwise join. The Faery Yurt, The Latibulum, The Den, the Hermitage’s cave and The Mopery are every one of them lit by a flame you could put your hand over. Here the sun is low, a hundred feet off and behind everything, so nothing has a lit face at all — the blades glow because the light is coming through them. That is why the greens go yellow while the ground stays dark, and it is a different warmth from tallow or varnish. There is no furniture in a meadow either; the only built things are the path and the fire ring. The fire is painted in the room’s own two golds and given no colour of its own, deliberately. A flame with an orange to itself would have made this the sixth flame-lit room on the street by the back door. Ryan’s brief pointed at 21 chapters of Braiding Sweetgrass read aloud, and they are published as doors rather than screens. The playlist is uploaded by The Anarchist Audio Library and is an unauthorised reading of a book that is in copyright — Milkweed Editions, 2013, Robin Wall Kimmerer living, publishing, and narrating the real audiobook herself. Every chapter plays and every chapter embeds, so nothing in the machinery would have stopped them going in beside the fire: love-embed.js only asks whether an id is well formed and check-jukebox.py only asks whether a video works. What stopped them is that this room’s whole argument is the honorable harvest — never take the first, never take more than you need, ask — and a page making that argument cannot serve somebody else’s entire book off its own surface while doing it. Ryan’s call once the provenance was put to him: keep both, her voice as the fire and these as a way out. make-sweetgrass.py refuses a reading marked as a screen, so the decision survives being tidied by somebody who thinks the doors look broken next to the presses. What is at the fire instead is Kimmerer in her own voice — her publisher, Bioneers, TEDxSitka, Harvard, the New York Botanical Garden, On Being, the Museum of Science, the Natural History Institute, the Commons KU — shortest first, so three minutes and an hour and a half are both a real option. Every id was resolved against YouTube on the day: status, playableInEmbed, length, title and channel, off one fetch of each watch page. That check is the only reason the two lists are two lists; the readings arrived looking exactly like the talks and the channel is what told them apart. The build refuses a talk whose channel is the readings’ channel, in either direction. The 21-strand teaching is somebody’s, and the video does not say whose. Seven generations behind, seven sacred laws, seven ahead. It was matched to its source rather than guessed at — the transcript panel was opened and read against the words, and it is Sweet Grass Teaching, published by Shawenim Abinoojii Inc., at 0:53, which was already in Ryan’s own field-guide list. The description says only “Made for Shawenim Abinoojii Inc.”, there is no name card at the end and the channel does not say, so the room credits the organisation and states plainly that the Elder is unnamed there rather than inventing a name. That is the herbarium’s refusal to guess at a binomial, applied to a person. make-sweetgrass.py counts the bundles and refuses one that is not seven — the opposite of check-counts.py’s rule and for the opposite reason: a count that belongs to somebody else is a fact to protect, not a total that goes stale. Nothing on that page teaches sweetgrass. Six teachings from Indigenous organisations, institutes and nations, Ryan’s selection, each linked and credited with one line of ours saying what it is about — and nothing anywhere instructing anybody how to harvest, braid or burn it, because that is not ours to hand out. A correction we owe is on the page rather than in a commit message. Our own glossary attributes a framework called reciprocal ethical unity to Barry Lopez and he never wrote the phrase; Star Stuff’s zine No. 72 went and read the essay. The room is quoting from the pages that carry the error, so it says so near the top instead of further down. When two of our own pages disagree, the one that checked wins. Three of the four passages were checked against the mirror and one could not be. The sheaf, the braid of stories and “becoming indigenous to a place” are verbatim on our own Nature, Place-Based Education and Offline pages. The Cajete and goldenrod-and-asters passage is on no page of ours, and archive.org’s search-inside was unreachable and Google Books rate-limited every attempt, so it is published on Ryan’s word and the liner notes say so rather than letting it sit among the checked ones looking identical. Zine No. 72’s own caveat on a fourth is still open and is recorded too. Ryan’s ten seconds of backlit bunchgrass is in there, and it is not sweetgrass. He said so when he sent it. It is already published by us on the Nature entry, underneath the line about immediate contact with the outdoors, which is exactly the argument: place-based means the ground you are standing on, not the sacred meadow somewhere else. The plant is deliberately not named to species — nobody here determined it, and a plant named on a page reads as a determination. VideoPress is the third origin this site will build a frame for, and getting it there took two goes. It was added to _headers by hand, confirmed in the file, and shipped — but that CSP line is generated by make-csp.py from a string literal of its own, so every later run put the old list back. The dev server serves no headers at all, so the room worked locally and the live site refused the frame; Ryan found it by pressing the button. The allowlist is one place now: love-embed.js’s ORIGINS array, which make-csp.py reads to build frame-src and make-sweetgrass.py reads to refuse a bad URL at build time. Both refuse outright rather than falling back to a default if the array is missing, because a silently narrowed frame-src is a room full of blank boxes and a silently widened one is a hole. Verified in a network panel: zero iframes and zero external requests on load, with eighteen presses on the page; one press produced exactly one iframe, at the right URL, with the right referrer policy, and left the other seventeen alone. The field’s sign for the pitch needed a light of its own, because the two on that board are taken. The yurt emits and the hermitage catches, so this one is carried: fireflies low in the grass, many small lights and no source you could point at, with the path going in and a thread of smoke where the clearing is. The fire is not drawn lit, because from the treeline the grass is taller than the clearing and what you can see from there is what gets drawn. Two name collisions, one of them caught by a tool and one by six sudden failures. check-classes.py refuses a custom property declared twice; and an unprefixed GLOW in check-contrast.py’s own Python silently repainted the Faery Yurt’s ember composite, turning six of Helen’s pairs red in a room nobody had touched. That is the --leaf collision arriving in a second file. The newcomer was renamed, scoped to its own block. Two layout faults the room’s own argument caught. The rule under each recording sat wherever its text happened to stop, so a row of two had its ground at two heights — in a room whose stated structure is that things stand on a line. Same for the three bundles of the braid. Both now fill their row and push the press to the foot. Two faults in one press, found by Ryan pressing a button. A facade is two elements — a <button> before the press and a <div> after it — and love-embed.js gives the replacement only the class facade, so anything the button was wearing evaporates. The portrait clip came out landscape and letterboxed; worse, the fire’s players rendered at 0×0 while the sound played, because align-items: flex-start on that column stopped the div stretching and the iframe inside it is absolutely positioned, so it contributes no size. The column defaults to stretch now and only the button opts out, and the portrait box is scoped from its container the way the Pebble Board already did it. Both had passed a check that confirmed one press produced one iframe at the right URL — which is a question about the DOM, where this was a question about paint. The rendered boxes are measured now: 16/9, 16/9 and 9/16. Two faces nothing else here sets — Eczar, whose serifs flare like a blade opening, and Alegreya Sans, a sans with a handwriting skeleton still in it. Sixteen new contrast pairs and two measured ornaments. New: data/sweetgrass.json, tools/make-sweetgrass.py. The room joins check-jukebox.py’s lists in the same commit that opens it. love.css gains §25 and the two cross-cutting sections renumber to §26 and §27.
2026-09-21-the-mopery
2026-09-21 — The Mopery, and a facsimile this site is not going to copy

The Mopery is open — a dark academia library, reading room and parlour, with two rooms behind it. Ryan’s brief: goth, brooding, vampire librarian, used book shop, moon phases, eldritch tomes. It is the first COLD enclosed room on this street, and that is the whole reason it can stand beside the other four. The Faery Yurt, The Latibulum, The Den and the Hermitage’s cave are each lit by one warm source and the light reaches the walls — canvas, plaster, panelling and curtain all go amber. This room has candles the whole way along every top shelf and the walls stay blue-black stone, because that is what a candle actually does: it lights about a foot of a very large room. Cosy is what those rooms are. This is what it is like to be let into a building after everybody has gone home. The type is the other half of it. IM Fell English is a face that was punched — Fell’s Oxford types with the ink spread and the battered counters left in — against the yurt’s Cormorant, which is high-contrast, clean and cut yesterday. Two warm serif rooms kept apart at the stroke rather than at the palette, which is the only place it holds. One scan is shown and one is pointed at, and the difference is a single line of metadata. The reading nook was meant to show a scanned page beside the text. The Library of Congress’s facsimile of The Raven in Poe’s own hand is the obvious candidate and it carries “reproduction prohibited without permission” along the foot of its own first leaf — that printing was made in 1949 for an exhibition at Yale, and loc.gov answers a script with a bot check rather than with its rights statement, so the notice is the only rights information anybody here had actually read. Copying it onto a CC BY-SA site would be relicensing somebody else’s asset under a licence it may not carry, which is the Penguin Pebbling problem with a different deck. Ryan then found one that says the opposite in as many words: an 1865 Tyndale & Mitchell printing, illustrations engraved on wood by Scattergood, digitised by Lehigh University and published by the Internet Archive under the Public Domain Mark 1.0. Three leaves of it are in the room and the whole book is linked. The facsimile is still linked and still not copied, and the nook says which is which and why. All twenty-six of Gustave Doré’s engravings are in the poem, from the 1884 edition by way of Project Gutenberg’s ebook #17192. Doré died in 1883, so they are out of copyright everywhere — the same test the Doomscroll applies to its poets. Ryan asked for them. Where each plate sits is our decision and the page says so. That edition printed the poem straight through and put the plates after it, each captioned with the lines it illustrates. Here every plate stands at the lines its own caption quotes, which is a reading decision rather than a reproduction of the 1884 layout — so the room states it rather than letting anybody assume they are looking at that book. And the captions caught a textual difference nobody was looking for. 2026-09-21-pebble-board
2026-09-21 — a noticeboard that is not a shopfront, and a rule that failed the person it was written for

The Pebble Board is street furniture, not a storefront. A room on this street is permanent and singular; a board is defined by being replaced, edition after edition, with the old ones kept. A shop whose entire stock is swapped out every gathering is a periodical, and giving it a shopfront would quietly have made every other shopfront look temporary. So it stands on the pavement outside the shops, in the same category as the signpost to the campgrounds. Your Room also already holds the one community storefront, and that one means something exact: one person decorates one room. The frame is constant and the paper is not — the second place on this street where two pages are meant to resemble each other, and the second is not a licence for a third. A noticeboard, like the Arcade’s cabinets, is one body with different things behind the glass. Each edition still gets its own share card, because the card is where the shortcut would be invisible. The first edition is Norah Hobbs’s, collected at a gathering on 2026-06-25 and built by her in the block editor before being rebuilt as a page. The cream, the tape, the tabbed drawers and the wording are hers. Twenty-one hotlinked thumbnails became twenty local files, and the security header did not move. Cached at build time instead. Verified in a network panel: every request on load is same-origin, and one press produced exactly one iframe at the right id with eighteen buttons untouched. Two of the twenty-one videos were not what the board thought they were, which is the argument for resolving ids rather than trusting them. OK Go’s “And the Adjacent Possible” had gone private since the gathering; the entry is kept in the data with what was measured, the way the Jungle Room keeps its dead cams. NEONI’s “Carry On Wayward Son” plays and refuses to embed, so it is a door dressed as a door rather than a play triangle that cannot play. Four images came off and their cards stayed on. A screenshot of the City of Austin’s Facebook post wrapped around a crowd of about forty identifiable strangers at a Pride event; a screenshot of an Instagram story carrying somebody’s phone status bar; a foundation’s product render credited as a photograph of two people wearing it. Two widely-reproduced memes were dropped for having no attributable source. The stories are all still there, in our own words, which is what the cards were carrying anyway. No total. The board arrived saying how many things had been collected. check-counts.py would have refused a typed one and a generated one would have passed — and still been wrong, because the pebbling cabinet refuses a tally on the grounds that pebbling is explicitly not about volume. Same practice, no game in the room, same answer. A lightbox, because a watercolour spread at 250px is not a watercolour spread. A native <dialog>, so the focus trap, the inert background and the return of focus are the browser’s rather than ours. The description is shown as words under the picture rather than only announced, so it reaches everybody. Escape is handled explicitly anyway: with the lightbox open and focus inside it, a real Escape keydown arrived undefended and the dialog stayed open. That may be an artifact of the browser it was tested in — but a modal a keyboard user cannot leave is not a thing to take on trust, and the fix is four lines. A rule was rewritten because it failed the person it was written to protect. This site said flatly that it does not publish photographs of children, reasoning that a parent can consent but the child cannot take it back in ten years. That reasoning was sound and aimed at the wrong case: it read as a ban on a teenage volunteer consenting for herself, and would have taken her own activity off the board while leaving the two adults standing beside her on it — which is what nothing about us without us exists to refuse, and that motto has no lower age bound. 2026-09-21-club-chronic
2026-09-21 — Club Chronic, and the room that refuses the one effect it obviously wants

Club Chronic is open. Freaks to the front: punk music and punk community, the story of scenes that built their own doors, every playlist we keep pasted up by the entrance, and a rack of records along the back wall. Ryan’s brief. It does not strobe, at any setting, and the room says so on the door. A punk club has exactly one obvious ambient effect and it can cause seizures. That looks like the campgrounds’ rule and is a different rule — the field is still because quiet is what it is for, and this room is still because the obvious idea here hurts people. A room whose whole argument is come in as you are cannot have a light in it that puts somebody on the floor. MAX GLITTER buys nothing in here and the copy says that is on purpose rather than unfinished. And it says out loud that a loud room is itself an access barrier. Volume, crowds, no exit, no quiet room, no seat — for a lot of us the gig this room is about is unsurvivable. A scene that lets anybody in and then builds the only entrance out of volume has not finished the job. The honest thing about this being a page is that you can leave mid-song and nobody notices. The zine table is the room this could have collapsed into, and the split is structural. Both are punk, both are photocopied, both are made of paper. But the zine is one sheet you hold, cut up with scissors and scattered at angles, and the page is the paper. 2026-09-20-hidden-attribute
2026-09-20 — the set said it was off while it was on, and the stylesheet was the one lying

Ryan found the television reporting the wrong thing about itself. A column of text beside the running video announcing THE SET IS OFF, overflowing its own box, and sometimes naming a different programme from the one playing. Three symptoms, and underneath them one bug and a half. The bug: [hidden] loses. The browser’s own rule for the hidden attribute is [hidden] { display: none } at specificity (0,1,0) — which any ordinary class rule that sets display ties with and then wins, because it comes later in the file. So offPanel.hidden = true did nothing visible. The script was correct and the stylesheet was overruling it, silently. The panel had never once been hidden. It was the third time in one room, which is the actual finding. The way-out link had it, the play button had it, and both were patched one selector at a time — which is exactly how the whole off panel was left still waiting to be found. The guard is in §2 now, for everything on the street, and the per-component patches are gone: doing it per component is what hid the third one. And the half: the panel was only ever written on the path that does not play. Retuning while the set was on built a new player and left the panel holding whatever had been tuned the last time it was off — so the stale text Ryan saw was not a rendering artefact, it was a real second bug wearing the first one’s clothes. What the panel says is derived from the tuned channel on both paths now. A panel that is only correct on one of two paths is a panel that will be found wrong. The overflow was real too, and the fix is that 16:9 is a floor rather than a ratio. A channel title runs to a hundred characters; at phone width that is four lines, and with the runtime and the button under it the panel wanted 215px inside a 152px screen — putting the one control that matters below the bottom of the set. Scrolling inside a television to find the play button is not a fix. The screen is a grid now whose row takes the height of the tallest thing in it, so the set is exactly 16:9 on every channel at normal widths and grows only on a phone, where 16:9 would be too small for the card to fit in. Nothing is truncated and nothing is unreachable, which matters more than a set that never moves. The runtime and the play button moved onto one line, because they are one sentence — how long it runs, and the control that starts it — and because it saves the set a whole row of height where the room is tightest.

2026-09-20-watering-hole
2026-09-20 — three benches in the Hermitage, and a check that stopped guessing at Latin

The watering hole is open, which finishes the room. Three tables pushed together under the long window: a herbarium, a solar bench, and a table of Star Stuff. A watering hole is where you learn from the people next to you, so nothing on these benches is a lesson — it is somebody else’s work left out where you can pick it up. One room, three postures, and that is what keeps the three zones apart. The cave is enclosed, round-cornered and dark and you are sitting in it. The campfire is seated too, and its cards are rounded because a bean bag has no corners. The workshop is flat-topped and square — worktops with a lip at the front, things laid out on them, and you are standing up. Every specimen in the herbarium is there because one of our own pages argues from it, and make-hermitage.py refuses one that is not. Dandelion, tulip and orchid off the sensitivity metaphor; a bamboo rhizome for Helen Edgar’s Autistic Rhizome; a fern frond because it is the picture our glossary reaches for to explain a fractal; moss, lichen, mycelium and an envelope with nothing in it, off four Star Stuff pieces. Nothing in it is named to species, and the check that enforces that had to be thrown away and rewritten. A Latin binomial typed from memory is a taxonomic claim nobody checked, wearing the one kind of authority a herbarium sheet has. The first version looked for Latin endings — and missed Taraxacum officinale, the single most likely binomial to end up on this table, then missed two more after two rounds of widening, while every widening walked it closer to firing on ordinary prose. A tripwire that is allowed to miss and at risk of crying wolf is the worst of both. So the shape is the check now and the English words are the allowlist: a name of one capitalised word and one lowercase word is refused unless the second word is one this table has declared. That catches every binomial rather than the ones somebody anticipated, and it costs one word added on purpose when a plain name like fern frond arrives. And the Faery Yurt’s tagline had been quietly taking display: flex and a 940px max-width from the street’s masthead since the room shipped. That one is a class name and not a design decision, so it is .yurt-tagline now; nothing of Helen’s moved, and the room renders pixel for pixel as it did. The share card is two grounds. Earth at the top with the lamp on it and the round door drawn on it, a band of lit plaster along the foot carrying dark type. That inversion is the room rather than a flourish, and a card that left it out would be advertising a different room. New contrast pairs for both halves; the brass moved from #C28F3C to #E3BB6A because a knob measured 1.93 against the lightest of the three woods behind it — a knob you could not see on the cabinet it is screwed to. The burrow’s two facades are in check-jukebox.py. A room with two of them is exactly the size at which somebody decides a list is not worth adding to a checker, and a dead station in a room built for people who are already flat is the worst place on this street to find rot.
2026-09-20-penguin-pebbling
2026-09-20 — a pebbling cabinet, and the licence that decided what it could be

Penguin Pebbling is in the Arcade. A shore, pebbles on it, three neighbours with nests. Walk into something to pick it up, carry it over, press GIVE. Every gift is taken and every one gets something different said back, because giving is how you find out who somebody is rather than a lock to pick. The first thing to say is that there is already a Penguin Pebbling game, and this is not it. Penguin Pebbling is thirty cards across all five locutions, by Helen Edgar and Ryan Boren, 2026, with Helen’s artwork. Go and play that one. The cabinet takes nothing from it — no cards, no prompts, no artwork, no five-locution structure. And the reason is a licence rather than modesty, which is worth writing down because it nearly was not noticed. The deck is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. This site is CC BY-SA 4.0, with no non-commercial clause. An adaptation would have dragged NC onto a page that cannot carry it; share-alike means it could not be quietly absorbed; and relicensing is not ours alone to do, because half the authorship and all the artwork are Helen’s. So the cabinet is built on the locution — coined by Amythest Schaber (Neurowonderful), documented by Stimpunks in 2022, written up by Helen at Autistic Realms in 2023 — which belongs to the community. Two of our own things with two different licences is exactly the case attribution exists for, and it is the first time on this site that a licence has changed what a page is rather than what it says at the bottom. It refuses a count, and that is the locution rather than a difficulty setting. No tally of what you gave, no total, no streak, nothing at the end. The neighbours bring you things on their own clock whether or not you have ever given them anything — built as a timer rather than as a reward, because a gift that arrives because you gave first is a trade. A number beside a practice that is explicitly not about volume would quietly make it about volume. The pale screen is the only one on the street, and the contrast work is why the pebbles have shapes. Everything on a shingle beach is a mid-tone including the shingle, so nothing on this screen is carried by its fill: every pebble, penguin and nest is drawn with the same dark outline, and check-contrast.py measures that outline against the three grounds and then each fill against the outline. That is the honest reading of WCAG 1.4.11, which asks about adjacent colours rather than about a fill against a distant background. But holding the fills to 4.5 against the outline squeezes them all light — and a narrow band of light tones is a narrow band of things nobody can tell apart. So the six things you can carry are six different shapes: a round pebble, a smooth one, a shard of sea glass, a speckled stone, a feather, a broken shell. Shape carries it, and the name said out loud on every pick-up carries it again. Thirteen new pairs, 195 in the file, none failing. The card inverts too, and had to. Gold on a pale sky measures 1.9, so the type is dark on light — the only share card on this street that is. It was decided by a measurement rather than chosen. A duplicate id, and a bug that would have been much worse anywhere else. The penguin’s drawing sits in the page’s <defs> as #peng and the player’s sprite was also id="peng", so getElementById returned the definition and the game threw on the first line of start(). It took thirty seconds to find because pressing START does something visible. The same mistake in markup nobody presses would have sat there, which is why the other cabinets’ cloned sprites were built out of <use> against one definition in the first place. All four arcade pages were swept; no others. So there is a checker for that now, and it immediately found a worse one. check-ids.py refuses a page that uses an id twice, and refuses a script that asks by name for an id no page loading it has. Run against the whole site it turned up seven elements sharing id="yurt-says" in the Faery Yurt — make-yurt-sound.py had been emitting a live region inside every sound tile, so six of them were dead markup that had never received a word, and love.js only ever reached the first. It had been live since the regulation nook shipped and nothing had said so, because a duplicate in markup nobody presses does not announce itself. The generator emits one shared region now. Broken on purpose with both real bugs put back; it named both. Two things found by looking at the screen rather than by any check. Every penguin was the same size on the same line, so there was no telling which one you were steering — the neighbours are drawn smaller and staggered up the beach now, and you are the one in front. And the nests were single filled ellipses that read as puddles the penguins were standing in; a nest is a rim with a hollow, which is also what the animal actually builds. And an honest note about the penguins, on the page. Adélie and gentoo penguins do build nests of stones, carry them about, and steal them from each other. The tidy romance — one penguin choosing the perfect pebble for its beloved — is the popular retelling rather than the finding. The locution is named after the image and is not weakened by that. A metaphor does not have to be a finding. There is no stealing in the cabinet, because the game is about the locution and not about penguins.
2026-09-20-otterly-adorbs
2026-09-20 — a second cabinet in the Arcade, in which floating gets you nothing

Otterly Adorbs. You steer an otter round a kelp bay. It twirls, somersaults, dives and floats on its back; three other otters keep their own rhythms; fish come through at feeding time and go again. Ryan’s proposal, and the name is his. It turned out not to be a blank sheet, which changed the design. The Stimpunks Solidarity Session has been leaving an otter cam running every Saturday for months — cameras on or off, some speaking, some in text, nobody has to watch. Helen Edgar wrote down what that was doing for her in Stimpunks Solidarity and Otters, and Star Stuff built The Stone You Keep (No. 58) on top of it, sourced to the primary literature. So the cabinet is built out of findings rather than out of charm, and otterly.js names the paper beside each one. Floating fills nothing up, and that is the single sharpest constraint in the build. No meter, no stamina, no bonus afterwards — the cabinet says so out loud the first time you roll over. Zine No. 58 refuses rest so you can produce in as many words: the otter is not recharging in order to forage better tomorrow. The friendly version of this game rewards resting, and the friendly version would have put a sentence on this page that another of our pages spends a spread refusing. It is written into CLAUDE.md so the next well-meant improvement gets stopped. A clam takes between 6 and 88 presses, and those are the real numbers. Two observers at Point Lobos in 1964 watched thirty instances over six days: a mussel took a mean of 35.5 blows, range 6 to 88 (Hall & Schaller). The game rolls in that range unrounded and reports your number with no target beside it. The urchin opens in a couple of goes and a stone does not help with it, which is Law et al. 2024 — some otters never carry one, because they are on the prey that does not need one, and the ones who do carry one keep their teeth. Nothing ranks the other three otters. Under food limitation a real population does not converge on one best way to be an otter; it fans out into specialists, each measurably better at its own thing (Tinker, Bentall & Estes, 2008). One of ours mostly floats, one mostly dives, one mostly turns in circles, and there is no scoreboard for any of it. The kelp does the holding. Float in the fronds and you stay where you are; float in open water and you drift. That is co-regulation stated as physics rather than as a metaphor, and it is the one mechanic that is also the reason the Saturday session works. It follows the zine’s correction rather than our own changelog. stimpunks.org’s week-28 entry describes the otter keeping “a favorite stone tucked in a pouch of skin” and returning to it “again and again”. No. 58 went to the primary and found the lifelong favourite rock in an armpit pouch is a popular retelling; what Hall & Schaller support is a stone kept and reused across successive food items within a bout of feeding. The game does the second thing. When two of our own pages disagree, the one that checked wins. A twirl is drawn frames, not a rotation, and that cost real work. Rotating the sprite would have been three lines — and would have made the room’s own comment false, because check-gentle.py reads rotation out of the computed matrix and this room says in its stylesheet that there is nothing there to read. So the otter has five drawn poses and a trick is a run through them. The angled poses are rotated, inside their own <svg>, where a transform is part of the picture the way a path’s d is. Frame-swapping is also what an actual cabinet did. The contrast checker found the seabed. It measured 1.10 against the water above it — invisible — and lightening the floor until it cleared 3:1 started swallowing the cobbles and the urchin that sit on it, which are the things a player reaches for. So the boundary is carried by a line instead, at 8.44 on the water and 9.25 on the bed. The information is “here is the floor”, and a line carries it perfectly well. Nineteen new pairs; 182 in the file, none failing. Buoyancy was winning an argument the player was trying to have with a clam. An otter is buoyant, so doing nothing takes you up — at the first setting that was about eight per cent of the bay a second, and it pulled you off the bed before you could pick a stone up. It is a quarter of that now, and it stops entirely while you are working on a shell, because an otter cracking something is holding itself there. Then the room split, and the share card is what decided it. Both games lived on one page for about an hour. Which meant a link to the otter game unfurled as a picture of a porcupine — the exact fault make-og.py exists to refuse, being committed by a room against its own second game. The Arcade is a foyer now, with the cabinets standing in it under lit marquees, and Quill Drift and Otterly Adorbs are pages with a machine on each. Three cards where there was one, and the two new ones are the screens: a flat dark field with Esmx and loose quills, and a kelp bay with an otter on its back. Those three pages share a carpet, a marquee, a cabinet build and a pixel face, and that is correct here. On this street that normally reads as the tidying instinct winning, so it is written into CLAUDE.md before somebody either “fixes” the similarity or cites it as licence to harmonise actual rooms. An arcade is precisely a room whose machines share a body and differ behind the glass. The worlds here are the screens, and a dark field and a kelp bay have nothing to do with each other. The chrome moved to a .arcade class so that the thing which styles and the thing which unfurls are never the same word — each page carries exactly one class make-og.py has a card for, and no ordering inside a class attribute decides anything. Each cabinet carries its own panels, its own refusals and its own credits. A single shared sidebar stopped working the moment there were two machines: a readout headed YOUR ESMX floating above an otter game is furniture belonging to nobody. The foyer keeps only what is true of every machine in the room — no timer, nothing chasing you, no sound, no memory, nothing moving until you press start. check-counts.py gained cabinets and games while this shipped and immediately refused two sentences calling one of them “the second cabinet”.
2026-09-20-stop-counting
2026-09-20 — the street stops saying how many rooms it has, and a checker to keep it that way

Ryan’s call: the number of storefronts is going to grow well past anything worth writing down, so nothing here states a total any more. Not the pages, not the stylesheet’s comments, not a generator’s published strings, not the docs. The street’s own description, its share card, llms.txt, the feed’s description, the liner notes, the campground’s lede and the empty storefront’s opening line all say something that stays true however many there are — no two rooms alike, one card per room, a row of shopfronts, a storefront with nothing in it. The change that opened the Arcade is the argument for this, and it is not a flattering one. That commit carefully updated the room count in twelve places — and shipped three sentences still carrying the old one. love.css went on describing the doors and the shopfronts by a number that had stopped being true the moment the seventh one landed, and CLAUDE.md went on giving the number of share-card designs as one fewer than existed. All three were written by the same session that was updating the other twelve, and nothing caught them, because nothing was looking. A total is a fact about the whole site that gets written in a dozen places and updated in one. So check-counts.py refuses a number or an ordinal sitting in front of a thing that grows when a storefront opens — rooms, storefronts, shopfronts, doors, worlds, card designs. It is deliberately small. The jukebox’s tracks and The Chappell’s are real counts of real data, generated from files holding exactly that many, and it leaves them alone. It starts at four, because the first draft refused its own fix. Written to catch any number from two upwards, the very first thing it flagged was “no two rooms alike” — the count-free phrasing this whole change exists to encourage — along with “two rooms turned out to be putting text on a background nobody had measured”, which is a finding rather than a claim about the size of the street. Below four, a number in front of these nouns is nearly always counting instances. A street’s total will be four and rising. Quoted text is skipped in prose and not in code, and the asymmetry is the point. A page or a doc has to be able to say what it corrected, so a count inside quotation marks there is evidence rather than a claim. In a generator every quoted string is a candidate for publication — make-og.py writes its card footers out of string literals — so there is no safe quotation, and the checker’s own docstring therefore describes the three stale counts rather than quoting them. It is the one place where a tool’s prose has to obey the rule it enforces. The first version scanned line by line and refused itself, because the quotation it makes its argument out of wrapped across two. Broken on purpose in all three shapes that actually shipped — a page’s prose (“the seventh storefront”), a stylesheet comment (“the six doors”) and a generator’s docstring (“eleven card designs”) — and it named all three with their file and line. Then the working tree was put back. One count it missed on the way, which is why it grew a word. The Arcade’s own source said the room “shares nothing with the six next door”, and the first rule sailed past it because next was not in the short list of words allowed to sit between a number and its noun. It is in the list now, and the sentence says the rooms next door. The share card changed with the street. Its footer read ONE STREET · SEVEN ROOMS · A FIELD PAST THE TREELINE and now reads NO TWO ROOMS ALIKE, which is the better line anyway: the count was never the interesting claim, and the thing it was standing in for is the one this site is actually about. The room numbers on the doors stay. room 04, room 05, ROOM 07 are addresses, and a house number has never told anybody how long the street is.
2026-09-20-second-yell
2026-09-20 — the second yell, and a duration that lies about itself

The yell button has two voices in it. The Playhouse holds a yell from Enigma, lent on 2026-09-20 — the first on that button from somebody other than the person who built the room. It is published under the name it came with, the room says whose yell it was out loud on the press, and it is credited in the liner notes as well. It carries no onward licence, unlike everything else here: CC BY-SA cannot be revoked, and a voice somebody lends us has to be one they can take back. Two tools refused it on arrival, which is what they are for. The file sat in audio/yells/ with no entry in data/yells.json, so make-yells.py stopped — a yell with nobody’s name on it is the one thing it cannot publish — and make-yurt-sound.py’s sweep of every audio file in the repo stopped on the metadata: com.apple, Core Media, and a creation timestamp to the second. Neither tool strips anything, and that is deliberate: what to do with somebody’s recording is theirs to decide, not a script’s. It was stripped once there was a decision to strip it. And the obvious way to check that strip is misleading. The instruction in both docstrings is to compare the duration before and after, because -c copy re-muxes rather than re-encodes. It went from 4.160s to 4.096s — 64 milliseconds apparently gone, which reads exactly like a bad edit. It is not. -map_metadata -1 drops the iTunSMPB tag, which is the container’s declaration of encoder padding, and the start offset went 0.044 to 0.000 with it. Decoding both files to raw PCM gives 196,608 samples each, identical at every one of them, same peak. The audio is untouched; the 64ms was never audio. Written down here because the check the tools recommend will keep producing that number, and the next person to run it should not go looking for what they cut off. The house rule rewrote itself, which is the whole reason it is generated. The Playhouse now says the button holds “2 recorded yells” rather than one. A claim a page makes about itself should not depend on somebody remembering to edit it. Verified in the network panel afterwards: zero requests to audio/ on load, one per press, and both names reached the live region.
2026-09-20 — a seventh storefront, with one cabinet in it

The street has an arcade on it. The Arcade is room seven, sixth door in the row, and it holds one game: Quill Drift, starring Esmx the Porkypine. Loose quills drift across a dark field, Esmx walks, and a quill joins the mane on contact and only on contact. No timer, no lives, no score, no streak, nothing chasing anybody and no way to lose a quill once it is in. The one rule is the mechanic, not a note at the bottom of it. A porcupine cannot shoot a quill — cannot throw, fire or launch one; it comes away in whatever touched it, and an attacker has to come to the animal. That is card No. 3 of the Quillery, sourced there to Uldis Roze. A spiky mascot invites precisely the opposite reading, so the game has no verb for it: there is nothing to aim, nothing to press but a direction, and nothing on the field but Esmx and the quills. “Non-violent” was the brief; refusing the one verb everybody expects is what it turned into. The point of the game is a variant, which is what the licence asks for. Twelve quills fill the mane, and what you are left with is a mane in an order nobody else walked into — written out in words beside the cabinet as well as drawn on the sprite, because a mane nobody can read is a mane nobody can tell anybody about. Esmx’s own page does not merely permit this: feel free to customise! Make variants of Esmx to represent your community. A correction, caught by Ryan mid-build and worth the space. The room shipped its first draft calling Esmx “our mascot and not ours”, and borrowed the framing from the Quillery, which says Kaya Oldaker’s artwork “is not ours to redraw stroke for stroke”. That is wrong about the facts. Stimpunks commissioned Esmx and holds the IP; Kaya is the artist. The credit line stays on every surface it was on — in the room, in the liner notes and in the drawing’s own markup — because holding the rights to a commission is not a reason to stop naming the hand that drew it, which is a different and better sentence than the one that was there. Attribution here is a courtesy as well as a licence, and it turns out the courtesy is the half that was doing the work. Esmx is drawn again rather than pasted in, and not because anybody needed permission. The originals are a download away and ours to use. A PNG would have been the only thing in the arcade that came from somewhere else, in a room whose whole argument is that it shares nothing with the six next door — and taking our own invitation seemed like the least we could do with it. The marks that make Esmx Esmx are kept: the pig snout, the earring in one ear, the chunk out of the other, and a mane that comes apart at the tips. An arcade in particular, because the mascot already came from one. Kaya’s notes say Esmx resembles a Sonic character or a Pokémon on purpose, due to their popularity within the Autistic community. Nothing of either is used here. The room is not a costume put on the mascot; it is where the mascot came from. The dial and the speed knob are two controls, on purpose. The dial governs the room — the cabinet glow, the marquee bulbs — and the game’s speed belongs to the player. The dial picks the knob’s starting position, Slow if you arrived on Gentle, and then stops having an opinion; all three speeds are offered at every dial setting. Tying the game to the dial would have made Gentle a different game, which is the “lite version” mistake with a joystick on it. And nothing on the playfield moves until a coin goes in — the jukebox’s consent model in a different costume, and the reason a room with a game in it does not make the dial lie. Motion the visitor started is not ambient motion. The cabinet also makes no sound at all, ever, at any setting; an arcade that is silent by choice seemed better than one that is silent until it isn’t. Everything moves with left/top, and that is a decision about the checker rather than about performance. Rotation and skew are what check-gentle.py reads out of the computed matrix, and a room that put its game behind a transform would be asking that tool to take the room’s word for something. There is nothing to take on trust if there is no transform to read. The two that are there are the sprite’s centring translate and a scaleX(-1) when Esmx turns round — both of which the tool already reads as layout, and both of which it can see. Broken on purpose with an unreset rotate(-2deg) on the cabinet marquee: it named p.cab-marquee and the matrix it found. 192 elements in the room, measured at all three settings, none tilting. Thirty-six new contrast pairs, two of them against grounds nobody chose. #0F1F24 is what the screen becomes under its scanline stripe and is the lighter of the two grounds the playfield makes, so it is the one that decides; #2D1C25 is the carpet under the cabinet’s own glow, where the headline and the eyebrow sit. The eight quills are in the list too — WCAG 1.4.3 does not reach a graphic, but a quill you cannot pick out of the background is a control you cannot use, and they are held to the body threshold rather than the 3:1 one so that nobody has to remember later which bar applied. Each quill also has a name, said out loud on contact, because colour is never the only channel here. 162 pairs, none failing; broken on purpose by dimming one grey, and the composite ground failed harder than the flat one, which is the whole argument for having both in the file. make-og.py refused the room until it had a card, which is exactly what it is for — the eleventh design, and the one that is mostly a drawing, because this is the only room whose subject is a character rather than an argument and a poster for a game showing nobody playing it would be a poster for the wrong thing. Esmx and the marquee bulbs are lifted out of the page rather than retyped, alongside the campground’s stream and the yurt’s crown, so the card cannot come to disagree with the room. The mane on it is the markup’s own default rainbow; the game only ever overwrites those twelve fills with what a player actually caught. Press Start 2P is the eighteenth family and the only face in the room. A pixel face is the one thing no other room on this street could have borrowed without turning into the arcade. 4.7KB, latin only, self-hosted like the other seventeen — verified in the network panel: every byte on the page comes from this origin, and the cabinet fetches nothing when you press anything, because there is nothing to fetch. Playtested, and the first build was over before its own instructions were. Six quills on the field at a reach of 7.5 filled a twelve-quill mane in about ten seconds. Dropping to five at 6.2 went too far the other way — a full lap of the field turned up one quill and the game went slack. Six at 7.0 fills a mane in something under a minute of walking, measured over a sixteen-leg random walk rather than guessed. “Six rooms” was written down in twelve places — the street’s description and its card alt, llms.txt, love.css’s own header, the liner notes, the campground’s lede, the feed’s description and the street card’s footer. It is seven now, and Your Room is the seventh storefront rather than the sixth. The derived files are derived, so make-sitemap.py and make-feed.py carried their own copies of the sentence and had to be edited at the source rather than in the output. The pad takes a press-and-hold or a single click, because a control that only works while a button is held down is not a control for somebody driving it with a switch or a screen reader. The arrow keys are bound to the playfield rather than to the document — arrow keys that stop the page scrolling from anywhere on it would be a trap — and Escape hands them back.
2026-09-20-check-gentle
2026-09-20 — a checker for the dial, and the windowsill it caught

The dial had nothing watching it. check-gentle.py loads all fourteen pages in headless Chrome, sets the intensity to Gentle, Regular and MAX GLITTER in turn, and reads what actually moves out of 2,253 computed styles — rather than reading the stylesheet and believing it. The global half was always safe: animation and transition are killed at Gentle with !important, and nothing out-shouts that by accident. The tilts were never safe. Every room sets its own rotations and resets them room by room, unprefixed, so a reset is one selector away from being outranked — and CSS does not warn when that happens. It applies the winner and says nothing. It found the Faery Yurt’s windowsill on its first run. A book at rotate(-3deg) and a pen at rotate(24deg), both still tilted for anybody who had asked the wobble to stop, because that room shipped without a single Gentle rule in it. Twenty-four degrees is not subtle. The room was a day old and two people had read it. The sill keeps its angles at Regular and MAX — they are Helen’s and they stay; the reset is the dial, which is our plumbing and applies to every room on the street. Rotation and skew are the wobble; a mirror and a translate are not. The tool reads the off-diagonal terms of the computed matrix, which are non-zero for exactly those two and nothing else, so a vine flipped with scaleX(-1) and a positioned layer pass without needing an exception. Transforms inside an <svg> are excluded on purpose: a transform on a <g> is part of the drawing, the same kind of thing as a path’s d, and flattening one would produce a broken picture rather than a calmer page. It checks the other half of the sentence too. “Never the words” means the visible text of a page has to be identical at Gentle and at Regular. It is, on all fourteen — which is the moment to write the check, rather than after somebody has a paragraph they would rather drop at the quiet setting. Broken on purpose three times before being believed, because a checker that has only ever passed is a checker nobody has tested. Restoring the near-miss on Enid’s wall — the tilt selector written one level too specific — and it names figure.polaroid. Hiding a .scrawl at Gentle and it reports the pages whose word count drops. Leaving an !important animation running and it names the element. Then the working tree was put back.
2026-09-20-the-wall-is-a-wall
2026-09-20 — the wall becomes a wall, and a tilt that nearly outranked the dial

Enid’s photographs were stacking in a single narrow column, and the prose panel beside them was being stretched to match: 1,291 pixels of bordered box holding 218 pixels of writing, and 1,073 of nothing. The row they sat in never carried align-items, so it defaulted to stretch — and the row one level up already had flex-start, which is the tell that this was an omission rather than a decision. It was correct the day it was written and rotted as the site succeeded. With the wall grey, the column was one note at 222px and the panel was 218px; stretch looked like alignment. Every photograph anybody sent added about 350px of emptiness to the panel next door, because aspect-ratio: auto is the no-crop promise and a portrait renders at full portrait height. The third photo is what made it impossible to miss. Nothing would have reported this — it is not a failing check, it is a room that looks slightly wrong and gets slightly wronger. So the wall is a wall now: sticker wall, then photographs across it, then the prose underneath. Polaroids are one fixed size, the way real ones are, and they pack across and wrap — the tenth photograph widens the wall instead of lengthening the page. Heights stay ragged, because the frame still adapts to each picture. Simulated eight photos in the page to watch it wrap: 3 / 3 / 2, the short last row staying short rather than stretching one polaroid to full width. The page is 1,175px where it was 2,860. Every other photograph leans the other way, because three in a row all tilted -2deg reads as one skewed strip rather than three separately pinned pictures. And that tilt nearly turned the wobble back on for the people who turned it off. The obvious selector — .polaroid-wall .polaroid:nth-child(even) — is specificity (0,3,0), and the Gentle reset is html[data-intensity="gentle"] .polaroid at (0,2,1). The decoration would have outranked the dial, in the one room whose photographs are of real people, and nothing here checks computed transforms so it would have shipped silently. It is written :where(.polaroid-wall) .polaroid:nth-child(even): :where() contributes no specificity, which holds the rule at (0,2,0) and under the reset. Read the computed transform at all three settings rather than trusting the arithmetic — Regular and MAX GLITTER tilt −2°, +1.5°, −2°; Gentle is none, none, none. The generator moved two spaces and learned nothing else. make-polaroids.py writes the wall between its markers and has no opinion about the container, so the restructure was ours to make; only its indentation changed, to match the new depth. Re-ran it against the rebuilt room and the output is byte-identical, which is the property that matters — the next photograph has to land in a row, not quietly restore the column.
2026-09-20-yurt-sounds
2026-09-20 — the regulation nook makes noises, and a hole between three tools

The Regulation Nook makes noises. All six of Helen’s tiles in the Faery Yurt are buttons now — blankets, squishmallows, fairy lights, cupcakes, coffee, cheese and pesto — and each plays a couple of seconds of Ryan making the appropriate noise. An easter egg Ryan and Helen wanted in her room. Each sound owns exactly one marker pair in the page and nothing else, rather than the tool generating the whole list: a tile whose recording is withdrawn goes back to being Helen’s own markup, and that has to be a change to one tile rather than a rewrite of six. An easter egg that still tells you it is there. A tile with a sound wears the same candlelit card as its neighbours, and a small ♪ 2s surfaces on hover and on focus; the button’s accessible name says it is a sound and how long. The discovery is meant to be “one of these is a button”, not “a page I was reading quietly made a noise at me” — a hidden noise would be the exact thing the dial and the press-to-play facades exist to prevent, arriving as a joke. At Gentle the marker is simply always shown, because the quiet setting should reveal more and never less. Nothing is fetched until you press. Verified in the network panel: zero requests to audio/ on load, one per press, and never two playing at once — pressing a second tile is a change of mind, not two people talking over each other. Whose voice it is is said out loud into a live region on every press rather than only filed in the liner notes, where it is also filed. Every runtime is measured off the file, not typed. The six labels say 2, 2, 3, 2, 4 and 2 seconds because that is what the containers report. Every press-to-play control on this street promises a duration before the press — the jukebox, the thirteen arches, the audio room’s sequence — and a hand-kept number is a promise one edit away from being false. Then the interesting part: three tools guarding audio, and a hole between them. make-readings.py refuses stray recorder metadata on passages, make-yells.py on yells, and the new tool on the yurt’s — and every one of them only ever looked at files its own data file named. Recordings sat in audio/ for an afternoon carrying com.apple.VoiceMemos (iPad Version 26.6.2), a creation timestamp to the second and a voice-memo UUID, belonging to no tool’s patch, one git add -A from being permanent in a public repository. make-yurt-sound.py now walks every audio file in the repo instead. Three guards with a hole between them is a hole. It refuses rather than strips. What to do with somebody’s recording is theirs to decide, and a tool that silently rewrote the files people dropped in would be worse than one that says what is wrong and names the file.
